<meta>This is the opening page of Hermann Oldenberg’s seminal work, "Religion des Veda" (1894). It establishes the historical and geographical setting of the Vedic period.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION.

## The Sources.

---

### Ancient India and the Ṛgveda.

The Vedic Indians, whose beliefs and worship we intend to examine, were settled at the time from which the oldest sources originate—this may be, according to the very uncertain estimates that are alone possible here, around the time of 1200 to 1000 BCE¹) — at the Indus and in the Punjab. They were divided into numerous small tribes, ruled by what were likely mostly minor <term>Rājas (kings or chieftains)</term> and a warrior nobility, alongside which even then stood a priestly nobility closed off like a caste. They lived in villages; the older texts show no trace of cities or urban life. Cattle breeding, especially of cows and oxen, far outweighed agriculture in importance: a relationship whose effects often appear in the sphere of religious life in many ways. The art of writing was absent; it was replaced in the priestly schools by the feats of an admirable power of memory.

The immigration of these tribes into India coming from the northwest, their separation from the <term>Indo-Germanic (Indo-European)</term> brother-tribes who had remained united with them the longest,

---

¹) I cannot consider the attempt by <note>Hermann Jacobi (1850–1937), a German Indologist</note> Jacobi (in the *Festive Greeting to Roth* <note>original: "Festgruss an Roth", a scholarly tribute volume for Rudolf von Roth</note>, pages 68 and following) to derive a significantly greater age for the <term>Ṛgveda (the oldest collection of Vedic hymns)</term> from astronomical observations to be successful.

<summary>This page introduces the historical context of the Vedic people, situating them in the Punjab region around 1200-1000 BCE and describing their social structure as a cattle-herding society without writing.</summary>

### Ancient India and the Ṛgveda.

the Iranians, lies in a distant past relative to the time of India’s oldest literary monuments. Yet, when compared to the vast spans of Egyptian or Babylonian history, it should likely be measured on a much smaller scale¹). For those moving southeast, the separation of the Indians from the Iranians represented a renunciation—or the final, concluding step in a renunciation—of participation in the great competition of nations, in which the robust masculinity of the Western nations matured. <note>Oldenberg reflects the common 19th-century European scholarly view that environmental factors and "racial mixing" determined the vitality of a civilization.</note> In the lush silence of their new homeland, those <term>Aryans (a term used here for the ancient Indo-European settlers)</term>, brothers to the most noble nations of Europe, mixed with the dark indigenous population of India. They increasingly developed the characteristic traits of Hinduism, enervated by a climate to which their physical type, forged in a temperate zone, could not adapt without severe harm. They were no less weakened by the idle enjoyment offered by this rich land following an easy victory over unequal opponents—defenseless "savages"—and by a life lacking great tasks, the steeling power of suffering, and the stern hand of necessity. The intellectual work produced by this people bears few traces of that laborious struggle which alone is destined to exhaust the depths of reality and bring one's own inner worlds to a vigorous, joyful maturity. With playful ease, they draped the surface of things in images that flowed from their own overabundant imagination—here graceful, there strangely ornate, rich in color but poor in firm, energetically drawn lines; sometimes blurring into one another, sometimes separating again, entwining in ever-new forms...

# The Character of the Ancient Indian People.

1*

Clear traces of this spiritual languor <note>The author uses "geistigen Erschlaffens" to suggest a loss of vigor or a state of relaxation common in 19th-century environmental theories about India.</note>, which rapidly became

the sacrificial songs and litanies with which the priests of the 
**Vedic Aryans** <term>Vedic Aryans: the ancient Indo-European speaking tribes who composed the Vedas</term> invoked their gods at temple-less
sacrificial sites, by the sacrificial fires scattered across the grass—
barbarian priests calling to barbarian gods <note>original: "Barbarenpriester die Barbarengötter." This reflects the 19th-century scholarly habit of labeling early ritualistic cultures as "barbaric" or "primitive."</note>, who came driving 
through the heavens and the atmosphere with horses and chariots 
to feast on sacrificial cakes, butter, and meat, and to drink 
courage and divine strength from the intoxicating **Soma juice** 
<term>Soma: a sacred, ritual drink made from a now-disputed plant, central to Vedic sacrifice</term>.

We must here, where our first task is to survey the 
sources for the knowledge of the **ancient Indian religion**, 
above all gain an insight into the particular nature of 
**Ṛgvedic** poetry.

The singers of the **Ṛgveda**, composing in an inherited manner 
for the grand and magnificent sacrifice performed with the 
complicated apparatus of the three holy fires—especially for 
the **Soma sacrifice**—do not wish to tell stories of the god 
whom they celebrate; rather, they wish to praise this god. 
They are not dealing with human listeners; their listener 
is, above all others, the god himself, whom they invite to 
graciously accept the sacrifice. Thus, they heap upon him 
all the glorifying epithets available to the flattering yet 
heavy-handed loquacity of an imagination that loves the 
bright and the gaudy. Here, there is no god at whose wink 
and the shaking of whose ambrosial locks upon his immortal 
head the heights of **Olympus** <note>original: "Olympos." The author contrasts the vivid, human-like imagery of Greek gods with the more abstract, epithet-heavy Vedic gods.</note> tremble; instead, there is 
a long series of gods, among whom each is as good as 
the next. When the singer addresses him, he is called very 
great or the greatest, very brilliant, very powerful, very 
beautiful to behold, and very generous to the pious: he 
annihilates all enemies, breaks all the fortresses of the enemies; 
with his strength, he has fixed the ends of the earth, the

# Ancient India and the Ṛgveda.

...spread out above. Everywhere superlatives prevail, not the limited or the formed. Only faintly and indistinctly do outlines emerge in the general glow of light in which this world of gods swims, distinguishing one form from another. One main effect in this glorification of the gods, however, is the playing with mysteries. It would be an exaggeration to say that the preference for this game runs through the entire **Ṛgveda**. Many a song, indeed long series of songs, speak of **Ushas**, the dawn resplendent in lovely charm; of **Indra**, the overwhelmingly powerful smasher of enemies, demons, and monsters; of **Agni**, the kindly shining guest of human dwellings, in a language from which the breath of fresh, simple nature has not yet escaped.

Next to these, however, stand masses of poems in which a different spirit breathes. If the song is meant to be "beautiful" to please the god, this means it should be *artful*; but above all, artful is the poem devised by the "knower" <note>The "knower" (German: *der Wissende*) refers to the initiated priest who possesses the secret knowledge of the ritual's inner workings.</note> and understandable to the knower alone, knowing how to half-show and half-conceal the thought in veiled hints. A poetry of this kind could only arise within the closed circles of priestly **sacrificial technicians** <term>sacrificial technicians: a term used by the author to describe priests who viewed ritual as a precise, almost mechanical science</term>. Among these priests, the posing and guessing of spiritual riddles formed a favorite sport; even the god, imbued with this priestly nature, indulges in it—for the gods love the hidden and hate the manifest <note>original: "die Götter lieben... das Verborgene und hassen das Offenbare." This translates a common Vedic sentiment, often expressed in Sanskrit as *parokṣapriyā vai devāḥ* (the gods love the cryptic).</note>. Delighted by the mysterious depths and subtleties of his own nature and by the mortal so well-versed in them, the satisfied god allows himself to be coaxed into granting favors. Thus the poets repeatedly repeat the old understood or misunderstood allusions, paradoxes, and riddles, and hunt for new ideas to outdo what has come before.

## Character of Rigvedic Poetry.

...words become fixed, playing an unclear game with mystic, shimmering colors—at times with great and deep concepts, at others with those that are by no means deep. One speaks of the **navel of immortality** and the **secret name of the cows**, the **first-born of Right** <note>original: "Erstgebornen des Rechts." In the Vedic context, this refers to *Ṛta*, the cosmic and moral order that governs the universe.</note> and the **highest heaven of speech**. One finds pleasure in tracing the essence currently being discussed—the god to be celebrated—through manifold forms of appearance and places of residence, with a particular fondness for pointing toward the **"highest hidden abode."** Libations of milk are frequently called "cows"; a wooden vessel is called "the forest"; the essence present within the product, from which that product originates, is pointed to through artificial allusions. Within the world of the gods, one discovers fathers who are the sons of their sons; one finds sons who are the fathers of their fathers, or daughters and sisters who are simultaneously wives or lovers. The seemingly ancient inclination of myth toward the motif of **incest** receives fresh nourishment from this taste for mysterious entanglements of kinship. Monstrosities, intentional absurdities, and riddles of this kind fill many songs entirely, strung together without interruption and piled one on top of the other.

In this priestly **master-song** <note>original: "Meistergesang." This implies a highly technical, formalised craft akin to the guilds of the later Middle Ages.</note>, which speaks in such a way of gods and divine things, there can be no full resonance, no eloquence of passion in what it has to say about the human soul and human destinies. It cannot possess the tones from which the warmth, depth, and the slight trembling of a pious heart speak. Of the abysses of distress and guilt, this poetry knows little; here, above all, the happy and the wealthy have their say—those who bring the great sacrifice to lay before the gods their desire for cattle and horses, for a long life and progeny. Or rather, it is not even these sacrificers themselves who speak,

<header>Ancient India and the Rigveda.</header>

...but rather the singers paid by them, who have emerged victorious in the competition among colleagues vying and intriguing for a lucrative commission, and who now practice their professional craft with a sober virtuosity for a sacrificial ritual <note>The German *Opfer* refers here to the *Yajna*, the central ritual sacrifice of Vedic religion, which became increasingly elaborate and regulated by precise rules.</note> whose overloaded complexity must, by its very nature, stifle all power and momentum. Where, in such a setting, could true, deep tones of the inner self originate? Where the broad, keen insights into the orders of existence? Where, within these narrow and shallow circumstances at the courts of small, rivaling dynasts, could one find the earnestness and pride of a great national consciousness shining through the religious ritual?

The external form which the singers of the Rigveda <term>Rigveda: The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational scriptures of Hinduism, composed in an archaic form of Sanskrit.</term> gave to their poems bore a character of simplicity that was not at odds with the essentially naive artificialities of the content. The language possessed little more than the elementary basic forms of sentence structure, which had not yet acquired the flexibility to express more complex movements of thought with their side-currents and counter-currents. Furthermore, the narrow scope of the verses—which almost consistently end with a completed sentence—hindered the construction of larger intellectual frameworks. This was especially true of the **Gāyatrī** <note>The Gāyatrī is a highly significant Vedic meter consisting of three sections of eight syllables each.</note> meter, which was particularly favored for song texts. The poets lacked the skill to organize and master the organic structure of such larger works. One idea was simply strung to another through constant repetition, just as chance dictated; individual elements were usually only touched upon with an allusion or a laudatory reference, rather than being unfolded in their full content. Whenever the poetic language departed from this simplicity of expression, it tended to lose itself in confused and unclear convolutions rather than rising to a freely moving variety. A pleasant interruption in the monotonous alternation of praises...

# Character of Rigvedic Poetry.

...and the darkly hinted secrets were formed by the frequent comparisons <note>These are similes or analogies used by the Vedic poets to link the divine and natural worlds.</note> that touch upon every sphere of human and natural life. The glowing sun and the star-adorned canopy of heaven, the tireless wind and the river with the surge of its waters rushing to the depths; the shepherd driving his flock and the deceitful gambler; the maiden going to a rendezvous or adorning herself for her wedding, and the blameless wife loved by her husband; the father’s care and the son clutching the hem of his father’s garment: these are, for the most part, frequently recurring themes in these short comparisons, full of fresh, vivid life. Their concise simplicity, however, is still a far cry from the rich poetic development of those parables <note>The author distinguishes between the brief similes of the early Vedas and the more elaborate, allegorical parables found in later Indian literature.</note> that later adorned the spiritual discourses and writings of the Buddhists.

<margin>+</margin>
The poetry of the sacrificial songs described here essentially reaches its end around the close of the Rigvedic era. Even in the youngest parts of the great collection of songs itself, it is no longer fully alive in the old way¹); the liturgical technique—which was becoming more firmly established and, one might say, increasingly rigid—prescribed specific inherited hymns for every point in the great sacrificial ritual <note>The author refers to the *Shrauta* rituals, which became so standardized that new compositions were no longer required or permitted.</note>. This left neither significant room nor any need for the continuation of this type of poetic production²). In its place, the poetry of philosophical and, especially, cosmogonic speculation <term>Cosmogonic: Relating to the origin of the universe; these hymns (like the famous Purusha Sukta) ask how the world was created.</term> begins to stir. There is also a growth in the number of narrative pieces, mixed from prose and poetic elements according to an ancient model³). A number of smaller ritual acts,

# Old India and the Rigveda.

...which had previously been performed wordlessly or only with short formulas that had not been elevated to a literary existence, were now endowed with songs—fashioned after the style of the old hymns belonging to the Soma sacrifice <note>The *Soma* ritual was the central, most complex ceremony of the Vedic religion, involving the pressing and offering of a sacred plant juice to the gods.</note>—or with long series of sayings in poetic form. This was the case for weddings and—what is particularly important for our investigations—for burials. Furthermore, it applied to various magical practices: the driving out of demons, the healing of illnesses, charms for married life, and the like. It is not this magic itself, which is ancient in its own right, but rather the literature of the songs or verses belonging to it that finds its beginnings in the latest parts of the Rigveda, only to then continue in rapidly growing volume through the younger Vedic texts.

Indeed, in the Rigvedic examples of this type, we may with great probability see the very first, or at least nearly the first, beginnings of this development. Otherwise, traces of the existence of such a genre of song <note>The author uses the term *Liedergattung* to describe the distinct literary category of these rhythmic spells.</note> would certainly have been preserved for us in the older layers of Rigvedic poetry as well¹). Presumably, the magical practices of earlier times were content, at least for the most part, with short prosaic incantation formulas. This is understandable enough: for if the use of metrical form <note>Specifically, the use of rhythm and verse as opposed to plain speech.</note> in the sacrificial songs was naturally based on the hope of awakening the god's pleasure through such "ornamentation of speech," why would one use ornamented, pleasure-inducing speech when, for example, addressing a demon to scare them away with threats? The penetration of poetic form into sayings of this kind is clearly a secondary process, stemming from the idea of the...

Thus, even when the poetic production of magic songs <note>The author refers to *Zauberlieder*, rhythmic or melodic hymns used for ritual power.</note> was at its highest bloom, the prose incantation <term>Zauberspruch; a spoken magic formula without a fixed poetic rhythm</term> always persisted alongside it; in many places, it seems clearly evident how a prose formula was subsequently versified, so that the original form clearly shines through. In particular, however, the old prose form of the magic spells has remained nearly intact in those spells of this kind which relate to the magical actions belonging to the great sacrifices¹); the conservatism of sacrificial practice granted a far-reaching, if not absolute, protection here against the introduction of poetic form. We shall have to return to the literature of magic spells and songs, which can only be briefly touched upon here, during our discussion of the *Atharvaveda* <note>The *Atharvaveda* is the fourth of the Vedas, primarily containing spells for healing, protection, and daily life.</note> and then during our presentation of the cult of magic. —

Let us now see what consequences arise from the peculiarities of Rigvedic poetry, as we have attempted to describe them, in terms of the estimation and use of this unique, direct source for the belief and cult of the oldest Vedic period.

It lies in the nature of this hymn-poetry that it touches upon the various areas of religious life and the store of myths very unevenly. All light falls almost exclusively on the great gods, who stand at the forefront of the *Soma* sacrifice <note>The *Soma* offering was the central high-ritual of the Vedic religion.</note> and in the refined cult of princes and the wealthy. The manner in which the singers of the Veda perceived the character of these gods and the relationship of humans to them emerges with almost perfect clarity. The individual deeds of these same gods appear less clear—in part, much less clear—with the sole exception of those standing in the foreground, such as Indra’s victory over Vṛtra <note>Indra is the king of the gods and god of storms; Vṛtra is the "Enveloper," a dragon or serpent representing drought whom Indra slays to release the waters.</note>. In epic texts, even the lesser of these deeds would command full interest at some point; however, within the narrow framework of the sacrificial hymns, the stereotypical praises and those principal deeds claim so much of the available space every single time that only brief allusions—often strung together in long enumerations—remain for the more incidental matters. Consequently, numerous corresponding passages in the great collection of songs usually point toward one and the same detail, while everything surrounding it, which would be indispensable for understanding the whole, remains in the dark. Since these myths have for the most part vanished from the interest of subsequent ages¹), any prospect of their reconstruction, and certainly of their interpretation, is completely cut off.

The rites of the sacrifice dedicated to the gods receive light that is just as unevenly distributed as the conceptions of the gods and their deeds. ### The Rigveda as a Source for the History of Religion.

However, this only establishes the facts for one side of this specific sacrifice. For the greater part of the associated concrete performances—for the magical actions connected with the sacrifice, such as the preparatory consecration <term>dikshā; a period of asceticism and purification intended to transform the sacrificer into a state of ritual purity</term> surrounded by various charms, which the sacrificer must undergo, and other such rites and observances, some of high cultural-historical significance—the Rigveda <note>original: Ṛgveda</note> fails us entirely. This is also completely true—aside from very sparse reports—regarding the other sacrifices. For example, regarding animal sacrifice <note>original: Thieropfer</note>, characteristically only its most magnificent form, the horse sacrifice <note>original: Rossopfer; the Ashvamedha, one of the most significant and elaborate royal rituals in ancient India</note>, emerges somewhat more clearly in two interconnected hymns; otherwise, we would learn little more from the Rigveda than the bare and fundamentally obvious fact that animal sacrifices were known. It is important to keep in mind that such gaps in the information we draw from the Rigveda are fully explained by the peculiar nature of these poems which, as already noted, mostly concern the Soma sacrifice—and indeed, only a specific aspect of it. This is reason enough to exercise the utmost caution when drawing conclusions about the "younger" origin of rites not mentioned in the Rigveda. We will have many opportunities to return to this point.

# The Rigveda as a Source for the History of Religion.

But the concepts of souls dwelling in the depths of the earth, of souls that hover and buzz around graves and human dwellings, of souls that have entered into animals, of ghosts: all this lies almost entirely outside the horizon of those funeral songs <note>original: Todtenlieder</note>. —

We conclude these remarks on the Rigveda <note>original: Ṛgveda</note> with the observation that within the immeasurably large masses of ideas deposited in these hymns, that which belongs to the stable core of the people's faith is often mixed indistinguishably with the artificial products of priestly speculation and especially with the momentary whims of individual poets. The nature of this literary production, as we have attempted to describe it—the competitive struggle of countless poets and poetic families, and that whole atmosphere of ever-increasing pursuit of mystery <term>Geheimnisshascherei; a tendency among Vedic poets to create obscure riddles or esoteric language to demonstrate superior knowledge</term>—sufficiently explains the lush proliferation of individual ideas, of attempts appearing momentarily and disappearing just as quickly to gain a new, striking, or mysterious appearance for well-known conceptual elements through new groupings.

The correct assessment of such momentary formations—though we certainly do not possess the means to identify them in every case—is one of the fundamental conditions without which we have no hope of correctly grasping the religious thought-world of the Rigveda. Research must not be satisfied with simply placing the ideas found in the ancient hymns—those that are consistent and those that are isolated and momentary—next to one another as if in a register¹). They must be seen in the right perspective

### The Yajurveda.

While the priests entrusted with recitations and chants—the **Hotar** <term>the priest responsible for reciting the Rigvedic hymns to invoke the gods</term> and **Udgātar** <term>the priest who sang the melodies of the Samaveda</term>—recited the songs of the Rigveda to praise the gods and invite them to the sacrifice, other priests, the performers of the actual ritual actions—the **Adhvaryu** <term>the "manual" priest who measured the ground, built the altar, and prepared the materials</term> and his associates—accompanied their hand movements with prose formulas of blessing or for warding off misfortune (*yajus*)¹). As a rule, these formulas were not addressed—or at least not directly—to the gods, but rather to the sacrificial implements being used at that moment, to the handle, or to the specific process then underway. They named these objects with mystical names which pointed to their own inherent secret power or to divine assistance. They addressed the circumstances of the sacrifice as representing analogous conditions of the universe, united with them by a mystical bond; they directed whatever happened on the sacrificial grounds toward a blessing for the patron of the sacrifice, or toward ruin for “him who hates us and whom we hate.” When the priest grasped any object, he did so “at the impulse of the god **Savitar** <term>a solar deity representing the restorative and impelling power of the sun</term>, with the arms...

# The Yajurveda. Sacrificial Magic Spells.

"...of the **Ashvins** <term>divine twin horsemen, healers of the gods</term>, with **Pushan’s** <term>a solar deity and protector of cattle and paths</term> hands.” To the winnowing basket woven from reeds, he said: “By rain you have grown”; when he placed the grain for the sacrificial food into it, he said to the grain: “May that which grew in the rain embrace you,” and he cleansed it of the husks with the words: “Removed is the demon, removed are the malignant spirits.” During the positioning of the cart laden with the sacrificial food, he touched the yoke-poles on the wagon-yoke with the spell: “A yoke <note>original: *dhūr*</note> you are; harm the harmer <note>original: *dhūrva dhūrvantam*</note>; harm him who harms us, harm him whom we harm.” When he poured water onto the flour during the preparation of the sacrificial food, he said: “The waters have united with the plants¹), the plants with the sap. Let the rich unite with the mobile²), the sweet with the sweet.” One sees how here the circumlocutions seek to represent the secret essence of the intended objects from all sides and thereby make the magic more effective.

It is probable that spells of this kind were already characteristic of the sacrifices of the **Indo-Iranians** <term>the common ancestors of the Vedic Indians and the ancient Iranians</term>; the **Avesta** <term>the primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</term> has preserved several that show exactly the character of the Vedic ones³). # The Yajurveda.

...[that] begin to appear individually, have already become common here¹). Thus, the form of these spells, compared with the admirable stability <note>original: *Festigkeit*</note> characteristic of the text of the **Rigveda**, must have been more fluid²); they must have been susceptible to progressive modernization to a much greater degree.

The yield that the literature of these **Yajus** spells <term>prose ritual formulas</term> provides for our knowledge of the **Vedic gods** is, of course, negligibly small compared to that of the **Rigveda**. The gods here are consistently a secondary matter; one gets the impression that they are merely placed here and there as a somewhat misplaced backdrop <note>original: *Staffage*</note>. Accordingly, what they happen to do—depending on the context of the sacrificial act—has only a very loose connection to their actual essence, which had already faded considerably for the compilers of the **Yajus**. The **Yajus** are all the more important for the knowledge of the sacrificial ritual, which they accompany step-by-step down to its most minute processes. In doing so, they push the historical evidence of these rituals back to a significantly higher antiquity; otherwise, our knowledge would mostly rely only on the later **Brahmana** <term>prose commentaries explaining the meaning and purpose of rituals</term> and **Sutra** <term>concise manuals of ritual rules</term> texts. Thus, the **Yajus** contribute an extraordinary amount to illuminating the ideas of the entire hidden spiritual event—the interplay of diverse natural and magical powers that was thought to take place in and around the sacrifice—and no less to the understanding of the means which the technique of the **cult** <term>the formal system of religious worship</term> believed it possessed to influence those processes and powers.

## **The Atharvaveda.**

The third Veda important for our investigations¹), the **Atharvaveda**, which in its poetic expression is both more agile and more careless compared to the **Rigveda**, continues—according to its main content—the poetry of magic songs <term>incantations used for protection or healing</term> as well as the songs and verses belonging to the customs of family life²). This type of poetry began to appear in the most recent parts of that Veda (see p. 8). The relatively short collections of verses for weddings and funerals contained in the last book of the **Rigveda** (p. 8) reappear here, having grown to a much larger scale; likewise, joined to the magic songs of the **Rigveda**—which are also largely repeated here—is an extensive new literature of incantations of all kinds: blessings for humans and livestock, banishments of disease-demons and other spirits, defense against hostile sorcery, and the like. 

Furthermore, partially extensive texts are added which do not deal with this "popular" magic, so to speak, but rather with new inventions of technical priestly ingenuity in the expansion or transformation of the great sacrifices into magical acts of various kinds. Then, in an alarmingly increasing frequency, there are texts which vary in the most detailed breadth a theme only touched upon relatively timidly here and there in the **Rigveda**: the merit of pious gifts presented to the priests. One could say that, from the perspective

In my opinion, it can be stated with absolute certainty that the collection of the **Atharvaveda** as a whole, as well as its individual elements, are younger than the **Rigveda**; nowhere do the language, meter, or content seem to me to confirm the view expressed by various researchers that any parts of this Veda—aside from those naturally taken from the **Rigveda** itself—reach back into the antiquity of the Rigvedic age. To what extent the world of ideas in this "magic poetry" nonetheless matches or even surpasses the sacrificial hymns in age, in terms of its content, will be investigated further in our description of the magic cult.

Scholars have sought to find traces of authorial circles in the **Atharvaveda** that are distinct from those of the **Rigveda** not only in terms of time: it seems that here, alongside the priests, the lower classes of the people are finding a voice. There is likely some truth in this; it is clear that the sphere of thought in which healing spells, love magic, or wedding customs move cannot, by its very nature, have the same exclusively priestly character as the liturgical poetry of the **Soma sacrifice** <term>a central ritual involving the pressing and offering of the sacred Soma plant juice</term>. But the reader of the **Atharvaveda** will still have the impression that even what was originally "popular," in the form it is presented to us here, has passed through priestly hands. For example, how the great wedding song and the entire mass of wedding verses are saturated with Vedic scholarship and a preoccupation with theological symbolism! Again and again, the priestly horizon of the authors betrays itself in comparisons and epithets. The poet who wishes to acquire "wisdom" <term>original: *medhā*, meaning inspired intelligence or spiritual insight</term> for himself through an incantation, calls upon that wisdom as "rich in holiness, moved by holiness, which the wise singers have praised, and from which the pious students have drunk."

All of this and much else must lead to the opinion that the social circles of the authors of the **Atharvaveda** are not to be sought too far from those of the **Rigveda**.

As a collection of magic songs, the **Atharvaveda**, along with its associated ritual¹), is naturally a primary source of inexhaustible value for understanding the entire population of "lower demons" and the clever tricks by which humans can win them over, reconcile with them, drive them away, or outwit them. It lies in the nature of the matter that the connection of most Atharvan songs with their corresponding magical manipulations is considerably tighter than in the hymns of the Rigvedic sacrificial cult, which rise to such much more abstract heights. As for the role played by the higher gods in <term>Atharvan poetry</term> <note>the hymns and spells found in the Atharvaveda</note>, what was already noted regarding the incantations of the <term>Yajurveda</term> <note>the Veda of ritual formulas</note> generally applies here as well: as often as the gods are mentioned, their actual nature usually has only a very superficial relationship, or none at all, to the content of the invocation. It is predominantly a matter of the goals of daily life and ancient <term>magic rites</term> directed at achieving them; these rites originally had nothing to do with conceptions of, for example, the storm god or the heavenly gods of light, and are certainly in part older than these. Naturally, efforts were still made to win over as large a number of heavenly helpers as possible for each respective purpose; thus, the simultaneous invocation of a multitude of deities is the regular and characteristic feature here, whereas the long praises of the <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>referring to the Rigveda, the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns</note> hymns are always addressed to only a single deity.

# The Gods in the Atharvaveda.

Songs, on the other hand, which are dedicated to the praise of a single god in the manner of the <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>referring to the Rigveda, the oldest and most prestigious collection of Vedic hymns</note> ones and dwell upon him more extensively, are relatively rare; the foremost occasion for composing such songs, offered by the <term>Soma sacrifice</term> <note>the central, highly complex ritual of the Vedic religion involving the juice of the Soma plant</note>, was, as we have already noted (p. 7), essentially exhausted. In those that are found—such as the great and beautiful hymn to the Earth (XII, 1) or the series of related songs to <term>Agni</term> <note>the god of fire</note>, <term>Indra</term> <note>the king of the gods and god of storms</note>, <term>Vāyu</term> <note>the god of the wind</note>, and various other deities (IV, 23 ff.)—one clearly feels, compared to the hymns of the <term>Rigveda</term>, a change in the way of thinking, in the entire coloring that the divine figures bear here. A more rationalistic tone prevails, a smoother and more fluid comprehensibility, a more direct connection with the world of the real and the visible. That hymn to the Earth names what the earth bears with a rich detail that would be hardly conceivable in the <term>Rigveda</term>: mountain and valley and plain, herbs of various powers, the trees, the lords of the forest who stand firm forever, and the grain, rice, and barley that grow on the rain-swelled earth: there is song and dance; there is battle and the drum resounds; there roam the animals of the forest, the lions, the man-eating tigers, and also the evil demons; winged birds fly about; <term>Mātariṣvan</term> <note>an ancient wind deity or spirit of the air</note> the wind stirs up vapors and shakes the trees.

### The Later Vedic and Extra-Vedic Literature.

The main content of the later Vedic texts written in prose (*<term>Brāhmaṇas</term>* <note>theological prose texts that explain the meaning and purpose of the sacrificial rituals</note> and *<term>Sūtras</term>* <note>manuals of concise rules for rituals, law, and domestic life</note>) is the sacrificial ritual. The ritual of the great sacrifices, especially the <term>Soma sacrifice</term> <note>the most important Vedic ritual, centered on the offering of the juice of the Soma plant</note>, was brought into a comparatively fixed form during an epoch that must be later than the completion of <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>pertaining to the Rigveda, the oldest and most influential collection of Vedic hymns</note> poetry ¹), moving away from the more fluid state of the oldest times. In this form—still containing countless variations in specific details depending on the different <term>schools</term> <note>referring to the "Shakhas" or traditional branches of Vedic study</note>—it is handed down in the extensive literature of the Brāhmaṇa and Sūtra texts, agreeing in general and in substance. We have already pointed out above (p. 11) that research has the task, and essentially also the possibility, of proceeding from this ritual to arrive at a picture of the older, simpler, and simultaneously more fluid form of the ritual for which the hymns of the <term>Rigveda</term> were composed. In this way, research into the history of cults moves constantly back and forth between the data of an older and a younger age, in such a way that with chronological progress within the literature, the mass of what we [know] about the whole ap[paratus]...

### Age of the Texts and Age of the Rites.

...paratus of the sacrifice <note>the specific tools, steps, and arrangements required for the ritual</note> is experienced, expanding more and more, the constant main question is naturally this: to what extent does this increasing wealth of our information depend on the addition of **new developments**, and to what extent does it depend on the **changed nature of the sources**? In the treatment of this alternative lies, one might say, the secret of success for investigations into <term>Vedic ritual</term> <note>the formal system of sacrifices and ceremonies described in the Vedas</note>. It would, of course, be an illusion to believe that the question is always solvable. But in many cases, there will indeed be a solution—either a certain or a probable one.

Some things will reveal themselves as new developments by the fact that they lead into circles of ideas that we recognize as only having become vibrant and developed at a later date; certain ritual concepts and practices are of such a nature that, if they were ancient, their traces could not be entirely missing from the older sources despite their characteristic gaps. On the other hand, for much that is not mentioned in those sources, the effortless clarity of this silence will combine with the observation that the developments in question cannot be explained by the circle of ideas of the younger <term>Vedic theologians</term> <note>the authors of the Brahmanas who provided speculative and symbolic interpretations of the rituals</note>, which is so well known to us as a whole; in such cases, we will frequently encounter the characteristic stamp—recognizable with increasing certainty by the practiced eye—of <term>survivals</term> <note>original: "Ueberlebsel"; a term referring to ancient customs that persist into a later era where they no longer "fit" the current logic</note> of ancient, distant layers of thought that are *incommensurable* <note>meaning they cannot be measured or understood by the same standards</note> with the views of the living Vedic present. Parallels—whether they lie within the circle of related nations <note>likely referring to other Indo-European peoples like the Iranians, Greeks, or Romans</note> or cross that boundary—we shall return to the significance of such parallels further below (p. 37)—will contribute to completing the proof for the high antiquity of the phenomenon in question, despite its recent attestation¹).

# The Later Vedic and Extra-Vedic Literature.

Besides describing the sacrificial customs, the **Brahmana texts** <note>ancient Indian prose texts that explain the symbolic and mythological significance of Vedic rituals</note>, as is well known, contain an attempt to interpret them. That these attempts were bound to fail very often is self-evident; the original meaning of countless rites was simply outside the horizon of these theologians, and they would not have been Indian if they did not constantly weave their own favorite speculations about the powers of nature and human life functions into their interpretations of the old customs. Amidst these obvious and serious flaws, the other side of the coin is easily overlooked; not infrequently, the Brahmana texts do offer useful explanations. Within these priests who spent their lives at the place of sacrifice, the genuine old logic of the art of sacrifice was not so dead that we moderns would have nothing to learn from them for the understanding of these processes, which seem so strange to us. Our representation of the sacrificial cult will attempt to make use of this source of instruction.

Later than the great sacrifices performed with the three fires <note>solemn rituals known as *Shrauta*, requiring three separate sacrificial fires and multiple priests</note>, the ceremonies of the domestic cult—such as the wedding, the consecrations for the child and for entry into adolescence, for the house, for fields, for herds, and so on—attained literary representation¹); we possess of them only

## Veda and Avesta.

An overview of the sources for our knowledge of the **Vedic** religious nature must not leave the closely neighboring literature of the **Avesta** <note>the primary collection of sacred texts of Zoroastrianism, ancient Iran's religion</note> unconsidered.

On the sides of both **Vedic** and **Avestan** research, there is currently a strong current aimed at the strict separation of one field from the other. Fundamentally, they argue, it is only language, as the most conservative factor in the life of nations, that connects both literatures¹). Thus, one must consider the **Veda** as a purely Indian, and the **Avesta** as a purely Iranian intellectual product, to be understood each on its own. # The Language of the Veda and Avesta.

The tendency to blur and merge national peculiarities, which seems to be a kind of natural necessity in newly cultivated fields of science, in my opinion overshoots the mark.

To stay with the language first, one can indeed claim that the language of the older **Vedic** hymns <note>the *Vedas* are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, composed in an archaic form of Sanskrit</note> stands closer in many respects to the language of many parts of the **Avesta** <note>the primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, written in Avestan, an Old Iranian language</note> than, for instance, to the language of the **Mahābhārata** <note>one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India, written in a later, "Classical" Sanskrit</note>. While the <term>phonetic shift</term> <note>original: *Lautwandel*; the systematic change of speech sounds over time as a language evolves</note> creates a gap between the **Veda** and **Avesta**—a gap that is hardly deeper than that between two distantly related Greek dialects or between **Old High German** and **Old Low German**—the two languages are linked by the agreement of their fundamental syntactic structures, the similar simplicity of sentence construction, and an essentially identical vocabulary. **Vedic** diction shares a significant series of its characteristic favorite expressions with the **Avestan**, but not with later Indian literature. Added to this is the close relationship of the metrical form and the overall poetic character: it has been noted that entire **Avestan** stanzas can be translated into **Vedic** solely on the basis of comparative <term>phonology</term> <note>original: *Lautlehre*; the study of the sound system of a language</note>¹); this may be extended to say that such a translation would often yield not only correct **Vedic** words and sentences, but verses through which the soul of **Vedic** poetry seems to speak²).

## However, the parallels in terms of religious and mythological content are hardly less significant than the formal ones

"...you out" <note>original: "dich heraus" (Fragm. 7 Westergaard); likely referring to the ritual plucking or taking of sacred branches</note>. To the tree from which he wishes to take the **Baresman** branches <note>bundles of twigs, usually pomegranate or tamarisk, used in Zoroastrian ritual</note>, he says: "Homage to you, good, holy tree, created by **Mazda**" <note>Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity of Zoroastrianism</note> (Vend. 19, 18). When he strikes the mortar pestle against the four sides of the mortar during the preparation of **Haoma** <note>a sacred ritual drink made from a plant of the same name</note>, he says: "A blow against the damned **Angra Mainyu**" <note>the personification of evil and destruction in Zoroastrianism</note>—"a blow against **Aeshma** <note>the demon of wrath</note> with the murderous weapon"—"a blow against the demons of **Māzana**"—"a blow against all demons and evil enemies of **Varena**" <note>Māzana and Varena were mythical regions inhabited by demons or "Daevas"</note> (Yasna 27, 1). Take, for instance, the following **Vedic** formulas relating to various situations of sacrifice: "I draw you for the inexhaustibility of the sea"—"You are protection, give me protection; homage be to you, do me no harm"—"The demon is burned, the monsters are burned"—"**Araru** <note>a specific demon in Vedic mythology</note> is struck away from the earth, the site of the gods' sacrifice," and so on.

In passing, I would also like to point out at least the possibility that a common form of presentation has been preserved in instructional lists of the following kind. On the Iranian side, Yasna 10, 16 (45 ff.): "To five things I belong; to five things I do not belong. To good thought I belong; to evil thought I do not belong. To the good word I belong; to the evil word I do not belong;" and so on. A very similar structure is found in Buddhist texts, for example: "A monk endowed with five qualities may not perform the ordination... His morality is not perfect, his contemplation is not perfect;" and so on. "A monk endowed with five qualities may perform the ordination... His morality is perfect," and so on. (Vinaya Piṭaka, Mahâvagga I, 36). Or: "There is an unauthorized denial of confession, and an authorized one. There are two... three (and so on up to ten) unauthorized denials of confession, and ten authorized ones" (followed by a list of these, always with the juxtaposition of opposites; Cullavagga IX, 3). Similar things occur very frequently. — One may also compare **Vendidād** 13, 44 (124 ff.): "A dog has the nature of eight kinds of people: the nature of a priest, the nature of a warrior" and so on (followed by further details), and with it Buddhist parallels such as the following (see my *Buddha*, 2nd ed., p. 204): "There are seven types of wives a man can have. Which seven are these? One who resembles a murderess, one who resembles a thief, one who resembles a mistress," and so on.

...back. How could it be otherwise? For even if it were correct—which is in fact only a very one-sided expression for a relationship that simply cannot be dismissed so easily—that in the **Veda** as in the **Avesta** we encounter two completely separate peoples, closed off in their peculiar character formation¹), it would still remain the case that even where historical fates impress a new stamp upon national identities, this can never and nowhere mean a new creation of the entire spiritual property out of nothingness. Instead, in countless remnants and traces, sometimes isolated, sometimes joined into compact masses, the old will project into the new age. Therefore, however radical the changes in the world of religious conceptions may appear—which are linked for us (though it must remain undecided here with how much right) to the name of **Zarathushtra** <note>the prophet also known as Zoroaster, the founder of Zoroastrianism</note>—the entire foundation of ineradicable mythical views and cult practices of all kinds must not be overlooked; these have survived from the most distant past into the Zoroastrian religion and connect it with the Vedic one.

It is true that, for example, such a primary figure of the ancient mythology as **Indra** <note>the Vedic king of gods and god of storms</note> has at least half-disappeared from the **Avesta**: and yet the victorious god **Verethraghna** <note>the Avestan personification of victory</note> also clearly enough marks the place in the **Avesta** where once the mighty, wild figure of the ancient storm god stood—the Vedic **Indra Vṛtrahan** ("Indra the **Vṛtra**-slayer") <note>Vṛtra was a serpent or dragon representing drought/obstruction, defeated by Indra to release the waters</note>. # Veda and Avesta.

The Avestan Ahura <note>the supreme deity of Zoroastrianism, Ahura Mazda</note> is the highest lord of right or order (Vedic *ṛta*, the same word as Avestan *asha*); just like Varuṇa <note>a major Vedic deity associated with the sky and moral law</note>, the Avestan Ahura forms a closely linked pair with Mitra; just like Varuṇa, Ahura is the first in a circle of seven light-gods; just as Varuṇa preserves the sun so that it does not fall from the sky (*ava-pad* <note>Sanskrit/Avestan: "to fall down"</note>), and as he clears its path across the vault of heaven, so Ahura holds the earth so that it does not fall (*ava-pad*), and clears the path for the sun and the stars.¹) And one can further add: the entire type of such gods²), who rush through the realm of the air on their chariots with swift steeds—bright and true, untouched or at least little touched by the traits of malice, cruelty, and lust that cling to the gods of other nations, though admittedly not sharing in the mystery of Olympian divine beauty—this type of the princely Aryan <term>Aryan</term> <note>In this context, the author uses "Aryan" in the 19th-century academic sense to refer to the common ancestors of the Indo-Iranian peoples.</note> elevated to heavenly heights is expressed in the Avestan world of gods just as well as in the Vedic. A similar situation exists with the closely related and mutually clarifying ideas of both nations regarding the first human and the first of the dead, the ruler of the dead: Yama, son of Vivasvant (Avestan: Yima, son of Vīvanhvant). There is a further similarity regarding sacrifice. Both peoples offered as their most noble gift the intoxicating juice of the Soma (Haoma), which the priests of both celebrated as the Lord of Plants—growing on the mountains, nourished by heavenly rain, and brought down by the eagle or eagles. In Iran as in India, the juice of the Soma plant was pressed out, purified with a hair sieve, and mixed with milk. The true Soma-drinker, however, is missing from the Avestan sacrifice,

# Relationship Between the Two Rituals.

The god Indra <note>the king of the gods in Vedic mythology, known for his strength and love of the intoxicating drink Soma</note> had been forced to yield the field to the Zoroastrian spiritualization of the religious essence; thus, the feast of the drunken god had faded here into a tangle of consecrations and all manner of remnants that had become merely symbolic. Yet, the original kinship of the rituals on both sides remains visible everywhere. For instance, at both the Avestan <note>ancient Persian/Zoroastrian</note> and the Vedic <note>ancient Indian/Hindu</note> sacrificial sites, there was a cushion or bundle of plants, originally intended to represent the seat of the deity. Both peoples named this with closely related names—the sacrificial grass <note>original: *Barhis*</note> and the sacred bundle of twigs <note>original: *Baresman*</note>¹). Even though the external form of its use had changed among the Iranians, it was still described by them—just as by the Indians—as "spread out" <note>original: *stereta, stīrṇa*</note>. In both countries, the pious sacrificer was consequently called "the man with the spread-out sacrificial grass or twigs." In both nations, a priest designated by the same name—the "reciter" <note>original: *Hotar* in Vedic, *Zaotar* in Avestan</note>—would sit and recite those prayers, whose close relationship in their poetic character we have already touched upon. Among the priestly pleas of the Zoroastrians for spiritual blessings, many formulas stand out that are common to both the Avesta and the Veda, placing before our eyes the prayer-language of the common Indo-Iranian period: the plea to pass over those who hate, to be preserved from the thief and the wolf, that cattle and men may thrive, that the steed may be swift in battles, that capable male offspring may continue the lineage, or even—as the petitioner placed himself entirely in the divine hand—the plea that everything may happen just as the deity wills.

When reading the Veda, one may yield to the impression far more than when reading the Avesta—whose circle of ideas is affected by shifts to a completely different degree—

# Veda and Avesta.

There is no doubt, of course, that on the path from that prehistoric period to the oldest Vedic hymns <note>the *Vedas* are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, composed in archaic Sanskrit</note>, the world of thought and the mode of expression became more complex and, at the same time, more formulaic. There is also no doubt that, in particular, the overgrowth of sacred poetry with allusions, mysteries, and tangled obscurity may be regarded as an essentially specific Indian development. 

But nothing indicates that the transformations which affected the soul of the people and religious thinking during these spans of time were even remotely as profound as, for example, those lying between the oldest Veda and Buddhism <note>referring to the shift from the early ritualistic religion to the later philosophical and ethical movement founded by the Buddha</note>¹). The change of geographical setting, which separated the pre-Indian and the Indian life-periods of these Aryan tribes, likely carried within it the seeds of immeasurable effects on the spiritual life of the distant future, but these effects did not develop from one day to the next. The pace of the transformations undergone by a nation’s culture accelerates with its progress, with the growing self-awareness and liberation of thought, and the emergence of individuality: the thinkers of the Upanishads <note>late Vedic texts focusing on philosophy and the nature of reality</note>, and perhaps on the other hand the circles of Zarathushtra <note>also known as Zoroaster, the ancient Persian prophet</note>, experienced and even brought about a profound shift in the entire inner world. Those older times, however, seem to have moved slowly along quiet tracks. Thus, we cannot consider it a justified endeavor,

### Indo-European and General Comparative Religion.

...hardt <note>Wilhelm Mannhardt (1831–1880), a pioneering German folklorist who focused on "lower mythology"—the spirits of the fields and forests</note> discovered correspondences in the field of lower mythology that led to such skepticism. And one must take care, alongside those premature comparisons—which essentially rely on etymologies and indeed on products of the "Storm and Stress" period of linguistics <note>Refers to an early, less rigorous era of language study where scholars often made bold, unproven links between words</note>—not to also discard the entire series of mythologically well-founded comparisons. It is certain that the Indo-Europeans already unified the shared nature of individual divine powers into the general concept of "gods" under a single designation (*deivos* <note>A reconstructed ancient word meaning "the shining ones" or "the heavenly ones"</note>). The etymological value of this term teaches us that even then, most of the prominent gods were thought of as heavenly beings. ¹) v. I must doubt this. I do not deny that the concept of Father Heaven back then may have been linked—whether with greater or lesser firmness—to the idea that the other gods of heaven are his children, although the naming of the gods as *deivo-* ("Heavenly ones") does not seem to prove much to me in that regard. ...to let the [world] of <term>Indo-European</term><note>A broad family of related languages and peoples, including Indians, Iranians, Greeks, Romans, and Germans</note> sky gods arise again would be roughly the same as if a linguist wanted to deny the entire prehistory of the Indo-European proto-language—which was rich in countless upheavals—and brand it as a fixed, original tongue.

They are also important insofar as they show us the world of Indian <term>cultus</term><note>The system of religious veneration and ritual</note>—which, to a superficial observer, appears self-contained and seemingly follows only its own laws—in its hundredfold relationship to non-Indian forms of worship. In this way, they teach us to understand the Indian material at many points as merely one instance of a type, alongside which many other equivalent instances exist.

I am under no illusion that anyone who dares to enter these research fields—which are so recently cultivated and yet so unimaginably vast—will err often enough, especially if they move within them only as a stranger. But the attempt must be risked; to renounce it would mean giving up on taking even the first steps on a path which, as much is certain, alone can lead to the solution of many of the most important riddles in Vedic religious history.

**Nature Deities and <term>Anthropomorphism</term><note>The practice of attributing human characteristics, forms, or personalities to non-human things like gods or nature</note>.** In the <term>Vedic</term><note>Relating to the Vedas, the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism, composed in ancient Sanskrit</note> faith, the entire world surrounding humanity is animated. ### The Lesser Spirits and the Gods.

We will not trace the evidence here that a stage with stronger **theriomorphic** <note>Having the form of an animal; from the Greek "therion" (wild animal) and "morphe" (form)</note> elements preceded the period of dominant **anthropomorphism** <note>The practice of attributing human characteristics, emotions, and forms to non-human beings, especially gods</note>. We will return to that at a later point. It is not our intention—and the time may not yet be ripe—to place the oldest elements of pre-Vedic history at the forefront of our presentation of **Vedic faith** <note>The religious beliefs and practices found in the Vedas, the oldest sacred scriptures of India</note>. Instead, we begin with what exists in the present...

...explains "that the Vedic myths of the gods did not flow directly from observations of nature, but rather primarily from the **ritual**, whose individual ceremonies were only then compared with natural processes." I shall refrain from discussing this theory here; what, in my opinion, should be said on this matter is *contained implicitly* <note>original Latin: "implicite"</note> in my own presentation of the myths and the ritual. Let me be permitted only a few words here to briefly express my view on the relationship between **myth** and **ritual**. The ritual contains the art of making the gods—who were conceived predominantly on the basis of observations of nature—either favorable or harmless to mankind. The myth describes how the Thunderer <note>A common epithet for Indra, the Vedic god of storms and king of the gods</note> fights for or liberates the imprisoned heavenly waters; the rites move him to perform this deed, or other equally heroic and gracious deeds, for the benefit of the pious. The primary means used by the rites for this purpose is that one feeds the god, gives him drink, prays to him, and praises him. This procedure bears no relation to the specific nature of the deeds that are peculiar to this particular god; on the whole, we learn nothing more from it about his personal characteristics than that he is a hungry, thirsty being who is susceptible to flattery (I say "on the whole"; in specific details, more is revealed here and there—for example, insofar as the time of sacrifice, the specific nature of the sacrificial animal, etc., can stand in a special relationship to the nature of the god). To be sure, the progressive growth of the entire system of worship can also lead to the conception of gods whose foundation lies entirely or largely within the world of the ritual itself (**Agni** <note>The god of fire and the messenger between gods and men</note>, **Soma** <note>The personified deity of the sacred ritual drink</note>, **Bṛhaspati** <note>The "Lord of Prayer," a deity representing the power of the priesthood</note>, etc.). And there can be rites that consist of the imitation of a mythical event (for example, the ***Sautrāmaṇī*** <note>A complex Vedic ritual involving the purification of the god Indra; it often involved the use of wine or sura alongside the usual ritual offerings</note>). Both the former and the latter, however, are special cases upon which a judgment of the overall relationship between myths and ritual must not be based.

# The Gods and Demons in their Relationship to Nature, etc.

...stands dominantly in the foreground of the **Vedic** <note>Referring to the Vedas, the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism, composed in archaic Sanskrit</note> period itself. Thus, we are concerned here with the relationship in which the great, predominantly human-like nature gods of the **Veda** stand to the natural objects or natural processes that correspond to them. 

This relationship varies significantly among the various gods; the degree to which the god becomes independent and humanized in contrast to their **natural substrate** <note>The underlying physical phenomenon—like fire or wind—that a god represents</note> is sometimes lagging and sometimes more advanced. The fire god **Agni** <note>The god of fire and the messenger between gods and mortals</note>, for example, exists in a substantially different relationship than the storm god **Indra** <note>The king of the gods and the deity of thunder and war</note>; the sun god **Mitra** <note>A solar deity associated with oaths and friendship</note> differs from the sun god **Sūrya** <note>The sun itself, often depicted as a celestial body or a god driving a chariot</note>. 

Besides various other factors—such as the influence of a name (which may or may not express the identity of the god with the natural object), the influence of the age of the concept, and the contrast between gods developed locally versus those adopted from outside—the primary deciding factor for this difference seems to me to be the form of the natural substrate itself. 

One might compare, for instance, the nature of Agni or **Ushas** (the Dawn) with that of Indra. Fire and the dawn offer a clear, self-contained appearance; one can actually see Agni or Ushas. In a thunderstorm, however, the form of Indra <note>To be precise, one should substitute the pre-Vedic predecessor here instead of the Vedic Indra, who is no longer truly a storm god</note> is visible to no eye. One certainly sees the dark mountains of the clouds from which Indra liberates the waters; one sees the waters; one sees the god's flashing weapon: but where is he himself? Here a gap remains, and the myth-making spirit fills this gap with the figure of a hero <note>Or possibly a divine animal, which the human-shaped god later replaced</note>, who is imagined to be all the more human-like <note>Or perhaps originally in an even purer animal-like form</note> the less a shape provided by nature limits the imagination. ### The Gods and their Natural Substrate.

A temporal factor also plays a role here. The constant presence of **Agni** <note>the god of fire</note>, and the regular movement of **Ushas** <note>the goddess of dawn</note> with her steady coming and going, places a restraint on mythical imagination. Meanwhile, in the case of **Indra** <note>the king of the gods and ruler of the storm</note>, freedom is granted from this side as well: it does not always storm, nor does it happen at regular times. Consequently, **Indra** will certainly move here and there according to unpredictable whims; he will perform deeds that have nothing to do with the storm and only exhibit the same character of heroic sublimity. 

And it will be possible—we shall return to this process in more detail later—that through the strong emphasis on this human-like, heroic being, which lures mythical ideas into new, independent paths, the connection with the natural event that originally stood at the center is forgotten. In contrast, the understanding of **Agni’s** essence, in the presence of the constantly visible natural object which bore the same name as him, could not possibly be extinguished.

To further illustrate the type of deity closely linked to a natural phenomenon, let us linger a bit longer with **Agni**.

Should one express the **Vedic** <note>relating to the Vedas, the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism</note> conception of **Agni’s** relationship to fire by saying that the latter is the preferred dwelling and sphere of influence for a god who also has other dwellings at his disposal? Or does **Agni** exist in an inseparable unity of essence with the fire? Is the element, one might ask, the house of the god, or is it the god's body?

The name **Agni** itself already supports the second view; the god is named "Fire." Wherever fire is, there he is; where there is no fire, I can hardly find anywhere that the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>The "Knowledge of the Verses," the oldest collection of Vedic hymns</note> presents the god as being present. Even when speaking of **Agni** hidden in the waters or in the plants, the god is not thereby [separated] from the fire— <meta>The page ends mid-sentence with the word fragment "ab-" (likely "abgetrennt" or "abgelöst," meaning separated/detached).</meta>

Whoever produces the sacrificial fire through the friction sticks <note>original: *Reibhölzer*—wooden tools used to start ritual fires by rubbing them together</note> does not first create an un-divine element and then call upon the god to enter it; rather, he creates the god or brings him to birth. “Men have caused **Agni** to be born with devotion from the friction sticks through the movement of their hands, the praised one.” “Mortals have generated the Immortal.” “Rub, you men, the wise one without falsehood, the knowledgeable, immortal, beautiful-faced one: the banner of the sacrifice, the first at the front; produce **Agni**, you men, the gracious one<gloss>²</gloss>).” Thus, phrases that attribute a human form to **Agni** are significantly rarer and less pronounced than, for instance, in relation to **Indra** <note>the storm god</note>: one sees **Agni’s** body before one’s eyes and sees that it does not resemble a human body.

The identification of the god with the natural object certainly encounters a difficulty specifically in the case of **Agni**, and to that extent, this example might not be the most favorable for illustration. Natural fire appears in an unlimited multiplicity of simultaneous phenomena. ### Agni and the Fire.

...beings were conceived, brought about the change: **Agni** became of the same kind and equal status to those beings; the “multi-kindled one” nonetheless became simultaneously the “one **Agni**” <gloss>¹</gloss>). The poets of the **Rigveda** <note>the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns</note> do not attempt to work through or resolve this contradiction between unity and multiplicity; among the multitude of countless Vedic riddles and paradoxes, they allow this one to remain as well. Thus we find, alongside the previously mentioned idea of the god being born anew every time from the friction sticks <note>original: *Reibhölzer*—wooden tools used to generate fire through friction</note>, another perspective—one that is admittedly isolated and, if I am not mistaken, foreign to the older layers of the text: the thought of the god entering or “descending” into the fire which human hands have produced or stoked.

### Agni and the Fire.

It is clear that this must be regarded as a transformation. Originally, **Agni** is the physical element endowed with a divine soul; only later does he become an idealized being who can be imagined as detached from the element itself. Just as we noted, the contradiction between the multiplicity of concrete, individual fires and the unity of the god must encourage this detachment. In other cases, however, the identity of the god with the natural phenomenon appears pure and undisturbed: this is the case with **Sūrya** <term>the Sun</term> and **Ushas** <term>the Dawn</term>, where a unique natural entity corresponds to a unique deity¹). Another example is the **Āpas** <term>the Waters</term>, whose natural multiplicity is reflected in the plural nature of the deity²). Wherever the dawn shines, the Vedic Indian sees the gleaming goddess revealing her bosom; where the sun rises, he sees the far-visible divine son of heaven; where the waters flow, the restless goddesses move along. The poet who speaks of a healing drink of water says that the **Āpas**, the goddesses, are a healing drink to be consumed³).

> ¹) In the case of the Dawn, however, it is well known that the **Veda** <note>The most ancient sacred scriptures of Hinduism</note> fluctuates between the idea of a single goddess returning daily and a series of ever-new dawns.
> ²) Is the female gender of the **Āpas** a factor in why a unified, ideal being did not develop here—following the model of **Sūrya** and others—as it did in the case of **Agni**?
> ³) Furthermore, alongside the divine type that remained closely tied to the natural element (the **Āpas**), the waters also show a progression toward a more independent personification: the **Apsaras** <term>nymphs, originally water nymphs</term>. The **Apsaras**, taking the form of beautiful divine women, can leave their element and experience various adventures among humans. Yet, a certain quality of "homelessness" clings to such activities, and their true home always remains the water, as shown by the story of the water-spirit **Urvaśi**, the "Melusine" of India <note>Melusine is a figure from European folklore, a feminine spirit of fresh water in sacred springs and rivers</note>. — One passage of the **Rigveda** <note>original: *Ṛv.*</note> (IX, 78, 3), moreover, still identifies the **Apsaras** entirely with their element: the **Apsaras** stream toward the **Soma** <note>A ritual drink made from a plant of the same name</note>, which means the liquid is being mixed with water.

**Obscurations and New Formations.** However, the connection between gods and the natural objects they represent is not always as clear in the **Veda** <note>The most ancient sacred scriptures of Hinduism</note> as in these previous examples. We cannot doubt that, like **Sūrya** <term>the Sun deity</term>, **Mitra** was also once a sun god; it seems almost equally certain to me that Mitra’s divine companion, **Varuṇa**, was a moon god¹). But in the hymns addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa, the relationship between the deity and the natural phenomenon appears quite differently than it does with, for instance, **Agni** <term>Fire</term> or **Ushas** <term>the Dawn</term>. In the consciousness of the Vedic poets, that direct connection is essentially non-existent; they only recognize a series of character traits for these gods. For us, these traits are traces of the original nature of the deity, but for the poets, they are simply established facts with no deeper symbolic meaning.

Mitra and Varuṇa are radiant kings who sit upon heavenly thrones and oversee all right and wrong among men. They have opened the path for the sun; the sun is their "eye." Here we find a trace of Mitra’s original nature, yet for the Veda, the sun is also Varuṇa’s eye. The belief arises that Mitra holds a special dominion over the day, and Varuṇa over the night—the latter being the only trait that points directly toward the moon. In place of the entirely faded natural significance, however, a human-like persona has been developed here in a much more advanced way than with Agni or Sūrya. One trait is enough to characterize the difference: Mitra and Varuṇa have the sun as their eye; Sūrya is an eye himself. 

An intermediate stage between the oldest state—in which Mitra must have been the divinely animated sun—and the Vedic detachment of the god from his physical natural body is shown in the **Avesta** <note>The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</note>. It portrays **Mithra** as the first of the holy gods to rise over the **Hara** <term>the mythical mountain of sunrise</term>...

...deepening of the inner spiritual life added increased weight, and which in turn contributed significantly to the disappearance of the natural significance of these gods. One could say that the religious element here particularly energetically helped to suck the lifeblood out of the mythological complex of ideas. Sun and moon, and whatever might occur with them, were no longer in the foreground. What mattered was the concept of all-seeing, all-just kings, with whom one sought to be reconciled and befriended. In place of the old feeling of helpless dependence on nature, it was increasingly human, social, and state conditions which provided the prototype for the concept of dependence on higher powers: dependence on the king, the strong warrior, the wise priest, the wealthy. Thus, the deified nature-being was replaced by the figure of a divine hero or benefactor who was increasingly emancipated from nature—in the case of **Mitra** and **Varuṇa**, by the figures of divine kings and judges.

...the old natural significance of **Varuṇa** <note>Originally a god of the sky and cosmic order, later a god of the celestial ocean and law</note> recedes behind the ethical and is obscured by it; those traits to which religious interest primarily attached itself further contributed to letting the original natural character of **Indra** blur: it was the powerful hero, bestowing victory and wealth, to whom prayers were primarily directed, not the storm-bringer.

In the field of mythology, it is no different than in that of language, which also sometimes faithfully preserves ancient formations, sometimes reshapes them in modern directions, or places entirely new formations alongside them. Just as the two transforming powers work on language—sound change <note>original: "Lautwandel"; the process by which spoken sounds change over time, often simplifying or "decaying"</note>, which is for the most part phonetic decay, and analogy <note>the process of creating new words or forms based on the pattern of existing ones</note>, which builds the new—so also in the history of divine figures and myths—and also, it may be noted in passing, in that of the <term>Cultus</term> <note>the system of religious worship and ritual practice</note>—two similar processes face each other: the fading, the emptying of the mythical

[foundations] rests. Now, furthermore, the metaphorical expression (mountain, river) stimulated a new series of ideas, namely that of the rivers springing from the mountains. <meta>This page continues the theoretical comparison between linguistic evolution and mythological development. While the previous page introduced the idea of "mythological decay," this page explores why mythology is harder to categorize than language due to the influence of human creativity and psychology.</meta>

...imagination and the filling of the empty vessel with new content. However, any attempt to trace mythological weathering <note>original: "mythologische Verwitterung"; the process by which the original meaning or natural origin of a myth erodes over time</note> back to such clear, law-like patterns as those science demonstrates in the processes of linguistic weathering is excluded from the outset. For, standing against the simple and firm "keyboard" <note>original: "Claviatur"; a metaphor for the limited and predictable set of speech sounds (phonemes) in a language</note> of phonetic elements that recur in countless words, the mythological field is faced with the most complicated variety of psychological factors which have influenced the fate of every individual idea. 

Analogy, on the other hand—whose power is undoubtedly active in both language and mythology—does not find in the latter a solid framework comparable to grammatical paradigms. Such a framework would allow research to trace the effects of analogy back to distinct, constantly recurring types, as is possible in grammar. Above all, the difference between the history of language and the history of myth is heightened by the fact that myths only partially unfold in the sphere of the unconscious, where linguistic changes move almost exclusively. Instead, priestly speculation <note>intellectual and theological interpretation by religious leaders</note> and poetic creativity intervene here, imparting to their products a character of "freedom." The effects of this freedom can only be observed and, in favorable cases, explained, but they can never be calculated in advance.

Such myths were likely never particularly numerous; they are originally very short—certainly not because the capacity for imagination or the skill of storytelling was insufficient for more complicated events, but because the material provided by nature itself contained very little.

In exchange, these myths tend to possess a weight and a power of persistence against the fluctuating stock of younger elements, which can be compared to the stability of impressions received in childhood. No matter how many of Indra’s deeds were recounted, the victory over Vṛtra always remained the most prominent.

When such myths—which, in comparison with more complicated younger structures, one might call mythological molecules or monads <term>monads: from the Greek 'monas' (unit); here used to describe the irreducible, fundamental building blocks of a myth</term>—join together into unions, the result should not be seen as a mythological image of a longer, more intricate natural process. Only the individual elements reach directly back to nature; their combination no longer reflects a chain of natural events, but is instead the free work of poetry and speculation. Above all, however, those monads do not grow through mutual union, but rather through the addition of elements from other origins. Imagination uses the old motifs as a starting point for its own independent creation¹). The...
