### The Gods and Demons in their Relationship to Nature, etc.

The great gods are conceived almost exclusively as good and benevolent, and in this way, they have largely displaced the friendly demons from their sphere of activity. It may be considered probable that those malevolent spirits developed, at least in part, from the souls of the deceased. We shall see how the ancient Indian faith—which in this regard continues the most ancient forms of belief—imagines the existence of the living to be surrounded by the souls of departed friends, but also by the malicious souls of enemies: these souls float about, sometimes invisibly in the near and far distance, and at other times manifest in ghostly, animalistic, and the most diverse other forms and deformities. They bring manifold danger to the living, as evidenced by the various precautionary measures that permeate the <term>soul cult</term> <note>The practice of honoring or appeasing the spirits of the dead (ancestors).</note>. The same process of the fading of old ideas and the addition of new ones—which transformed the thunder-god <term>Indra</term> <note>Indra is the chief deity of the Rigveda, a heroic warrior-god who wields the thunderbolt.</note> into the warlike achiever of all kinds of heroic deeds, and the moon-god <term>Varuṇa</term> <note>In later Vedic thought, Varuṇa is the guardian of moral order and the punisher of sin.</note> into the observer and punisher of all sins—could also allow souls to become disease-bringing and similar demons. These demons then naturally developed their own specific "specialties" or traits, relating to this or that particular type of mostly harmful influence on human destiny. Just as it is possible with many peoples—for example, the **Iranians**¹) who are so closely related to the Vedic nation—to trace the concrete tracks of such developments, I believe that much on Indian soil also points toward them. Later Indian literature is rich in stories, such as the one in the "Thirty-Two Throne Tales" <note>original: *Siṃhāsana-dvātriṃśikā*, a collection of Indian fables and legends.</note> about the man whose wife cheats on him and who, having died of grief over this, returns every night as an evil spirit to torment her²). <meta>This page continues the transition from discussing specific, often harmful spirit-beings (like Rudra) to exploring how Vedic thought developed more abstract divine archetypes. ...to briefly touch upon the types emerging in the divine world here.

If myth identifies the acting god in Indra for the actions visible in a thunderstorm, and points to the acting supernatural powers in Rudra and various demons for the actions felt by humans through illness, then in the following period, the inquiry progresses from these concrete types of action to more abstract ones. The most diverse movement permeates the life of the world: who is the stimulator of this movement? Thus, one creates the god "Impeller" or "Driver"—Savitar¹)—who is already fully realized in <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>Referring to the Rigveda, the oldest of the sacred Hindu scriptures, composed in archaic Sanskrit.</note> poetry. His name expresses his very essence: he stretches out his golden arms to drive all movement that takes place in heaven and on earth. He causes the sun to complete its daily course and lets the night come; he drives humans to begin their work in the morning and lets man and beast go to their rest in the evening²). Since the sun completes the most powerful movement in the universe itself and thus governs all other movement, Savitar naturally stands in a particularly close relationship to it, and there is a tendency to transfer the attributes of the sun god to him. But it would mean fundamentally misunderstanding the structure of this entire complex of ideas if one were to declare Savitar a sun god for that reason. The essential part of the conception of Savitar is not the idea of the sun, nor even the idea of the sun in a specific direction,

# Later Types of Gods: Savitar. 65

insofar as it drives life and movement: rather, the essential part is the abstract thought of this impelling itself. It provides, so to speak, the frame that encompasses the ideas concerning Savitar: where it is then, of course, not only not excluded but even natural that various old mythological materials, originating from more concrete circles of perception, fit into this frame. <margin>†</margin>

Just as in every epoch of linguistic history one finds, alongside word-forming elements whose activity has ended and which only exist in finished forms inherited from the past, those that are in full life and can be used by every speaker to produce ever new words, so must the highest vitality and productivity be attributed to the mythological mode of formation to which the god-figure of Savitar belongs—for the <term>Vedic</term> <note>Referring to the era of the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.</note> age and the age immediately preceding it. Just as they had the god "Impeller," so they had the god "Fashioner," the god "Maker," the god "Protector"¹) and numerous others, for all of whom the abstract idea of a specific kind of divine action provided the basis for the respective conception.

Another convenient and correspondingly popular way to form and name types of gods was the perception and designation of a god as the "Lord" (*pati*) of such and such entities. Thus, they worshipped a "Lord of Progeny" (*prajāpati*), a "Lord of Food" (*annapati*), a "Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoshpati*), a "Lord of the Field" (*kṣhetrasya pati*), and others. We wish to consider here one of these gods, who stands out most among them in the oldest texts and as the divine embodiment of a purely spiritual circle of ideas of special—

The essence of this god is indeed perfectly and adequately expressed by his name: he is "the oldest king of prayers," "the creator of all prayers." He himself sings the sacrificial hymns and speaks the magic-laden prayer and incantation formulas that awaken the gods' grace—"the utterance in which the gods <term>Indra</term>, <term>Varuṇa</term>, <term>Mitra</term>, and <term>Aryaman</term> <note>These are major deities of the Rigveda representing atmospheric power, cosmic order, friendship, and nobility respectively.</note> find their pleasure"—or he bestows such a prayer upon the human priest who has called upon him—"I place a brilliant word into your mouth," says Bṛhaspati to a priest who has sought his help for a rain-bringing sacrifice (<term>Ṛv. X, 98, 2</term> <note>Referring to the Rigveda, the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns.</note>). **Gods and Animals.** The relationship of the Vedic gods and demons to animals requires special consideration.

As we already touched upon above (p. 41), based on the analogies provided by <term>ethnology</term> <note>The comparative study of different peoples and cultures.</note>, one may assume a strong emergence of the animal element among gods and demons for the most distant prehistoric times. The god is frequently an animal or becomes an animal; he fluctuates between a human-like and animal-like being: one of the characteristic traits of the worldview of nature-based cultures is precisely this—that the boundary between the two is blurred for them.

If now, as we have seen, the <term>anthropomorphic</term> <note>A human-shaped or human-centered view of the divine.</note> conception had already achieved victory in <term>Indo-European</term> <note>original: "indogermanisch." Referring to the shared cultural and linguistic ancestors of most European and Indian peoples.</note> times for the great gods who direct the course of the world, numerous remnants and traces of the animal kingdom still protrude into the world of the gods within the <term>Vedic faith</term>. Here, it must first be emphasized that for the Vedic Indian, the actual animal he encounters—I am setting aside for now those cases in which the animal is merely the messenger or symbolic representative of a god—frequently appears, so to speak, in its own right as a carrier of demonic essence: so in-

### Animal Worship

...especially uncanny or harmful animals that are difficult to ward off, such as snakes; and among the useful ones, particularly the cow, the embodiment of all nutritional blessings. Even individual animals endowed with especially brilliant qualities can be granted a kind of personal deification. Concerning snake worship specifically¹) <note>original: "Schlangenverehrung"</note>, ceremonies involving offerings and invocations to the snake kings and snakes take place around the beginning and the end of the rainy season, during which the danger from snakes is particularly threatening. They are given water for bathing, a comb, makeup, flowers, eye ointment, and a strand of thread for clothing and adornment; the people entrust themselves and their families to these merciful beings. "Salvation to the divine hosts of snakes," it is said; the celestial snakes, the snakes of the air, the snakes of the cardinal directions, and the terrestrial snakes are invoked one after another. In a certain sense, the snakes are elevated here into the sphere of demonic supernaturalness; the imagination has extended their existence across the entire universe, but the primary focus remains the real, physical snakes and the protection against them²). — Similarly, we find the ants, for example, placed in the sphere of demonic essence when, to counter their overabundance, [appeals are made] to "the king of the white ants in the east, the king of the black ants...

Thus we find in the Vedic period that animals which provide any such occasion are worshipped as divine or demonic, both as a species and as individuals. Furthermore, the prominent, more or less human-like great gods are surrounded by a kind of divine animal world: numerous lesser gods, but especially beings hostile to the gods, disease-causing demons, and the like, are animal-shaped³). Thus, frequently—usually in longer lists of invoked gods—we find two beings who scarcely have the capacity to appear independently anymore and seem to be carried along merely as remnants from earlier circles of belief: the “Serpent of the Deep” and the “One-Footed Goat” (*ahi budhnya* and *aja ekapād*)⁴). ->### Animal-shaped Deities.<-

the mother of the seven <term>light-gods<note>Known as the Ādityas, these solar deities represent various aspects of the sun and social order</note></term>, herself—as her name suggests—representing freedom and closely linked in numerous <term>Vedic prayers<note>Ancient Sanskrit hymns from the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note></term> with the idea of liberation from the guilt of sin and all distress, is nonetheless also a cow; the gods descended from her are "cow-born": in the midst of a highly developed, ethically deepened circle of ideas, there remains a trace, it seems, of a primitive myth which allows the heavenly lights to be born from a divine cow¹). Furthermore, a number of animals appear as the property of the gods or as their servants: such as the eagle, who brings the <term>Soma<note>A sacred ritual drink in ancient India, personified as a god and believed to grant immortality or divine inspiration</note></term> to Indra; the divine hound Saramā, who tracks down the hidden cows; the cows themselves, which the god takes from his enemies; the steeds that pull Indra and other gods; the he-goats that pull Pūshan, and so on. In themselves, such animals are in perfect harmony with the prevailing <term>anthropomorphism<note>The practice of attributing human characteristics or forms to gods</note></term>; just as humans possess animals, the human-like god must also possess the same animals, or here and there, other animals will serve him, corresponding to the miraculous character of divine existence. Yet, in one case or another, the question may be raised whether the animal belonging to the god is not a remnant left over from the ongoing process of anthropomorphization—a remnant of an animal that the god once was, or whose form he used to take. We have already expressed the suspicion that the "Lords of the Steeds" (*aśvin*), the children of the mare, were once horse-shaped gods. If, during the horse sacrifice, a he-goat is added to the horse "as Pūshan’s portion, to announce the sacrifice to the gods" (**Rigveda** I, 162, 2–4)—that is, likely as a guide on the difficult path into the world of the gods—and if a similar thought is possibly at play regarding the he-goat that is burned along with the corpse during a burial⁴), then the assumption of a goat-form for Pūshan would give these rites a particularly distinct meaning. However, it is naturally not possible here to move beyond unprovable conjectures.

### The Gods and Demons in Their Relation to Nature, etc.

The connection with the gods who send them is, of course, particularly evident in the case of animals whose appearance was regarded as ominous. The bird of prey that alights with meat in its beak is described as "a dread bolt of lightning, sent by the gods"; the "bird that cries in the celestial region of the Fathers <note>The 'Fathers' or Pitṛs refer to ancestral spirits; the South is traditionally their direction</note> (the South)," already mentioned in the **Rigveda**, may surely be understood as having been sent by the Fathers; the female hyena howls "whether driven or of her own will"; the owl is the "bird that goes to the dwelling of the gods" and the "messenger of the evil spirits"; the "beast of prey with bloody maw, the blood-smeared one," and the "vulture that dwells among the corpses" are "messengers of **Yama**" or "messengers of **Yama** and **Bhava**" <note>Yama is the god of the dead; Bhava is a name for the god Rudra/Shiva</note>. If we take into account the belief in the appearance of eerie spirit-beings in animal form, it suggests the hypothesis that these god-sent animals were once creatures that possessed a demonic nature of their own and only later became servants of divine masters¹). —

Furthermore, the investigation into the relationship of the Vedic gods to animal forms must consider a number of cases in which, within the context of cultic ritual, an animal represents a god—that is, where the form of the <term>animal fetish<note>In this context, a 'fetish' is a physical object or animal believed to embody a spiritual power or deity</note></term> finds application.

The animal to which **Indra** is most frequently compared in the poetic language of the hymns—and which he is often directly named as—is the bull²). Here, according to the instructions of one school, a white or reddish-brown horse stands beside the singers; according to other authorities, it is a black horse. During their performance, the singers hold gold in their hands, undoubtedly as a symbol of the sun. The horse, too, likely represents the sun³), the black one clearly having a specific relationship to the setting of the sun.

### The Gods and Demons in their relation to Nature, etc.

A particularly clear example of the embodiment of the god in an animal is provided by the **"Spit-ox sacrifice"** <note>original: "Spiessrindopfer"; referring to the *Shulagava* sacrifice, where an ox was offered to the god Rudra to appease his wrath</note>¹) offered to **Rudra** <note>A fierce Vedic deity, the precursor to Shiva</note>. Next to the sacrificial fire, two huts are erected; a bull is led into one, the "Bestower of Grace" into the other, and "the Victor" is led into the space between them—according to traditional explanation, these are the "wife" and the "son" of that first bull. Water is given to the three animals, and they are allowed to touch the sacrificial food, which is then offered to the god Rudra, the wife of the god, and "the Victor."

With this, the main examples of **animal fetishes**—which characteristically involve domestic animals throughout—in the higher Vedic cult may be considered nearly exhausted. The role that such embodiments of the god play in the Vedic period is evidently not significant; one might say, it is no longer so. The entire direction in which at least the purer and higher currents of religious life moved did not favor that form of conceptualization. The dwelling place of the most important gods in the heights of heaven, the form in which they were conceived as being like heroic or royal humans, and the interaction in which one approached them during the sacrifice (which the gods were thought to visit invisibly)—not compelling them through magic, but winning their goodwill with gifts and pleas: all this was not conducive to being combined with ideas of the god's embodiment in animal form. That remains of animal fetishism, and presumably also new formations according to these old patterns, are nevertheless not entirely absent should not be surprising. The view which the...

### Animal Fetishes

The view that the Vedic age <note>The period in ancient Indian history (c. 1500 – 500 BCE) when the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, were composed</note> connected with this cultic use of animals does not seem to be that the full majesty of the god dwells in the bull or the horse—in the same way that **Agni** <note>The god of fire; the text uses the plural "Agnis" to refer to various manifestations of sacred fire</note> dwells in the flame or **Soma** <note>The god associated with the sacred ritual drink; "Somas" refers to the prepared portions of the plant</note> in the sacred herb. If that were the case, these animals would be shown other types of honors. Rather, there exists between god and animal a certain "commonality of substance," a connection of the kind that will continually occupy us later when we consider Vedic magical practices. 

In these practices, to bring about an effect or a state in a person or thing that cannot be achieved directly, the magician takes an image of that person or thing—or something similar to it, something coming from it, or something in contact with it—and performs the desired action upon that substitute. Thus, we will encounter manipulations with a burning brand, or with gold, or with a wheel, which are intended to influence the sun <note>In Vedic ritual, a golden disk or a rotating wheel often physically represented the sun's light and its movement across the sky</note>¹). In this very way, the animal seems to be conceived as a being in an inner connection with the god, and thus serves as a "handle" or instrument for magic directed toward that deity. The animal is not a constantly revered object of worship, but rather a **cultic utensil** that fulfills its role only for a specific moment. 

What we see here appears to be the faded remnant of an older way of thinking, which presumably once worked with a cruder identification between the god and the visible object. This older perspective would likely have left more abundant traces behind if—as was the case in **Egypt**—there had been a developed tradition of visual arts and the existence of temple- <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with "temple-complexes" or "temple-priests" on the next page</note>

---

¹) See below, page 88. We would have included the discussion of these cases, in which the wheel etc. plays exactly the same role as the horse or the bull here, if it did not conflict with the restriction of the current discussion to the relationship between animals and the gods.

6*

We cannot conclude our examination of the mythical world of animals without glancing at the relationships that belief establishes between animal and human existence. The idea of a substantial unity between animal and human—which, naturally, only survives as vestiges by the ancient Indian period—is expressed first in the belief in werewolf-like beings. To this category belong presumably the "human-tigers" <note>original: "Menschentiger"; similar to the concept of a weretiger</note>²) and then the **Nāgas** <note>Sanskrit: *Nāga*; supernatural beings, often depicted as half-human and half-serpent, who inhabit the underworld</note>³): apparent humans who are in truth snakes and whose snake nature, as an ancient Buddhist text states⁴), manifests on two occasions: during mating and in sleep⁵). Naturally, they can also transform into humans. Just as the ability to assume such forms is attributed to the human sorcerer, it naturally belongs to the god as well; the god's human-like nature essentially implies a similarity to a human who has reached the height of the magical arts.

# Totemism.

Above all, however, it will be important for research to collect the traces—which are likely also to be expected in ancient India—of a former belief in the descent of the human race, or individual human tribes and families, from animal (or plant) ancestors (**Totemism** <note>A system of belief in which humans are said to have a kinship or mystical relationship with a spirit-being, such as an animal or plant</note>¹)). It may be considered established that this belief, along with the customs attached to it, formed an almost dominant element of both the religious and social character among the majority of primitive peoples <note>original: "Naturvölker"</note> and then later, once the progressing understanding of reality had set the belief itself aside, it **left its traces behind for a long time in the form of survivals** <note>original: "Ueberlebseln"; a term used in early anthropology to describe cultural traits that persist even after their original function or context has disappeared</note>²). For ancient India, I can presently only offer the first beginnings of a collection of what are, in some cases, by no means certain remnants of this kind; here, almost everything remains for the future to do. First, I point to the Vedic tribal names of the Fish (*Matsya*), the Goats (*Aja*), and the Horseradish-people (*Śigru*). There was a priestly lineage of the Tortoises (*Kaśyapa*), whose progenitor, named "Tortoise," is a cosmogonic being <note>A being related to the origin of the universe</note> standing close to, or identified with, the creator of the world, **Prajāpati** <note>Sanskrit: "Lord of Creatures"; a Vedic deity presiding over procreation and the protector of life</note>. In the form of a *Kūrma*—this is another word for tortoise—Prajāpati [created] all creatures.

To summarize our findings—similar to our observations regarding animal fetishes—we find almost nowhere, or at least very rarely, a material object serving as a permanent representative of a god that is worshipped through continuous ritual. Magic, which utilizes the image of a thing (or something related to it) to influence the thing itself, extends throughout daily life and into religious ritual. For these purposes, ritual uses representations of the sun—such as a wheel or a flaming torch—instead of the sun itself. However, within the overall framework of <term>Vedic ritual: the system of ceremonies described in the oldest Hindu scriptures</term>, these creations of a magical nature, which are common to all eras and all peoples, hold no real significance. They remain disconnected from the vital, evolving currents of Vedic religious thought.

### The Multiplicity of the Gods.

The gods are conceived as being friendly toward one another, which is a natural assumption for these "friends of humanity" who all share a common inclination toward justice and goodness. "All the gods, of one heart and one mind, walk with a single will upon a straight path" (Rigveda VI, 9, 5). To be sure, friction does occur—for instance, <term>Indra: the king of the gods and god of storms</term> chases away the <term>Dawn: personified as the goddess Ushas</term>—

# Hosts of Gods and Divine Pairs.

...and breaks her wagon; he grows angry with the <term>Maruts: storm deities who accompany Indra</term> over the sacrifice of <term>Agastya: a legendary Vedic sage</term>—but on the whole, peace and alliance prevail in the world of the gods against their common enemies. Lower deities appearing in groups form the retinue of a greater god. However, it is particularly common for the gods to appear joined in pairs, endowed with the same majesty, as joint performers of the same deeds and recipients of the same sacrifices and praises. It is likely that this frequently repeated type of "divine pair"—firmly established in both poetry and ritual—was inspired by a single pair of deities who naturally belong together. Other, more arbitrary combinations of gods were then modeled after this original pair. This prototype can likely be found in <term>Mitra-Varuna: a dual deity representing social order and cosmic law</term>, the most prominent and most closely linked of these pairs in the <term>Rigveda: the oldest collection of Vedic hymns</term>. Evidence for this includes its great antiquity—it can be traced back to the <term>Indo-Iranian period: the era before the ancient Indian and Iranian peoples separated</term>—as well as its probable connection with the most noble of all natural entities suitable for such a pair of parallel gods: the sun and the moon. The modeled pairs¹) usually show <term>Indra: the king of the gods</term> in association with another god, whom one honors by admitting him into the fellowship of the mightiest god. A single hymn—or a collection of hymns—is dedicated to the pair that later achieves special significance in the younger <term>Vedic literature: later scriptures that expand upon the original hymns</term> (which focuses increasingly on speculations regarding sacrifice): the pair of <term>Agni: the god of fire</term> and

The world of the gods does not form a state with a recognized head, or at least only the beginnings of such a conception can be found. At one moment one god appears as the most powerful, the highest—we shall return to this fluctuation later—but two gods in particular stand out above the others: Indra and Varuna. While it is perfectly understandable in itself that divine figures could rise so powerfully from different spheres of natural life that no position lower than the first seemed high enough for any of them, another special factor comes into play to explain the competition between Indra and Varuna—if our assumptions about Varuna's prehistory²) are correct: alongside Indra, inherited from <term>Indo-Germanic: an older term for Indo-European</term> antiquity, stands Varuna, who originates from abroad; the faith of separate nations has [invested] in the one and the other such a fullness of power—

->### Indra or Varuna as the Supreme God.<-

...bestowed, so that as soon as both encountered each other, they were bound to contest the primary position as rivals. This meeting occurred during the <term>Indo-Iranian: the period before the separation of the Indian and Iranian peoples</term> era; thus, it is inevitable that the earlier phases of the conflict that may have unfolded here remain hidden in darkness. What we observe is this: in Iran, Varuna—the <term>Ahura: "Lord," referring to Ahura Mazda</term> of the <term>Avesta: the sacred texts of Zoroastrianism</term>—emerged victorious. This triumph could not fail him, the supreme lord of justice and purity, within the context of the <term>Zoroastrian: original: "zarathustrische"</term> doctrine dominated by ethical motives. In the <term>Veda: the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism</term>, however, Indra stands in the foreground. To be sure, many a word in the hymns addressed to Varuna also elevates him to the loftiest heights, and numerous comparisons between the two gods—above all the <term>dialogue of conflict: original: "Kampfgespräch," referring to a poetic debate between deities, likely Rigveda 4.42</term> between them, which we will examine more closely shortly—demonstrate that Varuna is seen above all others as a rival to Indra's greatness.

But the center of gravity of the cult and religious poetry ultimately falls on Indra's side. At the sacrifices of the warrior princes, for whom the singers composed their verses, the plea for power and victory—for the gifts Indra provided—necessarily drowned out the yearning for the forgiveness of sins and the grace of Varuna. Furthermore, liturgical poetry was primarily dedicated to the <term>Soma sacrifice: the ritual offering of the sacred Soma juice</term>; and the great Soma-drinker was Indra. Thus, alongside the praise of Indra, the thought of Varuna's majesty only occasionally moves to the forefront for the Vedic poet—perhaps where contemplation of the world's highest orders evokes it, or the feeling of being pursued by the anger of the god who punishes sins¹).

# The Multiplicity of the Gods.

...<term>Veda: the oldest body of Indian sacred scripture</term> that the outlines of the individual gods tend to blur into an indefinite, boundless formlessness. The imagination of the Vedic poet and the Vedic people lacks 그 secret of creative power which gave the gods of <term>Homer: the legendary Greek poet</term> their eternally living form. It would be an exaggeration to say that <term>Agni: the god of fire</term> or <term>Indra: the god of storms and king of heaven</term> possessed no individuality of their own for the Vedic poets. However, the specific features of their nature are almost entirely obscured by what they share with all gods, making them all appear similar—clothed in a uniform cloak of power, light, goodness, and wisdom, which the Vedic poets never tire of praising in the same stereotypical expressions. 

Various factors further contribute to the way the individual figures of the various gods became mixed and blurred. Many of them frequently overlap in the same functions. Help against evil demons is provided by the fire that burns them, but also by the wielder of the thunderbolt who shatters them, and several other gods as well. Thus, Agni and Indra overlap in a series of traits, and once a partial agreement exists, it naturally tends to expand beyond its original boundaries. The poet slips from one track of routine glorification into another, which then carries him further for a shorter or longer distance. Here, the tendency of the Veda to link the gods in pairs—touched upon earlier (p. 93)—will also have been an influence. By pairing Indra and Agni—

# The Blurring of Divine Personalities

...were glorified together, the attributes belonging to one god were extended to the other: <term>Agni: the god of fire</term>, who is normally not a drinker of <term>Soma: a sacred ritual drink</term>, became a Soma-drinker in the company of <term>Indra: the king of gods and storm-deity</term>; he became the "Slayer of Vritra" <note>original: "Vṛtratödter"; Vritra was a dragon-demon of drought slain by Indra</note> and the wielder of the thunderbolt; like Indra, he became the winner of the cows and the waters, of the sun and the dawn. Thus, the myth migrates from one god to another; research must be careful not to assign equal weight to the myth in both instances, but must distinguish between the original and the transferred versions. — Furthermore, certain activities that are, so to speak, mythologically "unclaimed," are particularly subject to constant fluctuation between various deities. For instance, the praise for having expanded the reaches of the earth and fixed the heights of heaven with its supports is sometimes paid to <term>Varuna: the god of cosmic order and the sky</term> as the lord of all laws, sometimes to Indra as the strongest, and sometimes to <term>Vishnu: a deity associated with the sun's stride</term> as the measurer of vast spaces. The poet, accustomed to ascribing the glory of such deeds now to this god, now to that, is then reluctant to let the other gods lag behind¹). — Further, the blending of divine types is promoted by the fact that the same natural entity appears in connection with different groups of mythological ideas. Water is initially animated by demons who are merely water-dwellers. But water also reveals itself—through observations of a quasi-scientific nature, which then become a source of myths—as the birthplace of fire: the fire-being dwells in the depths of the waters. In many areas, but nowhere more strongly than in the mythology of Agni, the same pattern repeats: reflection on the natural interconnectedness of diverse entities reveals one to be hidden within the other. Thus, alongside the somewhat natural blurring of types, a conscious tendency to identify all seemingly different things gains increasing importance. By seeking to unfold the hidden essence of a god in all its depth and versatility, one finds increasing pleasure in stating that this god is also what another god is. The most superficial contact—and perhaps sometimes even less—is enough for the singer to say:

> “You, O Agni, are <term>Varuna: the guardian of cosmic law</term> when you are born. You are <term>Mitra: the god of friendship and oaths</term> when you are kindled. In you, O Son of Strength, dwell all the gods. You are <term>Indra: the king of gods</term> for the mortal who pays you homage. ### Mixing of Divine Types

Tracing the path from the Vedic belief in gods to this pantheistic doctrine of Brahman <note>The "Brahmalehre" refers to the philosophical transition where the many gods are viewed as manifestations of a single ultimate reality, Brahman.</note> is not our task here¹).

---

¹) Only briefly shall we consider here the theory of Vedic “Henotheism” (M. Müller, *Origin and Development of Religion*, 312 ff.; *Physical Religion*, 180 ff.), defined as the “belief in individual gods who emerge alternately as the highest.” The Vedic poet—at least in large sections of the texts—attributes to every god he happens to be invoking at that moment everything that can be said of a divine being; each is, in turn, entirely independent, entirely the highest, and entirely divine. I cannot withhold my reservations regarding this idea of the Vedic singers' minds becoming so immersed in a belief in shifting, temporarily supreme and sole deities. I do not wish to speak of the hymns to “all the gods” so frequent in the <term>Ṛgveda: the oldest collection of Sanskrit hymns, dedicated to the deities of the Vedic pantheon</term>, in which all the major deities and hosts of minor ones are praised in succession. I merely point out that, as we see ever more clearly, the vast majority of Vedic hymns were composed for a specific ritual purpose: for the <term>Somaopfer: the Soma sacrifice, an elaborate Vedic ritual involving the offering of a sacred plant juice to the gods</term>, which even then, in its broad framework, encompassed the worship of nearly the entire ancient pantheon. The poets who sang of <term>Indra: the king of the gods and god of storms</term> or <term>Agni: the god of fire and messenger between humans and gods</term> with that seemingly henotheistic immersion in the worship of only one god, knew—as the experienced ritual specialists they indeed were—exactly where in the sacrifice, and before or after which other gods, the god they were currently glorifying belonged. In my opinion, the peculiarities of Vedic poetry that give the appearance of <term>Henotheism: a term coined by Max Müller to describe worshiping one god at a time as if they were the only supreme power</term> are explained, on the one hand, by that previously characterized vagueness of form inherent to the Vedic divine figures, and on the other, by the understandable courtesy shown by the singer or priest toward whichever heavenly lord he has the honor of addressing at that moment.

# SECTION TWO.

## The Individual Gods and Spirits.

### A g n i.

*The Pre-Vedic and the Vedic Fire God.*

If we ask about the prehistory of Agni, the Vedic fire god, we find that regarding the Indo-European <note>The ancestral culture and language group that includes most of Europe, Iran, and Northern India.</note> period, only very sparse and vague ideas about the religious significance of fire are naturally accessible to us. It may be considered probable that the myth of the descent of fire from its heavenly home dates back to that time. Furthermore, it is likely that the concern for the continuous maintenance of fire—which was self-evident for practical reasons—was already surrounded by certain ritual practices even then. 

Beside the demon-expelling magical fire, the sacrificial fire also appears to date back to the Indo-European period. Within the Italic-Greek-Aryan <note>In this historical context, "Aryan" refers to the Indo-Iranian branch of the Indo-European family.</note> cultural sphere, at least, there exists the custom of offering a gift to this fire itself when one uses it to convey offerings to the gods. Clearly, however, the personification of the power living within the fire was still quite shadowy—unlike, for example, that of the Indo-European storm god—otherwise, it could hardly have evolved into such diverse types as the female figure of Hestia-Vesta <note>Hestia (Greek) and Vesta (Roman) were the virgin goddesses of the hearth and domestic fire.</note> among the...

Greeks and Italians compared to the male fire god of the Asian peoples.

The picture provided by the comparison of the Veda <note>The oldest scriptures of Hinduism, composed in archaic Sanskrit.</note> and Avesta <note>The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, written in Avestan, a language closely related to Vedic Sanskrit.</note> for the Indo-Iranian era is much more definite. At that time, fire stood at the center of a highly developed cult; the care of fire was dedicated to a priesthood whose members were likely named "fire-men" <note>Referring to the *Athravans* in the Avesta and the *Atharvans* in the Vedas.</note> after it. These priests not only used fire to bring offerings to the gods but also dedicated offerings and worship to the fire itself. It was personified as a strong, pure, wise god, kind toward the house in which he was served with joy—a bestower of fame and nourishment, of herds and strong descendants, and also of spiritual power to his friends, but a destroyer to his enemies. Even the diversity of the forms and locations of fire—such as the fire of lightning, the fire that dwells in the wood of trees and is drawn out from it by friction, and so on—seems to have occupied the thinking of that era already.

If we turn now to the Veda, we see **Agni** <note>The Vedic god of fire and the mediator between gods and humans.</note> taking what is quite literally the most significant position in the cult and in religious poetry alongside **Indra**. One might even say that outside the sphere of the Soma sacrifice <term>Soma sacrifice: A central Vedic ritual involving the pressing and offering of the juice of the Soma plant, believed to be an intoxicating or energizing drink for the gods.</term>—with which the Rigveda <note>original: *Ṛgveda*; the oldest of the four Vedas, consisting of hymns to the gods.</note> is almost exclusively concerned—and the great cult practiced predominantly in the name of the warrior nobility, Agni has the decisive upper hand between those two gods who emerge roughly equally in the Rigveda. Between him and Indra, there is a perceptible difference in character. In Indra, the invincible, all-overthrowing strength is more prominent; in Agni, it is wisdom. The former is the great fighter, the latter the great priest¹). This is also shown in the blessings—

# Agni

Regarding the gifts one expects from both, there is a subtle nuance of difference: on Indra’s side, the elements of power, victory, and triumph are more prominent; on Agni’s, those of domestic prosperity, the blessing of children, and quiet growth come to the fore.

Despite the tendency of the Veda <note>The oldest scriptures of Hinduism.</note> to increase Agni’s importance, a faint trace seems to echo here and there through the language of the hymns of what was undoubtedly the view of an earlier age: that he—the spirit <note>original: "Dämon"</note> who goes about his business primarily on earth in human dwellings—was not perfectly equal in rank to the actual gods, the "Heavenly Ones." When he is called the messenger of the gods, when it is said that the gods have placed him in human dwellings, that they have appointed him to sacrificial service and granted him eternal youth as a reward, or even when expressions are used of him such as that he, the son of the gods, has become their father¹): he always appears in a certain unique position over against the compact mass of the "gods." Above all, however, it is noteworthy that Agni has as good as no share—and originally certainly no share—in the most noble drink of the gods, the Soma <note>A ritual drink made from a sacred plant, central to Vedic sacrifice.</note>. While it is often said of him that he blesses the person who brings him firewood, sacrificial butter, and worship, it is a rare exception for the pious man to appear as one preparing the Soma for him²). Will one not—

### Agni’s Position in the Veda. Agni’s Births.

—be permitted to assume that, by the time Agni reached his prominent divine significance, the basic structures of the <term>Soma sacrifice</term><note>The central ritual of the Vedic religion involving the pressing and offering of the sacred Soma juice.</note> were already established?

**Agni’s Various Births.** The myths of Agni, in stark contrast to those of <term>Indra</term><note>The heroic king of the gods and god of storms.</note>, report very few of the god's actual deeds. This seems to be related to the lesser degree of his <term>anthropomorphism</term><note>The attribution of human characteristics or behavior to a god.</note> already emphasized above (page 44). The speculations with which the Agni-hymns primarily concern themselves—besides their main theme, the appearance and activity of the god in that of his forms most present to the priest, the <term>sacrificial fire</term>—deal with the diversity of Agni’s various births, his forms of appearance, and his dwelling places. In no other deity were reflections of this kind so natural as in him; his wondrous birth from the <term>friction sticks</term><note>original: "Reibhölzern"; two pieces of wood rubbed together to generate the "sacred fire."</note> and his essential identity in heavenly forms alongside the earthly, and in hidden forms alongside the manifest, were bound to deeply occupy the "secret-mongering" of the Vedic priests and provide a favorite theme for the praise of the god.

Regarding the births or forms of Agni, sometimes two are mentioned, while at other times the favorite number of three appears; longer lists are also found. The epithet "the twice-born," which is applied to him several times, refers to his heavenly and his earthly nature¹):

> "We wish to serve you, Agni, in your highest birth; with songs of praise we wish to serve you at the lower place." "Let Agni hear us with his domestic faces; with his heavenly ones let the Never-Tiring hear us." "He takes his seat upon the lower..."

¹) Compare Bergaigne I, 28 ff., though some of his material should be disregarded. I consider the passage II, 35, 6, which appears particularly explicit to him, to be textually uncertain; instead of <note>original: "ca svàr"</note> "and the light of heaven," I would like to suggest <note>original: "sasvár"</note> "secretly."

# Agni's Births.

"They cherish his origins: one in the sea, one in the sky, and one in the waters" (I, 95, 3) — it is strange that the sea and the waters are distinguished here, and that there is no mention at all of Agni’s generation by human hands¹). I shall cite a few more passages which, without placing weight on a specific number, speak of the various births or forms of Agni. "You, Agni, the Shining One, are born from the heavens²), you from the waters, you from the stone, you from the forests, you from the plants; you, Lord of Men, are born as the possession of men in brilliance." "Offspring of the waters, offspring of the forests, offspring of the stationary, offspring of the moving; even inside the stone is his dwelling; like the lord of the settlements, the immortal one, full of wisdom³)." "Agni, your brilliance, which is in heaven and on earth, which is in the plants, the waters, O Adorable One, with which you have spread yourself over the wide air..."⁴).

What is meant by Agni’s heavenly birth, and what by his birth from the waters? For the heavenly Agni, the sun may be considered, or perhaps the lightning. The lightning, for its part, can be understood both as a heavenly being and as a being belonging to the realm of water; the cloud, its home, is after all—

# Agni.

In the Veda <note>The oldest layer of Sanskrit literature and Hindu scripture</note>, he is called "heavenly water." However, we shall see that for the Vedic conception—quite apart from lightning—fire is contained in all water, both earthly and heavenly, in a completely different sense. In cases where the Heavenly Agni and the Water Agni are mentioned side by side, I am generally inclined to believe that the former is to be understood as the sun, while lightning is either omitted or included within the deity's "water form"¹). Nevertheless, it must be admitted that the meaning which each individual passage associates with Agni's various forms or births often remains uncertain; the more important matter, however—how these forms themselves were envisioned—is quite well established. Let us consider them one by one.

The identity of Agni’s essence with the sun—or more precisely, the status of the sun as one of Agni's many manifestations—is an indisputable Vedic dogma. Agni "stands there with his brilliance, as the sun, spreading men over their dwellings." "Agni with bright brilliance shone mightily as the sun; in heaven as the sun he shone." "Agni, your rays that are in the sun, which spread across the heaven with the rays of sunrise," and so on²). However, it is very rare that this side of Agni’s nature is mentioned. It belongs, so to speak—

For on one hand, it is at the very least doubtful to what extent this interpretation was still vivid for the Vedic poets themselves; furthermore, it cannot be our intention to exclude the possibility of fluctuating ideas within the Veda. As a characteristic example of this fluctuation, I highlight <term>Aitareya Brahmana</term> <note>A collection of ancient Indian ritual instructions</note> VII, 7, 2, where lightning-fire is described in the same context as "heavenly fire" and immediately thereafter as "fire in the waters."

### Agni and the Sun.

...to complete the titles due to him—but only for that purpose—is he worshipped in this form as in others: as the heaven-born sun. Ordinarily, however, Agni is the earthly fire, which is compared to the sun in the sky rather than identified with it.
> "In the heart," it is said, "Varuṇa <note>A major Vedic deity associated with the sky, justice, and cosmic order</note> created will; in the water, Agni; the sun in heaven; on the rock, Soma <note>A sacred plant and the ritual drink pressed from it</note>" ¹), 
—one sees how, to the poet speaking without bias, the sun is one being and Agni another, placed in a different location by the Creator. After all, the sun was far too much a power in its own right for the conception of it as fire to have had real significance.

In ritual, the relationship between sun and fire seems to be reflected—alongside several other rites ²)—specifically in the morning fire sacrifice: at the time of sunrise—and similarly at sunset—the sacrificial fire ³) was stoked and a milk offering was presented. It may be conjectured—and non-Indian parallels support this assumption—that this act, which on one hand clearly represents the regular maintenance and service naturally due to the sacred fire itself, was on the other hand also a form of magic directed at the sun, at least in ancient times. By kindling the fire, one caused or promoted

The fire-drilling <note>The act of creating fire through friction with wooden sticks</note> should not be performed before sunrise (Maitrayani Samhita I, 6, 10). This is a parallelization of the two light-beings, which may well be the remnant of a closer and more concrete connection once imagined between them. A <term>Brāhmaṇa</term> <note>2) — a collection of ritual instructions and explanations</note> states quite explicitly: "By sacrificing in the morning before sunrise, he <note>the priest</note> brings him <note>3)</note> to birth; becoming radiant and shining, he rises. For the older period, however, passages from the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>5) — the oldest of the four Vedas</note> testify to the same view very clearly. Thus it is said: "Let us enkindle you, O God Agni, the shining one, the eternally young, so that your wondrous brand <note>6)</note> may shine in the sky." "Agni, you led the eternally young star, the sun, in the sky..."

### Agni and the Sun. Agni and the Lightning.

...upward, creating light for mankind" <note>1)</note>. The latter passage seems, as so often happens, to transform the daily recurring process into an event belonging to the creation of the world. Similarly, the circle of ideas we are considering here was inserted into the myth of Indra's attainment of the sun, which will be discussed later: as the Angirases <note>A group of semi-divine celestial priests or sages</note> split the rock and united their voices with the lowing of the cows, "then the sun became visible, when Agni was born" <note>2)</note>.

After the heavenly sun-Agni, we consider the one dwelling in the waters. The preference for the thunderstorm that has prevailed for a long time in mythological research has led to the tendency to see in this form of Agni exclusively, or at least preferably, the lightning <note>3)</note>; certainly unjustly for the Vedic age. It shall not be denied that the fire-nature of lightning or the lightning-affinity of fire is touched upon here and there by the Vedic poets — thus Agni is once called <note>4)</note> "the shining thunder that is in the realm of light" — but that is, so to speak, only an occasional marginal decoration...

<note>3)</note> Bergaigne (I, 10), in whose system it does not fit that the lightning is stamped as a female being by the grammatical gender of *vidyut* <note>original: "vidyut"</note>, and who finds the rare occurrence of the word *vidyut* strange, even goes so far as to claim that the actual designation of lightning in the Rigveda is Agni. Nothing can be more erroneous. Lightning is rarely mentioned because, in truth, people were much less occupied with it than modern research tends to assume: and those schemas of male and female entities, where lightning would have to belong to the masculine category, are simply a Procrustean bed <note>A metaphor for a rigid standard to which everything is forced to conform, even at the cost of distortion</note> for the actual ideas of the Vedic poets.

### Agni.

...in the image of Agni <note>1)</note>. Usually, where he is named together with lightning, he is compared with it—or it with him—and thereby clearly distinguished from it. It has been noted with good reason <note>2)</note> that the unsteady, fleeting nature of lightning is generally not favorable for it to develop into a distinct deity; it most naturally becomes a weapon or a tool in the hand of a god. It is the Indra myth involving the <term>Vajra</term> <note>Indra's divine thunderbolt weapon</note>, rather than the Agni myth, in which we primarily hear of lightning.

And yet, the conception of Agni dwelling within the waters—"clothing himself in the sea," or "enlivening the seed of the waters"—is one that stands out throughout the entire <term>Veda</term> <note>The most ancient body of sacred Sanskrit hymns and rituals</note>. A passage already mentioned above (p. 109) describes the god <term>Varuṇa</term> <note>A major deity associated with the sky, cosmic order, and the waters</note> creating "will in the heart, Agni in the water, and the sun in the sky." In this view, water is regarded as the true home of Agni in the same way that the sky is the home of the sun <note>3)</note>. One senses from this phrasing that the poet is expressing a thought that is vivid and living to him, rather than merely repeating the fossilized remains of a myth that has lost its meaning. Therefore, there must be some conception other than lightning that the Vedic people primarily had in mind when they spoke of Agni’s home in the water.

---

<note>1)</note> From the ritual, I mention as relevant to the relationship between Agni and lightning: the use of wood from a lightning-struck tree during the rite of establishing the sacred fire (<term>Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra</term> V, 2, 4), as well as the rite of <term>expiation</term> <note>A ritual performed to make amends for an error or omen</note> to be completed through an offering to "Agni in the waters" if the sacrificial fire had become mixed with "lightning-fire" (<term>Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa</term> XII, 4, 4, 4; <term>Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra</term> XXV, 4, 33; <term>Aitareya Brāhmaṇa</term> VII, 7; <term>Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra</term> III, 4, 7). Concerning another offering to "Agni in the waters," see below, p. 114, note 3.

### Agni and the Waters.

The way to determine this aspect of the nature of the waters—by virtue of which they could represent a home for Agni—seems to me to be indicated by the ancient connection between "Water and Plants," which had already become established in Indo-Iranian times <note>1)</note>. Just like the waters, the plants—the woods from which fire is produced by friction—are also a home for Agni, and the <term>Veda</term> <note>The sacred scriptures of ancient India</note> is fond of placing water and plants, or water and forests, side by side, specifically in relation to Agni’s dwelling places <note>2)</note>. However, in several passages, it provides even clearer clues regarding the nature of this relationship <note>3)</note>. "The offspring of the waters has entered into the fruit-bearing plants." "In the waters, Agni, is your seat; in the herbs you climb upward." "When he is brought down from the highest father, he climbs... the plants up into his dwellings" <note>4)</note>. We may interpret this thought as follows: water comes down from the "highest father," the sky; the plants then soak up their nourishment from the rain and from the terrestrial water that is identical in essence to it. Indeed, the plants are the "first-born essence of the waters," and "water is their nature" <note>5)</note>; in the—

### Agni.

In water, therefore, the power must be latently contained, which bursts forth as fire from the wood of plants. When the fire then returns to heaven as smoke—that is, as a cloud—the cycle is closed, which a verse of the **Ṛgveda** <note>The oldest collection of sacred Sanskrit hymns</note> describes very clearly: "The same water goes up and down in the course of days: the rain showers swell the earth; the flames of **Agni** <note>The Vedic god of fire</note> swell the sky" (I, 164, 51)¹). — Running parallel to these ideas and explaining them is the concept that **Amṛta** <note>The "nectar of immortality," a life-prolonging essence</note>—the power residing in plants that is given to the sick in the form of plant sap—is derived from the "seed" of **Parjanya**, the god who pours out the rain²).

One should not deny the probability that the thoughts described here regarding the connection between water and fire were given additional weight by the phenomenon of lightning born from the clouds. It may also be suspected that a third natural process played a part: the extinguishing of fire in water, which seemed to signify the fire's entry into the water and thus its latent remaining within it—"he hisses in the waters like a swan settling down," it is said of **Agni**³). The concept of Agni as being born from water led to a conflation of this god with a figure who was likely originally quite distinct from him: the "**Child of the Waters**" (*apām napāt* <note>Sanskrit for "Offspring of the Waters"</note>). This deity dates back to the Indo-Iranian period. In the Avesta <note>The sacred texts of ancient Zoroastrianism</note>, we find him as a spirit of the waters, living in their depths and invoked alongside them: rich in swift steeds—originally, these horses were likely the rushing waves—surrounded by women—the water-maidens—and governing the distribution of waters across the earth¹). Yet even in the Veda, his original nature **as a water god**²) clearly shines through the traits he adopted following his identification with Agni. Of the two hymns in the *Rigveda* addressed to him, one (X, 30), whose ritual use is precisely established³), concerns ceremonies that deal exclusively with water⁴), not with fire. When the priests set out to draw the water required for the sacrifice, the following verse is spoken:

> "You <term>Adhvaryus</term> <note>The class of priests who performed the manual labors of the Vedic sacrifice</note>, go to the water, to the sea; bring the sacrificial offering to the Child of the Waters: today his beautifully purified wave shall give that to you; to the..."

XIX). # Agni.

"...has ascended the womb of the side-going ones <note>original: *Seitwärtsgehenden*; a poetic reference to the flowing rivers</note>, standing upright himself, clothing himself in lightning"; at the conclusion, Agni is addressed directly, and in this context, he is hardly thought of as a being distinct from the **Child of the Waters**. The process underlying these data is likely not in doubt: an original water spirit <note>The German *Wasserdämon* refers to a supernatural spirit, not necessarily a malevolent demon</note> has—as was almost inevitable as a result of the increasingly popular speculations about Agni as being water-born, and under the influence of the tendency particularly characteristic of Agni to be identified with the most diverse types of gods—partially merged with Agni; for the other half, he has preserved his own nature. —

### Further Forms of Agni.

...the fingers of the one rubbing; one must rub with full exertion of strength: therefore he is called the **Son of Strength**. <note>A common Vedic epithet for Agni, referring to the physical force required to kindle fire by friction.</note>

There are still other forms of origin and existence for Agni, though they are mentioned hardly more than in passing. He dwells in stones, is born from stones¹): obviously referring to the spark coming from the flint. He dwells (in the form of animal heat, perhaps also as the clarity of consciousness) in humans, in the hearts of humans—"from our heart gazes the Many-Born"—and likewise in cattle and steeds, in birds and wild game, in everything that is two-footed and four-footed²). He dwells in the earth, which is called "pregnant with Agni"³), perhaps because the fire contained in wood was thought of not only as having reached that place through water, but also as rising from the soil into the trees that have grown out of the earth. Finally, the god who dwells in so many places could be envisioned as being spread everywhere, as the "offspring of the resting, offspring of the moving," as the "offspring of all that exists"⁴), as a power of life resting within the interior of all things. —

**Descent of Agni.** Standing unconnected alongside the ideas of Agni’s various births is the notion of his descent, or rather, his being brought down <note>The German *Herabbringung* suggests an external agent or mythic hero bringing fire to earth, similar to the Prometheus myth.</note>. In the former view, an earthly birth is ascribed to him as having equal status to his heavenly birth; in the latter, his earthly existence is derived from the heavenly one. In the former, Agni, a god, is born; here he is—at least according to the fundamental concept—brought down as a passive object. Can we... <note>catchword: Dürfen</note>

# Agni.

If we attribute the idea of this bringing down—which probably rests on the phenomenon of lightning—to the Indo-European <note>original: "indogermanischen"; the author uses the older German term for the Indo-European language family and culture.</note> period, as the Prometheus myth makes likely, then this passivity of Agni—similar to that of Soma <note>A sacred ritual drink and a god; like fire, Soma is often described as being "brought down" from heaven by an eagle.</note> in the myth of his descent—is easily understandable: the element had not yet become a personal god at that time.

The "bringer-down," the Prometheus of the Veda <note>The most ancient layer of Sanskrit literature and the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.</note>, is **Mātariśvan**¹). "The One," it is said of Agni and Soma, "Mātariśvan brought from heaven; the Eagle snatched the other from the rock." "The one who had hurried about on his paths, Agni, who had hidden himself—Mātariśvan brought him from afar, the one generated by friction from the gods." "Vivasvant’s messenger brought Agni here, Mātariśvan brought him—who belongs to all men—from afar"²). — **Vivasvant** is the first sacrificer, the ancestor of the human race³); his messenger brings to him, and thus to humanity, the fire from heaven, whose most noble virtue for the Vedic poet is its effectiveness during the sacrifice.

### Descent of Agni.

This is the sparse Indian form of the ideas which the profound Greek spirit elevated to the world-encompassing tragedy of the **Prometheus myth**.

The idea of the introduction of fire by the **Bhṛgus** <note>A legendary clan of ancient fire-priests in Vedic mythology.</note> is essentially different from the myth of the fire-bringer **Mātariśvan**. In the latter, the scene of the event is ultimately the lightning-streaked universe—even if the priestly poetry of the **Veda** <note>The oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism, composed in archaic Sanskrit.</note> understandably and characteristically highlights the sacrificial site, the "seat of **Vivasvant**." Here, however, we are dealing only with the spread of fire, specifically the sacrificial fire, by an ancient legendary priestly clan within human dwellings. The **Bhṛgus** do not fetch it from heaven; wherever the place they find the fire is mentioned, it is called the "abode of the waters." "The **Bhṛgus** have placed you among men . . . as a priest <term>hotāram: the primary priest who recites the hymns of the Rigveda</term>, **Agni**, as a welcome guest." "Him, whom the **Bhṛgus** have kindled, the treasure-rich one on the earth, the world's navel¹⁾ in his greatness . . ." "Those who performed pious service followed his footprints at the place of the waters like lost cattle. The **Uśij**²⁾, the wise **Bhṛgus**, found the secretly hidden one, searching in devotion." "The **Bhṛgus** have ignited you through songs of praise"³). It is not surprising that the imagination of **Vedic** poets occasionally connects **Mātariśvan** as the one who brings down the fire and the **Bhṛgus** as its ancient guardians and spreaders; for instance, such that **Mātariśvan** brings the fire to the **Bhṛgus**⁴),

->### Agni.<-

From the *Rigveda* <note>The oldest and most important collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns.</note> little more can be cited for this role than that Agni—in a passage that also makes him the creator of heaven and the waters and the progenitor of the two worlds—is said to have "begotten these races of men"¹). It is clear that this phrasing—amidst entirely different ideas about the beginning of the human race—represents only one of those countless notions appearing and then disappearing in the *Veda* <note>Ancient Indian sacred texts.</note> which attribute almost any deed to just about any god at some point: one should carefully distinguish this "weed" proliferating on the fertile soil of the Vedic poetic imagination from the stock of firm, permanent mythical concepts. I consider it idle to seriously investigate the origin of such notions, and I believe in particular that it was wrong to derive the one in question here from the identification of fire-making through the two friction-sticks <note>In Vedic ritual, two wooden sticks called *araṇis* were rubbed together to spark the sacred fire.</note> with the human act of procreation²). The sources teach us only that the friction of fire—as was obvious—was perceived as procreation and simultaneously as birth; conversely, in a magic spell promoting procreation, there is mention of the fruit "which the two **Aśvins** <note>Divine twin physicians in Hindu mythology.</note> have rubbed out with a golden friction-stick"; the later ritual also gives the two friction-sticks the names of the mythical couple **Purūravas** and **Urvaśī**³). ->### Agni as Father of the Human Race.<-

The comparison between fire production and human procreation is still far removed from the conception of fire as the creator of humans or as the first-created human, and I can discover no positive trace, at least, that the development of these ideas took such a course.

Far more firmly grounded in Vedic tradition than the view of Agni as the father of men is that of Agni as an **Angiras** <note>In Vedic mythology, the Angiras are a group of celestial beings or semi-divine seers who mediate between gods and men through sacrifice.</note>, as the preeminent Angiras (*angirastama* <note>original Sanskrit: *angirastama*; the suffix *-tama* indicates the superlative, meaning "the most excellent" or "the best of the Angiras."</note>). It may seem that this idea is not far from the first-mentioned one. The Angiras are the semi-divine ancestors of later priestly lineages: "our fathers the Angiras," "our ancient fathers the Angiras," "the Brahman priests the Angiras"; they "conceived the first law of sacrifice"¹); as companions of **Indra** <note>The king of the gods and god of lightning and storms.</note>, they broke open the rock that enclosed the cows through their priestly songs²). If Agni is now designated as an Angiras, as the preeminent Angiras, it may seem to imply that he is a "first" among the ancestors of humanity. However, I do not believe that this hits upon the origin and meaning of the expression in question. The Angiras are not simply the oldest humans in general; rather, as ancestors of historical priestly lineages, they are the oldest priests. But Agni is the priest *preeminently* <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐξοχήν (*kat' exochēn*)</note>, and therefore naturally an "oldest priest." Thus, he had to become an Angiras. And if he, the preeminent Angiras, also seems to be called the "father of the Angiras" in one passage³), this is just as understandable as a very small step forward from the established, secure body of concepts, while on the other hand...

**Agni and Humanity.** We shall now consider how the influence of <term>Agni</term> <note>The Vedic god of fire, central to the sacrificial ritual.</note> appeared to the Vedic Indian in actual life—his relationship to the present world and to humanity.

The function which is likely the oldest cultic use of fire, and which tends to appear even among the most primitive peoples, has been preserved in the Vedic Agni: his role as the burner and warder-off of evil spirits and all hostile sorcery. With his bright, sharp eye, he sees the hidden demons; he seizes them with his tongue, with his teeth of bronze; he strikes them with his arrow; he burns them with his glowing heat. In the discussion of the cult, particularly concerning sorcery, the rites in which the belief in this activity of Agni appears will be discussed in more detail; here, it must only be pointed out that Agni shares the role of "demon-slayer" above all with <term>Indra</term> <note>The king of the gods and god of storms.</note>, the lord of the <term>Vajra</term> <note>The thunderbolt or diamond-scepter used as a weapon by Indra.</note>—that is, at least according to the original conception—the wielder of the lightning weapon²): Agni, as lies in the nature of things, is more the burner, while Indra is the crusher of evil enemies. The impression is justified that this particular function on Agni's part is historically likely older, and also appears in the hymns of praise as more prominent and more deeply connected to his essence. In the ritual of demon-exorcism as well, Agni, or fire, plays a role in various forms

To Agni’s activity in the demon-expelling **magic fire** is added the blessing that the domestic and sacrificial fire bestows upon humanity. <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>Referring to the Rigveda, the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns</note> poetry emphasizes, as its entire character dictates, the **sacrificial fire** above all else; for this poetry, Agni’s most noble significance lies in his priestly dignity and in the service as a messenger that he performs between humans and gods. The poets of these hymns loved to glorify in him the divine counterpart of their own class, seeing the power of their own sacrificial art reflected in his power. Sometimes, it is pleasing to assign the qualities and duties of the various sacrificial priests, one after another, to Agni; however, he is primarily assigned the role of the **Hotar**, that is, the priest responsible for the recitation of the hymns that praise, invite, and call upon the god to enjoy the offering. This is likely because this priest—the master of the poetic art and of the persuasion that wins over the gods—was considered more noble than the sacrificial manual laborers who performed the actual physical work of the ritual, especially in his own eyes: for <term>Hotar</term> <note>The chief priest who recites the hymns of the Rigveda</note> priests are, after all—

<page-num>130</page-num>

...primarily the spokesmen in Vedic poetry. This prominence of the deified sacrificial fire—Agni, conceived as a mystical <term>Hotar</term> <note>The principal priest responsible for reciting the Rigvedic hymns</note>—which manifests from the beginning to the end of the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>The oldest collection of Hindu scriptures</note>, is evidently a relatively recent phenomenon. It stems more from the speculations of a professional priesthood than from the creative power of the living spirit of the people. In this positioning of the sacrificial god among the other gods, those claims are being prepared which the sacrificial caste later raised regarding their own precedence among men. The secretive "hide-and-seek" game of subtle conceits, which is already played in the Rigveda with the figure of the divine <term>Brahmin</term> <note>The priestly class</note>, finds its direct successor in the sacrificial symbolism of the later ritual texts, with all their inexhaustible and convoluted eccentricity¹).

Can we suspect that we encounter an older layer of concepts in those instances where Agni is celebrated simply as the guest in human dwellings, as the friend and companion of the people, and even of the domestic animals, without any special prominence given to the idea of sacrifice? Do we have here the echo of a view for which the most important thing of all was the fire of the hearth, the center of domestic existence—that fire of whose former religious significance a trace seems to have remained in the fact that, even in the fully developed ritual of the three sacrificial fires, the foundational fire from which the other two were always taken was called the "Householder’s Fire" <note>original: "Hausherrnfeuer"; referring to the Gārhapatya, one of the three sacred fires of the Vedic ritual</note>?

The <term>Gṛhya texts</term> <note>The Gṛhya Sūtras, or manuals of domestic religious rites</note>—which show us domestic worship in a significantly more popular form than was characteristic of the great cult of the three fires (even if they are by no means untouched by the exclusive priestly current)—give the clearest picture of how one [shaped] life...

# Sacrificial Fire and Domestic Fire.
<sig>9*</sig>
<meta>Digitized by Google</meta>

...that of the individual and the family, which was felt to proceed under the protection of Agni and in the closest dependence on his guidance. To him, invocations were addressed on the most varied occasions, such as the following:

> “May he be the gatherer of wealth. Do us no harm, neither the old man nor the boy. Bring healing to people and to cattle.”

At a wedding, offerings were made while praying for the bride:

> “May Agni, the <term>Householder’s Fire</term> <note>German: *Hausherrnfeuer*. This is the central hearth fire that was never allowed to go out, symbolizing the continuity of the family line</note>, protect her; may he lead her descendants to a ripe old age; may she be of blessed womb, a mother of living children; may she behold the joy of her sons!”

And when the bridegroom scattered roasted barley into the hands of the young woman, he spoke of this act as a

> “union of me and you: may Agni give his blessing to this.”

When a child was born, offerings were made on the tenth day, after the impurity caused by the childbirth had passed, with these verses:

> “May this glorious Agni bestow life upon you today; grant our life duration. Be life-giving, Agni, strengthened by the sacrificial food, your face full of <term>butter</term> <note>German: *Butter*. In Vedic rituals, this refers specifically to *ghee* or clarified butter, which was poured into the fire to sustain the god</note>, sprung from the womb of butter. Drink the butter, the sweet honey of the cow. As a father watches over his son, so watch over this child.”

Similarly, prayers were offered to Agni when the growing boy was brought to the teacher who was to initiate him into the knowledge of the <term>Veda</term> <note>The ancient body of sacred knowledge and hymns at the heart of Vedic religion</note>¹). The master of the house, returning home from a journey, honored his fire with the saying:

> “This Agni is blessed to us, this one is highly blessed to us. In our devotion to him, may we not come to shame. Let him place us at the forefront.”

This simple conception of the domestic Agni, untouched by priestly artifice, is by no means foreign to the poetry of the *Rigveda* <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, containing over a thousand hymns to various deities</note>. In the *Rigveda*, too, the pious man prays to—

# Agni.

Agni, that he might bless him "as a father blesses his son," and that he might be his "closest friend." He is called the "great householder who never goes away"; to him "the milk-cows return, the swift runners return, his own strong steeds return... the generous high-born ones gather at his side." "By his light, when he is kindled, the cows have awakened": those cows "whose names Agni knows through the sacrifice"¹. The singer, who has received rich rewards for his art abroad in the form of cattle, horses, and wagons, reports the gifts he has received to the local Agni upon returning home². While nothing here prevents us—in the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>The Rigveda, the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns</note> as in later texts—from thinking of this as the same sacrificial fire that was otherwise surrounded by such artfully intertwined and confusing priestly secrets: or rather, it is hardly doubtful that, as a rule, this very fire is intended. But this does not close the door to the suspicion that a tone of invocation continues here which was once addressed to a less exclusively sacrificial fire—to a fire whose nature as a participant, indeed as the center of the entire domestic life, allowed for an intimacy of language and interaction that does not easily recur in the worship of other gods.

The Vedic Indian perceives this friendship between Agni and man as one that the individual has inherited from his ancestors from time immemorial. Even if the appeal to such ancient friendship is also found with other gods, it characteristically appears nowhere so frequently and certainly nowhere in such a typical form as with Agni. Indra is praised—

### Sacrificial Fire and House Fire.

...as the god who bestowed victory upon this or that hero of the ancient world, *Agni* is, above all, the god whom the ancestors kindled and to whom they prayed. The fixed rules of the later ritual are well known, according to which, in every major sacrifice, *Agni*—as a god who had already belonged to the forefathers of the sacrificer—was invoked by reciting their names¹); in some passages of the *Rigveda* <note>The *Ṛgveda* is the oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational scriptures of ancient India, composed in Sanskrit.</note>, this custom seems, if not fully present, then at least to be in development.

One must not, however, be led by this to the conclusion that a direct physical *continuity* of the *sacrificial fire* took place from generation to generation; the ritual for the establishment of the sacred fire, which is known in all its details, excludes this idea, which would also stand in contradiction to the view that the death of the sacrificer pollutes his sacrificial fire and makes it unsuitable for further use.

But even if it was not a physical one, an "ideal" *continuity* of the fire worshiped by both fathers and sons was nonetheless felt—a connection in which people saw something more concrete than, for instance, the endurance of the friendship of *Indra* <note>The king of the gods and god of storms, often associated with personal heroism.</note> from one generation to the next. It is quite understandable that this special status—a closer blending with the family’s past—was granted specifically to the god who shared the human dwelling, who accompanied their life from day to day, and who watched the next generation grow up as the previous one grew old. While one speaks of an "*Agni of Bharata*"²), one would hardly speak of any other god in such a manner.

# Indra.

It is probable that even the Indo-European <note>original: "indogermanische." In the 19th century, "Indo-Germanic" was the standard term for what we now call Indo-European.</note> era¹) already recognized a thunder god distinct from the sky god—a blond-bearded or red-bearded²) giant of immense strength, the most voracious eater and drinker, who slays the dragon with his lightning weapon. It cannot be doubted that this same figure, in a form already somewhat close to the Vedic conception, was a part of the mythology of the Indo-Iranians. The Vedic *Vṛtrahan* <note>original: "Vṛtrahan." Sanskrit for "Slayer of Vritra." Vritra was a serpent or dragon who bottled up the waters of the earth.</note> (Indra as the slayer of Vritra) reappears as *Verethraghna* in the *Avesta* <note>The sacred scriptures of Zoroastrianism, the ancient Persian religion.</note>. Even if those myths so essential to his Vedic counterpart are missing from the Avestan god himself, the Armenian dragon-slayer *Vahaken* (= *Verethraghna*) shows—as has long been observed—that the stripping of the thunder myth and the dragon-slaying from the Avestan god is entirely secondary. We would be justified in claiming this even without such confirmation. In the Veda, we find Indra the Vritra-slayer endowed with a multitude of myths that were undoubtedly attributed to the thunder god only at a later date. This process clearly began partly in the pre-Indian period—though we will not undertake a detailed investigation of that here—but the growth of new legends and stories continued further on Indian soil. No other divine figure attracted the Vedic poets as powerfully as Indra; they attributed every trait of unconquerable strength and all the most mighty heroic deeds to him, the <term>Lord of Power</term> <note>original: "Herrn der Kraft," a translation of the Sanskrit epithet *Śacīpati*.</note>³).
