### The Battle with Vṛtra.

We add further details from other Rigvedic hymns.

The serpent had settled upon the “seven sloping paths”—the bed of the seven rivers, which he blocked. He lay there in ninety-nine coils. He had devoured the rivers, and since the rivers are within the mountain and later break forth from it, this even leads to the monstrous idea that “the mountain was in Vṛtra’s belly” <note>In Vedic thought, the "mountain" often symbolizes a rain cloud or the rocky enclosure holding the world's waters captive.</note>. The gods fear the enemy: “like old men, the gods retreated,” “before the serpent’s violence all the gods fled,” “retreating before Vṛtra’s hissing, all the gods, his friends, deserted him”—leaving Indra to stand alone, he whom the gods “placed at their head to slay Vṛtra.” Indra drank heroic strength from the <term>Soma</term> <note>A ritual drink of the Vedic religion, personified as a god, which provided divine inspiration and physical power.</note>; of his allies, the <term>Maruts</term> <note>A group of storm deities and sons of Rudra who serve as Indra’s companion warriors.</note> remain faithfully by his side, as does Vishnu, the god who traverses the universe in three steps: “Then Indra spoke, as he intended to strike Vṛtra: ‘Friend Vishnu, stride out further.’” As Indra takes the thunderbolt in his arm to kill the serpent, mountains, cows, and priests raise a shout of encouragement. Vṛtra, as he suffers the death-blow, is spoken of sometimes as one sleeping, sometimes his wheezing is mentioned, and as described in the hymn shared above, he produces lightning and thunder, mist and hail. Indra splits his head with the thunderbolt, or shatters all his joints. Heaven is terrified by the roar of the stricken enemy. Indra’s weapon opens the “udder of the mountain”; the rivers run to the sea like birds flying to their nests, or like chariots in a race for a prize. The gods cheer for the victor; the goddesses weave a song of praise for him. And the winning of the waters expands into the winning of all shining light. Just as the hymn shared above [mentions] the god, when he had struck the serpent, [gaining] the sun, heaven...

# Indra.

...and causes the dawn to arise, it says in other places¹):
> “When you, Indra, with your power, had struck Vṛtra, the serpent, then you let the sun rise in the sky, so that it might be seen.” “In your arms you carried the bronze <term>thunderbolt</term> <note>The German original uses *Donnerkeil* (thunderbolt), but as the author notes below, the weapon is more like a metal mace.</note>; you held the sun firm in the sky, so that it might be seen.” And a poet calls out to Indra: “Kill Vṛtra, win the sun!” —

If we survey the features of the myth collected here, it becomes obvious that there is no mention of thunderstorms or downpours anywhere²). A god fights a serpent-shaped demon and opens the interior of the mountains; the waters of the rivers stream forth from there toward the sea: that is what the Vedic poets say. One must not confuse this simple concept with the explanation that the poets meant clouds by “mountains” and rain-torrents by “rivers.” They did not; for them, the mountains were mountains and the rivers were rivers. If they had intended to speak of clouds and rain, the metaphor of mountains and rivers could not have recurred so consistently across countless passages without the actual subject ever being called by its right name. Where the poets truly mean clouds and rain, they use different expressions than the fixed ones found in the Indra-hymns. One might compare, for instance, the great hymn to <term>Parjanya</term> <note>The Vedic personification of the rain cloud and the god of the thunderstorm, distinct from Indra's warrior persona.</note>, the god of rain and thunderstorms (V, 83). There, the talk is of rain and again and again of rain and lightning and thunder; the god makes his rain-messengers appear; he creates the rain cloud; the <term>Maruts</term> <note>A group of storm deities who act as Indra's companions.</note> bestow rain from heaven; one prays to Parjanya: “you have let the rain fall, now cease.” He strikes the trees, and with a roar of thunder he strikes the evildoers;

> “Indra has opened the path for us, the bearer of the thunderbolt; he has struck down Vṛtra, who held the streams encompassed . . . Again and again, Indra's heroic deed is to be praised, that he cut the serpent to pieces. With the thunderbolt, he has smashed the enclosures; the waters ran, longing for their course” ³).

From this it is clear: for the Vedic poets, Indra’s victory is not about a thunderstorm, but about the fact that the mighty god caused the locked springs to burst forth from the depths of the rock, which, as rivers, bring blessings to human fields⁴). # Indra.

That the <term>Vajra</term> <note>Sanskrit: *vajra*. The divine weapon of Indra, typically translated as "thunderbolt," though its physical nature varies in description.</note> was originally a lightning weapon is a fact that comparative mythology leaves beyond doubt. However, we must strictly distinguish between the original substance of the myth and the meaning it held for the Vedic poets.

For the <term>Rigveda</term>, one can speak at most of isolated remnants and traces of this old perspective—traces that in part are surely only apparent. This is because the incidental flourishes and momentary inspirations of individual poets could, and inevitably did, in many places take on an indistinguishable similarity to such traces. Indra is called the one "to whom the rain belongs"; a singer who identifies himself with Indra says: "I gave rain to the mortal who honored me"; in the context of the liberation of the waters, a "younger" hymn uses the expression "heavenly waters." At his thundering, it is said, the fixed and the moving tremble; he hurled thunder into the jaws of <term>Vṛtra</term> <note>The "Obstacle" or "Encloser," a serpent-demon who bottled up the world's waters until slain by Indra.</note>; he created the incomparable projectiles of heaven. Indra drove the serpent from the wide plains; he blew it away from the atmosphere and struck it down from earth and heaven¹).

The weight of these hints pointing toward the thunderstorm-nature of the <term>Vṛtrakampf</term> <note>The battle with Vṛtra.</note>—hints which might seem to be present in such expressions—will not be overestimated by anyone who considers their rarity within the enormous mass of the Indra-hymns, and who remembers how often in the Rigveda the power and deeds of every god are occasionally painted with traits that are foreign to his truly canonical form.

Difficulty has been found in rediscovering the atmospheric character of Indra’s dragon-fight; for the Vedic commentators as well as for the poets¹) Indra is now the storm-god who brings rain²). However, this does not change the fact that for the singers of the *Rigveda* <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the ancient sacred scriptures of Hinduism.</note>, he was the splitter of earthly mountains and the liberator of earthly rivers. —

### The Subjugation of the Panis and the Winning of the Cows.

Alongside the winning of the waters, the <term>Veda</term> <note>Sanskrit: *veda*, "knowledge." The primary body of ancient Indian religious texts.</note> presents the "winning of the cows" as Indra's second major achievement.

It may be doubted whether this deed belonged to Indra from the very beginning. Alongside the version predominantly represented in the *Rigveda*, which refers to this god, there is a narrative that by all appearances should be judged as a second, and indeed older, form of the same myth. <term>Trita Āptya</term> <note>A minor Vedic deity associated with the preparation of Soma; he often appears as an earlier hero-figure whose feats were later attributed to Indra.</note>, encouraged by Indra, fights the three-headed, serpent-bodied <term>Viśvarūpa</term> <note>The "All-Shaped One," a demonic figure.</note> (the All-Formed), the son of <term>Tvashṭar</term> <note>The divine artisan or celestial builder in Vedic mythology.</note>; he strikes off his three heads and "lets the cows out"³). "For Trita," says Indra, "I brought forth the cows⁴) from the serpent." Evidently, the actual main character is Trita; Indra was likely only subsequently associated with this deed as the recognized achiever of all the greatest heroic feats⁵).

<page-num>144</page-num>

<header>Indra.</header>

This is also supported by the form in which this same myth appears in the *Avesta* <note>The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, written in the Avestan language.</note>. Thraetaona <note>An Iranian hero who corresponds to the Vedic Trita.</note>, of the lineage of Āthwya, kills the serpent with three mouths, three heads, and six eyes. What he liberates, however, are not cows, but two beautiful women¹). But the fact that the connection between the killing of the three-headed monster and the liberation of the cows—as attested by the *Veda* in contrast to the *Avesta*—is original is demonstrated by the myths of the classical peoples <note>Refers to the ancient Greeks and Romans.</note>. Heracles <note>Greek hero known for his strength and twelve labors.</note> kills the three-headed Geryon, and Hercules <note>The Roman equivalent of Heracles.</note> kills the three-headed Cacus and carries away the herds of cattle which belong to the monster or which it had stolen from the god and hidden in its cave.

Contrasting with this Indo-European form of the myth involving a three-headed monster, another version exists in the *Veda* which is humanized and infused with motifs of earthly—specifically priestly—everyday life. It seems to bear a predominantly Indian character, although it is not improbable that at least its beginnings date back to the Indo-Iranian period²).

One should note that the Avestan passage stands in a context concerning the claim of spiritual persons to the sharing of earthly goods: exactly as in the *Veda*, the myth appears as a glorification of the Brahmin’s <note>A member of the highest, priestly caste in Hindu society.</note> claims to gifts of cows.

# The Recovery of the Cows.

The enemies appear here as a whole troop; they are called the **Paṇis** <note>The Paṇis are depicted in the Vedas as a class of wealthy, stingy individuals who withhold cows and wealth from the gods and priests.</note>. In the *Ṛgveda* <note>The Rigveda: the oldest and most important of the four Vedas, the sacred scriptures of ancient India.</note>, the Paṇi appears quite frequently as a figure from real life, to be understood in a thoroughly realistic way and free from any mythical accessory: it is the archetype of the wealthy man—naturally enjoying a particularly sharp unpopularity among singers and priests—who is stingy with sacrifices and the associated gifts to the clerical class¹). The Paṇis—so our myth relates—possess herds of cows which they keep hidden in a rocky cave in the farthest distance, beyond the **Rasā** <note>A mythical river said to encircle the world or the atmosphere.</note>, the river that flows around the world. Indra’s messenger, the divine hound **Saramā**, has leaped across the Rasā, tracked down the cleft in the rock, and heard the lowing of the cows. She demands the cows in Indra’s name, but is rejected with mockery by the Paṇis²). Now Indra himself approaches with the **Angiras** <note>The Angiras are a group of celestial seers or ancestral priests who assist Indra in his exploits.</note> or with the “seven priests,” the ancestors of the priestly lineages. The cave opens of its own accord, or Indra opens it for the Angiras, or else they themselves open it “through their words” or “through their litanies,” “through their sound,” “singing,” “with kindled fire”—the conception is clearly that these first among human priests sing and recite at a sacrificial fire just like their descendants, and through the magical power of this act, they open the sealed rock³). They have opened the rocks "through the **Ṛta**" (that is, the Right or Cosmic Law)¹); it is understood as a process belonging to the law of the eternal world order that they had to perform this deed. **Agni** <note>The Vedic god of fire and the personification of the sacrificial flame.</note> also appears here and there as a participant (see above, pages 99 and 111): it is understandable that, alongside the sacred chant—as just mentioned—the sacrificial fire is also present. This is doubly understandable if we are correct in relating the entire myth to the attainment of light (page 149); the kindling of the fire is a magical act that brings about the rising of the sun. Above all, however, alongside the priestly fathers, another divine figure is named as an actor: **Bṛhaspati**, the "Lord of Prayer"²); his role is fundamentally no different from that of the **Angiras**, as he himself is regarded as belonging to their lineage. He, the personification of the power of the sacred word and sacred song, opens the cave "with songs heated by fire." He shatters it and drives the cows out just as one breaks an egg and pulls out the young bird, or as one extracts marrow from a bone. **Vala**, the demon of the cave, laments for the abducted cows like forests for the leaves that winter has stolen from them. In this way, the cows—and with them all the abundance of food—are won for humanity and for the priests: **Saramā** has found the firm enclosure of the cows "from which the human tribes take their nourishment"; the Angiras have "found all the food of the **Paṇi**"; Indra, as the first, [has opened the stall] "for the Brahmin...

### The Winning of the Cows.

...found the cows," "made the cow easily attainable for the Brahmin." However, the winning of the cows is closely connected with the winning of light, the Dawns, and the sun; the passages that yield this connection are exceedingly numerous. The priestly fathers "drove out the cows, calling toward the Dawns"; "they found the light." "The Red One <note>The "Red One" refers to Uṣas, the personified goddess of the Dawn.</note> became visible through the cow’s shining [milk?]¹)." The evil darkness vanished; the heaven shone; the light of the goddess Dawn arose; the sun stepped upon the wide fields, beholding right and wrong among mortals." When Indra followed the cows with the fathers, "he found the sun dwelling in the darkness." The fathers, who shattered the rock, "found day and the sun, the light of the Dawn." "Through the **Law** (<term>ṛta</term> <note>Ṛta is the principle of cosmic order and truth that regulates the universe in Vedic thought.</note>) they cast the stone apart, splitting it; the **Angiras** <note>A group of semi-divine ancestral seers who act as mediators between gods and men through ritual song.</note> roared (that is, they began their song) together with the cows. For salvation, the men sat around the Dawn; the sun became visible when **Agni** <note>The god of fire and the personification of the sacrificial flame.</note> was born." **Bṛhaspati** <note>The "Lord of Prayer," a deity who personifies the power of the sacred word to influence the gods and the cosmos.</note> "found Dawn, sun, and fire; with his song he scattered the darkness." "He drove out the cows, splitting the cave through the holy word; he hid the darkness and let the sun be seen.²)"

If we now ask for the interpretation of the narrative, the dominant motives of its form as presented in the **Rigveda** <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational scriptures of Hinduism, composed in archaic Sanskrit.</note> seem to come clearly to light. The main characters are, above all, the human and divine prototypes...

of the priesthood: the fathers of the priestly lineages and the deified ideal priest, the heavenly house-priest <term>Purohita</term> <note>A Purohita is a domestic chaplain or family priest who performs rituals to ensure the prosperity and protection of a household or kingdom.</note> Bṛhaspati. ## Interpretation of the Myth

...presses <note>referring to the ritual preparation of the Soma drink</note>, a friend of the pressers . . . He gathers together the food of the <term>Paṇi</term> <note>In Vedic myth, the Paṇis are demonic figures who hoard the world's wealth and cattle in a cave.</note> as booty and distributes the beautiful possession to his worshipper” (Rigveda V, 34, 5 ff.).

One may certainly grant a high age to this mythical reflection of priestly life-claims¹); however, it is obvious that the explanation for the original **Indo-Germanic** <note>A term used by 19th-century scholars for what we now call Indo-European, referring to the common cultural and linguistic ancestors of many European and Indian peoples.</note> myth has not been found by this means.

I am inclined to believe that it concerns the winning of the **Dawns** from the dark rock of the night sky²). This explains why, in Greek myth, there are red cows and their hiding place is in the extreme West—at the furthest possible distance from the point where the liberated Dawns appear to humanity. It also explains the prominent connection in the <term>Vedic</term> <note>Refers to the Vedas, the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism, written in archaic Sanskrit.</note> myth between the winning of the cows and the attainment of the morning light. As is well known, the image of "red cows" representing the Dawns is still vibrant in the poetic language of the <term>Veda</term>³). And in a series of passages, Vedic poets speak of the goddess of the **Dawn** in expressions that unmistakably recall the story of the cow-winning or refer to it quite explicitly. It is said of the Dawn that she “opens the darkness as cows their pen.” “You have,” the poet says to her, “the gates of the solid rock—”

**The Winning of Light.** The winning of light, the sun, and the dawn—which appears linked with the discovery of the cows in the myth discussed here—is also frequently attributed to Indra independently of that deed. He fixed the sun in the sky; he made it shine; he stabilized the heavens with its supports and spread out the vastness of the earth. Thus, he appears as the accomplisher of all those works and the founder of all those orders that are also attributed to **Varuṇa** <note>The Vedic god of the celestial ocean and cosmic law.</note>²). Must it not have been the strongest of all the strong who gave the greatest goods to mankind, who wrested them from the enemies for him, and who assigned their place to the mightiest entities such as the sun and the heavens? —

**Indra’s Victory over the *Dāsas*.** The deeds of Indra spoken of so far—the victory over **Vṛtra** <note>The dragon or serpent-demon of drought who held back the waters.</note> and the winning of the cows—stand alone, each an incomparable event in itself. There follow deeds that form a series of instances of the same type; these perhaps seem more similar to each other to us than they were in reality, for it is likely due to the brief form of the mentions—with which the poets of the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>The oldest collection of Sanskrit hymns, central to Vedic religion.</note> usually satisfy themselves when listing these deeds—that so few individual traits have been preserved for us here.

These stories consistently involve the subjugation of enemies referred to as *dāsa* or *dasyu* <note>Sanskrit terms for "enemy" or "servant," used in the Vedas to describe both demonic foes and the non-Aryan indigenous peoples encountered by the Vedic tribes.</note>. These are the standard terms with which the Indian **Aryans** <note>The Sanskrit-speaking people of the Vedic period.</note> name the dark-skinned original inhabitants. Thus, from the outset, the view is suggested that we are dealing here with the echoes of historical events: the overcoming

---

¹) Here and there, however, the winning of the sun looks like a consequence of the victory over Vṛtra (cf. above p. 139 f.), for example, Rigveda I, 51, 4: „When you, Indra, with your power, had struck down Vṛtra, the serpent, then you let the sun rise in the sky so that it might be seen“ (more in Bergaigne II, 191 <note>original: "Bergaigne II, 191" refers to the work of Abel Bergaigne, a prominent 19th-century French scholar of the Vedas.</note>). I am inclined to believe that we should think here not so much of the natural phenomenon of the sun's reappearance after a thunderstorm, but rather, so to speak, of a poetic motif: after overcoming the most terrible danger, after surviving the hardest struggle, follows the acquisition of the luminous goods.

The defeat of these enemies in battles—which strained the people's strength until nearly the time of the poets or even into their own era—appeared as the deed of the warlike, all-powerful god, whom only the **Aryan** <note>The Sanskrit-speaking people of the Vedic period.</note> knew how to win over as a friend. It will indeed become clear that the boundary line between the subjugations of the **Dāsas** <note>A term used in the Vedas for both earthly enemies and atmospheric demons.</note> as historical events and the purely mythical deeds of the god—the overcoming of enemies who might be compared to the **Titans** <note>The giant deities of Greek myth who fought against the Olympian gods.</note> or the giants of the **Edda** <note>The primary source of Norse mythology.</note>—is not a sharp one. 

This should not be surprising. For the Vedic poets and storytellers, the distinction between mythical and historical events—in which our modern research takes such great interest—did not exist. For them, the earthly opposition between the Aryans and the dark *Dāsas* continued into the world of gods and demons; the hostile demon stood on the same level as the hated and despised "savage," and was perhaps, in many cases, actually nothing other than the god of a wild tribe. Likewise, the particularly impressive figure of an enemy leader could take on traits like those worn by the devils of myths. 

Thus, we must be prepared from the outset for uncertainties in these boundaries. Correcting them remains impossible given the "fog" that lies over both the historical and mythical elements of this study,¹) and especially given the hopeless scarcity of the evidence that the **Rigveda** <note>The oldest collection of sacred Indian hymns.</note> provides us here. But here too, the researcher who wishes to discern any figures within such fogs of the Rigveda must constantly hold fast to one principle: a relationship whose effect...

### The Victory over the Dāsas.

...in this chaos of countless intersecting uncertainties, a trait is preserved at some point, it must not for that reason be simply dropped from the investigation. Character traits that are mixed with features of a contradictory nature in some places can nonetheless be the decisive ones; the goal is not to simply line up opposites in a uniformly flat light, but to distinguish the fundamental essence from secondary alterations.

Thus we believe, despite the reservations that are inevitably necessary, that we can approach the nature of the type of **Indra-deeds** <note>The legendary exploits and battles attributed to the god Indra.</note> that concern us here in the following considerations.

In significant frequency, references to the **Dāsa** (**Dasyu**) <note>The *Dāsa* or *Dasyu* were the indigenous peoples encountered by the Aryans; in the Rigveda, the terms are used for both human enemies and demonic figures.</note> as the opposite of the **Aryans** <note>The *Aryas* or Aryans were the semi-nomadic people who composed the Vedic hymns.</note> occur throughout the **Rigveda**. The Indian warrior, an Aryan himself, deals with both Aryan and **Dasic** <note>original: *dasisch*; pertaining to the Dāsas.</note> enemies;¹) he prays: "May we conquer Dāsa and Aryan with your help" (X, 83, 1); "Whoever plots battle against us, O Indra, you much-praised one—the godless, whether Dāsa or Aryan: may the enemies be easily overcome by us; through you may we defeat them in battle" (X, 38, 3). Most often, however, the Aryans are spoken of as the friends and victors, standing in contrast to the defeated Dasic enemies. "You (Indra) have conquered the Dasyus; you alone have won the lands for the Aryan" (VI, 18, 3). "Distinguish the Aryans from those who are Dasyus. Subdue and punish those who observe no laws, bringing them under the one who spreads the **sacrificial grass** <term>Sanskrit: *barhis*; the sacred grass strewn upon the altar during Vedic rituals.</term>" (I, 51, 8). Thus we come to know the **Dāsas** <note>The indigenous inhabitants or "enemies" encountered by the Vedic Aryans.</note> as the "black skin," and the Dāsa women in another passage as "having a black womb" (II, 20, 7); a further characteristic of the Dāsas is that they are "noseless" (V, 29, 10), which likely means they are flat-nosed. > "You have," says a poet to Indra, "struck the wealthy **Dasyu** <note>Another term for the Dāsa enemies.</note> with the mace; alone with your helpers you came, Indra. They turned their heads away there, Indra, the non-sacrificers fighting with the sacrificers, when you, the mighty lord of the tawny horses, blew away the lawless ones from both worlds from heaven" (I, 33, 4. 5).

One sees that these Dāsas are enemies of a different kind than the serpent **Vṛtra** <note>The personification of drought or chaos, often depicted as a dragon or serpent slain by Indra.</note> or the three-headed monster **Viṣvarūpa** <note>A three-headed demonic figure in Vedic mythology.</note>: they are human enemies, of whom exactly those things are said which the scorn of the Aryan devotee was bound to say above all else about the "wild" people who stood against him: their skin is black and they do not sacrifice to the gods. They are those enemies of whom old Indian royal names tell, such as **Trasadasyu** <term>original: *Trasadasyu*; "he before whom the Dasyus tremble"</term> or **Dasyavevṛka** <term>original: *Dasyavevṛka*; "the wolf for the Dasyu"</term>.

# The Victory over the Dāsas.

...the **Dāsa** <note>A term used in the Rigveda for the indigenous enemies of the migrating Aryans.</note>, struck down, and you have blessed **Divodāsa** <note>A famous king of the Bharata tribe often aided by Indra.</note> with radiant blessings"¹). The "castles" of the **Dāsas** are mentioned with particular frequency; these were fortifications built with primitive skill which Indra and his human companions destroyed. These strongholds formed the objective of the struggle—a more realistic objective than the rivers in the battle with **Vṛtra** <note>A dragon-like demon representing drought, whose defeat releases the cosmic waters.</note> or the "Cows of the Dawn" <note>A mythological reference to the light of morning being freed from a cave.</note>—between the **Aryans** and the **Dāsas**.

Fabulous numbers of such castles are often mentioned: an embellishment of pious eulogy, which nevertheless does not cast doubt on the historical character of the core of these events.

> "Pouring sleep over **Cumuri** and **Dhuni**, you have killed the **Dasyu**; you were gracious to **Dabhīti**. Then even the old man with his staff won gold. Indra did this in his **Soma**-intoxication" (II, 15, 9).

### Indra.

"...brought wood and cooked the sacrifice with songs" (VI, 20, 13). And the following verse further completes the picture: "He (Indra) surrounded the captors of **Dabhīti** <note>A Vedic Rishi or king often mentioned as being protected by Indra.</note>. With blazing fire, he burned all their weapons, but he led him back along with cattle, steeds, and chariots: Indra did this in a **Soma**-trance <note>original: "Somarausch"; a state of ritual ecstasy or divine intoxication brought on by drinking the sacred Soma juice</note>" (II, 15, 4).

One of the **Dāsas** whom Indra overcame, **Ṣuṣhṇa** <margin>1) Regarding the name, compare page 155.</margin>, seems to carry a strongly mythical air. However, even here I consider it not improbable that historical events ultimately lie at the foundation, which have been embellished with supernatural trappings. **Ṣuṣhṇa's** opponent and conqueror is **Kutsa**. To help him, Indra strengthened himself with potions at the home of the sorcerous **Uṣanā** and had a weapon forged by him. For **Kutsa’s** benefit, he performed a miracle concerning the sun. We have compiled some of the verses that refer to this battle:

"You (Indra) helped **Kutsa** in the killing of **Ṣuṣhṇa**; for **Atithigva** you overcame **Ṣambara**. **Arbuda**, as great as he was, you trod down with your foot: from of old you were born for the slaying of **Dasyus** <term>Dasyutödtung: the ritualized or heroic act of killing the non-Aryan enemies known as Dasyus</term>" (I, 51, 6).

Indra stands with **Kutsa** on the same war-chariot, drawn by the steeds of the wind, and Indra himself resembles **Kutsa**. Therefore, in a verse that seems to present the god and his human friend returning home together from battle, it is said to Indra: "Come home, your spirit filled with the <term>Dasyutod</term> <note>the death or defeat of the Dasyu enemies</note>. May **Kutsa** remain in your friendship, he who desires it. Sit both of you down in your dwelling, identical in appearance: the virtuous wife <note>original: "rechtliche Weib"; referring to Kutsa's wife, who cannot distinguish her husband from the god because they look so much alike</note> will find it difficult to distinguish between you" (IV, 16, 10). A hero of light would always be presented as a friend, and a demon of darkness always as an enemy of the singer; however, one who is a friend in one context and an enemy in another will be — like **Divodāsa Atithigva** — a human being, or at least the ideal representative of a human kinship group that was friendly to some singers and hostile to others.

**Kutsa** fights with the **Dāsas**, whose real leader or ideal representative is **Śuṣṇa**. At first, **Kutsa** is hard-pressed by his enemies. The outcome depends on whether the day will last long enough. ## The Asuras. 
Some passages assign the title of "**Asura**" or "Son of the **Asura**" to the **Dāsas** defeated by **Indra**. This leads us to examine the concept of the **Asura** here, which, as is well known, presents difficult problems for research²). The word **Asura**, which in the later Vedic language designates only beings hostile to the gods <note>demons</note>, appears in the older texts alongside this—and indeed predominantly—as an epithet of gods; likewise, among the Iranians, the same word appears in the form **Ahura**, as the name of the most sublime of all gods <note>Ahura Mazda</note>. How should this change, which seems to have led from the meaning "God" to the meaning "Devil," be explained?

Attempts have been made to attribute the peculiar fate of the word **Asura** to national conflicts, to a clash between the Vedic Indians and followers of another faith. Indian tribes who had remained foreign to the actual Vedic culture, or perhaps Iranians, followers of the doctrine of **Zarathustra** <note>Zoroaster</note>, opposed the cult of the Vedic people with their worship of the **Asura**, and thus their gods were treated by the latter as devils. It seems to me that this hypothesis, as ingenious as it is, nevertheless [is based on] concrete traces in tradition <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence</note>...

absolutely cannot be supported. The clues that this evidence provides point rather in another direction. If one examines more closely the old usage of the word *Asura* for gods—which, as mentioned, disappeared from the Vedic texts in later times—one finds that it is not used for all gods with equal preference; it is not simply synonymous with *deva* <term>deva: The common Sanskrit word for a deity or celestial being, derived from a root meaning "to shine."</term>. Rather, there are differences between the gods here which suggest a specific nuance of meaning inherent to the word *Asura*. This nuance turns out, in my view, to be precisely of the kind that explains the convergence of the gods and the hostile beings under a single shared name. Among the gods, the title *Asura* is applied with particular frequency precisely to those whose *māyā*—that is, their "secret power"—is most often discussed. It is exactly this *māyā* <term>māyā: In the early Vedas, this refers to a mysterious, supernatural power or craft used to create or transform, rather than the later meaning of "illusion."</term> that is a characteristic trait of the evil enemies as well, whether they be of a human or demonic nature. Thus, regarding the gods, the name *Asura* appears with *Varuṇa* <note>Varuna is a major Vedic deity associated with the sky, water, and cosmic law (Rta).</note> or the divine pair *Varuṇa-Mitra* with a frequency that stands in sharp contrast to *Indra* <note>The king of the gods and god of storms.</note> or *Agni* <note>The god of fire.</note>¹. It is specifically *Varuṇa* or *Mitra-Varuṇa* upon whose *māyā* the imaginations of the Vedic poets dwell most frequently². In this context, *māyā*—which is inherently neutral regarding the distinction between noble skill and low arts³)—takes on the character of a magnificent power that manifests gloriously in the wonders of the universe. Agni, who has long dwelled in dark concealment, crosses over "from the non-god" into the camp of the gods, "from the side unworthy of sacrifice to a share in the sacrifice." He renounces "Father Asura," and thus the Asuras lose their magic power (*māyā* <note>original: "māyā"; here referring to supernatural or deceptive power</note>); **Indra** kills **Vṛtra**, and the gods' dominion over the world is decided²). —

### The Asuras. Historical Events.

**Historical Events.** Just as in the victories over the **Dasyus** <note>A term used by the Vedic people to describe both supernatural demons and the indigenous tribes they encountered in India.</note>, historical occurrences still shine through in other parts of the hymns to **Indra**: for instance, when Indra is praised as the one who brought forth **Turvaşa** and **Yadu**. These are the eponymous ancestors of two closely connected Aryan tribes who, alongside friendly mentions, are occasionally named by the poets in a hostile tone—the surest sign of historical reality.¹) Indra led Turvaşa and Yadu from afar and made the rivers crossable for them. "Indra, the lord of strength, the wise one, brought over Turvaşa and Yadu, even though they could not swim" (IV, 30, 17): the lord of all battles is also the patron of the migrations that were moving through the river-rich land at that time. — The battles of King **Sudās** reach entirely into historical times; to him, Indra gave victory in response to the prayers of his priests, the **Tr̥tsu**, among whom the highly famous **Vasiṣṭha** <note>One of the most revered sages (rishis) of ancient India, credited with composing much of the seventh book of the Rigveda.</note> seems to have stood at the head with his kin at that time.²) Indra caused the enemies to perish in the floodwaters. "The path they took to the **Parushṇı** <note>The ancient name for the Ravi River in the Punjab region.</note> became their downfall. Even the swift found their rest there. Indra subjected the swift enemies to Sudās, the man to those of **emasculated speech** <note>original: "entmannt Redenden"; likely a translation of the Sanskrit term 'mṛdhravāc,' referring to those who speak a foreign or "broken" tongue.</note> . . . All at once, Indra [destroyed] all their strongholds, their seven fortresses with might..."

# Indra.

"Broken" <note>Referring to the destruction of enemy fortifications; original: "zerbrochen" (Rigveda VII, 18, 9. 13).</note>. One sees how the turn of phrase so characteristic of the subduing of the **Dasyus** <note>The enemies of the Vedic tribes, often depicted as demonic but here clearly associated with human foes.</note>—the "fortresses broken by Indra"—appears here in the context of undoubtedly historical battles. "Thus with them (the descendants of **Vasiṣṭha**)," it continues in reference to these and related struggles, "Indra crossed the stream; thus with them he struck down **Bheda**; thus in the **Battle of the Ten Kings** <note>A pivotal historical battle mentioned in the Rigveda where King Sudās defeated a confederation of ten tribes.</note> Indra helped **Sudās** through your prayer, O Vasiṣṭhas" (VII, 33, 3). To him, the granter of victory in combat, who directs the fates of battles from his war-chariot drawn by two bay horses, **Vajra** <note>The thunderbolt, Indra's primary weapon.</note> in hand, the warriors turn their prayers again and again. It is he "who is to be invoked by the heroes and by the fearful, who is called upon by the fleeing and by the victors" (I, 101, 6). "Men on both sides call upon him at the clash: in the struggle for life and death, they made him their protector" (IV, 24, 3). "With a few," they say to him, "you kill the more numerous enemy who is arrogant in his strength—with the friends who are by your side" (IV, 32, 3). We conclude this collection with the first verse of one of the principal battle hymns (X, 103), which, according to one of the younger **ritual texts**¹) <note>The *Gṛhya-Sūtras*, which describe domestic rituals and customs.</note>, the royal house priest is to recite while looking at the king heading into battle: "The swift one, whetting his horns like a fearsome bull, the striker, the shaker of the lands, the roarer with ever-open eye, the sole hero: a hundred armies at once has Indra conquered." —

Indra is the conqueror of the goddess <term>Ushas</term> <note>The Vedic personification of the Dawn</note>.
> “You, Indra the Great, have crushed the daughter of Heaven, <term>Ushas</term>, who performed great deeds. ### Indra’s Character.

The farce of the good-for-nothing monkey and the scandalous stories that happened to Lord and Lady Indra because of him may conclude our overview of the primary Indra legends. We shall now attempt to summarize the image of the Vedic Indra in just a few words. He is the greatest of the great, the strongest of the strong, bull-like; he is violent yet good-natured; when in a good mood, he is inexhaustibly generous; he is a drinker and a brawler, noisy, kicking up dust, and smashing everything to bits. He is a friend to his friends and an enemy to his enemies: the friend, above all, of the great...

Indra is neither the master nor the servant of a vast world plan or eternal law <note>original: "ewigen Rechts"</note>¹); likewise, he is not an educator of humanity toward order, morality, and art. Yet it is his strong arm that has brought humanity its highest goods: fertilizing water, light, and the abundance of food for the herds. People call upon him for power and victory; he stands at the center of the cult as it was practiced at the sacred fires of princely sacrificial patrons. Even in the minor cult of daily life—in actions performed for the prosperity of house and offspring, of herds and fields—one encounters Indra often enough—how could it be otherwise?—but the true home of the worship of Indra is not here. Its element is war, the splendor of victory, and the Soma-rapture <term>Somarausch</term> <note>the ecstatic state induced by the ritual drink</note> of magnificent sacrifices with throngs of praying, singing, and officiating priests, with rich sacrificial rewards of horses and chariots, of herds and gold. —

### Soma, the Drink of the Gods²). 

The drink that inspires Indra to perform his deeds is the pressed juice of the Soma plant.

The concept of an intoxicating drink for the gods seems to date back to the Indo-European <term>indogermanisch</term> <note>a historical term for the shared linguistic and cultural ancestry of many European and Indian peoples</note> era. A drink that demonstrates a mysterious, ecstatically exciting power in humans must be of a divine nature; it must be the special property of the gods. Thus, the Soma of the "Indians" <note>referring to Native Americans in this 19th-century anthropological context</note>, through which they transport themselves into a state of supernatural inspiration, is tobacco, which they call the "sacred herb"³); also

²) Compare the discussion of Soma in the section on the Cult.
³) Tylor, *Primitive Culture* <note>original: "Anfänge der Cultur"</note> II, 419.

Even in the belief system of the Indo-European <term>indogermanisch</term> <note>a historical term for the shared linguistic and cultural ancestry of many European and Indian peoples</note> period, the home of the drink of the gods seems to have been heaven; even then, as shown by the designation of the gods as the "Heavenly ones" (*deivo-*) <note>original: "*deivo-*"; the Proto-Indo-European root for "god" or "shining one"</note>, people were accustomed to recognizing heaven as the actual seat of all divine essence. From its heavenly storage place, a bird—the god's bird or the god himself in bird form—fetches the drink or steals it from the jealously guarding demon: the eagle of Indra, the nectar-bringing eagle of Zeus, or Odin carrying away the mead as an eagle. Perhaps—though we can naturally only offer conjectures here—even before the separation of the peoples <note>referring to the migration of Indo-European tribes into separate cultures like the Greeks, Germans, and Indo-Aryans</note>, the drink of the gods was already associated in a very special measure primarily with one god: the great divine drinker and drunken one, the wildly powerful god of the storm. Finally, it may be assumed with probability that the concept of divine immortality was already linked to the drink of the gods (<term>Amrita</term> <note>Sanskrit for "non-death" or immortality</note>, <term>Ambrosia</term> <note>Greek for the food or drink of the gods</note>) for the Indo-Europeans. Just as human life is sustained by food and drink, and especially by the medicinal draught that conquers death—at least for a time—so too must divine existence rest upon the consumption of a drink whose essence is immortality¹).

The view that the gods drink the heavenly drink and the narrative of the acquisition of this drink can hardly be regarded as a nature myth <note>a 19th-century school of thought that interpreted all myths as poetic descriptions of natural phenomena like clouds or the sun</note> in the sense that any events occurring in the sky provided the decisive impetus for the development of these ideas²). <meta>This page continues the exploration of the divine drink Soma, moving from its earthly origins as an intoxicant to its mythological status as a heavenly substance fetched by a bird and its possible associations with honey and the moon.</meta>

<header>Soma.</header>
<page-num>177</page-num>

The starting point was the concrete, earthly intoxicant; its mysterious properties led people to see in it the drink of the gods. And this heavenly drink—which naturally no other being could bring as well as a bird flying toward heaven, and specifically, of course, the strongest and fastest of birds—was then touched by that motif so frequently active in mythology¹): the tendency to view all the highest goods as being snatched or carried away from a guarding enemy. We have no reason to recognize any specific natural phenomenon in this enemy, just as we cannot identify one in the thieving bird itself.

This is not to deny that this circle of ideas could have gained a firmer footing through natural processes that were believed to be linked to the concrete intoxicating substance. It is likely that among the Indo-Europeans <term>Indogermanen</term> <note>a historical term for the shared linguistic and cultural ancestry of many European and Indian peoples</note>, it was honey-mead to which the dignity of the divine drink was attributed. Thus, the conjecture deserves belief that the widespread ideas regarding the heavenly origin of honey or honey-dew²) <note>original: "Honigthaues"</note> were not without influence on the myth of the divine drink. Furthermore, one cannot reject at least the possibility that even the moon—the dispenser of heavenly dew³), which appears to be drunk up by divine beings as it wanes—was imagined in the most ancient times as the seat or quintessence of that heavenly substance⁴).

# Indra.

If we move from the shaky ground of conjecture regarding the beliefs of the Indo-Europeans <term>Indogermanen</term> <note>a 19th-century term for the common ancestors of Indo-European speaking peoples</note> further to the consideration of the Indo-Iranian period, we find that the ancient honey-mead has been replaced by the pressed juice of the Soma plant. The pressing and offering of this drink, organized and glorified through complicated rites, became one of the most noble—likely *the* most noble—celebrations of the higher cult. Now, alongside the old mythical heavenly home of the divine drink, a second home appears: the Soma plant grows on the mountains. The Avestan <note>referring to the Avesta, the primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</note> liturgist praises clouds and rain that let the body of the Soma grow upon the mountain peaks; a skillful god formed it and set it down upon the great mountain Haraithı (Elburz); from there, birds marked with sacred signs carried it in all directions. Furthermore, the sacrificial drink, now filled with "demonic" <note>here meaning "supernatural" or "divine" power, from the Greek *daimon*</note> power, has—much like the sacrificial fire—become a mighty god: a fact characteristic of the atmosphere of priestly sacrificial artistry in which one already moves during the Indo-Iranian age. The detailed correspondence with which the Veda <note>the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note> and the Avesta celebrate the blessings of this helpful god points back to this period: he grants swift steeds and excellent children; he, the King of Plants, provides medicine and removes death and all the snares of the wicked.

This constitutes, in its basic features, the prehistory of the Vedic Soma; we now turn to the Veda itself.

Here, it becomes very clear how the two circles of ideas—that of the ancient Indo-European heavenly drink and that of the younger Indo-Iranian mountain Soma—intersect. On the one hand...

O." / "antea citato"</note> 20 ff., E. H. Meyer *Indo-European Myths* II, 589, and the literature collected by this researcher in *Germanic Mythology* 81.

-># Soma in Heaven and on the Mountain.<-

In a series of passages, it is the mountain that is very emphatically designated as the home of **Soma**. To treat this mountain—as many modern mythologists seem to take for granted—simply as an equivalent for a cloud is fundamentally mistaken. This view is most decisively excluded by passages that contrast **Soma’s** mountain home with the heavenly home of another being. Of the world-orderer **Varuṇa**, it is said: “In the forests he spread the air, in the horses swift strength, in the cows milk. In hearts **Varuṇa** has created the will, in the waters **Agni**, in heaven the sun, and **Soma** upon the **Rock**” <note>Rigveda V, 85, 2</note>. And in a song to the pair of divine sacrificial patrons **Agni** and **Soma**: “One (namely **Agni**) was brought by **Mātariśvan** from **Heaven**¹); the other was stolen by the **Eagle** from the **Rock**” <note>Rigveda I, 93, 6</note>. But just as surely as the mountain is regarded here as the home of **Soma**—expressly distinguished from heaven in accordance with concrete reality—other passages name heaven. “Swift as thought he stormed along and penetrated the iron fortress; flying to heaven, the fair-winged bird brought the **Soma** to the wielder of the thunderbolt” <note>Refers to the god Indra. Rigveda VIII, 100, 8</note>. “The darting **Eagle**, carrying the herb from afar—the bird, the joyful intoxication—he brought the **Soma**, gripping it firmly, he who is joined with the gods, stealing it from that heaven above” <note>Rigveda IV, 26, 6</note>.

Spirited verses, evidently belonging to a narrative whose prose components are missing, describe the deed of the bird:

The divine personality attributed to <term>Soma</term> lags noticeably behind figures like <term>Indra</term> or <term>Varuṇa</term> <note>One of the oldest Vedic deities, associated with the sky, water, and cosmic law</note> in terms of developing a distinct, human-like character. The tangible presence of the god <term>Soma</term> on the sacrificial grounds—physically manifest as the <term>Soma plant</term> and the <term>Soma drink</term>—placed limits on the poets' ability to fully anthropomorphize him. While the poets praise <term>Soma’s</term> wisdom and radiant majesty, they speak very little of a human-like form or human-like actions. When the text mentions his heroic deeds or miraculous works, it usually attributes <term>Indra’s</term> deeds to him (since he is the drink that inspires <term>Indra’s</term> frenzy), or it lists those vague, general feats shared by almost all the gods: for instance, that he has spread out the earth...

However, <term>Soma</term> himself is invoked almost exclusively in those hymns addressed “to the one undergoing purification” <note>original: *an den sich Läuternden*; these are the *Soma Pavamāna* hymns found in the ninth book of the Rigveda</note>, in the magical songs sung over the drink as it passes through the <term>wool sieve</term> <note>A strainer made of sheep's wool used to filter the crushed plant juice</note>. Like racehorses racing across the track in pursuit of glory, like streams flowing into the depths, like rain floods pouring over the earth, they hasten toward <term>Indra</term>. <term>Soma</term> clothes himself in the “cow-garment”—the milk mixed into him—; he wraps himself in solar radiance and, through his own power, causes the sun itself to shine. The singers chant beautifully adorned songs about him, just as mother cows low to their calves.

These <term>Soma</term> hymns are full of a formless tangle of images and mystical phantasms. How different this is from the poetry that Greece dedicated to the <term>Dionysian</term> <note>Relating to Dionysus, the Greek god of wine, ecstasy, and theater</note> intoxicant and its god! Here, we find the dullness of a solemnly pious magical trance surrounded by ritual secrets; there, the irresistible, beauty-transfigured release of all the depths of a soul inspired by wine and the divine. —

# Soma and the Moon.

...can be proven in the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the ancient sacred scriptures of India</note>: the identification of Soma with the moon¹). We already touched upon the idea above (p. 177) that such a concept regarding the heavenly seat of the drink of the gods may have been ancient. In the vast majority of the Rigvedic hymns, however, traces of this seem either to be entirely missing or to be of only secondary importance²). Among the nearly overwhelming amount of imaginative wordplay heaped upon the concept of the deified drink in the Soma hymns, there is much that can be interpreted as an embodiment of Soma in the moon³), but the fact that this interpretation is merely a possibility in each case diminishes its likelihood. I am more inclined to believe that these are, in fact, connections of a different nature. Very frequently, Soma is placed in relation to concepts of heaven, light, and the sun. He has caused the sun to rise, shines like the sun, purifies himself in the sky, looks down from heaven, and fends off the darkness through his light; the <term>Amrita</term> <note>The drink of immortality; original: *Amṛta*</note> is hidden among the lights of the third heaven⁴). One sees that where an allusion to a specific celestial light exists beyond the general sphere of light and heaven, it is the sun to which Soma is thought to have a mystical connection. This relationship likely rests primarily on the fact that, like <term>Indra</term> <note>The king of the gods and god of storms</note> and <term>Agni</term> <note>The god of fire</note>, this god is also a champion of light against the darkness—

### Varuṇa, Mitra and the Ādityas.

**Mitra-Varuṇa**¹), closely bound to one another, stand at the head of the **Ādityas** <note>a group of celestial deities, sons of the goddess Aditi</note>; one of them, the greatest of all, is **Varuṇa**. The total number of the **Ādityas** is seven²), but nowhere does the **Ṛgveda** <note>the oldest collection of Indian hymns</note> provide a list of the seven names. If it is at all possible to assemble the series of names found in various places into a list of seven to—

---

¹) Regarding the name **Varuṇa**, see below p. 194 note 1. As far as **Mitra** is concerned, according to traditional interpretation, the word would initially mean "friend" in an appellative sense <note>as a common noun</note> and the god would therefore have his name from it. It seems more probable to me that the process was the reverse. The god **Mitra** was—already in Indo-Iranian times—invoked during the conclusion of contracts and alliances of friendship. The ritual used for this is not known; statements in the **Veda** can perhaps be interpreted as meaning that a <term>fetish</term> <note>a physical object believed to have spiritual power</note> representing **Mitra** was smeared with butter and in a ceremonial manner somehow set up or laid down (cf. **Ṛv.** V, 3, 2; VI, 15, 2; VIII, 74, 2 and generally the passages which speak of **Mitra** as *suhita* <note>meaning "well-placed" or "well-disposed"</note>); also, a walking together of the parties concluding the friendship-bond through seven steps (**Ṛv.** X, 8, 4) seems to have taken place. Thus, the god **Mitra** is the embodiment of the contract, the bond of friendship, and so *mitra* (initially clearly as a masculine noun) in the **Veda** as in the **Avesta** <note>the sacred texts of ancient Persia</note> comes to the meaning "bond" and then also in the **Veda** to the meaning "ally" or "friend."

²) "The seven divine **Ādityas**, with whom, Soma, protect us" (**Ṛv.** IX, 114, 3). To bind the **Ādityas**, one drives in seven pegs (Taitt. Saṃh. II, 3, 1, 5): a ritual all the more significant as it is preserved in a text that, dominated by the belief in the twelve-fold number of the **Ādityas** (see below), could no longer understand it. In **Ṛv.** X, 72, 8-9 (cf. Av. VIII, 9, 21), there is mention of an eighth child of **Aditi**, the one "sprung from the dead egg" (*mārtāṇḍa*), whom the mother had rejected, while she "went to the gods with the seven." Whatever the meaning of this myth may be, the number seven is authoritative as the number of the living, active **Ādityas**, all the more so since this number is confirmed from the Iranian side (see below). — If the younger Vedic texts state the number of the **Ādityas** to be twelve, this is based on the well-known mystical-symbolic parallelization of god-groups and the **poetic meters** <note>original: *Metra*</note>: in this, the **Jagatī** <note>a meter consisting of 12-syllable lines</note> meter falls to the **Ādityas**.

-># The Circle of the Ādityas.<-

combine [the lists], the fact remains that the very necessity of resorting to this artificial and uncertain procedure is indicative of the uncertainty surrounding the individuality of the minor **Ādityas**: an impression further reinforced by the superficially allegorical character of some of these names, such as **Amṣa** ("Portion") and **Daksha** ("Skill")¹). Indeed, we hear almost nothing of these individual gods; they possess a collective character which simply repeats, on a smaller scale, the traits belonging to **Varuṇa** and **Mitra**. Consequently, it is not surprising that a later Vedic text²) presents a completely different list of the **Ādityas** that in no way matches the points of reference found in the **Ṛgveda**. The number seven is evidently not based on the fact that there were exactly seven divine personalities considered to be **Ādityas**; rather, that number formed a fixed framework which was filled—or rather, hardly even attempted to be filled—by inserting individual gods.

These exact same conditions recur in the **Avesta**³); therefore, these Vedic facts must essentially date back to the Indo-Iranian period. Two great gods, **Mithra-Ahura**, are closely linked to one another; one of them—**Ahura**—the greatest of all, stands at the head of the circle of the **Amesha-spenta** <note>the "Bounteous Immortals," a group of six or seven divine beings in Zoroastrianism who assist the supreme god Ahura Mazda</note>. The total number of the **Amesha-spenta** is seven; the abstract names of the minor gods among them ("Health", "Immortal-

# Varuṇa, Mitra, and the Ādityas.

One receives the impression that the connection with the natural entities, whose number of seven formed the basis of this conception, had already been severed—at least for a portion of the gods concerned—back in the Indo-Iranian period.

The character of **Varuṇa** and the **Ādityas** in general—just like that of the Avestan ***Amesha Spentas*** <note>the "Bounteous Immortals" of Zoroastrianism</note>—is summarized in the idea of a heavenly kingship that governs all orders of the world and whose physical manifestation carries the attributes of the highest light, specifically sunlight¹). The title King (*rājan*) or Prince (*kshatriya* <note>a member of the ruling or warrior class</note>) is assigned to them far more than to any other gods, though not exclusively; the texts speak predominantly of their sovereignty, their beautiful sovereignty, and their most sublime sovereignty, and the like²). The nature of these gods stands out particularly clearly when one contrasts them with **Indra**. It is as if one sees the gods of a more highly civilized world standing next to a barbarian god. There [Indra is] an all-powerful hero who has something of a divine brawler about him, the most bottomless of drinkers, and not without a touch of humor. Here [the Adityas are] the quietly shining majesty of a holy kingship that preserves the orders of the cosmos and punishes sin. “The One kills the enemies—”

But before we further develop the relationship of Varuṇa and the Ādityas to the idea of a supreme world order, we must dwell a moment longer on their physical attributes. In general, these can be summarized in the words: **Heaven — Light — Sun**. From the wide heaven, Mitra and Varuṇa look out over the world. In the highest heaven, they mount their chariot. # Mitra and the Sun.

...accustomed to speaking of a living sun god in the consciousness of this age. But in the *Atharvaveda* <note>the fourth Veda, a collection of hymns and incantations</note>¹) we read—unfortunately, it must be admitted, amidst a rather wild mixture of ancient mythological fragments and modern speculations—the following phrase used for the all-encompassing supreme God who lives in all beings: “In the evening he becomes Varuṇa, Agni; he becomes Mitra when rising in the morning.” This means that in the evening, the god identifies himself with the nocturnal bearer of light, Agni <note>the Vedic god of fire</note>, and at the same time with Varuṇa, whom we encounter here—as in the passages to be discussed later—as the ruler of the night; in the morning, however—what else could the rising being, who is then called Mitra, be but the sun?

I know of no passage in the *Veda* <note>the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note> where the identification of Mitra with the sun appears with such clarity as it does here. Much more frequent are expressions which, while not identical, are closely related in content, distinguishing the roles of Varuṇa and Mitra based on the contrast between night and day or morning. Thus in the *Atharvaveda*²): “What Varuṇa has pressed together, Mitra shall bend apart in the morning.” And then, throughout the entire *Brahmana* literature <note>ancient Indian commentaries on the Vedas</note>, there are numerous passages that repeat the same idea in various forms: that the day belongs to Mitra and the night to Varuṇa, or that Mitra created the day and Varuṇa the night³). It seems to me that there can be no doubt about the result of all this: in their original meaning, we are dealing here with gods of the Sun (Mitra), Moon (Varuṇa, known in the Iranian tradition as Ahura), and the five planets¹).

I believe further that this statement can be followed, with at least great probability, by a further claim: the <term>Indo-Iranian</term> <note>the ancient people who shared a common language and culture before diverging into the branches that produced the Indian Vedas and the Persian Avesta</note> people adopted this circle of gods from an external source.

As strongly as the agreement between India and Iran is emphasized in this particular mythological field, the comparison with the deities of other Indo-European peoples <note>such as the Greeks, Romans, or Germans</note> fails completely. Here, however, a second sun god appears; here a moon god appears whose natural significance—to all appearances—was already forgotten or nearly forgotten in Indo-Iranian times in favor of ethical attributes. Furthermore, in this circle of the "highest lords of the world," there appear gods of the five planets who had likewise become unintelligible in their original nature. The <term>Vedic</term> <note>ancient Indian</note> and <term>Avestan</term> <note>ancient Iranian</note> peoples hardly concerned themselves with these planets, which, moreover, were even reckoned among the evil powers in the Iranian faith. 

Is it not probable, then, that the Indo-Iranians borrowed these figures from a neighboring people who were superior to them in their knowledge of the starry heavens—that is, in all likelihood, from the **Semites**²)—borrowing them, perhaps, as something that was only half-understood from the very beginning³)? And when one surveys the world of the Vedic gods from this perspective, does one not indeed receive the impression that this tightly-knit circle of light-gods stands out from the other beings of the Vedic Olympus as something peculiar and foreign?

# Foreign Origin of the Ādityas. — The Ṛta.

Is not Varuṇa alongside Indra—the world-ruling sovereign beside the strong, thirsty brawler (we already touched upon this contrast above on page 188)—the representative of an older, higher culture? Is he not the witness of a stimulating contact between the people who then stood at the threshold of India and the culture of more western nations¹)? Earlier, it seems, than the <term>Indo-European</term> <note>the broad group of peoples including the ancestors of the Greeks, Romans, Germans, and Indians</note> peoples, the **Semites** had matured to a serious ethical contemplation of life. Is it a coincidence that it is precisely here—where we believe Semitic influence was felt—that the belief in powerfully acting natural forces takes its most decisive turn toward the ethical?

### The Ṛta.
The presentation of these conjectures, which proceeded from the physical essence of Varuṇa and the <term>Ādityas</term> <note>a group of solar deities, sons of the goddess Aditi, often associated with moral laws</note>, has finally led us over to the role these gods play as *lords of the world order* and as *highest guardians over right and wrong*. In this context, we must seek above all to reach an understanding of the relationship in which Varuṇa and the Ādityas stand to the idea of <term>Ṛta</term> (*"Order"*). Thus, it will be appropriate here to insert some remarks on the significance of this idea within the <term>Vedic</term> <note>referring to the Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of India</note> view of natural and human affairs.

Already in <term>Indo-Iranian</term> <note>the historical period before the ancestors of the Indians and Persians split into separate linguistic and cultural groups</note> times, reflection on the order ruling the world—on the occurrence, preordained by a higher power, of what must or should happen—had led to the creation of this concept of Ṛta (roughly, *"movement"*). For the priestly world-view of that age, this concept already stood in the foreground of—

The world-ordering fathers "have led the sun up into the sky according to Ṛta," which is itself "the bright, visible countenance of Ṛta," while the darkness of a solar eclipse, which shrouds the sun by breaking the natural order, "acts contrary to the commandment" (*apavrata*). # The Ṛta.

Vedic poets praise it as "the *Ṛta* <note>the fundamental principle of cosmic order and truth</note> of the cow guided by *Ṛta*"; *Agni* <note>the Vedic god of fire</note>, the fire that dwells mysteriously in waters and plants and bursts forth from the friction-sticks, is called the "offshoot of *Ṛta*," the one "born in *Ṛta*." In the actions of men, *Ṛta* acts as the moral law which—to use the phrasing foregrounded by the Vedic style—commands truth and walking on the straight path. "*Ṛta* and the True" is a standing phrase; *anṛta*—"that which is not *Ṛta*"—is frequently used as the opposite of "true." Contrasted with the person who harms his fellow man through deception or malicious sorcery is the honest man, "who strives after *Ṛta*." To his twin sister *Yamī*, who wishes to entice him into incest, *Yama* <note>the first mortal and king of the dead</note> says: "What we have not done before, how shall we do that now—speaking *Ṛta* yet seeking *Anṛta*?" "For him who follows *Ṛta*, the path is beautiful to walk and free of thorns."

However, among the realms in which *Ṛta* manifests itself in the Vedic hymns, that of the <term>cult</term> <note>the system of religious worship and ritual sacrifice</note> stands out particularly. It seems to me that one gives the idea too narrow a turn if one understands *Ṛta* in this context only as the technically correct, ritually regulated course of performing the cult. Rather, it is meant that the great orders of the cosmic whole live and act within the sacrificial process. Just as the rivers flow in obedience to *Ṛta* and the dawns return at the appointed time, so too it happens "under the harnessing of *Ṛta*" that *Agni*—"the offshoot of *Ṛta*," "who does his work with *Ṛta*"—is kindled for the sacrifice; "on the path of *Ṛta*" he brings the sacrificial food to the gods. At the same time, the sacrifice is also touched by the moral side of the concept of *Ṛta*, insofar as it stands as the embodiment of the true and the right, in contrast to the hidden intrigues of sorcery allied with evil spirits. "I call the gods, free from sorcery; with the *Ṛta* I do my work, I create my thinking." Even if the weight placed on the relationship between *Ṛta* and sacrifice in the phrasing of the <term>Veda</term> <note>the oldest body of sacred Sanskrit hymns</note> may seem disproportionately significant, we must keep in mind that here, priests are consistently speaking of their own priestly work. For them, this work stands at the center of all thought and action. In fact, we must maintain that the essential core of the idea of *Ṛta* is the concept of a physical and moral world order. Its sacrificial meaning <note>original: "sacrificale"</note> rests on the fact that the sphere of the <term>cult</term> <note>the system of religious worship and ritual</note> appeared—and necessarily had to appear—to the Vedic poets as being particularly and powerfully permeated by the currents of that world order.

*Ṛta* itself has not been personified. Those phenomena, reaching far and wide through the entirety of the world, which led to the concept of *Ṛta*, were held together by a bond of deep, inner similarity. However, they nowhere forced the imagination to see a single personality acting within them all at once. Consequently—and we shall return to this shortly—while they could associate with already established divine figures, they were more likely to generate the idea of an impersonal power. It is true that a certain touch of concreteness clings to *Ṛta*¹). One finds attempts at a localization, however vague: the dawns come, awakening, from the "seat of *Ṛta*"; or the sacrificial site is envisioned as the "seat of *Ṛta*." # The Ṛta. 199

Now, however, just as the power of *Moira* had to be reconciled with that of *Zeus*, so too in Vedic belief—or more correctly, in the belief of the Indo-Iranian people²)—the concept of the world-ordering *Ṛta* had to be balanced with the sovereign power of the gods, "over whose will no one lives, even if they had a hundred souls"³). Above all, it was *Varuna* and the *Adityas* <note>a group of solar deities who uphold the laws of the universe</note> whose royal character meant that an activity similar to that of *Ṛta* was attributed to them. In their sovereign majesty, they, above all other gods⁴), had to appear as the founders and directors of the lawful order in both nature and human life. The *Dawns* shine forth according to the *Ṛta*, it is said once; another time the *poet* has them—appearing the same today and tomorrow—follow the great *ordinance* (*dhāman* <note>original: "dhāman," referring to a divine decree or established order</note>) of *Varuna*. The *moon* wanders shining through the night."

### Varuna, Mitra, and the Adityas.

It is the nature of humanity to violate Varuna’s command day after day, just as subjects might violate the command of their king. Yama <note>the first mortal and later the king of the dead</note>, appealing to the *Ṛta* <term>Ṛta: the fundamental cosmic and moral order of the universe</term> while rejecting the advances of his sister Yami, also speaks of the “great ordinance of Mitra and Varuna.” Thus, the content of the *Ṛta* concept aligns with the ordinances (*dhāman* <note>original: "dhāman," referring to a divine decree or established order</note>) and the commands (*vrata* <note>original: "vrata," meaning sacred law or vow</note>) of Mitra and Varuna. Consequently, it was inevitable that alongside statements viewing the *Ṛta* as a world-encompassing power—independent of any deity who might have founded or ruled it <note>¹) Read, for example, Rigveda IV, 23, 8–10.</note>—others are found in which it is conceived as the creation of Varuna. On the other hand, there are passages that make Varuna, so to speak, a supreme servant of the *Ṛta*. This plurality of views—very similar to the fluctuations in the Greek poet Homer’s ideas regarding the relationship between Zeus and *Moira* <note>original: "Moira," the personification of Fate</note>—is the natural result of different, independently developed lines of thought intersecting within the contradictory sphere of Vedic belief, which remained largely untouched by rigid dogmatic definitions.

“The rivers,” it is said, “the son of Aditi <note>referring here to Varuna</note>, the Orderer, has allowed to flow; they go their way according to the *Ṛta* of Varuna.” Heaven and earth “promote the *Ṛta* of Mitra.” Here, the poets speak of the *Ṛta* of Varuna or Mitra in the same sense as they do of their ordinances or commands; the *Ṛta* appears as something originating from or belonging to these gods, just as they themselves are once called the “two lords of the *Ṛta*, of light.” However, they are portrayed more as executors, administrators, or the highest adherents of the *Ṛta* rather than its masters when they are called “guardians of the *Ṛta*,” “charioteers of the *Ṛta*,” or “leaders of the *Ṛta*,” and when it is said that they “have grown up in the dwelling of the *Ṛta*.” One sees that the nuances...

# The *Ṛta* and the Gods.

...una, in which the concept of the relationship of Varuna and the gods associated with him to the *Ṛta* <term>Ṛta: the fundamental cosmic and moral order that governs the universe</term> appears, are varied; it is consistent throughout, however, that these specific gods are placed in an especially close relationship with that power of the world order.

Alongside them—evidently receding in comparison to them—there is primarily one other god who plays a similar role: Agni <note>the Vedic god of fire and the mediator between gods and men</note>¹). This is understandable, for in him the most powerful orders of natural and, above all, cultic <note>relating to the performance of religious rituals and sacrifices</note> events are manifested. As the closest divine companion of human life, he—the “Overseer of the Statutes”²)—sees through all sinful deeds, distinguishes between good and evil, and recognizes what is done intentionally or out of recklessness. As an enemy of darkness, as a banisher and burner of evil demons, he also burns human wrongdoers who violate the commands of Varuna and Mitra³); he is a champion of right and order.

However, just as this side of Agni’s nature can only be placed in the proper light within the context of the entire ethical concepts of the Veda, so too must our presentation of Varuna and the Adityas <term>Adityas: a group of solar deities, sons of the goddess Aditi, who uphold the laws of the universe</term> yield a substantial—perhaps even the most essential—part of its content to that discussion which is to occupy us later. **Varuna as Water-God.** Regarding a side of Varuna’s nature that was secondary during the Vedic age—the correct understanding of which has long been established—a few words here will suffice: his relationship to the waters. Varuna, or more frequently the pair Mitra-Varuna, causes it to rain; they are among the gods most frequently invoked for rain. This is a very natural function for these great heavenly rulers from whose high realm the rain falls—perhaps also, ultimately, a consequence of the widespread ancient notion that the moon sends the rain¹) <note>In many ancient cultures, the moon was believed to be the source of dew and moisture, contrasting with the drying heat of the sun</note>. While this connection was naturally no longer understood by the Vedic poets, their phrasing occasionally seems to express the original idea directly. For instance, it is said of the heavenly waters: “In whose midst King Varuna moves, looking down upon truth and falsehood <note>original: *Wahrheit und Unrecht*</note> among men, may the honey-dripping, shining, purifying, divine waters bless me here” (Ṛv. VII, 49, 3) <term>Ṛv.: Rigveda, the oldest and most sacred collection of Hindu hymns</term>. ### Varuṇa, Mitra, and the Ādityas.

Aditi is a personified concept. Her name clearly expresses her essence. It means "unboundness"; we might translate it more simply as "freedom." Human beings are threatened by the shackles of guilt and suffering; it is the *Ādityas* <term>Ādityas: A group of solar deities, the sons of Aditi, who uphold cosmic law</term> above all who control these shackles and to whom one prays for liberation from them. Thus, a goddess could be imagined as the mother of the *Ādityas* who embodies an existence released from all fetters and bestows this upon mankind—one to whom the bound person prays and says: "Who shall give us back to the great Aditi, that I may see father and mother?" (I, 24, 1). In this way, Aditi is invoked along with other liberating, debt-canceling deities:

# Aditi.

"Mitra and Aditi, may the god Savitar <term>Savitar: A solar deity in the Rigveda who represents the divine impulse and the rising sun</term> proclaim us as guiltless to Varuṇa <term>Varuṇa: A deity who acts as the guardian of cosmic law, often depicted holding a 'noose' to bind sinners</term>"; in one passage we read: "in guiltlessness, in Aditi-hood" <note>original: "Aditischaft"</note>¹) or better "in guiltlessness, in freedom from bonds"—where the allusion to the name of the goddess in the expression for freedom cannot be overlooked. Furthermore, we find Aditi as the redeemer from distress (*amhas* <note>Sanskrit for "narrowness" or "constriction," often used for spiritual or physical suffering</note>), as mistress of wide pastures, of wide hurdles, as the all-encompassing one, as presiding over the lot of wholeness (*sarvatāti* <note>Sanskrit for "perfection" or "unimpaired health"</note>): everywhere, the contrast to bondage in guilt and suffering, which constitutes the true essence of the goddess, clearly stands out.

I cannot consider it correct to dissipate this concept of "unboundness"—which is so closely linked with the most tangible wishes and worries of one’s own life—into that of "infinity," and to allow the figure of Aditi to be rooted in the imagination's striving toward the infinite expanses of space beyond the sun and the dawn. Nor, in my opinion, should one interpret Aditi as "imperishability" by applying the idea of "freedom from bonds" to time, or—by introducing a natural element—as daylight in its imperishability. By doing so, one pushes to the center what has a justified place only at the periphery. What is correct, even self-evident, is primarily this: that once "Freedom" was personified and linked by kinship to Varuṇa and his group of gods, concrete attributes were assigned to her—presumably from the very beginning—that corresponded to the luminous and sovereign nature of those deities, especially since the concepts of light and freedom were closely intertwined. "Who prays today for the blessing of the gods? Who praises the Ādityas and Aditi for light?" "We proclaim the glory of the god Savitar, of Aditi, the order-strong light that does not harm."

# Varuṇa, Mitra, and the Ādityas.

"I praise you, the guardians of the great order (*ṛta* <term>ṛta: the fundamental principle of cosmic order and truth in Vedic thought</term>), Aditi, Mitra, and Varuṇa, the high-born." The dawn is invoked as "the face of Aditi." — Furthermore, Aditi—as the mother of the highest lords of the world and not least as the bearer of an abstract name so inviting to speculation and secrecy—was bound to have a strong tendency to be linked with the mysteries of the world's most distant origins. In the cosmogonic <term>cosmogonic: relating to the origin of the universe</term> speculations that are characteristic of the younger part of the Rigveda, she appears as the one who gives birth to the father of the gods, Daksha ("Skill" or "Dexterity"), and at the same time is born from him; there is talk of "existence and non-existence in the highest heaven, at Daksha's birth, in the womb of Aditi." We are content to touch briefly upon these features of Aditi’s image; a sober consideration will not be misled by them in judging the point where the root and center of the entire concept lies.

One particular detail should be pointed out here: the designation of the cow as Aditi, and Aditi as a cow, which is repeatedly found in the Rigveda as well as in later texts¹). "Do not kill the innocent cow, the Aditi," says a verse used in rituals where a cow intended for sacrifice is set free²). And in another passage: "The milk-cow Aditi swells for the righteous, for the man who offers sacrifices, O Mitra and Varuṇa." In later rituals, the address "Aditi" is common for a cow appearing in the context of sacred rites. ### The Two Aśvins.

Regarding the nature of the two Aśvins,²) it seems certain at first glance that these twin gods are connected with the light phenomena of the breaking day. The celebration of the Soma pressing <term>Soma: a sacred, ritual drink central to Vedic sacrifice, believed to grant immortality and divine inspiration</term> is introduced in the early morning by the recitation of the "Morning Litany" (*prātaranuvāka*).
