# The Aśvins as Morning Deities.

The golden, bright, thought-swift chariot of the Aśvins <note>The twin "Horsemen" of Vedic mythology, known for their healing powers and for heralding the dawn</note>, drawn by flying steeds or even by birds, moves in its circuit (<term>vartis <note>Sanskrit: a turning, orbit, or regular path</note></term>) around the sky; the frequent emphasis on this circuit seems to show that it was regarded as a firmly established one. “Let us today call your chariot, O Aśvins, whose wheel-rims are undamaged, which travels around the heaven.” “Your chariot goes around heaven and earth in a single day”¹). Thus, the word “earth-encompassing” (<term>parijman <note>Sanskrit: wandering or moving around</note></term>) is used with particular preference for them and their chariot. It is also said of them that they “encompass the sun in the distance”²).

When one compares the language of the Aśvin hymns with that directed toward the other morning deities, a certain difference is clearly felt. Something is missing here of the vivid descriptiveness with which the text speaks of Agni <note>The god of fire, who shines through the darkness</note> shining through the night, or of the bright Dawn <note>Uṣas, the goddess of the morning</note> who awakens the human races to their work. And if one looks among the easily observable natural phenomena presented by the break of day, one finds nothing that corresponds to the image of these dual beings driving across the sky, shining before the sun.

***

The [bright] appearance of the Aśvins is also connected to the conception of them as being rich in honey, as dispensing honey, of the honey-skin <note>A leather bag or bottle used for liquids</note> that lies on their chariot, and of the whip (<term>kaśā <note>Sanskrit: whip</note></term>) with which they sprinkle honey (materials found in Bergaigne II, 433 ff. <note>Refers to Abel Bergaigne, a French scholar who wrote "La Religion Védique"</note>). It is clearly a matter of neither the gift of moisture from the clouds nor of the Soma <note>A sacred ritual drink</note>; in those cases, the constant prominence of the idea of honey specifically with the Aśvins would remain unexplained. It seems to me that we should think of the **morning dew**.

## The Two Aśvins.

There must, therefore, have been a crystallization of the original concept—a shifting of its individual elements—causing the poets to repeat things they no longer understood, which had become incomprehensible due to that very shift. Our task is to identify the natural phenomenon that fits at least a part—the characteristic part—of the data provided by the hymns, and which must be structured in such a way that the alteration (which displaced the data that no longer fits directly) can also be understood.

It seems beyond doubt to me that this natural phenomenon can only be the Morning Star <note>The planet Venus when it appears in the east before sunrise</note>¹). Alongside the fire kindled in the early morning, the Dawn, and the Sun, it is the only power of light to which the imagination—which adorns the break of day with divine figures—and the cultic worship moving around the break of day could assign the place where we find the Aśvins. The timing of its appearance, its bright essence, and its flying movement in a fixed path around the sky, returning day after day like the Sun and the Dawn, all fit the Morning Star. Only the duality of the Aśvins does not fit. But does it not confirm the accuracy of our interpretation that we only need to assume a single, easily understood shift to reveal the strikingly appropriate meaning of even this trait? The concept of the Morning Star cannot be separated from that of the Evening Star: that is the second Aśvin. Thus, the only remaining discrepancy between nature and myth is that while the Morning Star and Evening Star are eternally separated, the two Aśvins are joined together as two morning beings. > "Sacrifice in the morning and set the *Aṣvins* <note>The twin Vedic deities associated with the dawn</note> in motion. One does not worship the gods in the evening; it is not pleasing to them."

Could not this preference for the morning over the evening in the ritual cult lead to the concept of the morning-and-evening pair of gods—otherwise unchanged—shifting entirely to the morning? Consider the significance that the Dawn <note>The goddess Uṣas</note> holds in Vedic sacrificial poetry, while the evening twilight effectively does not exist for it. Furthermore, compare the exactly similar shift that transformed the pair of the Sun and Moon gods, *Mitra* and *Varuṇa*, into two gods enthroned together whose shared eye is the Sun, so that only traces still point to the contrast between the star that rules the day and the star that rules the night. Indeed, traces seem to have been preserved, partly of the originally separate existence of the two *Aṣvins*, and partly of their connection to the evening. The Veda <term>Veda: the oldest body of sacred Hindu scriptures, composed in archaic Sanskrit</term> celebrates the Aśvins as saviors from all distress. This character trait of the divine pair dates back to the Indo-European period, as shown by the comparison with the Dioscuri <term>Dioscuri: "the sons of Zeus," the twins Castor and Pollux in Greek mythology, often associated with the constellation Gemini</term>. The star that heralds the approach of saving daylight after the danger-filled darkness of the night was greeted as the manifestation of a help-bringing deity. In particular, the Aśvins—just like the Dioscuri—were saviors from the perils of the sea²). The Veda frequently attributes a ship or ships to them as vehicles; they are called upon to bring treasures “from the sea or from heaven” (I, 47, 6); it is said to them: “Far around the sky goes your chariot when it approaches from the sea” (IV, 43, 5). Thus they rescue Bhujyu from the sea, who, as it is said in one passage, was abandoned by evil companions, or as it is stated elsewhere, his father Tugra “had left him as a dying man leaves his possessions.” “Then you showed your strength in the sea, where there is no support, no standing ground, no handhold, when you led Bhujyu home, you Aśvins, who had boarded your hundred-oared ship” (I, 116, 5)³).

### The Aśvins as Saving Deities.

The songs addressed to the Aśvins <term>Aśvins: twin Vedic gods of the dawn, characterized by their youth, beauty, and role as miraculous healers</term> are full of praise for such deeds. As is the manner of the hymns, what was surely known to everyone in vivid detail is always only alluded to in a few words. Beside Indra <term>Indra: the king of the gods in Vedic mythology, a warrior deity associated with thunder and strength</term>, the Aśvins are the true heroes of the stories concerning divine acts of grace: to Indra belong primarily those involving the subduing of enemies, while to the Aśvins belong those concerning bloodless rescue from hardships of all kinds.

One will not succeed, nor should one attempt, to interpret such tales as mythical reports of natural phenomena in which the morning star plays a role. The sailor beset by the sea, the aging maiden, the wife of the eunuch—these are humans and nothing but humans, in whose wondrous fates the inventive joy of the storyteller allowed the grace of the deities (who are helpers in need and misery above all others) to be demonstrated.

<header>Rudra.</header>

# Rudra.

Rudra is often regarded as a storm god. In any case, he cannot have held this meaning for the consciousness of the Vedic poets. The hymns to the Maruts <term>Maruts: a group of storm deities in Vedic mythology, described as a restless army of young warriors</term> show how the rushing of the winds is described in the Veda <term>Veda: the oldest body of sacred Sanskrit literature, consisting of four collections of hymns and ritual texts</term>: the lightning flashes and the downpours pour through the atmosphere over the plains of the earth, the mountains tremble and the forests bow in fear when the army of the mighty gods roars over them. None of this is found in the songs to Rudra. Their very consistent content is quite different: the fear of the arrows of the terrible archer, the plea that he spare man and cattle from plague and death, and that he might grant his wonderful healing remedies.

“Praise the glorious, the young one on his throne, whose attack is powerful like that of a fearsome beast. Have mercy on the singer, Rudra, who praises you. Let your hosts strike down others than us. May Rudra’s weapon fly past us, may the great wrath of the impetuous one pass by. Unstring your strong bows for our friends, the generous ones; graciously have mercy on children and grandchildren” (II, 33, 11. 14). “The red boar of heaven <note>original: "rothen Eber"; a common epithet for Rudra, suggesting his wild and powerful nature</note>, the impetuous one, whose hair is wound like a shell <note>original: "zur Muschel gewunden"; a reference to the *kaparda*, a braided hairstyle or top-knot characteristic of Rudra</note>, we call upon him with devotion. May he, who carries the best medicines in his hand, grant us protection, shelter, and rescue... Do not strike us, Rudra, neither great nor small, neither the growing nor the grown, neither father nor mother nor our own dear bodies” (I, 114, 5. 7).

The small number of hymns addressed to Rudra in the Ṛgveda <term>Ṛgveda: the oldest of the four Vedas, containing over a thousand hymns dedicated to various deities</term> is evidently due to the fact that, because of his uncanny nature, he was not ranked alongside the other...

<summary>This page argues that Rudra was not primarily seen as a storm god by Vedic poets, but rather as a terrifying archer who brought disease and death, while also possessing unique healing powers.</summary>

Just as little should one be deceived by the language of the <term>Ṛgvedic verses: the individual stanzas or hymns of the Rigveda</term>—which, after all, move in the channels of formal priestly expression—regarding the character of wild terror that was obviously inherent from the beginning to the concepts relating to <term>Rudra: a powerful deity associated with the wild, storms, and hunting, later identified with Shiva</term>. The image to be gained here from the younger Vedic texts, to which we now turn, certainly shows essentially ancient features; it is solely due to the peculiarities of tradition if these features are less clearly marked in the oldest collection of hymns.

A <term>Brāhmaṇa text: a category of Vedic prose that explains the significance of rituals and myths</term>²) relates how the creator of the world, <term>Prajāpati: the 'Lord of Creatures,' a primordial creator deity</term>, had committed incest as an antelope buck with his daughter as an antelope doe <note>This myth explains the origin of the constellation of the Deer (Mriga) and the hunter (Rudra/Sirius), symbolizing the punishment of a cosmic moral violation</note>, and the gods searched in vain for someone who would be capable of punishing him for this guilt.

> “Then they gathered all the most terrible substances that dwelt within them into a pile: from that, this god was born.”

His appearance is terrifying. Even the <term>Ṛgveda: the oldest of the four Vedas, containing hymns to the gods</term> describes him as red; the red color is connected—likely as the color of blood—with death and everything terrible³): red are the clothes of those condemned to death; the funeral wreath consists of red flowers; red implements are used in lethal magic. In the younger Vedic literature, it is said:

> “Blue-black is his belly, red his back. With the blue-black he covers the enemy and rival; with the red he strikes the one who hates him⁴).”

If, given this multifaceted nature and omnipresence of Rudra, we were to raise the question of where the starting point and core of this entire conception lies, I would consider the traditional interpretation of this god as a **storm god** to be rather unlikely. It is true that he is called the father of the <term>Maruts: Vedic storm deities known for their collective power and noise</term> and that they, as a result, are named “Rudras,” but this does not prove that he is a personification of the same natural phenomenon as the Maruts. “No one knows their birth,” is said of the Maruts in the <term>Ṛgveda: the oldest of the four Vedas, the sacred scriptures of ancient India</term> (VII, 56, 2): thus, when they are called children of Rudra, this may flow from the idea that the winds come storming toward the dwellings of men from the same mysterious distance—from the wilderness of forest and mountain—just as suddenly as Rudra with his disease-bringing arrows. -> ### Rudra as Mountain and Forest God. 223 ### <-

...significance by the fact that they stand amidst countless others, which connect the god just as much with the most varied other natural phenomena.

More firmly and deeply than the relationship to wind and weather, the connection to mountains and forests—as well as his harmful, disease-bringing power—seems to be established in Rudra's nature. Although the god is thought to dwell in all places, mountains, forests, and trees stand out in the texts as his foremost residences; there, the one armed with a bow dwells as a wild hunter. Elements of different origins may have converged in this circle of ideas, which it would be daring to try to disentangle from one another. One might think of the possibility¹) that the concept of harming spirits <note>original: "schadender Seelen"; referring to the belief that the souls of the dead could return to cause illness or misfortune</note> has increased here to dimensions that equal the greatness of the heavenly gods. Above all, however, one may believe that from the image of Rudra, the traits of a mountain and forest god emerge—traits which, as is self-evident, are easily reconciled with this concept of spirits. He stands there sometimes as a unified person in divine greatness, and sometimes divides himself into a limitless multitude of "Rudras"²). We have here, I believe, a relative of those European types whose nature **Mannhardt** <note>Wilhelm Mannhardt (1831–1880) was a seminal German folklorist whose work compared rural folk traditions with ancient mythology</note> has so masterfully developed: the **Fauns** and **Silvans** <note>Deities of the woods and fields in Roman mythology</note>, the forest-men, wild folk, <term>Fanggen: Alpine forest spirits or hags often depicted as wild or moss-covered</term>, and the like. From the wasteland, from mountain and forest, the spirits of sickness or the arrows of disease come to human dwellings³): these are the armies or the projectiles of the "mountain-wandering" [Rudra].

**The Maruts.**

**Rudra.** And just as his European counterparts—for example, **Mars Silvanus** <note>original: "Mars Silvanus"; a Roman deity associated with both the protection of the state and the wild forests and fields</note>—are invoked for the prosperity of the herds,¹) so too is <term>Rudra</term>, the Lord of Cattle. It is quite understandable that such a god—who originates entirely from "lower" mythology <note>Refers to local, folk, or nature-based spirits rather than the high "celestial" gods of the heavens</note> and is foreign to the circle of sublime, heavenly powers, a god surrounded by eerie dread and bearing the character of raw savagery—could more easily than all other ancient deities prove susceptible to blending with the wilder creations of a degenerating Hinduism. Thus, in the course of historical development, he provided a primary element for the genesis of the most terrifying of all Indian gods, <term>Shiva</term> <note>original: "Śiva"</note>.

### Other Deities.

After our detailed discussion of the main figures of the Vedic pantheon, the description of most of the remaining deities may be kept considerably shorter.

->Vāyu. Vāta.<-

...described as youths who arrive in magnificent attire, with sparkling spears, wearing gold ornaments on their chests, riding in their chariots drawn by spotted mares or antelopes. Storms, downpours, and lightning accompany their procession. "The winds they have harnessed as steeds to the wagon pole; the sons of <term>Rudra</term> <note>The Maruts are frequently called the 'sons of Rudra,' linking their stormy nature to the wild god of the mountains</note> have turned their sweat into rain" (V, 58, 7). They cause the rain to rise from the sea and pour down upon the earth; they shake the earth and the mountains; the forests bow in fear before those passing by; they create darkness in the middle of a bright day when they flood the earth with the torrents of <term>Parjanya</term> <note>The Vedic god of rain and thunder</note>.

Alongside these wind-gods who appear in throngs stands the wind as an individual deity, appearing in two forms under the names *Vāyu* and *Vāta*. These names represent the contrast between two developmental phases of the same concept.

Both *Vāyu* and *Vāta* mean "wind"; however, the first word is remarkably rare in the <term>Veda</term> <note>The oldest layer of Sanskrit literature and the foundation of Hindu scripture</note> in this literal, everyday sense, while the second is the common term used in daily speech. Accordingly, *Vāyu* is a wind-god in much the same sense that <term>Indra</term> is a storm-god. His connection to the actual natural phenomenon has faded; in stereotypical phrases, he is invited to arrive with his long line of teams (<term>niyutaḥ</term> <note>original: "niyutaḥ"; refers to the specific teams of horses or steeds harnessed to a deity's chariot</note>) and to enjoy the <term>Soma drink</term> <note>A ritual offering made from a sacred plant, central to Vedic sacrifice</note>, of which the first portion belongs to him, the swiftest of all gods, according to ancient sacrificial order.

*Vāta* is quite different. Ritual etiquette grants him no distinguished place. Instead, the perception of the blowing wind with its roaring freshness clings to him indelibly. "I will praise Vāta's chariot in its greatness. Breaking everything, his thunderous noise advances. He touches the sky, spreading a red glow; he moves along swirling up the dust of the earth . . . He wanders in the realm of the air..."

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Vedic wind deities, moving from the ritualistic Vāyu to the more elemental Vāta, and introducing Parjanya, the personification of the rain-cloud and thunderstorm.</meta>

# Parjanya.

...he travels on his paths; he does not rest for even a single day. The friend of the waters, the first-born, the holy: where was he born? From whence did he spring? The breath of the gods, the life-germ of the world <note>original: "Welt Fruchtkeim"; referring to the wind as the vital spark or embryo of all existence</note>, this god wanders wherever he wills: his roaring is heard, but his form is not seen. To him, to **Vāta**, we wish to bring offerings” (X, 168).

It is characteristic how the connection of the wind with thunder and rain is expressed in two pairs of gods. **Vāyu** is consistently paired with **Indra**: both are gods who are highly celebrated in the sacrificial ritual, yet their original significance as natural phenomena has faded. In the same way, **Vāta** is connected with **Parjanya**. **Parjanya**<gloss>¹</gloss> is the actual, living god of thunder and rain from the Vedic age. We pointed out above (p. 140) how the entire conceptual sphere of the thunderstorm—which appears stagnant in the hymns to Indra, showing that the poets themselves no longer fully grasped it—fills the hymns to **Parjanya** with the freshest natural truth.

> “He strikes the trees, and the evil sorcerers he strikes. All beings are afraid of the mighty weapon-wielder. Even the innocent man flees before the bull-strong one when **Parjanya**, thundering, strikes the evildoers. Like a charioteer whipping his steeds with a lash, he lets his rain-messengers become visible. From afar rises the lion’s roar when **Parjanya** creates the rain-cloud. The winds blow forth, the lightnings fly, the herbs shoot upward, the sun swells with moisture <note>original: "feucht schwillt die Sonne"; likely referring to the sun being obscured or softened by the humid, rain-heavy atmosphere</note>. Nourishing sap is born for all creatures when **Parjanya** blesses the earth with his seed... You have rained rain: now cease. You have made the desert wastes traversable. You have created herbs for food, and for the creatures you have found wisdom” (V, 83).

# Vishnu.

<note>original: 15* ; This is a printer's signature mark used for bookbinding.</note>

Next follow several deities who do not represent—or at least not in a way recognizable to us—specific natural beings or powers, but rather correspond to certain types of action or specific spheres of activity.

**Vishnu** plays a thoroughly minor role in the *Veda* <note>The oldest layer of Sanskrit literature and Hindu scripture</note>. The deed that stands at the center of his myth, and which nearly exhausts its content, is his measuring out of the world with three steps¹.

> “Three times has a god stepped forth, the lord of wide seats, there where the gods enjoy pleasures.” “Three times has this god stepped across this earth... Over this earth **Vishnu** has stepped, helping man to find a dwelling place... wide habitation he has created.” Over the earthly realm he has stepped far with three steps toward a wide-dwelling life. “Two steps of the sun-like one the active mortal beholds; into the third, no one dares, not even the flight of winged birds.” “In his three wide steps dwells all that is.” “He who alone holds the threefold world, heaven and earth, all that is”². The third step leads to the place where **Vishnu** “rules beyond this atmosphere”: “this highest place of **Vishnu** is forever beheld by the generous ones³ like the eye⁴ that spreads across the sky”⁵.

¹ Do the three steps of **Vishnu** belong together with the three steps that, according to Zarathustrian <note>Zoroastrian</note> belief, the *Amesha Spentas* <term>Amesha Spentas: "Holy Immortals," a class of seven divine entities in Zoroastrianism</term> took from the earth to the sphere of the sun? Three steps of the priest in the *Avestan* <term>Avesta: The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</term> ritual imitate these divine steps, just as in the *Vedic* ritual the sacrificer takes three steps to represent the three steps of **Vishnu** from heaven to earth or from earth to heaven. Cf. Darmesteter’s French translation of the *Avesta* I, p. 401; Hillebrandt, *New and Full Moon Sacrifices*, p. 171 ff.

# Vishnu.

It is customary to see in Vishnu a sun god; his three steps are said to signify the rising, the zenith, and the setting of the sun. While it may not be impossible that obscurations and shifts have transformed an original sun god into the Vedic <note>Referring to the era of the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, c. 1500–500 BCE</note> Vishnu, I cannot consider it likely. Indeed, every more definite trace of a solar nature is lacking. The concept of light plays no greater role for Vishnu than it does for roughly every other Vedic god. Furthermore, relationships of any established antiquity to the course of the day—to morning, noon, and evening—can hardly be discovered. The three steps fit this last-mentioned triad quite poorly. As shown by what was cited above, the ideas regarding where these steps took place are not free from fluctuations. At times the god has stepped across the earth three times; at times he has taken the steps there where the gods enjoy their pleasures; at times the three steps seem to be brought into relation with the threefold world (earth, atmosphere, heaven)¹: yet the idea that the third step is a unique, most sublime one, leading into the mysterious world of the highest height, remains prominent, whereas the evening step of the sun rather descends into darkness.

To me, the dominant motif in the conception of Vishnu² appears to be the vastness of space: Vishnu is the god who strides through this vastness, thereby in a sense ordering it and acquiring it for mankind. The word "wide" (*uru*), but above all the preposition that denotes spreading apart, the preposition *vi*, are the

²) I am speaking of this conception in its Vedic form. I do not deny that it may have a broader pre-history; for us, if it existed, it remains obscure. Perhaps it would the ex- <note>The text ends mid-sentence in the original German: "Vielleicht würde sie die Er-"</note>

The emphasis does not fall on the fact that he gave the earth to humans to inhabit, but rather that he *measured out the expanses* of the earth for human dwelling; not on the fact that he dwells on high, but that it is the *highest height* which he ascended only with his third step. I am inclined to believe—and the previously mentioned uncertainty of the specific interpretation in the *Rigveda* <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the ancient sacred hymns of India</note> strengthens me in this view—that the triple nature of the steps did not correspond to a concrete natural concept from the very beginning. The number three likely owes its position here only to the general favor this number enjoys in mythological imagination. It is also merely a reflection of a general tendency of this imagination when the third step appears as the particularly sublime and mysterious one²). In this context, Vishnu’s alliance with Indra <note>The king of the gods and god of storms</note> also becomes easily understandable. Given this prominence of **vi** in expressions relating to Vishnu, one may ask whether the name of the god himself might not be derived from this same preposition, which would then mean "the one striving into the distance." To be sure, the linguistic accent is not favorable to this interpretation.

# Pūshan.

> “Friend Vishnu, take your wide strides! Heaven, give space so that the thunderbolt may exert itself against you. We both wish to slay Vṛtra <note>The serpent-demon who blocks the waters, representing chaos and drought</note> and let the streams flow: as Indra <note>The king of the gods and god of storms</note> drives them, may they go their way freely”¹).

There is likely no doubt about the role assigned to Vishnu here. He appears as the slayer of Vṛtra and the liberator of the streams only in a superficial assimilation to Indra. However, just as the Vedic poets love to link those deeds which establish the order of the world and the happy existence of humanity with the victory over Vṛtra, so Vishnu must accomplish his own characteristic deed alongside the slaying of Vṛtra: he must take the three steps and through them create the wide battlefield for Indra’s victorious struggle.

### Pūshan.

Pūshan is active in the most diverse situations; yet the recurring characteristic of his influence lies in the fact that he knows the ways, shows the ways, and leads the ways; he protects against wandering and getting lost, and knows how to lead back the strayed and find the lost. He has been considered a god of agriculture and cattle breeding, but he protects agriculture and cattle breeding only insofar as he guides the furrow drawn by the plow in the right direction, and as he—with the

---

...the role which the legend of the Brāhmaṇas <note>Ancient prose commentaries on the Vedas</note> (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa I, 2, 5, 1 ff. etc.) assigns to him in the battle of the gods with the Asuras <note>A class of powerful beings often in conflict with the gods</note>. He is a dwarf, and the Asuras declare themselves ready to leave the gods as much of the earth as he covers while lying down. The gods eventually obtain the entire earth. It is an obvious idea that the winner of the most immense expanses must himself be the smallest. — Also the idea of Vishnu dwelling on the mountain, of him as ruler of the mountains (Bergaigne II, 417; Taittirīya Saṃhitā III, 4, 5, 1), is easily explained in this context; his natural place is where the most powerful expanses of space meet the eye.

¹) Rigveda IV, 18, 11; VIII, 100, 12. The second verse clearly gives the words of Indra to Vishnu.

stays: there they have—it seems during their slumber—prepared fertility for the fields, guided the rivers on their course, and created herbs on the heights and water in the depths. Some have wanted to see in the Ṛbhus the genii <note>protective spirits</note> of the three seasons; the twelve days they sleep are said to be the "Twelve Nights" <note>The *Zwölfnächte*, a traditional period of midwinter rest</note> around the winter solstice, during which the course of the year, as it were, rests. Then it would not be far-fetched, in the division of the one cup into four, to think either of the four months into which each season is divided, or—especially obvious to enthusiasts of lunar myths—of the four lunar phases¹). Interpretations of this kind must only be accepted as conjectures of the most uncertain sort; the brief allusions in which the songs speak of the experiences of the Ṛbhus do not provide a sufficient basis for a somewhat reliable judgment.

# Goddesses.

**Goddesses.** Divine women and maidens take only a small part in the governance of the world and destiny in the Vedic faith. To be sure, since ancient times, phenomena associated with the idea of female beauty and, above all, maternal fertility²) led to divine-female personifications such as the Dawn <note>German: *Morgenröthe*; Sanskrit: *Uṣas*</note>, Mother Earth, river goddesses, water nymphs, and so on; however, within the whole of the faith and cult, these goddesses remain in the background. As corresponds to the historical position of the Vedic religious nature, their figures are still completely untouched by the character of holy prudery <note>The author suggests that early Vedic texts describe goddesses with a frankness regarding the body that later eras might have found scandalous</note>. The Dawn, who

# Ushas.

The water nymphs, equally blessed with beauty as with fertility, are rich in manifold love adventures. But the uninhibited naturalness of such depictions has none of that atmosphere of sultry and refined sensuality about it which, for example, surrounded the figure of Astarte <note>A major goddess of the ancient Near East associated with fertility and sexuality</note>: just as the Vedic cult—which was by no means poor in moments of ribald coarseness in word and deed—nonetheless remained a stranger to the Semitic intertwining of the sanctuary and the brothel <note>The author is contrasting the "naturalistic" descriptions of the Vedas with the institutionalized "sacred prostitution" that 19th-century scholars often attributed to ancient Near Eastern religions</note>.

In the ancient poetry of the hymns, Ushas, the Dawn <note>German: *Morgenröthe*</note>, has been celebrated above all other goddesses with a preference that far exceeds her actual importance in the sacrificial ritual¹). Together with the other morning deities—**Agni** <note>The god of fire</note>, who illuminates the darkness, and the **Ashvins** <note>The divine twin horsemen</note>—hymns were addressed to her in the earliest dawn of the day of the **Soma** sacrifice <note>The central ritual of the Vedic religion involving the pressing of a sacred plant juice</note>, before the birds raised their voices. These hymns were not connected with any physical offerings. Permeated by the poetry of the early morning and free from references to the mystical subtleties of sacrificial technique, these poems possess a charm that the actual sacrificial songs lack—those songs which were performed while the Soma was being pressed, while the offerings were being poured into the...

# Heaven and Earth. Sun and Moon.

Heaven and Earth, Sun and Moon, mountains and rivers, **Gandharvas** <note>Nature spirits or celestial musicians</note> and **Apsaras** <note>Celestial water nymphs</note>, trees and herbs. — In the Vedic faith, Heaven and Earth are divine powers of only shadowy significance; it has been rightly remarked that alongside the Earth goddess **Gaia**, we find here not a personified **Zeus**, but rather a primordial **Uranus**. To be sure, expressions inherited from ancient times speak of "Father Heaven" and "Mother Earth"; they provide mankind with rich gifts and "drip with fatness and sweetness." Heaven in particular regularly receives the epithet of the "wondrously powerful" (*asura*) <note>While *asura* later came to mean "demon," in the oldest Vedic hymns it was a title of honor for high gods, meaning powerful or lordly</note>. However, Heaven and Earth never attained a more vivid personification or a distinct prominence in the religious cult¹. Not much is different regarding the Sun and the Moon: we are not speaking here of the likely non-Aryan sun god **Mitra** and moon god **Varuṇa**, whose relationship to the great celestial bodies was no longer—or hardly—understood in the Vedic era. In their case, the obscuring of their original nature-meaning corresponded to their development into divine personalities filled with the deepest ethical content. Instead, we are dealing here with the sun god who was simply called "Sun" (**Sūrya**)² and the moon god who was called "Moon" (**Mās**, **Candramās**). As for **Sūrya** in particular, he is a thoroughly benevolent god who drives away evil spirits with his light; it is not the killing power of the sun's heat that serves as the deciding motif here. Yet, compared to divine beings like **Indra**, **Agni**, or **Varuṇa**, **Sūrya** recedes far into the background. The conceptions of...

²) In the *Avesta* <note>The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</note>, he is called **Hvare**, who relates to **Mithra** much as the Vedic **Sūrya** relates to **Mitra**.

->Sun and Moon.<-

**Sūrya**'s <note>The primary sun god of the Vedas</note> form and nature are full of fluctuations: at times he is the eye of the gods, at others a shimmering horse; sometimes, like a hero traveling abroad, he is pulled in his chariot by seven golden-colored mares; or, like a young man in love, he follows his beloved, the goddess **Dawn** <note>original: *Morgenröthe* (Uṣas)</note>¹). Alongside him, there is also a female personification of the sun, the goddess **Sūryā**; she has been preserved in myths that depict the sun as a divine bride. The union of this sun-maiden—here also understood as the "daughter of **Sūrya**"—with the **Aṣvins** <note>The divine twins, often associated with the transition from darkness to light</note> has already been discussed (p. 212). However, the marriage of **Sūryā** to **Soma**, the Moon, is considered the prototype of the human wedding and is celebrated in a hymn whose recitation was among the most distinguished adornments of the wedding ceremony. In this myth, the **Aṣvins** were the suitors and **Agni** <note>The god of fire</note> was the leader of the bride's procession; the various parts of the chariot on which the bridal journey took place, and the bride’s equipment, were equated in a mystical-fantastical interplay with the great powers of the sacrifice and the universe, with which priestly speculation loved to occupy itself²).

Along with such divine beings as the Sun and the Moon, frequent lists name others which, at first glance, seem even less developed into living figures than the former. "May the treasures, may the mountains, the waters, the bounty-bestowing gods, the herbs and the heaven grant us this; united with the trees, may the earth and both worlds (heaven and earth) protect us." ### Water and Rivers.

"...may the four quarters of the world be for our welfare; may the firm mountains be for our welfare, may the rivers be for our welfare, may the waters be for our welfare"¹). A closer look reveals that instead of these colorless notions of divinely animated "mountains," "waters," "rivers," and "trees," one can clearly recognize—or at least suspect—richly shaped hosts of lesser, mostly local deities filled with multifaceted life. These were the beings felt to surround human existence and influence the daily course of human destiny.

Let us dwell first upon the waters and rivers. The waters are envisioned as **Mothers**, "the heavenly and the flowing ones, those dug from the earth and those arising of themselves, the bright, purifying ones striving toward the sea" (VII, 49, 2). They contain within them all healing remedies; they wash away evil and every guilt. Filled with life, they meet the person who approaches them. They keep watch in the house over his well-being²). When the priests fetch water for the sacrifice, they speak to the waters: "To him who led you out of your prison to freedom, who redeemed you from the great curse, to **Indra** <note>The king of the gods, who famously slew the dragon Vritra to release the trapped waters</note> send your sweet wave, as a joyful drink for the gods, O you waters. Send him your sweet wave, your fruit of the womb, you waters, the fount of sweetness—your wave, whose back shines with butter <note>original: *Butter* (likely *ghṛta* or clarified ghee, a sacred substance in Vedic ritual)</note>, which is glorified at the sacrifices. Hear my call, you abundant waters!" (X, 30, 7. 8). When a water barrel is set up, one pours water into it with the verse: "You abundant waters, you rule over possessions; right wisdom you carry within you, and immortality. You are mistresses of wealth and the blessing of offspring: may such power Sa— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely referring to *Sarasvatī* or a similar blessing of strength</note>

---

¹) **Ṛv.** <note>Rigveda</note> VII, 34, 23: 35, 8.
²) Thus **Hiraṇyakeśin** <note>An ancient teacher of domestic rituals (Gṛhyasūtra)</note> (G. II, 4, 5) prescribes placing a water vessel at the head of a woman in confinement <note>A woman who has recently given birth</note> with the verse: "You waters, watch in the house. As you watch among the gods, so watch over this woman, adorned with the blessing of children."

# Rivers.

"...grant [Sarasvati] to the singer"¹). Naturally, among all waters, the rivers are the most glorified. To the rivers **Vipash** and **Shutudri**, which the tribe of the **Bharatas** wished to cross during a military campaign, **Vishvamitra**, the singer of the tribe, spoke: "Listen, sisters, to the singer. From afar have I come to you with chariot and train. Bow down; be easy to cross; reach not up to the axles, you streams, with your floods" (III, 33, 9). Highest of all rivers in the veneration of the pious, however, stands the **Sarasvati**, upon whose banks important cult sites of the aforementioned Bharata tribe—evidently of great significance for Vedic sacred affairs—must have been located. The goddess **Bharati**, that is, the personified sacrificial offering of the Bharatas²) and the river goddess **Sarasvati** are invoked together³) at a fixed place in the ancient **Apri litany** <note>A series of propitiatory hymns used to introduce animal sacrifices</note>. "Sarasvati," one prays to her, "best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses! We are like those without fame: create fame for us, Mother" (II, 41, 16). She is the promoter of prayers; she once gave the Bharatas the mighty king, the glorious son **Divodasa**, to the prince **Vadhryashva**⁴).

While these river goddesses have maintained the closest connection between the deity and their natural foundation <note>original: *Natursubstrat*</note>, other female water deities, the **Apsaras** <note>Celestial nymphs or water spirits often associated with water and fertility</note>, have evolved into much freer personifications, reaching a more complete detachment from the natural essence from which their existence emerged—

However, the regular connection in which the **Apsaras** <note>Celestial nymphs or water spirits often associated with water and fertility</note> appear with male spirits, the **Gandharvas**, will justify inserting a consideration of the latter at this point, although they seem to have only secondary relations to the world of water.

The evaluation of the ancient Gandharva type—which can be traced back via its Vedic name to the **Indo-Iranian** age²)—is exceedingly difficult. The testimonies of the **Rigveda** <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational scriptures of Hinduism</note> concerning these beings, who appear sometimes individually and sometimes in groups, are so obscure and ambiguous, their form is so greatly faded and, to all appearances, so blurred by the transfer of the name to such diverse mythological beings, that only an indefinite and uncertain result seems attainable.

Like their companions, the beautiful Apsaras, the Gandharvas in the **Veda** have very diverse locations and spheres of activity. But just as it remains clearly recognizable with the Apsaras that their nature as water nymphs forms the starting point for everything, it may be suspected that the Gandharvas too were originally more specifically localized—

They are of hideous appearance and devour the beings that come into their domain. They seem not so much to be the personifications of the respective body of water as specimens of the general type of demonic monsters who have taken up residence in the water. However, the Buddhist stories naturally also know water deities in the other sense: such as the deity of the **Ganges**, to whom one offers sacrifices when crossing the river, **Jataka** <note>A collection of stories about the previous lives of the Buddha</note> vol. ->## The Gandharvas.<-

...more clearly defined demons. And by all appearances, they were demons who go about their business in the high regions of the sky and the realm of the air; we could call them **spirits of air and light** <note>The original German uses "Elben," a term for elves or nature spirits similar to the Germanic 'Alfar'</note>.¹) The **Rigveda** <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, foundational Hindu scriptures</note> speaks of "the heavenly Gandharva, the measurer of the air realm"; it has the Gandharva appear "in the bottomless spaces of the air," standing "upright upon the vault of heaven."²) In the **Atharvaveda** <note>A later Veda containing hymns and charms</note> as well, in a passage that assigns the sea as a home to the **Apsaras** <note>Celestial nymphs or water spirits</note>, it is said to the "heavenly Gandharva," "whose skin shines like the sun": "your place is in heaven." The Gandharva, who haunts the bride during the wedding and is chased away from her vicinity, "has departed, the god, to his highest dwelling."³) In a series of passages, a Gandharva is more or less clearly identified with some specific heavenly being of light or a celestial light phenomenon:⁴) for example, with the sun, the fixed—

Beside the activity of the Gandharvas in the realms of air and light—which we have considered so far and which apparently forms the starting point—they are also imagined as carrying out their nature in various other natural domains. Particularly in the water. **Yama** says to **Yamī**, the first man to his sister, the first woman: "The Gandharva in the waters and the water-woman <note>original: *Wasserfrau*, referring to an Apsaras</note>, that is our highest kinship and siblinghood." And Soma, the drink of the gods, which is poured into the water during its sacrificial preparation, is called "the Gandharva of the waters,"³) which likely means the spirit <note>original: *Dämon*</note> who carries out his divine nature in the water after the manner of Gandharvas. Does this transition of the heavenly Gandharva to the water Gandharva relate to the identity of the heavenly cloud-water and earthly waters? As beautiful, shining divine youths—the representatives, so to speak, of the heavenly *gilded youth* <note>original: *jeunesse dorée*; refers to wealthy, fashionable young people</note>—the Gandharvas are the natural lovers of the charm-adorned divine maidens, the Apsarasas. A Brahmana <note>a collection of ancient Indian ritual commentaries</note> text describes how a Gandharva sits in the midst of the Apsarasas and enjoys himself on a swing: whichever one he points to and says "**you there**," she loves him.²) During the Horse Sacrifice <note>the *Ashvamedha*, a major Vedic ritual</note>, the priest speaks of the Gandharvas: while doing so, he points to the handsome youths who are present in the festive gathering. He then speaks of the Apsarasas and points toward the beautiful young women.³) This leads to a further sphere in which the activities of the Gandharvas move: as lovers of women, they concern themselves with their sexual lives; the female reproductive organs are the mouth of the Gandharva **Viṣvāvasu**.⁴) Here too, similar to their relationship with the Soma <note>the sacred ritual drink</note>, they appear at times as kind and helpful, and at other times as hostile. They and the Apsarasas can grant or withhold fertility; for this reason, people turn to them when they desire offspring.⁵) In later times, the living being that comes from a previous existence and enters the womb at the moment of conception to become an embryo is specifically called "the Gandharva." # The Apsaras. 251

But we return to the female counterpart of the Gandharvas, the Apsaras, who have already been mentioned many times in the preceding pages. Their name, "the water-wanderers," clearly expresses their original nature; they are water nymphs, the Indian sisters of the Nereids <note>in Greek mythology, these were sea nymphs who often accompanied the god Poseidon</note> and the swan-maidens. "The Apsaras of the sea have flowed toward the Soma," says one of the oldest passages that mentions the Apsaras (*Rigveda* IX, 78, 3), in reference to the water poured into and mixed with the drink of the gods <note>Soma was a ritual drink of immense importance in Vedic religion, believed to grant immortality and divine inspiration</note>. "In the sea, I am told, is their seat, from where they go back and forth in an instant" (*Atharvaveda* II, 2, 3). "To the river the Apsaras shall go, to the shore of the waters" (*Atharvaveda* IV, 37, 3): in this way, they are driven away from human proximity. In a lotus pond, the Apsaras Urvaśī swims around with her companions when her abandoned husband Purūravas finds her again: a poet of the *Rigveda* prays to "Urvaśī together with the rivers" (*Rigveda* V, 41, 19). And in later literature, passages are exceedingly frequent that describe the Apsaras enjoying themselves at forest ponds, on riverbanks—especially the banks of the Ganges—and similar places¹. But just like the Gandharvas, the Apsaras also spread from their original home into the most diverse regions of nature. The nymphs of the water ascend to the heights and carry out their existence in the waters of the atmospheric realm and in the heavenly world; the goddesses who accompany the Gandharva Viṣvāvasu are called "the Cloudy, the Lightning-like, the Starry"; "in the highest heaven, the Apsaras smiles at her beloved"². And on the earth, the water nymphs

The Apsaras are adorned with the highest, sense-delighting beauty and are mistresses in all the arts of love. Alongside their divine lovers, the Gandharvas, humans also enjoy their favor. Connected to them in India is that ancient legend which is at home in Greek poetry as well as in today’s folk beliefs, and is equally widespread among civilized and <term>indigenous peoples<note>original: *Naturvölkern*, a common 19th-century term for non-industrialized cultures</note></term>⁴)—the legend of the marriage of a divine woman to a human husband. This is the saga of Thetis <note>the Greek sea nymph and mother of Achilles</note>, of Melusine <note>a female water spirit of European legend</note>, of the tree goddesses, and of the Blessed Maidens who live in marital community with humans⁵). ## The Apsaras. 253

The Indian heroine of the story is the Apsaras **Urvaṣi**, and her husband is King **Purūravas**¹). As is standard in these divine-human marriages, the duration is tied to a condition—dependent on the husband respecting some taboo-like prohibition—and so it is here. Purūravas must never show himself naked to the nymph. This is probably, as parallel stories of other peoples suggest, a modification of a more original version in which it was the goddess who could never be seen naked in her true, superhuman form²). The **Gandharvas**, who do not wish to leave the Apsaras to a mortal man, use a trick to ensure the condition is broken. They stage a noise in the night; Purūravas leaps up naked from his wife's side; lightning flashes; she has seen him and vanishes. Lamenting, he wanders through the land until he sees the Apsaras swimming like swans and playing with one another on a lotus pond—among them, his lost one. He begs her to speak to him, but she turns him away: “What shall I do with these words of yours? I have departed like the first of the dawns. Purūravas, go home! I am as difficult to catch as the wind!” He despairs; he wants to throw himself into an abyss; he wants the wild wolves to tear him apart. She³) comforts him, not without scorn: “Purūravas, you shall not die, nor throw yourself into the abyss; the evil wolves shall not devour you. With women there is...”

# Deities of the Soil and Mountains. 255

...and to increase the number of horses, and to grant long life to humans themselves. "Lord of the Dwelling, dispeller of plagues, you who take on all forms: be a kind friend to us" <note>original Latin/Sanskrit context: Rigveda VII, 54</note> ¹). — Upon the farmland rules the "**Lord of the Field**" (<term>Kshetrasya pati<note>A Vedic deity invoked to bless the soil and ensure a bountiful harvest.</note></term>), to whom one offers sacrifice or shows reverence when the field is plowed ²). The **fertile field** (<term>Urvarā<note>Personified as a goddess of the productive, cultivated land.</note></term>), "crowned by the threshing-floor," the **furrow** (<term>Sītā<note>Originally the personification of the agricultural furrow before becoming the heroine of the Ramayana epic.</note></term>), and their divine protectors stand on the boundary between the realms of earth-spirits and vegetation-spirits. — The mountains, too, are divinely animated—"the masculine, firmly established ones, joyfully reveling in the abundance of food" (<term>Rigveda<note>The oldest collection of Indian hymns.</note></term> III, 54, 20). We hear little of their divinity, but it may be assumed that when the <term>Rigveda<note>RV III, 53, 1</note></term> speaks of **Indra** <note>the king of the gods</note> and **Parvata**, who ride to the sacrifice in a great chariot bringing blessings, "reveling in the abundance of food," **Parvata** here is what his name "Mountain" seems to signify: a mountain god. Similar to **Indra**, and like the mountain gods of later literature, he is conceived anthropomorphically <note>imagined in human form</note> as the companion of the mightiest god, riding along in his chariot. It is likely no coincidence that the same expression is used for **Parvata** as we found just before, in the immediate vicinity of this very passage, applied to the mountains: "reveling in the abundance of food" ³).

### The Forest Woman.

Since <term>Apsarases<note>Celestial nymphs or water-spirits in Hindu mythology, often associated with natural beauty.</note></term> were considered to have their playgrounds there, the mixing of these closely related elf types—air elves and water nymphs with tree elves—as seen here, is not surprising.

Just as there is an individual "Lord of the Forest," the forest as a whole is spiritually animated. In the <term>Rigveda<note>The oldest and most important collection of Vedic hymns in Sanskrit.</note></term>, we encounter the Forest Woman (<term>Aranyānī<note>The Vedic goddess of the forest and wild animals.</note></term>), a relative of the forest maidens, forest wives, <term>Skogsnufvar<note>original: "Skogsnufvar"; Swedish forest spirits, also known as Skogsrå.</note></term>, and <term>Green Ladies<note>original: "Dames vertes"; French forest spirits or "Green Ladies" found in folklore.</note></term>, whom <term>Mannhardt<note>Wilhelm Mannhardt (1831–1880), a pioneering German scholar of folklore and mythology who specialized in "spirit of the corn" and tree worship.</note></term> has so masterfully described. ## Later Evidence Regarding Tree and Forest Deities.

It is easily understood why there is little mention of tree and forest deities in the <term>Rigveda<note>The oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns, focusing primarily on major atmospheric and cosmic gods.</note></term>; for the poetry of the great sacrifice, these lower beings recede into the background before the mighty deeds of <term>Indra<note>The king of the gods and the god of thunder and rain in Vedic mythology.</note></term> and the world-ruling power of <term>Varuna<note>A major Vedic deity associated with the sky, cosmic order (rta), and justice.</note></term>. It is more striking that tree deities do not play a larger role in the <term>Atharvaveda<note>A later collection of Vedic texts containing charms and spells for daily life, where one might expect more "folk" spirits.</note></term> and the ritual of small domestic sacrifices;¹) it seems, in fact, that one may conclude their significance in the folk belief of the era represented by those texts was less substantial than it appears, for instance, in early Buddhist literature. However, the fact that a belief in deities of this kind was not absent even in Vedic antiquity is made clear by the materials we have collected, and would otherwise be self-evident even without them. Thus, it will appear practical and not unjustified if we seek to complete the incomplete picture of ancient Indian belief in tree and forest spirits provided by the <term>Vedas<note>The large body of religious texts originating in ancient India, composed in Vedic Sanskrit.</note></term> with some data from later literature—I choose the Buddhist texts here. This is a procedure intended to be nothing more than a <term>makeshift solution<note>original: "Nothbehelf"</note></term>, but given the overall state of these questions, it should hardly run the risk of adding inappropriate features to the spots in the picture left empty by the Vedas.

In the stories of the Buddhists, tree deities form a particularly popular <term>staffage<note>Background or decorative figures used to flesh out a scene.</note></term>; among all deities of lower rank, they appear to be those with the most human—

I, 13 in Winternitz, *Ancient Indian Wedding Rituals* 101.

As a rule, however, the god is most firmly linked with the tree (or the climbing plant, the bush, etc.²)) that forms its dwelling—as long as it lives; indeed, the deity is essentially understood directly as a <term>tree-soul<note>The concept that a tree possesses its own conscious spirit or "soul," similar to the Greek idea of a dryad.</note></term>. When a swan speaks to the deity of a <term>Palāśa<note>A sacred tree (*Butea monosperma*) often called the "Flame of the Forest" because of its bright orange flowers.</note></term> tree, one verse uses the expression: "The swan spoke to the Palāśa"³). When a newly growing tree endangers the existence of an older tree, one says to the deity of the latter: "That one will break your limbs"⁴). The deity fears that branches will be cut from the tree; to a monk who wants to cut down a tree, she says: "Do not destroy my house, Venerable One, in order to build a house for yourself." Finally, on this occasion, the arm of a child of the deity is cut off⁵). We find here the understandable further development that, as soon as the tree begins to be the deity's house instead of her body, her children now also share this house with her. Thus, it is also imagined that if the tree is destroyed, perhaps by a storm, the deity takes her children by the hand and departs, homeless, seeking a new shelter⁶). If the tree deity wishes to appear to humans, she usually shows herself in the branches, but she can also emerge entirely from the tree and freely walk around— in any form, for example, as an old <term>Brahmin<note>A member of the highest priestly caste in Hindu society.</note></term>.

# Later Evidence Regarding Tree and Forest Deities.

...walk about¹). To humans, tree deities are generally friendly, provided they are not provoked. People pray to them for whatever they desire and offer them vows; one worships them by circumambulating the tree with the right side turned toward it <note>This refers to the ritual of *pradakshina*, a gesture of respect in Indian religions where one walks clockwise around a sacred object.</note>, by clearing the ground around the tree of weeds, scattering clean sand, and offering perfumes, garlands, lights, and sacrificial gifts²). — However, alongside the deities who inhabit and animate individual trees, Buddhist stories also recognize forest beings of a different kind: giants dwelling in the forest, "wild-folk," and the like; they embody not the friendly life of the tree, but rather the horror and dangers of the forest, or they are forest-dwelling versions of the general, widespread types of harmful demons. These monsters stalk people traveling through the woods and devour them. Such a being appears as tall as a tree, misshapen, with black hands and feet; another forest spirit takes the form of a man seeking honey in the trees; he has set out poisoned honey-dishes to kill travelers; another man-eating forest spirit has kidnapped a human woman and lives with her in his cave³). While it is hardly feasible to claim a <term>Vedic<note>Referring to the oldest layer of Indian literature and religion, dating roughly from 1500 to 500 BCE.</note></term> origin for any of these specific details, it can nevertheless be claimed with high probability that, in its overall character, this belief in wild forest-dwellers dates back to Vedic antiquity and even beyond it into the most remote prehistoric times.

## Evil Demons.

The small demons of many kinds, which surround the daily existence of humans, are predominantly, but by no means exclusively, harmful in nature. Friendly spirits hold sway in the fields, filling the grain with abundance and helping with the harvest: among these are “Rich-in-Milk,” “Hundred-hand,” “Thousand-hand,” “Amasser,” and “Piler-up” <note>Original German: "Milchreich," "Hunderthand," "Tausendhand," "Anhäufer," "Aufhäufer." These are personifications of the desired abundance of the harvest.</note>. Divine weaver-women are called upon when a bride puts on her wedding gown; they are meant to clothe her with long life. The girl who cannot find rest due to the longing of love is roused from her bed by the god “Awakener” <note>original: "Aufscheucher"</note>. On the battlefield, battle-demons hold sway, led by Arbudi <note>A demon or spirit mentioned in the Atharvaveda, associated with the horrors of war and the confusing of enemies.</note>, who is invoked to carry terror and death into the ranks of the enemy¹).

It is hardly possible and would be pointless to fully survey demons of this kind; the essence of each is exhausted in the single action that constitutes its specialty and is usually expressed in its name. However, a more detailed consideration is required for the essentially uniform mass of harmful demons, who primarily threaten the life and health of humans, but also otherwise frighten and plague them in the most diverse ways. They are spirits that, on the whole, have no relation to natural phenomena and natural forces²); their essence lies precisely in being the causes of harm and ruin within the sphere of human existence. That many connections show themselves between them and the souls of the deceased has already been pointed out above (p. 60 ff.)—

---

²) Yet demons like the <term>Gandharvas<note>In this context, nature-spirits who bridge the gap between celestial beings and earthly demons, often associated with fertility, music, and occasionally causing madness.</note></term>, whose conception arises from natural phenomena, can unfold an activity similar to those [harmful demons] and thus assimilate to them; cf. above p. 249 ff.

Furthermore, in X, 87, 10, where Agni <note>The god of fire, often invoked to consume demons with his flames.</note> is invoked to destroy the three "peaks" of the Rakshas, to destroy its ribs, and to tear the root of the Yātudhāna into three parts: here too, it is clearly a matter of one and the same being. If in VIII, 60, 20 a prayer is offered for the turning away of the Rakshas, of the Yātu of the Yātu-rich, the two concepts are indeed distinguished, but these words are in turn accompanied by VII, 104, 23, where, just as here, there is talk of the Yātu of the Yātu-rich and the Rakshas of the Yātu-rich. Should the explanation for these occurrences be that Rakshas is the generic concept and Yātu is the specific concept? What the specialty of the Yātus consists of seems to result from the fact that alongside *yātu*, the concepts *yātudhāna* (feminine *yātudhānī*), *yātumant*, and *yātumāvant* frequently appear (see, for example, the passage just cited, VIII, 60, 20). It is unlikely that *yātudhāna* could mean anything other than "container of the Yātu," that is, the sorcerer who is inhabited by the Yātu, makes use of it, and can be seen in a certain way as identical to it: therefore it is not surprising that occasional confusion occurs between *yātu* and *yātudhāna* (Rigveda VII, 104, 16, if *āyātu* is a descriptive compound, like...

it seems). Thus, *yātumant* and *yātumāvant* are evidently sorcerers connected to a *Yātu*. Therefore, we must understand <term>Yātu</term> <note>A term specifically associated with sorcery and the spirits summoned by magicians.</note> specifically as that kind of evil spirit used by sorcerers to cause harm (compare Avestan <note>Avestan: the ancient East Iranian language of the Zoroastrian scriptures.</note> *yātu* = sorcerer). VII, 104, 23); the person who employs a *rákshas* is called *rakshás*, *rakshasvín*, or *rakshoyúj* ("yoking the Rakshas"): just as it is a common accusation that so-and-so is a *yātudhāna*, there is also debate about whether someone is pure or a *rakshás* (Ṛv. VII, 104, 23; cf. I, 35, 10). — In the terminology of evil beings, the concept of the <term>Piśāca</term> <note>Often depicted in later folklore as flesh-eating demons.</note> stands somewhat further apart from the closely related terms <term>Yātu</term> and <term>Rakshas</term>. In the Ṛv. <note>Rigveda: the oldest collection of Vedic hymns.</note>, the word is found only once (in the form *piśāci*, I, 133, 5, alongside *rákshas* and clearly distinguished from it). In later literature, the <term>Piśācas</term> are frequently mentioned and usually distinguished from the <term>Rakshas</term> and <term>Yātu</term>: thus, in the Taitt. Saṃh. II, 4, 1, 1 <note>Taittirīya Saṃhitā: a primary text of the Black Yajurveda school.</note>, the three classes of beings—gods, humans, and manes <note>Ancestral spirits or the "fathers" (Pitrs).</note>—are opposed by the three hostile classes of <term>Asuras</term>, <term>Rakshas</term>, and <term>Piśācas</term>. Compare also Av. <note>Atharvaveda: the Veda of formulas, spells, and incantations.</note> I, 35, 2; V, 29, 11; VI, 32, 2; Hir. G. I, 11, 8; Baudhâyana in Ludwig V, 421. On the other hand, the identification of the <term>Piśācas</term> with the <term>Yātu</term> occurs in Av. V, 29, 9. The predominant specialty of the <term>Piśācas</term> in causing harm is evident from the fact that they are quite often called *kravyād* <note>original: "kravyād", meaning "raw-flesh eater."</note> (see e.g., Av. V, 29, 9; VIII, 2, 12; XII, 3, 43): this word is practically a synonym for <term>Piśāca</term> and may be regarded as the regular designation for these beings in the Rigveda (VII, 104, 2; X, 87, 2. 19; 169, 2). — From all these classes of beings, the <term>Asuras</term> (cf. above p. 162 ff.) are on the whole separate; they are the enemies of the gods in their mythical battles, not the enemies of humans in present life. A characteristic of how they are, in a sense, perceived as <term>Rakshas</term> pushed back into prehistoric divine experiences is Taitt. Saṃh. VI, 2, 1, 5. 6. Occasionally, however, they do appear as enemies of humans belonging to the present, e.g., Av. VIII, 6, 5; Kauṣ. Sūtra 87, 16; 88, 1.

### The Damage Caused by Demons.

The time of evil spirits, like that of the souls of the dead, is primarily evening and night. For Agni the Rakshas-slayer <note>Agni is the Vedic god of fire; here he is invoked in his role as a protector against demons</note>, one who is pursued by <term>Rakshas</term> <note>Malevolent spirits or demons in Hindu mythology</note> prepares a sacrificial cake at night, "for at night the Rakshas wander about"; "the night belongs to the Rakshas, so it is taught." One addresses a blessing to the night: "O Night, rich in colorful treasures, let me pass safely through you"; then "the monsters and Rakshas of the night do not find one." At night, the Rakshas poisoned (?) the blood of the gods. At night, the Rakshas seek to kill the person who has completed the sacrificial initiation (<term>dikshā</term> <note>A ritual of preparation or consecration for a religious ceremony</note>), but Agni the Rakshas-slayer watches over him. In the east, the Rakshas have no power, "for the rising sun drives back the Rakshas in the east" $^1$). But the dark time of the new moon especially belongs to the evil spirits, who in this regard also correspond to the souls of the deceased. A magic song of the <term>Atharvaveda</term> <note>A sacred text of the Vedas containing hymns, spells, and charms</note> is directed against "the devourers (?) who have set out in swarms on the night of the new moon," another against the flesh-eaters, "who go hunting around the new moon" $^2$).

The harm that these spirits, who go about their business in the dark, inflict upon humans is, naturally, not very consistent with the ideas regarding demonic or diabolical influence belonging to more advanced forms of faith. It involves very concrete damage, specifically to life and health; the greedy spirit satisfies hunger and thirst with the flesh and blood of humans. The

# Evil Demons.

The usual way it reaches its goal is by entering into the human. Thus it is said of a disease-demon: "Winged flies the <term>Jāyānya</term> <note>A type of demon in the Atharvaveda, often associated with wasting diseases or tumors</note>; he enters into the human"¹). And one prays to <term>Agni</term> <note>The Vedic god of fire, who acts as a protector of the home and a consumer of demons</note>: "Do not let the <term>Rakshas</term> <note>Malevolent spirits or demons</note> enter into us, nor the <term>Yātu</term> <note>A term for sorcery or a class of demons associated with black magic</note> of the Yātu-senders²)." Specifically, the mouth seems to have been considered the entrance for spirits; while consuming food and drink³) or otherwise, they slip inside: for this reason, during a magical ritual to drive out a <term>Piçāca</term> <note>A class of flesh-eating demons</note>, anyone entering the room is commanded to wipe their tongue with a hemp cord⁴); evidently, there was a fear that the expelled spirit would fly into the newcomer's mouth. But the mouth is not the only gate for spirits; the demons who endanger childbirth slip in through the woman's private parts⁵). Once they are inside the human, they devour his flesh, suck out the marrow, drink his blood, and cause all kinds of illness. One prays to Agni to restore to the sick person what the Piçācas have torn off, shredded, carried away, or eaten from him; "We awaken flesh and the breath of life in the body"⁶). In the spirit, the Rakshas cause madness; they rob speech of its power, so that one loses in a debate ⁷). Naturally, they are particularly dangerous at the most important occasions—

To those familiar with the wedding ritual, the numerous rites aimed at driving away evil spirits are well known; I will limit myself here to highlighting the practice of shooting small sticks into the air, which is accompanied by the following incantation:

> “I pierce the eye of the <term>Rākshasas</term> <note>Malevolent spirits often depicted as shapeshifters or man-eaters</note> who prowl around this bride as she approaches the fire.” ¹)

If, after the wedding, sexual abstinence is imposed on the young couple for a certain period—three nights or even longer ²)—it seems certain to me that the original meaning of this ancient custom, which was clearly no longer understood by the <term>Vedic Indians</term> <note>The people of the Bronze Age Indus Valley and Ganges Plain who composed the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note>, must be sought in the fear of spirits. These spirits might slip into the woman during intercourse and endanger the fruit of the womb, or even impregnate the woman themselves—for spirits are, of course, lustful ³). By pretending to refrain from consummating the marriage, one misleads them. I will pass over the customs associated with pregnancy and delivery here, which likewise stem from the fear that spirits might devour the fetus, transform a male fetus into a female one, or cause other harm ⁴). Our later examination of the burial ritual will show us the evil spirits that lie in wait for the deceased and their survivors.

->Demons and Fluids. — Human Heroes.<-

[...harmful powers] acquired through contact, which to divert from oneself and direct toward the enemy is one of the most distinguished tasks of the art of magic. The presentation of the cult of magic, which will be given further below, must complement our discussion of evil spirits by describing the defensive actions directed against them; it must also concern itself with the struggle of humans against such substances or fluids <term>fluida</term> <note>Oldenberg uses this term to describe semi-physical, semi-magical forces or influences, similar to the concept of "miasma" or contagion</note> and endeavor to clarify the way these latter operate.

### **Humans. Priestly and Martial Heroes.**

Besides gods and demons, humans appear in Vedic narratives of various kinds—which, unfortunately, mostly become known to us only through brief hints—either acting on their own or alongside those higher beings. Sometimes the deeds of fictitious ancestors of either humanity or specific human lineages are recounted; sometimes—often, of course, linked to such ancestors—etiological myths <note>Myths that explain the origin or cause of a custom, name, or natural phenomenon</note> appear; sometimes one is dealing with underlying historical memories, and sometimes clearly with free creations of an imaginative, storytelling fantasy. Everywhere, it is the real human world from which the conceptions of these legendary humans originate. I consider it unlikely that the humanly conceived heroes or patriarchs of the <term>Veda</term> <note>The oldest layer of Sanskrit literature and the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note> are to be understood as faded gods <note>original: "abgeblasste... Götter"</note>¹) who have sunk to the earthly sphere, or as demons, or even directly as the embodiment of natural powers. The fathers of the human race certainly participate in the victorious deeds that established the natural order, or they accomplish them themselves: the winning of the sun, the dawns, and so forth. But

### Humans. Priestly and Martial Heroes.

their role, however, is not to represent a natural force themselves; they are not, for example, genies of light, but entirely and only humans; the idea is precisely that, in alliance with the gods, the magical power of the first humans achieved those great successes. Or when a human hero, King Purūravas, appears as the husband of the beautiful nymph, he is not to be interpreted as a "thunder-hero" who has an adventure with a "cloud-woman," nor as the sun following the dawn. It is by no means a matter of a married couple of equal supernatural rank; rather, it is essential that a human stands opposite the goddess¹). Purūravas is a relative—elevated into the heroic sphere—of those men who, in modern folk belief, enter into marital unions with "Blessed Maidens" <note>German: *Seligen Fräulein*; benevolent female spirits of Alpine folklore</note>, "Fanggen" <note>Female tree spirits or wood-wives from Tyrolean tradition</note>, "Forest Spirits" <note>Swedish: *Skogsnufvar*; alluring female wilderness spirits</note>, and so on²): such beliefs refer to real humans, behind whom nothing of a super-human or extra-human nature is hidden.

In the ancient tales, alongside royal and martial heroes who perform deeds of indomitable strength against human and demonic enemies, there also appear heroes of a priestly nature. The horizon of the <term>Brahmanical</term> <note>Relating to the Brahmins, the priestly varna or class in Vedic society</note> poets was, after all, filled with the interests and claims of their families, and with the power of sacrifice—particularly their own mastery of sacrificial art, which was inherited from their priestly ancestors. Since the texts preserved from the ancient period are almost exclusively hymns to the gods and not epic poems, the intervention of the gods naturally comes to the fore everywhere: human deeds recede behind the deeds that the gods performed for humans or, at most, alongside humans.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of human figures in Vedic mythology, specifically moving from heroic and priestly figures to the conceptual "First Human" who stands at the beginning of the human race. # The First Human.
### 18*

At the head of the human race stands the figure of the first human.

The clusters of ideas surrounding this figure are still entirely in a state of flux; thus, it is not surprising that various examples of this type exist side by side. We have already encountered *Vivasvant* <note>A solar deity and the father of the human race in Vedic tradition</note>, the first sacrificer, in an earlier context (p. 122): it is characteristic that in the conception of the first human, a special emphasis is placed on the role of the first sacrificer. Just as in the *Avesta* <note>The sacred texts of Zoroastrianism, closely related to the Vedas</note> *Vivanhvant* is "the first mortal who prepared the *Haoma* <note>The Avestan equivalent of the Vedic Soma, a ritual plant and drink</note> for the physical world," in the *Veda* it is *Vivasvant* to whom his messenger from heaven brings down the fire—the governing power of the sacrifice. *Agni* <note>The god of fire</note> himself becomes the messenger of *Vivasvant*; the prayers of *Vivasvant* drive the *Soma* <note>The sacred ritual drink of the Vedic people</note> to flow; and the priest, connecting the current ceremony to its primeval prototype, calls the place where the sacrificial work is performed "the site of *Vivasvant*." — Standing in the closest connection¹) with *Vivasvant* are, on one side, *Manu* (meaning "the human"), and on the other, *Vivasvant’s* son *Yama* (meaning "the twin")²), who begets the human race with his twin sister *Yamī*. "Father *Manu*" is essentially a double of *Vivasvant*: he is the living figure of the first human in the Vedic period, while *Vivasvant*, who had stood in the foreground of belief during the earlier Indo-Iranian age, is in the process of fading. Just as with *Vivasvant*, the *sacrificial* <note>original Latin: *sacrificale*</note> aspect of the original human is particularly prominent in *Manu*. Like the "site of *Vivasvant*," it is the "dwelling of *Manu*" in which the Vedic priest performs the sacrifice in which he himself officiates—

²) In the *Avesta*, *Yima* is the son of *Vivanhvant*.

The *Avesta* <note>The sacred texts of ancient Persia</note> speaks of Yima as the king of a golden age, and the *Veda* also calls Yama a king. Here, to be sure, only one side of his kingship remains. The first human was also the first to die, the king of the realm of the dead who grew to divine dimensions: thus, we shall have to return to Yama when discussing the conceptions of life after the death.

# Divine Descent of Humans.

— would have been granted a more significant religious weight, and the concept in question was no more fixed in a stable form than the cosmogonic <note>theories about the origin of the universe</note> or theogonic <note>theories about the origin of the gods</note> ideas of the *Veda* <term>the Veda: the most ancient sacred scriptures of Hinduism</term> in general. Sometimes, Heaven and Earth—the great parental pair of all existence—are interpreted as the father and mother of humans as well; occasionally, *Agni* <term>Agni: the god of fire and messenger to the gods</term> is spoken of as the father of human creatures (p. 125 ff.); in another passage, the twin pair of primeval humans, *Yama* and *Yami*, say to one another: "The *Gandharva* <term>Gandharva: a celestial being or nature spirit often associated with water and music</term> in the waters and the water-woman, that is our highest kinship and siblinghood" (X, 10, 4)¹). Standing completely independent alongside these ideas are others, such as the priestly, ornate, yet possibly ancient conception of the origin of humanity from the body of the great thousand-headed and thousand-footed primeval man (*Purusha*). The gods offered a sacrifice using him as the sacrificial animal. From this sacrifice arose all creatures: horses and cattle, goats and sheep. From the sacrificed *Purusha* arose heaven and earth, sun and moon. From his face came the *Brahmin* <term>the priestly class</term>, from his arms the prince <note>the *Kshatriya* or warrior class</note>, from his thighs the farmer <note>the *Vaishya* or commoner class</note>, and from his feet the *Śūdra* <term>the servant or laboring class</term> (X, 90).

Individual human lineages also have their own independent origins from the gods. Sometimes divine fathers are mentioned, sometimes divine mothers, or both. *Vasiṣṭha* is miraculously fathered by *Mitra* and *Varuṇa*; *Urvaśi* the *Apsaras* <term>Apsaras: a celestial nymph or dancer of the heavens</term> is his mother (VII, 33, 11 ff.). And just as of *Manu*, the father of the entire human race, the poet also says of the patriarchs of priestly families like *Kaṇva* and *Atri*: "These are linked to the gods; from them comes our race" (I, 139, 9).
