# Humans. Priestly and Martial Heroes.

These ancestors of the great Brahmanical clans <note>original: "Gentes", a Latin term for kinship groups</note> are the "seven priests" whom we encountered earlier (p. 276) performing sacrifices alongside Manu <term>Manu: the mythical first man and progenitor of humanity in Vedic tradition</term>. Here, in another instance, we find the archetype of human founders of earthly orders—the initiators, so to speak, of human life. The clan-based system is more sharply defined among the Brahmins <term>Brahmins: the priestly and scholarly class of Vedic society</term> than within the princely class; it encompasses everyone within a specific number of lineages. Thus, it was easier for a conception of a fixed circle of related individuals to develop around priestly ancestors than around princely ones.

These ancient Brahmins and masters of the sacrificial art naturally took center stage in the mythical history imagined by their priestly descendants. This was because their interest was not focused on the founding of secular or political institutions, but on establishing sacrificial protocols and acquiring essential human assets like light and livestock. In this pursuit, the leading role fell to priestly sacrifice and sorcery, rather than to princely military might. The "seven Rishis" <term>Rishis: ancient inspired poets or seers of the Vedic hymns</term> or "our fathers" or "the Angiras" <note>The Angiras are a group of celestial seers who helped establish the first religious rites</note>¹) have "ordered these beings while sitting in the sunless and sunlit atmosphere"; they have "found the hidden light; with a powerful incantation, they produced the dawn"; "like a dark horse adorned with pearls, the fathers decorated the sky with stars; they placed darkness into the night and [light] into the day—"

---

¹) Compare what was noted regarding this name above on p. 127. Just as we have just encountered the seven priests as sacrificial assistants to Manu, the Angiras also form the retinue of Yama <term>Yama: the god of death and the first mortal to die</term> in the afterlife. During the sacrifice for the dead, one venerates "Yama, accompanied by the Angiras," and prays: "Sit down, Yama, upon this sacrificial grass, united with the Angiras, the fathers" (*Rigveda* X, 14, 4).

# The Priestly Heroes.

Above all else, however, they split the rock with their prayer and with blazing fire—the rock that enclosed the cows hidden by the envious Paṇis <term>Paṇis: a group of mythical demons or misers who stole and hid the celestial cattle</term>; in this way, they secured the blessing of nourishment for themselves and for all of humanity²).

Most of what is recounted in ancient tradition regarding individual priestly heroes lies outside the realm of pure mythology. These stories are predominantly demonstrations of priestly skill and power, manifesting in historical events or in idealized occurrences where the image of actual history was elevated and condensed. Naturally, supernatural elements are not lacking. There, stories were told of how the seven Ṛshis <term>Ṛshis: the seven legendary seers of ancient India</term>—appearing here as a collective group—obtained for the wife of King Purukutsa (perhaps a widow in dire need) a hero son, "Trasadasyu, won through sacrifice, the vanquisher of enemies equal to Indra, the demigod." It seems this tale (Rigveda IV, 42) was preceded by a verbal contest <note>original: "Kampfgespräch", a formal poetic or theological debate</note> between Indra and Varuṇa, the two rivaling high gods. The queen, along with her priests, turned to them, and once reconciled and united, the gods granted her that favor (cf. p. 96).

Or, the priestly clan of the Viṣvāmitriden <note>The descendants of the sage Viṣvāmitra</note> told of their ancestor: how he made the rivers crossable through his prayer for the chariots and the baggage train of the Bharatas; how he obtained the help of Indra for King Sudās through Soma sacrifices <term>Soma: a sacred ritual drink used to honor and empower the gods</term>; and then, after victory was won, how he performed the horse sacrifice <term>Horse sacrifice: the Ashvamedha, a grand ritual performed by kings to assert sovereignty</term> for him. Perhaps this narrative already contained hints of the deadly enmity that divided the rival priestly clans of the Viṣvāmitras and the Vasiṣṭhas, and—

# Appendix.

## Good and Evil Gods. The Divine and the Moral World.

The description of the individual Vedic gods requires a supplement: we must raise the question of the relationship of these gods to good and evil. This, however, primarily takes the form of a question regarding whether their character is beneficial or harmful to humanity.

Among a people advancing victoriously and living in a secure order and rich abundance, an optimistic view of the world's course was bound to prevail—a belief that sees blessing-bringing friends in the most noble powers of the universe. This friendly character truly dominates among the gods of the Vedic <term>Pantheon: the collective assembly of all the gods within a particular religion</term>. It is true that many troubles also come from supernatural powers, but on the whole, it is only the host of lesser demons, goblins, spirits of disease, and the like, to whom such harm is attributed. This corresponds to the fact that illnesses and plagues did not appear to the observer to stem from the great, regularly governing natural entities, but rather from the unpredictable malice of isolated agents; thus, the ancient type of small, harm-bringing demons could be preserved largely unchanged here. But the most distinguished, all-encompassing powers of nature, such as the sun, fire, and the thunderstorm, provided the visible foundations for a happy human existence. Thus, among the great gods of the <term>Veda: the oldest sacred scriptures of ancient India</term>, there is only one in whom a harmful nature comes to the fore: <term>Rudra: a powerful and unpredictable storm god, often feared for his arrows of disease but also petitioned for healing</term>. Other hostile beings such as <term>Vṛtra: the "Obstacle," a serpent-like demon who withheld the world's waters</term>, the begrudging restrainer of water currents, large enough to stand as an equal opponent against <term>Indra: the king of the gods and wielder of the thunderbolt</term> and to make the gods flee with his snorting, are presented as overcome and destroyed; thus they contribute to the idea

## Good and Evil Gods.

...to further increase the beneficent power of the gods, who have eradicated such evil.

The benevolent nature of a god like Indra is, of course, conceived entirely within the sense and limits of human benevolence, which demands reciprocity and is not untouched by change and arbitrariness <gloss>1</gloss>). Indra is a friend to the one who offers sacrifice, the <term>Soma-presser: a worshiper who prepares the sacred, intoxicating Soma juice to offer to the gods</term>, but he kills the one who does not sacrifice—the miser—and destroys his hearth and home. He is no more above playing tricks on mortals through deceit and guile—especially when his sensuality provokes him—than the Homeric gods of Greece. Naturally, he is just as subject to these desires as he is to a powerful thirst and, occasionally, the consequences of too much heavy drinking <gloss>2</gloss>). He is also easily angered; the idea that he wavers inconsistently in his friendship is not foreign to the <term>Rigveda: the oldest collection of sacred Sanskrit hymns</term>.

> “Who then may praise him? Who may so provide for and sacrifice to him, that the Gracious One might bless him forever and make him mighty? As one sets one's feet forward, one after the other, he uses his art to make the last into the first. He is called a hero, taming the powerful one after the other, leading them forward one after the other. He hates the one who prospers, this King of both worlds; Indra seizes the districts of men for himself. He casts away the friendship of one; with others, he moves in shifting impulses. Shaking off what does not follow him, Indra presses forward through many autumns” (VI, 47, 15—17).

Incidentally, one should hardly place special weight on the phrase regarding Indra’s “hatred toward the one who prospers” <note>This concept of divine envy toward human success is a common theme in ancient religions, most notably seen in the Greek concept of *phthonos*.</note>. # Grace and Wrath of the Gods.

...said to be that Indra strikes down the arrogant, the godless, and the wealthy miser; here the poet—who is preoccupied with the uncertainty of all human fortune in the face of a divine power that plays with destiny—goes so far as to use that expression regarding the god's hatred toward the fortunate: a statement that, standing isolated as it does in the poetry of the <term>Rigveda: the most ancient collection of sacred Sanskrit hymns</term>, would hardly be considered sufficient to grant the idea of the <note>original: "Neide der Götter"</note> "Envy of the Gods" a place in the reconstruction of the Vedic worldview.

In contrast to the notion of the dangers brought by Indra's wrath, there prevails by far a trust in his inexhaustible grace, to which the pious man—who has been a friend of Indra from of old—feels entitled. To the petitioner, "he diminishes nothing of his desires." "No one can say: he does not give." "As the storm clouds pour down rain, so Indra pours out treasures of horses and cattle": one would find no end if one sought to collect all such similar passages from the Rigveda. The same, however, applies—perhaps on a smaller scale—to almost all the other gods, here and there with individual traits that correspond to the nature of the specific god—such as with <term>Agni: the god of fire and the hearth</term>, with the prominent nuance of the intimacy of a divine housemate—: the fundamental tone everywhere is a secure confidence in the often-tested, rich grace of the gods.

The relationship with <term>Rudra: a fierce deity of the wilderness and storms, often associated with both destruction and healing</term>¹) forms an exception; with his bow, he showers arrows of devastating pestilence upon men and cattle. In his case, the world of harmful powers, otherwise restricted to the region of lower demons, reaches into that of the great gods. The

# Good and Evil Gods.

The <term>ritual worship: original "Cultus"</term> of Rudra—at least regarding the precautions a sacrificer must take against this dangerous god—stands on the same level as the rituals performed for evil demons and the spirits of the dead. <note>original footnote 1: See the description of the ritual practice below.</note> However, the tone of the hymns addressed to him does not differ quite as much as one might expect from the invocations to benevolent deities. It is, after all, natural that the fear of an uncanny god is expressed less clearly in what one says to him than in what one *does* in his presence. Furthermore, Rudra—the healer of the very same diseases that he himself sends—is not entirely lacking in benevolent qualities, which a poet would naturally find reason to praise. Nevertheless, the dangerous nature of the god emerges at every turn in these hymns. The people beg him not to strike the "great or the small," neither father nor mother, nor one's own life, nor cattle nor horses; they pray that his heavenly hosts might strike down others instead; he is described as being as terrifying as a wild beast. It might be a simple oversight that provokes his anger—perhaps an awkward invocation or a prayer offered at the wrong time while he is already occupied by other worshippers <note>original footnote 2: Rigveda II, 33, 4.</note>—but on the whole, the pleas for mercy addressed to him sound as if one expected his attacks even without any provocation, let alone a serious moral transgression.

Having seen how the gods' beneficial or harmful actions toward humanity follow from their specific characters and temperaments, we must now particularly consider the role that concepts of right and wrong, or sin, play in the relationship between humans and the divine.

## The Gods and the Law.

...originally completely independent of the belief in gods or its earlier developmental stages. In and of itself, it is not immediately clear why spirits—and especially those preeminently powerful spirits called gods—should be any more inclined than humans to be friends of justice and enemies of injustice, or why they should be so at all. Historical development, however, soon moves beyond this separation of the two spheres, leading to a connection between the gods and the law. While this connection is generally not absolute, it is nonetheless predominant: the gods are conceived as the friends of what is right. Just as every god is assigned their own particular sphere of activity within the cosmic whole, certain deities may take this specific task upon themselves—using their strong arms to ensure that justice prevails over wrongdoing.

It is not our task here to trace the older phases of the development just mentioned; instead, we shall attempt to describe the stage it reached during the <term>Vedic period: the era in ancient India (c. 1500–500 BCE) when the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, were composed</term>.

The general portrayal of the gods possesses ethical traits only on the surface. For the religious consciousness of the time, the essential quality of a god is that of a powerful friend; in the hymns of praise dedicated to him, his power is magnified to an immeasurable degree. His moral sublimity, however, is not elevated in the same way. To be sure, qualities such as "true," "deceitless," and the like are attributed to all the gods, <note>original footnote 1: See the compilation in Bergaigne III, 199. [Translator's note: Referring to Abel Bergaigne’s "La religion védique d'après les hymnes du Rig-Veda"].</note> but such <term>epithets: descriptive titles or adjectives</term> recede far behind others like "great," "mighty," and their equivalents. These terms show little more than that a certain goodness and straightforwardness are expected of a god, just as they are of a righteous man. What was noted above (page 282) regarding <term>Indra: the king of the gods and god of thunder and war</term> illustrates the limitations within which such qualities must be understood. The best confirmation that the Vedic gods possess little...

### Good and Evil Gods.

The further course of Indian religious history shows how little these concepts were designed to adopt more than a superficial ethical coloring. For an era as deeply moved by moral problems as that of ancient Buddhism, the pinnacles of ethical perfection lay entirely elsewhere than in the regions of the divine world; the existence of a Buddhist god essentially consists of nothing more than "rejoicing in heaven" for immeasurable spans of time.

However, a different relationship to morality—distinct from that which a god has simply by being a god—can be found in the deity's individual character. As we have already explained above (p. 195 ff.), from Indo-Iranian times onward, the *<term>Ādityas: a group of solar deities, sons of the goddess Aditi, who represent various aspects of social and cosmic order</term>* and especially the greatest among them, *Varuṇa*, were conceived as the founders and protectors of *<term>Ṛta: the fundamental law or cosmic order that governs both the physical world (like the seasons) and the moral world (truth and justice)</term>*, setting them apart from other gods. As gods of the great lights of the sky—according to their original nature—they embody the order of all events most visibly manifested in the firmament; as all-seeing, they are also knowers of even the most secret human sins. "They see through what is crooked and straight; everything, even the highest, is close to the kings." "Whoever stands and whoever goes, whoever wavers, whoever sneaks in secret and whoever rushes forward, what two people discuss while sitting together, King Varuṇa knows that as a third participant"¹). The all-seeing power of these gods is embodied in their "spies" <note>German: *Späher*; these are divine agents or watchmen who observe human behavior</note>, who never close their eyes²). # The Gods and the Law. Guilt.

Might the explanation for why the **primary emphasis** in the religious development of both the Veda <note>The oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism</note> and the Avesta <note>The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</note> falls on Varuṇa (called Ahura in the Avesta) lie in this role—which was added to the original nature-significance of the <term>Ādityas: a group of celestial deities representing social and cosmic order</term>—as the observers of all sins? This is despite the fact that the Sun (Mitra) would naturally be placed before the Moon (Varuṇa)—a sequence that is also proven by linguistic evidence (p. 193 note 1) to have existed initially. Of the two great Ādityas, Varuṇa is the god who rules the night: sins seek the protection of the night, and so it is he, rather than his companion who rules the day, who must take up the struggle against sin and the protection of <term>Ṛta: the fundamental cosmic and moral law</term>¹).

However, wherever we investigate the views on sin and atonement, we notice the side-by-side existence and partial mixing of the same two great series of ideas that we encountered earlier when considering the relationship of Varuṇa to Ṛta (p. 199 ff.): on the one hand, the conception of sin as an entity that brings ruin to the guilty party through its own inherent nature; and on the other hand, as something that brings ruin through the intervention of the deity.

It is necessary to dwell a little longer on this point and to consider the ideas regarding the way sin operates more thoroughly.

## Good and Evil Gods.

Just as diseases and similar harmful forces are thought of as substances—sometimes solid, sometimes as fleeting as air—that one can wash away with water, burn with fire, banish with magical amulets, or remove in various other ways, so too is **sin** (Sanskrit: *enas*, or *āgas*) envisioned. Why should one understand this power, which brings harm to the perpetrator, in any other way than based on the model of other harmful powers? It is viewed with the same physical reality attributed to the others¹). The idea of a **fetter** or **noose** in which the sinner becomes entangled is particularly frequent. This conceptualization is shared by sin and other destructive powers: thus, people speak of the "fetters of death" or the "fetters of disease," or disease itself is called the "fetter of Perdition" (<term>Nirṛti: a goddess associated with decay and the abyss</term>). The sinner, though perhaps appearing free and happy on the surface, is nonetheless held by a bond from which he cannot break free. Here, the idea of a sin-punishing god naturally arises—as the one who applies the fetter or casts the noose—but this element is by no means essential. The fetter is simply the sin itself, which clings to the guilty party with its inherent destructive power. Thus, one prays to Soma and Rudra for liberation from the:
> "**sin bound fast to our bodies**, which we have committed,"

and one prays to Varuṇa:
> "**Release from us the sin** which we have committed"²).

This noose of sin seems to be imagined as being cast in the form of a snare in which the wrongdoer is caught: thus, one prays

It is self-evident that this external, one might say sensory, understanding of sin manifests in the fact that the subjective element—the sinful will—is still far from being the decisive factor. What matters most is the objective reality of the sinful act. Even sin committed unknowingly or in sleep²) is considered sin. Furthermore, this entire prevailing mode of thought—particularly the notion of sin as a substance that produces illness—leads to a consequence characteristic of all early stages of ethical contemplation: the idea that guilt by no means clings to the guilty party alone, but can pass to other people through various paths³). Most naturally, it passes from the father⁴) to the son. # Guilt

...will be completed in the discussion of the cult of atonement <note>original: "Sühncultus"</note>; there it will be shown how diverse forms of magic were directed toward the removal of that substance, how it was washed away, wiped off, chased away, burned, or overcome like a disease through healing herbs. Here it should only be further emphasized how these views of guilt and atonement necessarily posed serious obstacles to the internalization and deepening of moral consciousness. Where guilt, just as it could attach itself externally, could also be removed through external means—where waters washed away "whatever deception one has committed, whatever injustice one has sworn" (Rigveda I, 23, 22)—it was difficult for feelings more serious and profound than a superficially cautious dread of contact with the dangerous substance of guilt to develop; one remained far from the requirement of an overcoming of guilt taking place in the depths of the inner self. With spells similar to those used to drive away fever or to bring prosperity to the herds, one also secured the help of Agni <note>The Vedic god of fire, who acts as a mediator and purifier in rituals</note> in order to be reinstated "back into the world of the good" by him, especially if one had "promised what one did not intend to fulfill" (Atharva Veda VI, 119). In a tone of calm businesslike efficiency, far removed from any trace of inner emotion, one prayed to him:

> "Whatever we have failed in through incantation, through dismissal, through address <note>These terms likely refer to specific ritual formulas or spoken errors during a ceremony</note>, while sleeping or waking: all evil deeds, the hated ones, may Agni carry far away from us¹)" (Rigveda X, 164, 3).

# Good and Evil Gods.

One would misunderstand the currents running alongside each other if one believed that the stance of Ancient Indian religious thought regarding the idea of guilt was fully and exhaustively expressed in forms of such superficial cleansing magic <note>original: "Sühnzauber"</note> and sacrificial atonement. Yet there is no lack of expressions from the spiritual poets in which the voice of the soul, haunted by the awareness of its sins, can be heard in a serious and urgent manner from the depths. Such expressions tend not to concern themselves with the removal of impersonal "sin-substance" <term>Sündsubstanz: the early Vedic belief that sin was a physical, contagious material that could be ritually washed or scraped away</term> brought about by magic or the action of a helpful god. Instead, they deal with the reconciliation of divine wrath that punishes sin. And so we are led to speak of a second side of the concept of sin: guilt, which we have previously seen as an entity acting through its own power, must now be considered in its connection with divine wrath and the divine intervention for the maintenance of the moral order¹).

Just as the impersonal physical and moral law of the world <term>Ṛta: the fundamental cosmic order or "truth" that governs both the natural and moral worlds</term> coincides with the "Commands of Varuna" <note>Varuna is one of the oldest Vedic deities, the guardian of the cosmic order and the judge of human morality</note> (p. 199 ff.), so too is sin a violation of Varuna's commands or ordinances. One prays to Varuna: "If we have violated your ordinances through thoughtlessness, do us no harm, O God, for this sin <term>enas: a Vedic term for sin, crime, or misfortune</term>."²) The fetters or snares,

It seems to me that this view—which has indeed found its supporters²)—is based on an incorrect estimation of the significance of one-sidedly selected sentences and incompletely considered expressions. Above all, it must be remembered³) that the word *māyā* <gloss>māyā: a term often translated as "illusion" in later philosophy, but in the Vedas, it refers to a mysterious, supernatural power or transformative skill</gloss> in itself possesses neither a low nor a noble connotation; it simply means any secret skill that performs deeds reaching beyond the general horizon. It is Varuṇa's *māyā* that he sends the dawns, that standing in the air he measures out the earth with the sun as if with a measuring-rod, that the sun walks across the sky and then clouds hide it, and the honey of the rain drips down to the earth⁴). It is clear that in all of this, it is not a matter of cunning and malice, but solely of secret, incomprehensible skill. That this skill may also take the form of trickery in individual cases need not be excluded; however, even if that appears in the Veda as a primary quality of Varuṇa, one is by no means justified in the view that cunning and malice form the basic character of this god. His power is a friend of justice (<term>Ṛta: the fundamental cosmic and moral order that the gods must uphold</term>); it protects the right and punishes the sins even of the strong and the cunning.

They are called "strong in the Right"; "they have grown strong in the dwelling of the Right"¹). <note>The "Right" refers to *Ṛta*, the fundamental cosmic and moral order of the universe.</note> What is said of all the gods applies to them as well: "Splendid is the grace of the gods who walk in straightness" (I, 89, 2). Wherever the contrast between straight and crooked, between honesty and double-tonguedness <note>In the Vedic context, being "double-tongued" refers to hypocrisy or lying.</note> occupies the Vedic poet, the gods—and among them, first and foremost, Varuṇa and the Ādityas—appear throughout as the friends and protectors of the good.

However, one must certainly not measure this alliance between Varuṇa and the Right by modern Christian standards. Deceiving an enemy was considered good and right by the Vedic Indian²), and it would have seemed questionable to him to hope for a victory over the crafty person except through superior craftiness. The poets say it themselves: the deceptive spirits of Mitra and Varuṇa pursue the sins of men; for the deceiver, their snares <note>Original: *pāśas* — the literal "nooses" or "bonds" used by Varuṇa to bind those who break his laws.</note> are open. Against the good and pious, however, Varuṇa is true and faithful; where he is angry or causes harm through his deceptive arts, the person he pursues knows—unlike with the anger of Rudra <note>Rudra, a fiercer god, was often seen as striking unpredictably; Varuṇa’s punishments, by contrast, were seen as the direct consequence of a moral failing.</note>—that it is **sinful guilt** for the sake of which Varuṇa punishes him³). And since he himself does not confront the god with arrogant defiance, but rather seeks to recognize his guilt and reconcile with Varuṇa, he trusts that the god will show himself to him not as a malicious and spiteful enemy, but as a kind and merciful one.

# Varuṇa as the Punisher of Sins.

...inherited from our fathers, and those which we ourselves have committed with our own bodies. Set Vasiṣṭha <note>The legendary sage and traditional author of this collection of hymns</note> free, O King, like a thief who steals cattle, like a calf from its tether.

> “It was not my own will, Varuṇa; it was delusion, drink and gaming, passion and thoughtlessness. The elder falls into the error of the youth. Even sleep does not keep one free from wrongdoing.
> 
> “Like a servant I wish to satisfy the Gracious one, the zealous God, so that I may be guiltless. The God of the Aryans <note>The Indo-Iranian people of the Vedic period</note> has given thoughtfulness to the thoughtless; the Wiser one advances the clever to wealth.
> 
> “May this song of praise, O Varuṇa, you who are free, penetrate to your heart. May it be well with us when we rest, and well when we move. Protect us always, you Gods, and give us well-being.” —

Just as the god overcomes the deceits of the wicked with his own superior cunning, so the man in this song—driven to penance not by an internal consciousness of guilt itself, but by the fear of divine punishment—will undoubtedly be found wanting when weighed in the scales of modern virtue. Can it surprise the historian if the ancient prayers of the Veda are not in full harmony with the ethical tastes prevailing today? The penitent approaches the god with a measured, dignified bearing; there is no passionate outburst of pain or fear; the language he speaks is calm, almost cool. However, the gravity of the awareness that the divine guardian of justice pursues sin—and at the same time, the trust in forgiving grace toward the repentant—has found an expression here whose simple and profound eloquence, rare in the poetry of the Veda, will still be felt today. This hymn may well appear as one of the highlights in the realm of that religious poetry. —

# Good and Evil Gods.

Varuṇa and the Ādityas <note>A group of solar deities who uphold the cosmic and moral order</note> are the most prominent, but naturally not the only, protectors of the law and punishers of sin. To satisfy the religious need to see the world of justice linked with the world of the gods, the figure of Agni <note>The god of fire, who dwells in the sacrificial flame and the domestic hearth</note> also presented itself alongside them.¹) We have already touched upon this fact elsewhere (p. 201) and identified its obvious causes. Invocations are addressed to Agni that are quite similar to those addressed to Varuṇa: he is asked to make amends for guilt, not to let the petitioner suffer for the sins of others, and to loosen the bonds of sin so that one may stand guiltless before Aditi <note>The mother of the gods, representing the infinite and liberation from bondage</note>. The difference between these prayers to Agni and those to Varuṇa is, first of all, that the former appear less prominently among all sorts of other invocations in the Agni hymns, while they form the main content of the songs dedicated to Varuṇa. 

But even aside from that, Agni's special nature is expressed in several specific nuances. Varuṇa is the highest, but Agni is the scrutinizer of right and wrong who is closest to humanity. The god who dwells within human habitations, the mediator between Earth and Heaven, is also the natural mediator between human justice, human guilt, and their divine judges: a mediator first by reporting on humans to the gods above, and then by interceding for them as a faithful friend, deeply rooted in daily interaction with them. “How will you, Agni, reproach us before Varuṇa, or before Heaven? Which of our sins? How will you speak to the gracious Mitra, or to the Earth? What will you say to Aryaman, what to Bhaga?”²) <note>original: “Wie wirst du, Agni, uns vor Varuṇa, wie vor dem Himmel schelten? Welche unsrer Sünden? Wie wirst du zum gnädigen Mitra, zur Erde sprechen? Was wirst du dem Aryaman, was dem Bhaga sagen?”</note>. “You, O Agni, knowingly turn—”

Furthermore, a series of Vedic statements that place him in contrast to Varuṇa show quite explicitly that it was not Indra who was known as the actual master of right and wrong. One can already count it here when Indra is once celebrated as the fighter and destroyer of those who break the law of Mitra and Varuṇa (X, 89, 8. 9): the sin is simply a violation not of Indra, but of those gods; and after them, as the decisive ordainers of the law, comes Indra, who places his strong arm at the disposal of their statutes. # SECTION THREE.

## The Cult.

---

### General Overview.

Human action toward the gods and spirits seeks to win their favor and to keep their ill-will at bay. The dual nature of this endeavor—and the double nature of the <term>cult</term> <note>Derived from the Latin 'cultus,' meaning the care, labor, and ritual attention directed toward the divine</note> as both the care and the defense against supernatural powers—are in close contact with one another without, however, completely overlapping. For the effort to protect oneself from a malevolent god or spirit can only take the form of "defense" when the enemy's superior power does not exclude all hope for the success of human strength and skill; in the other case, even toward a hostile god, only the means of ritual care remain, through which one moves him to depart of his own accord or, while lingering, to turn his wrath into kindness.

The cult of the great <term>Vedic</term> <note>Pertaining to the Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of ancient India, which detail the hymns and rituals for the gods</note> gods therefore presents itself under all circumstances as care: as a nurturing which, because the great gods were regarded overwhelmingly as benevolent powers, only relatively rarely exhibits the trait where the worshipper seeks to remove the god by praying to and feeding him: this is the characteristic

### The Cult as Nurturing and Defense.

...peculiarity specifically of the <term>cult of Rudra</term>¹ <note>Rudra is a fierce Vedic deity associated with storms, hunting, and disease; he is often seen as a precursor to the god Shiva. His worship often focuses on pacifying his potential for destruction</note>. Among the lesser demonic powers, on the other hand, hostile forces predominate. Humans believe themselves to be a match for these through power and cunning, and above all through the assistance of their friends, the great gods who bring blessings; here, the <term>cult</term> <note>The system of religious worship and ritual</note> therefore takes on the predominantly defensive form of open—and occasionally hidden—warfare². Finally, the cult of the dead shows a double face. The souls of the departed ancestors are at once friendly and uncanny powers to their children; they require nurturing, but as soon as they have received this, a defense is mounted against them to ensure that they do not impose their dangerous proximity upon the living beyond the allotted time³.

The nurturing of the god—from the modest gifts given to the small beings in the spirit realm up to those great offerings with which the wealthy sacrificer honored the high and highest lords of this realm—consists primarily in the gift of food and refreshing or intoxicating drink, which is to say, in <term>sacrifice</term>: whereby it is understood that this hospitable reception of the god also includes certain secondary attentions, such as the offering of a comfortable seat, fragrances, and the like.

# Worship: A General Overview

...or at least can encompass. Gifts of clothing seem—and this is noteworthy—to occur only in the <term>cult of the dead</term> <note>Rituals and practices intended to care for and honor deceased ancestors (Manes)</note>, not for the gods, who were nevertheless also imagined as clothed; likewise, as far as I can see, one does not encounter gifts of items belonging to the god's equipment, such as weapons, chariots, and the like. Property objects, moreover, that go beyond what pertains to personal use, do not seem to have been dedicated to the god in the <term>Vedic cult</term> <note>The religious practices described in the Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of India, roughly 1500–500 BCE</note>. This is likely due on the one hand to the fact that the basic features of cultic custom date back to an age to which developed private property—and thus the idea of a divine private property—was still foreign; on the other hand, it will be related to the lack of temples <note>Literally "god-houses"</note> in which such property could have been stored.

In addition to the gifts, there are naturally inviting and praising speeches, often in metrical <note>poetic</note> form, as well as song and, here and there, instrumental music; one also sought to delight the god through dance performances. The dialogues encountered not infrequently in the ritual—theological riddle-questions <note>Known as *brahmodya*, these were ritualized intellectual competitions between priests</note> with their solutions as well as conversations of obscene content—are perhaps also at least partially to be regarded as intended for the entertainment of the god. In contrast, some other acts belonging to the cult, during which one might think of a similar explanation—for example, chariot racing, arrow shooting, dice games, sexual acts—are to all appearances not dedicated to the delight of the god, but rather <term>magical acts</term> <note>Acts intended to produce a direct supernatural result through the ritual itself rather than through the favor of a deity</note> through which the sacrificer sought to secure for himself strength, luck, the fertility of his wives, and so on¹).

### The Petitionary Sacrifice, Atonement Sacrifice, and Thanksgiving Sacrifice.

...whether in general, or to win specific manifestations of the

In a certain sense, the **atonement sacrifice** is a special case of the 
petitionary sacrifice: here, it is forgiveness, the non-punishment of a 
guilt, toward which the petition is directed¹). We reserve the 
more detailed discussion of the atonement sacrifice for its own section. 
Actual **thanksgiving sacrifices** are completely, or at least 
nearly, foreign to the <term>Vedic cult</term> <note>The religious system of the Indo-Aryans during the period in which the Vedas were composed (c. 1500–500 BCE)</note>, just as the word "to thank" 
is foreign to the Vedic language. Rites that could be taken 
for thanksgiving sacrifices seem, upon closer inspection, 
to prove themselves consistently or almost consistently to be 
**petitionary sacrifices**. Such is the case with the first-fruits sacrifice 
of the field crops²), which quite obviously does not look 
back at the blessings already received, but toward new blessings 
requested from the gods for the future—incidentally, it seems,

# Cult: General Overview

The **thanksgiving sacrifice** after the birth of a son¹) is in fact entirely a **petitionary sacrifice**; the explicit intention, as stated, is to purify the newborn "with the splendor of holiness, to bestow upon him sharpness, to bestow upon him the blessing of food, to bestow upon him the power of the senses, and to bestow upon him cattle." Even in cases where—as is demonstrably the case—the later popular custom of the <term>vow</term> <note>A promise made to a deity to perform a ritual or gift if a specific prayer is answered.</note> was practiced as early as the Vedic period²), it was clearly not a thanksgiving sacrifice: the gift promised to the god in the event of a specific grant of grace, and paid to him after its occurrence, is naturally nothing other than a petitionary sacrifice with a delayed timing. Against several other cases of sacrifices that one might be tempted to interpret as thanksgiving sacrifices, closer examination likewise reveals doubts. A list of kings who were consecrated with the "great anointing sacred to Indra" says of each that he "traveled victoriously over the whole earth and sacrificed the sacrificial horse"³). Should the horse sacrifice then be understood as a thanksgiving sacrifice for great victories...

### Cult: A General Overview.

...established the fires, illness befalls him; let him move out... "The fires love the village," so it is said. Longing for this, desiring to return to the village, they will likely make him healthy, so it is taught. Once he has become healthy, he should offer a **Soma sacrifice** <note>original: *Somaopfer*; a central Vedic ritual involving the pressing and offering of the juice of the Soma plant</note> or an **animal sacrifice** or an ordinary sacrifice and dwell again in the old place. Or [he may do so] without such a sacrifice. Perhaps here, as one might believe by analogy with some of the cases discussed previously, we have a **petitionary sacrifice** <note>original: *Bittopfer*; a sacrifice performed to request a specific favor or outcome from a deity</note> intended for future health: however, one can hardly deny that such a petitionary sacrifice looks very similar, at the very least, to a **thanksgiving sacrifice** <note>original: *Dankopfer*; an offering given in gratitude for a favor already received</note>, and one may suspect that precisely this kind of petitionary sacrifice could easily have served as the starting point for the development of thanksgiving sacrifices. —

It must now be asked: how does the sacrifice work? By what path does it procure the sought-after blessings for man?

Without doubt, the original conception is the following: The sacrifice goes to the god as a gift brought to him; the **sacrificer** <note>original: *Opferer*; the person for whose benefit the ritual is performed</note> hopes that it will act upon the god’s disposition, not in the form of compulsion, but by awakening his mighty goodwill, which then manifests itself toward the human being¹).

May this conception be attributed unchanged to the **Vedic period** <note>The era in ancient Indian history (c. 1500 – c. 500 BCE) when the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, were composed</note>?

Anyone who observes without bias the language that the sacrificial poets of the **Ṛgveda** <note>Rigveda; the oldest of the four Vedas, consisting of hymns to various deities</note> use toward the gods will essentially answer this question in the affirmative. The original conception has remained the dominant one; even if some

# Mode of Action of the Sacrifice.

Even if elements of other origins have attached themselves to it, these cannot seriously call into question the character of the whole. Throughout the entire **Ṛgveda** <note>the oldest collection of Hindu hymns, dating to approximately 1500–1200 BCE</note>, we find the same thought repeated in countless variations: this sacrificial food, and especially this drink—for it is primarily a matter of the **Soma** <note>a sacred ritual drink made from a plant, believed to provide immortality and strength to gods and humans alike</note>—is intended to satisfy, delight, and strengthen the god¹). This is expressed drastically by a story contained in a later Vedic text²): **Indra** <note>the king of the gods and god of thunder and war</note> goes to **Suṣravas** <note>a king or figure mentioned in Vedic lore</note> and says: "Sacrifice to me, I am hungry." The latter sacrifices, and now Indra walks about with the sacrificial cake in his hand. — The god, as goes without saying, loves the **sacrificer** <note>the person who pays for and benefits from the ritual</note>; he certainly has indulgence for the poor man who can only give a little³), but he hates the stingy. He will contentedly bestow his gifts upon the generous man, just as he has bestowed them upon him in the past. "Drink, grow strong!" says the Ṛgveda, "for the Soma drinks are yours, the pressed ones, Indra, now as before. Just as you drank the old Soma, Indra, so may you, the Praised One, drink the new today . . . Arise, bring it here! No one shall hinder you! For we know you, the lord of treasures. Indra, whatever your great gift is, grant it to us, Lord of the tawny steeds" (III, 36, 3. 9). "Enjoy the Soma, satisfy your longing with it: then turn your mind to bestowing treasures" (I, 54, 9). "The hero possesses unswerving strength through Indra, through his men, he who presses deep Soma-pours for you, o **Vṛtra-slayer** <note>an epithet for Indra, who defeated Vṛtra, a serpent or dragon representing drought</note>, and prepares them with water" (VII, 32, 6). "I became"—Indra speaks—"the promoter of the sacrificer; in every battle I have overcome those who do not sacrifice."

->### The Mode of Efficacy of the Sacrifice.<-

This is the conception and mood that permeates the entire breadth of <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>pertaining to the Rigveda, the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns</note> sacrificial poetry, as expressed in hundreds, even thousands, of passages: a view whose recurring appearance among peoples of the most diverse origins justifies us in regarding it as the standard and characteristic view for long periods of human culture.

Now, however, further developments emerge from this foundation. First, in several passages of the <term>Rigveda</term>, there is the view that the sacrifice does not so much awaken the favor of the god as it captures the god through a kind of magical compulsion, subjecting him to the will of the sacrificer. Thus it is said¹): "Even if others than we hunt him (Indra) with cows²) like herds (of hunters) hunt game, lying in wait for him with milk-cows" (VIII, 2, 6). To Indra, a priest who invites him to his sacrifice says: "May others not hold you fast with them like bird-catchers [capture] a bird" (X, 49, 1).

### Sacrifice Compelling the Gods.

...hunting Indra, ambushing him, and holding him fast like bird-catchers are the rivals of the speaker: their efforts to win the god's favor are deliberately cast in a malicious light, and the question to Indra seems to shine through: will you really allow yourself to be held fast by them, as if you were a bird and they the fowlers?¹)

With all this, it is not intended to deny that traces of the view regarding the power of the priest over the god—which was later carried to such extremes <note>The author refers to the later Brahmana period of Indian religion, where ritual mechanics were thought to be so precise they forced the gods to act.</note>—reach back into the oldest <term>Veda</term> <note>the Rigveda, the earliest collection of Indian sacred hymns</note>; we only wish to reduce the significance of these traces to their proper measure. However, the primary origin of that view seems to me to lie in a development to which the most significant effects in the history of sacrifice must generally be attributed: the fusion of two originally distinct spheres of thought and action—sacrifice and **sorcery**. Clearly, the method of one who seeks to win over a god through gifts, perhaps to gain his help in destroying an enemy, is fundamentally different from the method of one who burns an image, clippings of hair, or the like belonging to that enemy, believing that by doing so he burns the enemy himself. The former achieves his goal indirectly by swaying the will of a powerful ally; the latter achieves it directly through an impersonal chain of cause and effect. This second method is the way magic works; there is no doubt that the way sacrifice works was originally conceived in the first manner²). But there is also no doubt that in the—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between sacrifice and sorcery. # Cult: A General Overview

In practical life, the close contact between these two procedures must have led to various mixtures even at very early stages of cultural development. Magical acts were often similar to sacrificial acts, and they increasingly came to resemble them—or combined with sacrifices¹) wherever the conceptual sphere of sacrifice held dominant sway in the world of ideas. In such cases, the specific mode of action belonging to magic was transferred to the sacrifice itself. On the other hand, the environment of the sacrifice—saturated with ideas of divine proximity and mysterious success—offered a terrain that invited the practice of <term>sorcery</term> <note>German: Zauberei; the attempt to compel supernatural results through ritual mechanics rather than prayer</note> like no other. Individual secondary actions belonging to the sacrifice as its constituent parts could have originally fallen within the realm of sorcery, or a magical character could have been introduced into them. Furthermore, the endeavor to explain sacrificial rites in all their often quite accidental particulars could hardly lead anywhere else than to the discovery of effects similar to those of magic within them. Not least, the sacrificial priests, in order to demonstrate the indispensability of their own art to the people, must have cultivated and intensified the notion of a magical power inherent in the sacrifice. Finally, the mixing of sacrificial acts and magical acts was significantly fa— <note>The text breaks off here at the start of the word "befördert" (facilitated/promoted), continuing on the next page.</note>

->### Sacrifice and Magic ###<-

—cilitated by: the mixing of prayer-formulas and magical spells—of the word that persuades the will of the god just as one would a human, and the word that, by virtue of its <term>correspondence</term> <note>The belief that a ritual word or action is cosmically linked to the thing it represents</note> with the object or process it designates, brings about effects in the world of objects. This is similar to how an image relates to the object depicted, or a severed body part relates to the whole body in a state of magical correspondence. Prayer is an essential part of sacrifice; if prayer takes on some of the effects of a magical spell, then these effects must naturally benefit the sacrifice itself.

Beside the already discussed beginnings of the idea that sacrifice possesses a power that masters even the gods, many other views encountered within <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>Refers to the Rigveda, the oldest collection of Hindu hymns (c. 1500–1200 BCE)</note> sacrificial poetry can be traced back to this reinterpretation of the sacrificial idea in the sense of magic. Just as sacrifice captures the will of the gods with its magical power, it can also bypass this will and influence things and events directly through magic, without the assistance of the gods¹. This is seen above all in the sacrifice of the first ancestors, which is elevated to a state of mythical immensity. They, the achievers of the great deeds that gave the world its shape, were the first sacrificers and the first to offer prayer (p. 278 ff.): thus, the sacrifice and the prayer—or the <term>magical song</term>—must have been the instrument of their power.

***

¹) A rich collection of material on the direct effect of sacrifice, not mediated by the action of the god, is provided by Bergaigne <note>Abel Bergaigne (1838–1888), a French scholar of Sanskrit whose work "La Religion Védique" is a standard reference for Vedic studies</note> I, 121 ff. However, many things that do not belong there must be filtered out: above all, the magical rites cited on p. 123 (mostly from *Rigveda* X). It is a fundamental error of Bergaigne's to place these in the same category as sacrifice, whereas it should instead be a matter of separating them from the latter as a distinct type, and then tracing the mutual influences of the two types.

From this universal sacrifice, sacrificial songs and sacrificial melodies were born; the meters were born from it; the sacrificial formula was born” (X, 90, 6. 9).

The magical power <note>original: "Zaubermacht"</note> of that pre-worldly sacrifice has not been lost to the sacrifice of the present; although its effect is often—as lies in the nature of the matter—not sharply distinct from the effect mediated by divine grace, the belief in such an independent magical power for the **Rigvedic period** <margin>And, it may be added by way of conjecture, for much older ages.</margin> is not to be doubted. # Sacrifice and Magic. — The Atonement Cult.

...settled down to the sacrificial work:

> “Then he poured out the heavenly waters of rain from the sea above to the sea below. In that sea up there, the waters dwelled, held fast by the gods: they flowed, poured out by the son of **Ṛshṭisheṇa**, sent by **Devāpi** <note>Devāpi was a legendary figure who acted as a priest to win rain for his brother's kingdom</note> in torrents¹).”

One sees how here the conception slips away from its initial direction: first, the gods were meant to give rain in their grace; now the priest himself pours it out through the magical power <note>original: "Zaubermacht"</note> of his sacrificial art.

Given the current state of research, the attempt may only be ventured for certain parts of the ritual field—we will often have to occupy ourselves with this in the following—to determine in detail where, in the ancient form of sacrifice, speculation on the direct, magical control of objects played a role. How the entire sacrificial system was overgrown by this belief in the later Vedic period is shown by every page of the **Brāhmaṇa texts** <note>Prose commentaries on the Vedas focused on the intricate details and mystical meanings of rituals</note>.

### Atonement Sacrifice and Atonement Magic.

The atonement cult <note>original: "Sühncult"</note>, to which we must return here in somewhat more detail following the indications given above (p. 305), moves in two directions. These correspond to the different lines of thought that intersect in the conception of the nature of guilt <note>original: "Schuld"; in this context, it implies a mixture of moral sin, ritual error, and cosmic debt</note> (see above p. 287): directions whose clear fundamental distinction is not canceled by the fact that they understandably meet and intertwine in many ways in individual acts of atonement. Insofar as guilt is, on the one hand, a violation of the divine will and thus a provocation of divine wrath, the atonement is addressed to the god; one seeks to please and appease him through gifts and signs of submission.

# Atonement Sacrifice and Atonement Magic.

On the other hand, insofar as guilt <note>original: "Schuld"; suggesting both a moral failing and a physical taint</note> is conceived as a fluid adhering to the guilty person—much like the pathogens of a disease—the atonement cult presents itself as a series of magical manipulations. These are designed to detach this substance, this fluid, to destroy it, or to divert it to harmless distances, so that the guilty person may become free and pure,
> “as one covered in sweat is freed from his impurity when he has bathed,” “as the winged bird is freed from the egg”¹)

This way of thinking also allows for a turn in which the god assumes the role of the liberator: namely, in cases where the removal of the substance of guilt is not achieved through the direct effectiveness of magic, but where the power and skill of the god are called upon for help. One can see that here the god’s position relative to the process of atonement is fundamentally different—more external and incidental—than when the liberation from guilt is placed within the soul of the god and understood as an act of his forgiving grace.

Atonement sacrifices, which make the attainment of this divine grace their primary objective, clearly lie entirely within the sphere of the ordinary sacrificial cult <note>original: "Opfercultus"</note>. Their occasion is special, but they themselves are sacrifices like any other, usually offered to <term>Varuṇa</term> <note>The Vedic deity of the celestial waters and the guardian of Ṛta (cosmic and moral order)</note> in order to appease him, the divine guardian of the moral world order and punisher of sins. Such is the sacrifice—for it is most likely such a case—to which that beautiful and profound prayer of a <term>Vasiṣṭhide</term> <note>A descendant of the sage Vasiṣṭha, belonging to one of the most famous priestly families of the Rigveda</note> belongs, which was shared above (p. 296).
> “When will I be close to <term>Varuṇa</term> again?”
—he seeks to see his guilt and goes to ask the wise; but they all tell him with one mind: it is <term>Varuṇa</term> who is angry with you²). Exactly in the

# Propitiation of the Gods and Removal of the Substance of Guilt.

The atonement sacrifice for the breach of an oath of loyalty (Ts. II, 2, 6, 2) <note>Taittirīya Saṃhitā, a core collection of Vedic hymns and ritual instructions</note>, for example, follows the forms of an ordinary sacrifice: a sacrificial cake offered to <term>Agni Vaiśvānara</term> <note>Agni (the god of fire) in his aspect as "belonging to all men" or the universal fire</note>. Presumably, it was this specific form of Agni that the person swearing the oath had invoked, and it is in this form that the god is now asked to be appeased by the offering and to forgive the transgressor.¹)

However, a series of other acts of atonement are of an entirely different nature. The most prominent act of atonement in the regular festival calendar forms part of the second of the three great four-monthly festivals—the celebration of the <term>Varuṇapraghāsās</term> <note>A seasonal ritual held at the beginning of the rainy season to secure the favor of Varuṇa</note>, which takes place around the start of the rainy season. Using barley that has been roasted in the southern sacrificial fire—the fire reserved for unclean and eerie rituals—cakes are prepared in the shape of plates. One plate is made for each member of the household, plus one additional cake: this one is for

---

guilt as an adhering substance or, more precisely, as a bond <note>original: "Fessel"; often used in the Vedas to describe Varuṇa’s "noose" that ensnares the guilty</note> into which Varuṇa is asked to enter and loosen (Verse 5).

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Varuṇapraghāsās ritual, specifically examining how the act of "sacrificing away" guilt functions more as a physical disposal or magical destruction than a traditional prayer for mercy. ### Removal of the Substance of Guilt.

One can see how here, alongside the <term>Varuna sacrifice</term> <note>A ritual dedicated to Varuṇa, the Vedic deity who oversees cosmic law and punishes moral failings</note>—in which the mercy of the god is implored in the manner discussed above—there stands an act of an entirely different nature: the ceremony involving the plate-shaped pastries. Its character as a "sacrifice" is only superficially attached to it. The technical term <term>ava-yaj</term> <note>Sanskrit: "to sacrifice away" or "to discard through offering"</note> encountered here and in similar cases points primarily to a "putting away." The priestly imagination, operating within the framework of sacrificial systems, has reinterpreted this disposal as an act of offering. This is much like the reinterpretation that occurred with the burning of objects after a standard sacrifice; because these items had taken on a "consecrated" character, they could not be brought back into contact with profane, everyday life without danger. The guilt of the household members is thought to adhere to these plates—the guilt of a specific person to each individual plate. Through the offering, or more accurately, through the burning of the plates, the guilt itself is burned.

A similar burning of guilt has been inserted into the ritual of the <term>Soma sacrifice</term> <note>The central and most complex of the Vedic sacrifices, involving the pressing and offering of the sacred Soma juice</note>—inserted quite loosely and at a seemingly random point, as far as can be discerned. The priests cast splinters of wood from the sacrificial post into the fire, one for each of the following incantations:

> "You are the sacrificing-away of the guilt committed by the gods. You are the sacrificing-away of the guilt committed by men... by the ancestors... of the guilt committed by oneself. For guilt after guilt, you are the sacrificing-away. Whatever guilt I have committed knowingly and whatever I have committed unknowingly, you are the sacrificing-away of all that guilt."

Here, too, it is clear: what is called "sacrificing away" is essentially nothing other than "burning away." It is a purely physical destruction of guilt, performed without any invocation of divine grace¹).

# Expiatory Sacrifice and Expiatory Magic.

When ceremonies of atonement of this kind are incorporated into the context of the high cult <note>The formal, public religious ceremonies conducted by professional priests</note>, one will be all the more certain to encounter them in abundance within the sphere of the low cult—among the incantations and magical acts tied to the accidental occurrences of daily life. Indeed, the magic songs of the **Atharvaveda** <note>The fourth Veda, primarily consisting of spells, prayers, and charms for healing and protection</note> and the corresponding ritual instructions of the **Kauśikasūtra** <note>A manual detailing the practical application of the Atharvaveda's spells</note> do not disappoint this expectation. 

Thus, the purification of brothers is described, who have transgressed by the younger marrying before the elder <note>In Vedic social law, it was considered a ritual sin for a younger brother to marry before his elder brother</note>. By a body of water, fetters made of reed-grass are placed upon them, a symbol of the bonds of guilt; they are washed and sprinkled; thereupon the fetters are thrown, one over the other¹), into the foam of the water and allowed to float away: "Disappear with the foam of the river," says the associated incantation²) addressing the evil³). — Whoever has spoken an untruth shall rinse their mouth

This can itself also be spoken of in accordance with the sense discussed above: that through the sacrifice, the god's inclination toward punishment or other harm is appeased, and his alliance is won against threatening misfortune.

# Removal of the Substance of Guilt.

...I suspect yet another meaning. The guilt, which perhaps will be atoned for later, first has a claim to take full possession of the person of the guilty party: this taking of possession finds its visible expression for everyone in those observances¹).

As for the previously mentioned procedures for removing guilt—such as burning it away, washing it off, and the like—one sees that these are exactly the same methods by which a disease is warded off through magic. We are dealing here with the thought patterns of an age that saw guilt primarily as a kind of harmful substance <note>The author refers to the concept that "sin" was not just a moral state but a physical "stuff" that stuck to the body</note> adhering to a person, such that it stood on the same level as other harmful things and was treated similarly. Therefore, the term in the Vedic language that comes closest to the meaning of "atonement," <term>prāyaçcitta</term> <note>Sanskrit: A ritual act of atonement, penance, or rectification</note> or *prāyaçcitti*²), actually encompasses much more: it includes the sacrifice to be offered or whatever else is to be done in cases of crimes or offenses, the neglect of sacred duties, all disturbances—whether intentional or unintentional—of the normal course of a sacrifice, but also other events of all kinds that indicate an impending misfortune: such as when a wife or a cow gives birth to twins, or when someone

...is made a duty to withdraw from human interaction and the like (**Āpastamba** Dh. I, 9, 24, 13; 10, 28, 13; 10, 29, 1; **Manu** XI, 47 etc. <note>Ancient Indian legal and ethical texts</note>).

### The Share of the Sacrificer and the Priests in the Sacrificial Food.

A fundamental feature that the Indian sacrifice shares with those of many other peoples is that, alongside the god, humans also partake in a portion of the sacrificial food: the organizer of the sacrifice, provided that as a Brahmin he is qualified for this enjoyment which exceeds the powers of an ordinary person¹), and alongside him or on his behalf, his sacred representatives, the priests. The formula belonging to this act, which in its present version is quite modern, certainly dates back to high antiquity in terms of its content: it is the "invocation of Iḍā"—that is, the deified essence of the cow and the abundance of nourishment contained within the cow²). It says there: "Iḍā is called forth . . . may Iḍā call us forth. The cows are called forth with the milk that is added to the Soma <note>A ritual drink of great importance in Vedic religion</note>; may the cows call me forth with the—"

---

¹) Whether this restriction, which appears in the later Vedic texts, already applied in the time of the Rigveda <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational scriptures of Hinduism</note> does not seem to be positively determinable; given the whole situation, I would consider it probable.

²) Regarding Iḍā as a cow, see page 72 above. Of the abundant testimonies regarding this animal goddess in the later Vedic literature, I share only a brief selection. Addressing the cow as Iḍā in Yajus-verses <note>Sacrificial formulas</note>: *Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā* III, 27, *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* VII, 1, 6, 8, *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* VI, 3, 8 etc. Formula for the "invocation of Iḍā" (see above in the text): "Invoked is the cow whose footprint is butter" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* I, 7, 7): the "butter-footprint," however, is the standard characteristic of the goddess Iḍā. According to the narrative in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* I, 8, 1, she arises from the sacrifice of butter, sour milk, sour cream, and curd offered by Manu <note>The progenitor of humanity in Hindu mythology</note>; liquid butter remained in her footprint.

### Human Consumption of the Sacrificial Food

"—milk that is added to the Soma <note>A sacred, intoxicating ritual drink used in Vedic ceremonies</note>. Called forth is the milch-cow with the bull; may the milch-cow with the bull call me forth. Called forth is the cow whose footprint is butter; may the cow whose footprint is butter call me forth," and so on: a litany originating from pastoral life and pointing to a form of sacrifice involving food products derived from the cow—perhaps even the cow herself—as the gift dedicated to the gods. After the recitation of this litany, the priests and the sacrifice-organizer <note>original: "Opferveranstalter"</note> enjoy their share of the sacred food¹). During the offering of sacrificial cakes, just as in animal sacrifice, this portion is cut according to essentially the same rules; it is clearly evident in the rites that the meaning of the act is the same in every instance. In the Soma sacrifice as well, the priests and the sacrificer receive their portion of the holy intoxicating drink.

What meaning, then, did antiquity associate with this participation of humans in the meal of the gods? Here we encounter a theory to which the investigation of corresponding customs among the Semitic peoples led an outstanding researcher who died all too young²): that the fundamental idea of sacrifice was not that of a tribute from man to god, but rather that of a community—conceived as a blood kinship—between the god and his worshippers, based on the shared consumption of the flesh and blood of the sacrificial animal. Only later, according to this view, did the idea of a gift to be made to the god in sacrifice displace this original perception.

As far as the Vedic ritual is concerned, of which alone we have to speak here, I find in it, just as much—

²) Robertson Smith (*Religion of the Semites* Vol. I).

## The Share of the Sacrificer and the Priest in the Sacrificial Food

...in the ceremonies themselves, as well as in the accompanying prayers and verses, there is absolutely no indication of a conception of the sacrificial meal as a **covenant meal** <note>original: "Bundesmahl"</note> or as the establishment of a **blood brotherhood** <note>original: "Blutsbrüderschaft"</note>. The blood of the sacrificial animal was not consumed at all, but was instead poured out for the evil spirits. Furthermore, in the offerings made to the gods, the invocations do not align with the direction that one would expect according to that theory. The prayer is not: "God [Name], eat together with us so that you may become one of us." Instead, it is repeatedly: "God [Name], accept, eat, and drink what we give you; thrive yourself and let us thrive"¹). And the actual consumption of the food and drink does not take place in any form that places any weight on a sense of community between god and man. First the god eats; something remains, and that is what the humans eat later. Why? Surely because the food from which the god has eaten is considered to be filled with a mysteriously blessed *fluid* <note>original: "Fluidum"; referring to a spiritual essence or aura</note> communicated to it through the proximity and grace of the god—a powerful **"medicine"** <note>original: "Medicin"</note>, which man—naturally only a man capable of such consumption²)—

The attempt to please someone and make them favorably disposed by giving them food to eat is conceivable even without the concept of private property.

-># Magical Power of the Consumed Sacrificial Food #<-

We thus find, in the most diverse forms, the view that the substance belonging to the sacrifice confers power—specifically the kind of power implied by the nature of each particular sacrifice—upon humans, and even upon animals and inanimate things, when it is consumed, smelled, or rubbed on. The resulting explanation for the rule that the sacrificer must partake of a portion of the sacrificial food is further confirmed by the exceptions: those cases in which this consumption was avoided.

Greek sacrificial ritual prohibited the consumption of sacrifices intended for the **Manes** <note>The spirits of deceased ancestors</note> or for **chthonic** <note>Underworld</note> deities, as well as **piacular** <note>original: "Piacularopfer"; sacrifices made to atone for a sin or appease divine anger</note> sacrifices; in these instances, the offerings were presented as **holocausts** <note>original: "Holokausten"; here used in the original Greek sense of a "whole-burnt" offering where the entire animal is consumed by fire and none is eaten by the worshippers</note>. The underlying idea is clearly that the consumption, which is otherwise health-bringing, would in these cases instead be dangerous due to the contact of such a sacrifice with sinister or angry deities.

We find something quite similar in the ritual of the **Veda** <note>The oldest layer of Sanskrit literature and the foundation of Hindu ritual</note>. Sacrifices to sinister beings, such as the souls of the dead or **Rudra** <note>A fierce Vedic deity associated with storms, the hunt, and unpredictable danger</note>, are surrounded by manifold precautionary measures, among which the avoidance of consuming the sacrificial food is particularly prominent. "He consumes nothing of it . . . thereby he makes it something consecrated to the Fathers," says a **Brāhmaṇa** <note>A ritual commentary on the Vedas</note>¹). In the ritual of the flour-ball offering <note>The Piṇḍapitṛyajña, where dumplings are offered to ancestors</note> to be presented to the **Manes**, it is indeed prescribed that the dumplings laid out for the ancestors are afterwards placed in a bowl and the sacrificer smells them instead of eating them: "that is the portion of the sacrificer (in the sacrificial food)"—says a **Brāhmaṇa**²). Evidently, this represents

***

¹) *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* XII, 5, 1, 12.
²) *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* II, 4, 2, 24; compare *Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra* IV, 1, 20. — One should compare the materials belonging to an analogous context in *Kātyāyana* V, 9, 13 ff.; *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* II, 6, 1, 33; *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* VIII, 16, 3. 12.

->### The Share of the Sacrificer and the Priests in the Sacrificial Food ###<-

Smelling represents a compromise between the dread of a food that has been in contact with the dead and the rule that the sacrificer is to partake of the sacrificial food¹). We find something similar in a sacrifice through which someone who wishes for death <note>Referencing rituals performed by those seeking a transition to the next life or a spiritual end</note> achieves their goal. Here it is prescribed: from the introductory consecration <note>original: "Weihe"</note> onwards, one may only smell what would otherwise be eaten²). Here, too, it is the connection to death that excludes the actual consumption of the sacrificial food.

Occasionally, the view arises that the same consumption which a person better prepared through consecrations may safely risk is, for the less prepared, replaced by smelling. This occurs during an offering of sour milk³), which is connected to the **Pravargya** ceremony <note>A highly potent Vedic ritual involving a heated clay pot and milk, considered so powerful it was originally kept secret</note>—a rite affected by a certain "holy eeriness" and therefore passed down as secret knowledge. While the priests who have received the **Dīkshā** initiation <note>A formal consecration or "spiritual rebirth" required before participating in major sacrifices</note> eat from the sacrificial remains here, the others are—if not strictly required, then at least encouraged—to limit themselves to "breath-consumption" <note>original: "Athemgenuss"</note>, that is, the smelling of the food⁴).

Regarding the cattle sacrifice to **Rudra** <note>The fierce, unpredictable Vedic god of storms and the wilderness</note>, the dangerous god, it is prescribed: "He shall not eat of it. One shall bring nothing of it into the village"—the sacrifice having been performed at a place invisible from the village—"for this god lies in wait for living beings. He shall keep his people far from the vicinity of the sacrificial site"⁵). The reason for not consuming the sacrificial food could hardly be more evident than it is here; the

# Avoidance of Consuming the Sacrificial Food #

The abstinence in question is simply one of many precautionary measures necessitated by the dangerous nature of certain sacrifice-receiving beings¹), just as the previously mentioned relocation of the **Rudra sacrifice** <note>A ritual dedicated to Rudra, the fierce Vedic god of storms and the precursor to Shiva</note> to a spot that cannot be seen from the village—meaning Rudra also cannot see the village from there—is another such measure. The obvious conclusion from the materials collected here is in full harmony with our other results. If the consumption of the sacrificial food by humans is omitted during sacrifices to beings such as **Rudra** <note>A fierce Vedic deity associated with storms and disease, the precursor to the god Shiva</note> or the souls of the deceased, then it cannot have been the communal meal between man and god—and the brotherhood based on that community—which formed the actual and essential center of the sacrifice. From the **Vedic** <note>Relating to the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note> sacrificial ritual at least, that supposedly fundamental idea of sacrifice would have disappeared. As for the opinion that this idea nonetheless lay at the foundation of later developments in the unimaginably distant past, it is poorly supported by the fact that the actual appearance of the customs in the **Veda**—which would have once been permeated by this idea—suggests simple, clearly coherent interpretations of their own, independent of that hypothesis.

## Magic Fire, Sacrificial Litter, and Sacrificial Fire.
### The Triple Sacrificial Fire.

**Ethnology** <note>The study of different peoples and their cultures</note> introduces us to an ancient form of religious rites in which there were indeed sacrifices and a sacred fire, but no *sacrificial fire*. The sacrificial gift was handed over to the god or spirit by means other than through the fire; the fire itself, not yet tasked with the messenger service between

...entrusted to both the human and spirit worlds, was initially effective only as a **magic fire** <note>German: *Zauberfeuer*; fire used for its inherent supernatural power rather than as a vehicle for offerings</note> for the scaring away of evil demons.

This magic fire now converges in the **Vedic cult** <note>The system of religious rites described in the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note> with fire in its more recent application: the **sacrificial fire**. Distinguishing between these two types is all the more difficult for us because they undoubtedly became frequently mixed and shifted against one another even for the ancients themselves at an early stage. Given the foundation of those cultic habits, which were overloaded with sacrifices of every kind, the performance of a sacred act in the presence of a blazing fire naturally led to the logical consequence that, as a rule, a sacrificial offering had to be cast into this fire. A starting point for interpreting the use of fire is provided by the rites of many **primitive peoples** <note>German: *Naturvölker*; a 19th-century ethnological term for indigenous societies or those without industrialization</note> whose cultic practices do not recognize the sacrificial fire proper. In those cultures, all important acts are usually performed in the presence of fire: during childbirth, a fire blazes next to the **woman in labor** <term>Wöchnerin: a woman in the period of confinement immediately following childbirth</term>, which protects her and the child from the predations of spirits; the ceremony through which the grown boy is accepted into the circle of men; the performance of various customs such as haircutting and the like; the offerings to gods or spirits; and finally the burial. All of these require the proximity of a fire so as not to be disturbed by evil spirits. Anyone familiar with the near-universal use of this magic fire across the earth who approaches the Vedic ritual will certainly recognize that same fire in a great many cases, even where that ritual prescribes the presentation of sacrificial offerings. The **childbed fire** <note>original: *sūtikāgni*; the fire kept in the room where a woman has recently given birth to ward off demons</note> is a custom shared with indigenous peoples.
> "One takes away," says **Hiraṇyakeśin** <note>An ancient Indian teacher and author of a *Gṛhyasūtra*, a manual for domestic religious rites</note>¹), "the domestic sacrificial fire and brings in the childbed fire. This is used only for warming (vessels and the like)."

Besides this practical purpose, however, it is naturally used above all for **magic**. The author continues:
> "Sacred acts are not performed with it, except for fumigation. He fumigates the child with small grain mixed with mustard seeds"

—and there follows a series of incantations against the evil spirits sent by the spirit-king, who wander through the village at night and drink from skulls: **Agni** <note>The Vedic god of fire, acting here as a protector</note> is to burn their lungs, liver, and heart.

And just as it watches over birth, the fire also watches over the most important stages of life for the growing Indian. The boy's hair is moistened with lukewarm water and then shorn while blessing-bestowing verses are recited. However, there is no mention of using that fire for the presentation of a sacrificial offering.
