The most prominent use of fire in this cult <note>original: *Cultus*</note> is, however, as is well known, another: as a **sacrificial fire**, it conveys the offering to the gods. To be sure, not every offering was handed over to it. In certain cases—namely where the gift was directed to water deities—one sacrificed into the water¹); in the sacrifice for the dead, pits were the receiving points for the offerings²); there were also offerings to **Rudra** <note>a storm god of the Vedic period, often considered an early form of the god Shiva</note> and Rudra-like demons, which were thrown into the air, buried in a molehill, hung from trees³), and the like. But on the whole, it can still be asserted that the Indian ritual in its present form is based entirely on the use of the sacrificial fire.

In its present form: for, I believe, even apart from the cases just cited of sacrifice in water, etc., even where fire is actually used, the trace of another preceding state still shines through clearly. We may here connect to the description which **Herodotus**⁴) <note>a Greek historian from the 5th century BCE</note> gives of the animal sacrifice of the Persians. When the Persians wish to sacrifice, he says, they do not erect altars and they do not light a fire. The sacrificer "dismembers the sacrificial animal limb by limb and boils the meat; he spreads out the softest grass, preferably clover, and places all the meat upon it. When he has laid it down, a **magus** <note>original: *Magier*; a priest of the ancient Persian religion</note> standing nearby sings the **theogony** <note>original: *Theogonie*; an account or song regarding the origin of the gods</note> over it—this is, according to their account, the accompanying chant—for they may not perform any sacrifice without a magus. The sacrificer then takes the meat away again after a short time and does with it as he pleases." ¹) The etymological meaning seems to be something like "cushion" or "padding"; compare the Sanskrit terms *upabarhaṇa* <note>a pillow or cushion</note>; *upabarhṛhat* <note>referencing a protective covering</note> Rigveda V, 61, 5; *upa barbṛhi* X, 10, 10.

During the consecrations and offerings belonging to the sacrificial ceremony, the Baresman was touched in various ways; the offering was brought near to it or poured over it (Darmesteter p. 114, 185, 189, 409, 411, 416, 421, 422, 426, 429, 436 etc.); the various parts of the Baresman, specifically the right and left sides, represented different deities: the right side represented the souls, in a perhaps not coincidental agreement with the Vedic significance of the right side (the south) as the region of the souls.

The original identity of this Baresman with the Vedic Barhis, long suspected but also frequently contested, seems to me hardly doubtful. Consider the following. Both words, even if different in their suffixes, belong in all appearance to the same linguistic root (*baresman* would be the Vedic **barhman*; it likely has nothing to do with *brahman* <note>the ultimate reality or the priestly caste</note>). Both designate a plant-based element appearing in the ritual—branches in the one case, grasses in the other; in both the Veda and the Avesta, this element is the bearer of special holiness or proximity to the divine. With the Barhis (Hillebrandt, *New and Full Moon Sacrifices*, p. 64) as with the Baresman, a binding band plays a role. Particularly important, however, is that regarding both Baresman and Barhis, the fixed verb *star* or *fra-star* (compare the Vedic *prastara* bundle, which is associated with the Barhis; Hillebrandt p. 64) is used. It is clear that *fra-star* cannot originally mean "to bind together," as the traditional translations of Justi and Darmesteter suggest; it must originally mean "to spread out" <note>cognate with the English word "strew"</note> and points with great probability to a form of the ritual which, similar to the Vedic ritual, involved a spread-out vegetable covering. (Note also that the Avestan *barezish*, which designates something like a mat or cushion and exactly corresponds to the Vedic *barhis*, is also accompanied by the verb *star*). # The Sacrificial Litter.

...is the place where the gods receive the sacrificial gift—more precisely, the essence or soul of the gift, as its physical body is later taken away by the humans. Meanwhile, on the Indian sacrificial ground, the fire flames next to the **Barhis** <note>sacred grass spread on the ground to serve as a seat for the gods</note>. This fire is the "mouth of the gods," as the **Rigveda** <note>the oldest collection of Indian Vedic hymns</note> so often describes it, through which they consume the sacrifice. Comparing Persian customs with Indian ones suggests that the Indian practice of placing the **Barhis** and the sacrificial fire side-by-side preserves a trace of an old, primitive form in which one was accustomed to handing over the offering to the god¹). On the other hand, it also represents the innovation of a more advanced sacrificial technique. The way the Vedic poets speak of—

---

—"one who has spread the **Baresman**" is exactly like the Vedic term ***stīrṇabarhis*** <note>literally "one who has spread the sacrificial grass"</note>. It is also noteworthy that in the **Avesta** <note>the sacred texts of Zoroastrianism</note>, the primary elements of sacrifice and holiness—Fire and **Baresman**, Fire, **Baresman** and **Haoma** <note>a sacred ritual drink</note>, or Libation and **Baresman**—are named together in a solemn manner. This mirrors how the **Veda** mentions the blazing fire and the spread **Barhis**, or fire, **Barhis**, and **Soma** <note>the Indian ritual equivalent of Haoma</note>, or the **Barhis** and the sacrificial offering itself (compare *Vendidad* 3, 16; *Visperad* 2; and on the other hand *Rigveda* IV, 6, 4; X, 21, 1; *Vajasaneyi Samhita* XV, 49).

By what path and for what reasons the transition occurred—from a sacrificial litter resting on the ground to the portable, sacred branches known in the **Avesta**—remains for specialists in Iranian studies to investigate. I must leave it to them to determine if the ancient **Barhis** merged here with a originally different element. Regardless of the result they reach, I do not believe that the points brought forward here regarding the connection between these two types can be dismissed. This remains true even if, in the Persian sacrifice described by **Strabo** <note>an ancient Greek geographer</note> (XV, 3, 14), one finds branches spread on the ground to receive the offering alongside the "bundle of thin tamarisk rods" <note>original Greek: *ῥάβδων μυρικίνων λεπτῶν δέσμη*</note> held in the hand. (I owe the reference to this passage, and many suggestions regarding this question, to G. Hoffmann).

¹) Compare the collections of **Tylor** (*Primitive Culture* II, 389) regarding the sacrificial methods of various indigenous peoples.

# The Sacrificial Litter.

[The offering] was placed there, where the seat of the gods was, upon the sacrificial litter, and was received by them there. Non-sedentary shepherd tribes could not believe that the presence of their gods was bound to unmovable, fixed natural landmarks; here we encounter the holy site of their ritual practice <term>cultus: the system of religious ritual and veneration</term>, the wool-soft grass carpet that could be spread out with equal ease anywhere. The presence of the god, who has been summoned onto it, hallows it—that is, it makes it dangerous for common <note>original: "profane"</note> touch: therefore, after the ritual act is finished, the Indian sacrificer throws the ***Barhis*** <note>the sacred grass spread on the ground</note> into the fire, evidently according to the original meaning to make it harmless¹).

### Magic Fire, Sacrificial Litter, and Sacrificial Fire. The Triple Sacrificial Fire.

The treatment of objects that have been affected by the **contagion** <note>original: *contagium*; refers to the belief that holiness or spiritual power can be physically transferred through touch</note> of holy or uncanny powers during sacred rites could also be significant for the history of the sacrificial fire that we are examining here. Specifically, it raises the question of whether this type of burning represents the transition—or at least *a* transition—from a sacrifice consisting of merely laying down a gift to a sacrifice performed with holy fire¹). What was to become of the gift once it was laid down, after its inner essence was believed to have been enjoyed by the gods? Whatever the god had seized could bring danger to humans. It was a natural impulse to secure oneself against this danger by burning the remains. This burning, by removing the feared object from the earth, carried it toward heaven with the upward-swirling smoke, thus—

---

> [The power] that struck the killed animal has entered into the heart-spit, says the ***Śatapatha*** <note>The *Śatapatha Brahmana*, a foundational ancient Indian text describing Vedic rituals</note> (as cited above, § 8); the original meaning is possibly that something of the "soul-substance" of the killed animal still clings to it. Other cases of burial in the context of both cult practice and magic are frequent; it may be seen as an echo of this sacred burial when the **Buddha**, approaching death, instructs **Cunda** to bury the remains of the food he offered—the last meal the Buddha enjoyed (*Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* page 41, Childers edition). No firm boundary can be drawn between burying and burning; it is not only in the treatment of human corpses that we find both procedures side by side (compare the ***Pāraskara*** <note>A manual of domestic religious rules</note> III, 8, 12 in the ritual of the cattle sacrifice to **Rudra**: "he throws the intestines smeared with blood into the fire, or they bury them in the ground"). Finally, alongside burying and burning, we should mention washing or washing away in water. This is used similarly to remove impure, ghostly, or disease-bringing substances, as well as to dispose of those "fluids" which carry the holiness—and therefore the danger—emanating from the gods. Reference is made here to the discussion on the sacrificial bath (***avabhṛtha***) (further below in the section "**Dīkṣā** <note>consecration</note> and Sacrificial Bath").

### The Fire of Removal and the Sacrificial Fire.

...to that place where the most distinguished deities had their habitual residence. Thus, the transition from disposal via fire to offering via fire is natural and obvious. In one respect, however, this transition brings about a contradiction. People imagined the gods descending onto the **Barhis** <note>A sacred mat of grass spread out during Vedic rituals for the gods to sit upon</note> to enjoy the sacrifice, yet simultaneously sent the sacrificial food up to their heavenly dwelling. That the first side of this dilemma represents the older as well as the more deeply rooted way of thinking is beyond doubt. But in quite a few passages of the *Rigveda* <note>The "Knowledge of Verses," the oldest collection of Hindu hymns</note> we also encounter the other view¹). The contradiction inherent here perhaps emerges nowhere as sharply as where a poet from the family of the **Vasishthas** <note>A famous lineage of Vedic seers or rishis</note>, wavering between the two points of view, says:

> “Agni, lead the gods here so that they may enjoy the sacrificial food. May they rejoice here with Indra as their head. Bring this sacrifice to heaven, to the gods. Protect us always with prosperity” (VII, 11, 5). —

Our previous discussions have already taught us about two types of fire usage preserved in the **Vedic cult** <note>The system of rituals described in the Vedas, centered on fire sacrifice and hymns</note>, which can easily be understood as precursors to the sacrificial fire: the **magic fire** flaming alongside the sacred action to scare off evil spirits, and the fire that consumes the remains of the sacrifice and the like, which have become dangerous to humans through divine contact. Another rite preserved in the Vedic cult, which might likewise have gained a certain significance in the evolutionary history of the sacrificial fire, is the burning of certain parts of the sacrificial animal for the purpose of creating a scent that attracts the gods²). In the state of the ritual currently before us, however, the single fire, "the domestic," and the three fires stand independently alongside one another. # The One and the Three Sacrificial Fires.

Additionally, the establishment of the three fires signifies the founding of a larger **cult center**; numerous **Brahmins** <note>Members of the priestly caste in ancient India</note>, sacrificial priests, and others residing in the home of the **patron of the sacrifice** <note>The *Yajamana*, or the individual who pays for and benefits from the ritual</note> gather at such a center¹). Certain main ceremonies are common to the ritual of the one fire and that of the three: the daily morning and evening offerings, and the celebration of the **New Moon** and **Full Moon**, are performed in essentially the same way with one fire as with three, though the former uses a simpler form. This is a **sacral doublet** <note>A situation where two different versions of the same ritual exist simultaneously</note> that is quite likely to be considered a secondary development rather than an original practice. Other actions, however, belong only to one sphere or the other; for instance, the consecrations belonging to family life <note>Known as *Samskaras*, such as birth or marriage rites</note> are performed only with the single fire, while the **Soma sacrifice** <note>The most prestigious Vedic ritual, involving the juice of the Soma plant</note> is performed only with the three fires²).

Regarding the specific nature of the three fires, it has been expressed not as a mere conjecture but as a self-evident certainty³) that one should see in them the fusion of three different **fire services** <note>Distinct traditions or lineages of fire worship</note>. This idea is plausible, but I can find nothing in the actual conditions of the **Vedic ritual** <note>The system of ancient Indian ceremonies described in the Vedas</note> that would confirm it—not even traces of such a distribution of sacred acts among the various fires that would allow the tasks linked to each fire to be imagined as the exclusive **sacral property** of any one particular group of priests⁴). # Magical Fire, Sacrificial Strew, and Sacrificial Fire. The Triple Sacrificial Fire.

All three fires work together during the same rites, such that a specific character dominates, or at least prevails, in the role of each. At the head stands the *Gārhapatya fire* <term>original: Gārhapatyafeuer; the "fire of the householder"</term>, which is clearly the representative of the ancient domestic and hearth fire; it alone is maintained constantly, and from it the other two fires are newly taken for every sacrifice in which they are required. A person setting out on a journey first takes leave of the *Gārhapatya*, then from the *Āhavanīya fire* (see below); on the other hand, the one returning home first greets the *Āhavanīya*, then the *Gārhapatya fire*: the latter is thus regarded, in a sense, as being in the center, so that one leaves it first and returns to it last¹). The second fire already touched upon here, the *Āhavanīya fire* <term>original: Āhavanīyafeuer; the "fire of offerings"</term>, is situated to the east. A *Brāhmaṇa* <note>A category of Vedic instructional texts that explain the meaning and practice of rituals</note>³) points out the difference between the two²) in the following words:

> "That is the *Āhavanīya*. It is not there so that one may cook in it what is uncooked. Rather, it is there so that one may sacrifice in it that which is already cooked."

The *Gārhapatya* therefore serves, so to speak, as the fire for practical, human use, such as for preparations like the cooking of the sacrificial food, the heating of the vessels⁴), and the like; the *Āhavanīya* is the flame in which the gods [receive] the—

As a domestic fire, it is also recommended—and this is perhaps the most widespread regulation regarding this—to maintain the fire into which the sacrificer, as a Brahmin student <note>a young man studying the Vedas under a teacher</note>, placed a log for the last time as part of his student duty, or the fire with which the wedding ceremonies were performed for him. # The Laying of the Holy Fires.

During the four-month festivals that accompany the course of the seasons, and at the Soma sacrifice <note>a central Vedic ritual involving the pressing and offering of the juice of the Soma plant</note>, a new fire is kindled by friction and united with the old *Āhavanīya* <note>the eastern-most of the three sacred fires, used for offerings to the gods</note>¹): this is evidently an act of refreshment and strengthening, and possibly also a remnant of a treatment of the holy fire different from the one prevailing in the traditional ritual—namely, its periodic replacement with a new fire.

Allowing the old fires to go out and, perhaps after an interval, laying new ones was considered necessary whenever the old ones had brought no luck to the sacrificer; one then celebrated the ceremony of "re-laying" (*punarādheya*).

### **Sacrificial Food and Sacrificial Drink.**

In the field of Vedic sacrifice, the natural principle is also confirmed that man offers to the god exactly what is welcome to him as his own food²). There are exceptions here and there, but this is clearly the rule.

If we initially set aside animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice, we encounter as sacrificial food all the main products of agriculture and livestock breeding: at the head of the list is milk in its various states (sour milk, etc.), butter, and the two most noble grains, barley and rice³), which were processed into various cooked and baked dishes. The correspondence between the properties of the god and the gift brought to him, already mentioned regarding non-animal sacrifices, emerges much more distinctly in animal sacrifice. A clear tendency—though by no means without exception²)—is evident to make the sacrificial animal mirror the god, above all in gender, but also in color and other characteristics.³) This phenomenon, which also recurs among indigenous peoples <note>German: *Naturvölkern*; a historical term for non-industrialized or tribal societies</note>, is perhaps not fully explained by the somewhat vague idea that the god is particularly pleased to see the animal that resembles him. For example, in the offering of a black sacrificial animal to obtain rain: "it is black, for this is the essence of rain; with that which is its essence, one wins the rain for oneself."³) A blood-red sacrificial animal is offered by priests dressed in red and wearing red turbans when the goal is the destruction of an enemy.⁴) Such a practice is not a late priestly over-refinement, but rather bears the stamp of the most ancient magical practices.

The sacrificial animal was killed using expressions—similar to those found among other peoples—intended to keep the participants free from the guilt of a blood-deed. The animal was told that it was not dying: "You do not die, no harm comes to you; you go to the gods on beautiful paths" (Ṛv. I, 162, 21). The act of killing was euphemistically called "gaining the animal's consent." The killing was carried out by suffocation or strangulation without bloodshed; in doing so, they sought to avoid the animal making a sound

...uttered; the main participants of the sacrifice turned their backs until the death of the animal had occurred.

The parts of the sacrificial animal dargebracht <note>offered</note> to the god are divided in a very striking way into two masses, the offering of which constitutes two completely separate acts of the sacrificial ritual. Once the animal has been killed, an incision is first made through which the *omentum* <note>original: *netz*; the fatty membrane or "caul" surrounding the internal organs, which is the richest in fat</note> is pulled out¹). This is cooked and offered with all solemnity. The ritual texts prescribe the distribution of gifts to the priests and acts of purification after this action²); it is clear that a transition or break is made here. Afterward, the rest of the animal is carved up, and after first offering a rice cake, portions of the individual parts are sacrificed to the god³). Other portions are consumed by the priests. What remains is distributed among the priests, the sacrificer, or any Brahmins <note>the priestly caste of ancient India</note> who desire it⁴), except for the tail piece, which is reserved for a concluding ceremony primarily dedicated to the wives of the gods. Thus, the offering of the omentum and the offering of portions from all other suitable body parts form two separate actions. For the sake of illustration, I will share a few more sentences from Āśvalāyana's⁵) description of the Ashṭakā <note>A specific seasonal festival or rite in the Vedic calendar</note>—

I cannot resist the suspicion that we have here the last remnant of an ancient, even more pronounced preference for the omentum; specifically, that there was a time when, of the entire animal, the omentum was—I will not say the only part given to the god—but at least the only part burned for the god. <margin>¹) XV, 732. ...offered on the altar, the rest eaten by the priests. In the thank offering¹⁾ <note>Also known as a peace offering or *Shelamim*, where the meal was shared between God, the priest, and the worshiper</note>, the fatty portions were offered on the altar: “it is a fire for a sweet savor to the Lord”; the remainder partly falls to the priests, and partly is consumed by the offerer with his family and guests. — We turn our gaze here to the sacrificial customs currently practiced among the Zulu people, as described by native witnesses heard by Callaway²⁾. They kill the sacrificial bull and skin it. Then they take some of the fat from the omentum <note>The fatty tissue surrounding the internal organs</note> and burn it with incense; the house is filled with the scent of the burning omentum, and they believe then that they have prepared a sweet savor for the spirits of their people. The meat of the sacrificial animal, however, is laid down; the spirits come and eat of it. In the morning, it is found untouched, but the spirits have licked it. —

From all this, the burning of the omentum is clearly explained quite independently of the burning or non-burning of the rest of the animal's body, and independent of the idea that the deity's food must be sent to them in the form of sacrificial steam. Fat vapors are produced for the god “for a sweet savor”³) even in an age that is still accustomed to laying out the actual sacrificial meat for the god and then, after the deity has invisibly claimed their portion, handing it over for human consumption: this method of treating the sacrifice, observed among many indigenous peoples, has also left its traces in the Indian ritual, as we attempted to show above (p. 341 ff.). # The Sacrifice of the Omentum #

In the present use of fire for the purpose of generating scent, we may perhaps once again recognize one¹) of the starting and ending points from which fire attained its significance as a sacrificial flame—acting as a carrier of offerings to the heavenly dwellings of their recipients.

The blood of the sacrificial animal was poured out in the Vedic ritual for the <term>Rakshas (demonic beings in Indian mythology who often disrupt rituals)</term>²). The possibility cannot be denied that this contains a remnant of sacrificial forms from an ancient time in which the consumption of blood played a significant role. However, the explanation may also lie closer to the surface. Just as the waste products of the grain used in a pastry sacrifice were thrown to the Rakshas³), so the blood may have been left to them as waste, a way to pay off the "lower folk" of the spirit world⁴). In this, the conception of these beings—who prey upon life and health—as bloodsuckers likely played a part as well.

In connection with animal sacrifice, the question of the existence of human sacrifice in the Vedic period must also be touched upon here⁵). The only completely reliable trace of this seems to me to be that which concerns the so-called <term>building sacrifice (the practice of placing a victim in the foundations of a new structure to ensure its permanence)</term>. Among the ritual instructions for the construction of the brick fire altar—which, as is well known, was surrounded by particular ceremonial pomp—known as the <term>Agnicayana (the 'piling of the fire-altar')</term>, one finds the rule that five sacrificial animals—man, horse, ox, ram, goat—are to be offered to various gods.

### Sacrificial Food and Sacrificial Drink ###

The most distinguished offering of the Vedic cult is **Soma**. In the sacrifice, man does not only satisfy the hunger and thirst of the god, but he also helps him to achieve an intoxication in which the man then participates himself. We have already noted in another context that the idea of the intoxicating drink of the gods, especially the thunder god, and in connection with that—as can be concluded with full certainty—the use of such a drink in the cult, can with great probability be traced back to the <term>Indo-European (the ancient common ancestors of many European and Indian cultures)</term> age and related to an intoxicating honey-mead characteristic of that time (p. 175 ff.). We saw that in the Indo-Iranian period, the pressed juice of the **Soma plant**²) took the place of the honey drink; it was provided with various additions, among which the addition of milk stands out particularly; it

# The Soma. #

undoubtedly dates back to the Indo-Iranian period¹). In the Veda, the Soma drink is frequently called *madhu* ("honey"): the obvious assumption has been made that the <term>Indo-European (the ancestral language and culture of many European and Indian peoples)</term> name for honey-mead (*medhu*) was inherited here for the altered drink, much like the Greeks, who had transitioned from mead to wine, yet preserved the old name *methy* <note>original: μέθυ</note> for the latter. This assumption may be correct; however, it seems to me that another explanation for that naming of Soma is also possible and, for several reasons, even probable. To the Vedic poets, the words honey, honey-rich, and the like are very common for liquids they wish to describe as sweet or generally pleasant. Honey—that is, sweet milk—dwells in the cow; butter is called honey-rich or simply honey; even the waves of the water and the air are called honey-rich. All kinds of imaginative wordplay are attached to the substance of honey, the preeminent carrier of sweetness for the Vedic age. 

According to this, even without the aid of the Indo-European honey-mead, it is entirely understandable from the Veda alone if Soma is named there as honey or honey-rich; regardless of how it might have actually tasted, pious expression naturally could not help but praise its sweet flavor. This applies fully to the Soma that was actually mixed with sweet substances, such as milk or honey, as well as in cases where particular mythological qualities of the deity in question led the poet’s imagination toward the idea of honey²). Regarding its distribution among the deities, it appears mainly in the cult of the <term>Ashvins (the divine twins of the Vedic pantheon)</term>. It is also likely that the mixing of honey with Soma represents a simple sweetening, similar to that with milk, whose connection to the prehistoric divine honey-drink is entirely doubtful.

Is it then the case that Soma was ever a popular drink of the <term>Aryan (the ancient Indo-Iranian)</term> people? I doubt it, and yet I believe I do not truly contradict the principle that man gives to the god in sacrifice what is a pleasure for himself. One must consider that, by all appearances, the role assigned to Soma in the ritual was not invented for it first. It inherited this role from an older drink, entering a situation that was already complete and hieratically <note>sacred or priestly</note> established. # Soma. Inedible Offerings. #

We conclude this overview of sacrificial foods and drinks with the remark that here and there—this point was already touched upon during the discussion of the sacrifice of donkeys and horses—substances that are neither edible nor drinkable are presented as sacrificial offerings or added to them. Various magical manipulations performed with an object can, under the hands of zealous ritualists, transform into the "sacrificing" of that object. The sacrifice can be regarded as a magical means to transport a substance into the sacrificer or into other beings, or otherwise to bring it into their possession. Whoever desires a long life offers a hundred nails made of <term>Khadira wood (the wood of the *Acacia catechu* tree, known for its hardness)</term> on the night of the full moon: perhaps as a "nailing down" of life through the hundred years that one desires. ### **The Sacrificer and the Priests.**

The center around which the Vedic <term>cult (the system of ritual worship)</term> moves is the sacrificial fire, or the three sacrificial fires of the individual: the <term>yajamāna (the person who pays for and benefits from a sacrifice)</term> or "lord of sacrifice" (*yajñapati*) is this individual, not a tribal or political association. When it is stated in numerous passages of the <term>Ṛgveda (the oldest collection of sacred hymns)</term> that "the Vasiṣṭhas pray to <term>Agni (the god of fire)</term>," or that "<term>Indra (the king of the gods)</term> is praised by the Bharadvājas during the pressing of <term>Soma (the sacred ritual drink)</term>," and such, this does not point to the <note>original: "sacra"</note> sacred rites of those specific clans. Instead, it only means that <term>Brahmans (the priestly caste)</term> from the house of the Vasiṣṭhas or Bharadvājas officiated at sacrifices for wealthy, presumably royal organizers, and composed these hymns for that purpose. Given the general circumstances of Indian public life, the community as such—the state—is the least conceivable entity as an organizer of sacrifice. There are indeed sacrifices which, by their nature, are offered for the welfare, or at least partly for the welfare, of the whole. In these cases, the organizer of the sacrifice in the technical sense is the King. This is true of the <term>Horse Sacrifice (a grand royal ritual to assert sovereignty)</term>, where a characteristic prayer shows that it was not about the welfare of the King alone, but also about that of the people. The <term>Adhvaryu (the priest responsible for the physical manual labor of the ritual)</term> prayed:

> "In holiness may the Brahman be born, full of the radiance of holiness. In royal power may the prince be born, a hero, a marksman, a strong striker,"

As far as the "third estate" <note>the *Vaishyas*, or commoner class of farmers and merchants</note> is concerned, it is telling that the farmer himself is not mentioned; instead, the "high lords" were more interested in the fields and the livestock. However, there was no ritual form through which one could have prayed and sacrificed in the name of the "people" as a collective; the <term>Horse Sacrifice (Ashvamedha)</term> was and remained exclusively a sacrifice of the King.

It would require an investigation into ancient Indian constitutional and private law to explore these brief suggestions further. Here, I will only point out what is—as far as I can see—the only exception (and one hardly worth calling significant) to the rule that the sacrificer is an individual: it concerns those <term>Soma (a sacred ritual drink)</term> sacrifice complexes that extend over a long period, often a year, known as <term>Sattra (literally "sessions")</term>. In these, a number of Brahmans joined together in such a way that, while they divided the usual priestly functions among themselves, each of them was considered an equal "Lord of the Sacrifice." This was based on an agreement such as the following:

> "Whatever we shall gain through this ceremony, through this animal sacrifice, that belongs to us together. Good deeds belong to us together. But if anyone does something evil, that belongs to him alone"²).

# The Sacrificer and the Priests.

...be viewed as a sacrifice, it would be premature to attempt to decide. —

Standing beside the performer of the <term>cult (the system of religious worship)</term> are the priests he has commissioned to act on his behalf. "Every petition that the priests make during the sacrifice belongs solely to the sacrificer¹)."

We now know how far removed Vedic India was from an ideal state of "childlike freedom," in which every person would have felt entitled to approach the deity as their own priest without any outside mediation. The ancient custom of employing specific individuals—those endowed with special knowledge and particular "magical" qualities—to mediate the interactions with spirits and gods (an interaction filled with difficulties and dangers) had already led to the formation of a more or less distinct priestly class, indeed a <term>priestly caste</term>, in the pre-Vedic period. The <term>Rigveda (the oldest collection of Hindu hymns)</term> shows us a specific circle of families, such as the **Vasishthas**, **Vishvamitras**, and **Bharadvajas**, who were the masters of the art of proper sacrifice and prayer. We will not attempt here to provide a full picture of the social status of this **Brahman caste**; however, the role played by these priests in the ritual cult must occupy our close attention.

At this point, we should first point out the obvious consequence of the principle just discussed—namely, that because Vedic India knew no **public sacred rites** <note>original Latin: *sacra publica*</note>, there were naturally no **public priests** <note>original Latin: *sacerdotes publici*</note>. In particular, the type of priestly "college" or formal assembly—such as the Roman **Pontifices** <note>the highest-ranking priests in the Roman state</note> or the **Salii** <note>the "leaping priests" of the god Mars</note>—was entirely absent, and for good reason. Such a state-authorized continuity of the keepers of specific priestly knowledge or skills would have required a level of organized public life that was foreign to the Vedic people.

---

<page-num>373</page-num>

# The Priests.

Distantly comparable to those <term>colleges (organized groups of priests with specific duties)</term> is perhaps what may have actually formed their prototype: the circle of the priestly family or the priestly clan created by nature, such as the aforementioned **Vasishthas** and **Vishvamitras**. An essential difference, however, is that each of those ancient corporate bodies held its own specific branch of sacral functions as its sole owner or sole authority, whereas the Vedic priestly families, by and large, practiced the same <term>cult (system of religious worship)</term>—primarily the same **Soma cult** <note>The ritual preparation and offering of the sacred Soma juice</note>—following the same basic procedures.

Differences between the families did nonetheless exist, which would certainly prove to be all the greater the further back in time we could trace the situation; and presumably, if our tradition were more favorable, many a special cult and specific rite held in the possession of individual families would come to light alongside the main cult common to all¹). Clearly, however, the entire development moved toward the disappearance of these peculiarities.

Contributing to this on one hand may have been that the connection of the cult with a specific holy site or a specific holy object—the entire spirit of cultic local traditions rooted in the soil—seems to have been only weakly developed, if not entirely absent. On the other hand, that general equalization will have been promoted precisely by the absence of a state organism which—as happened in the ancient <term>commonwealths (such as the Greek or Roman city-states)</term>—would have placed cultic specialties in the service of the whole and thereby preserved them in their unique character. Thus, with the increasingly decisive retreat of the family, all weight finally fell entirely upon the individual; his concern was

In this context, a new distinction replaced the old family differences, though it was of a fundamentally different nature: the ever-increasing scope of ritual science inevitably brought about specialization. The "**triple knowledge**" <note>This refers to the *Trayi Vidya*: the Rigveda for reciting, the Samaveda for singing, and the Yajurveda for the physical ritual actions</note> of the reciting, the singing, and the performing priests diverged, leaving it open to the individual to choose his field of study.

The relationship between the sacred patron and the priest he employed took two main forms: the priest functioned either as a **house priest** (**Purohita**) or as a **sacrificial priest** (**Ṛtvij**). That is to say, he either managed the administration of the <term>cult (system of worship)</term> performed in the name of a royal lord, or he filled one of the specific priestly positions prescribed for a single, individual sacrifice.

The **Purohita**, in the ordinary sense of the word, is thought of entirely as being in the service of a king, just as, conversely, the king is thought of as employing a **Purohita**. "Now concerning the position of the **Purohita**," says a **Brāhmaṇa**¹) <note>A category of Vedic prose texts explaining ritual</note>. "The gods do not eat the food of a king who has no **Purohita**. Therefore, if a king wishes to sacrifice, he should make a Brahmin his **Purohita**, so that the gods will eat his food." Occasionally, of course, **Purohitas** are mentioned in a broader sense: for instance, in the regulation that at the point in the sacrifice where, for a patron of the **Brahmin caste**, his ancestors are named as sacrificers blessed by **Agni** <note>The god of fire and the messenger between gods and men</note>

It provides us—especially when we supplement the information from the **Vedic** ritual and legal texts with the rich non-Vedic materials, notably those of Buddhist narrative literature and the great Epics²)—with a clear picture of the status of such a spiritual-courtly dignitary.

The King appoints the **Purohita**³), who seems, as a rule, to have held his office as long as the King’s and his own life lasted. Narrative literature frequently has the son become **Purohita** after the father’s death; thus, a certain degree of heredity seems to have developed—though whether this was already the case in the **Vedic** period remains an open question—even if it was more a matter of fact than a legally established rule. The relationship between King and **Purohita** is likened almost to a marriage; the act of appointment is made similar to a wedding, in that the same verse is prescribed for it with which the bridegroom must take the hand of the bride: "I am he, you are she; you are she, I [am he]..." <note>original: "Der bin ich, das bist du; das bist du, der [ich bin]". It shows the <term>Purohita</term> in the highest splendor with the King, sitting behind him on the state elephant as they solemnly ride around the city—the <term>Purohita</term> who, alone with the Queen and a servant, accompanies the King as he flees a besieged city—and even the wicked <term>Purohita</term> who is struck down by the people alongside a wicked King. Everywhere, the <term>Purohita</term> stands in the closest proximity to the King, showered with glory and wealth.

There is no doubt that such splendor was already granted to the <term>Purohita</term> in **Vedic** times; even then, this dignity was the highest goal of aspiration for a <term>Brahmin</term>. However, the absolute peak was reached by those who—as is attested in several cases—united the <term>Purohita</term> dignity of two or three kingdoms within themselves. Such a position would be unthinkable without the overwhelming development of a priestly prestige that towered far above weakly developed royal personalities. It lies in the nature of things that such goals were most accessible to the most skillful and unscrupulous intriguers, and that achieving them predestined the lucky winner to play a leading role in the machinery of courtly cabals.

The <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>The oldest of the sacred Hindu scriptures</note> already identifies the entire prosperity of the kingship as resting upon the <term>Purohita</term>, the "Guardian of the Kingdom," as an ancient saying calls him; "the King rules securely...

# The Purohita.

"In a cozy home, there flows an ever-swelling abundance of food, and the subjects bow willingly to him before whom a <term>Brahmin</term> <note>A member of the highest, priestly caste in Hindu society</note> goes," says that <term>Veda</term> <note>Ancient Indian sacred scriptures; specifically the Rig Veda IV, 50, 8</note> with a clear view toward the dignity of the <term>Purohita</term>, the "one placed in front." In detail, the image provided by legal texts and narratives regarding the political and general public activity of the <term>Purohita</term> does not possess perfectly defined outlines; this is quite natural given the fluid nature of ancient Indian state administration, which was not bound by fixed legal norms. The <term>Purohita</term> is expected to be knowledgeable in law and government, to stand at the forefront of all state business, and to advise the King, who in turn should act according to his counsel. We find him instructing the King—specifically teaching him the sacred texts—judging in the King’s name, and both imposing penances and deciding matters of property. During a change of government, in cases of difficult succession, he can intervene and take the necessary measures.

It is not appropriate here to touch upon these duties and rights of the <term>Purohita</term>'s office except by way of a brief indication. We must primarily concern ourselves with its sacral side, in which the root of its entire power lies. It is likely not saying too much to describe the <term>Purohita</term> in a sacral sense as the King’s *other self* <note>original: "alter ego"</note>. We have already mentioned the invocation of **Agni** <note>The Hindu god of fire and messenger to the gods</note>, in which, at the point where the ancestors of the sacrificer were to be named, the ancestors of the <term>Purohita</term> were named instead. During the <term>Horse Sacrifice</term> <note>original: "Rossopfer"; a major Vedic ritual (Ashvamedha) used by kings to assert their sovereign empire</note>, the King—at least according to the view of some teachers—is meant to perform certain offerings using the sacrificial fires of the <term>Purohita</term>¹). In the fasting through which the King must atone for errors in the administration of criminal justice, the <term>Purohita</term> is also expected to participate²).

The main point, however, is that the highest orders for all royal sacrifices and other ritual acts must originate from him. With the most varied variations, the ritual texts tell how the gods, when things went poorly for them in their battle against the demons, turned to their <term>Purohita</term> <note>A court priest and spiritual advisor</note>, the god <term>Bṛhaspati</term> <note>The divine priest who serves the gods in Hindu mythology</note>: "Find for us a sacrificial act through which we may gain victory over the demons." We cannot conclude these remarks about the Purohita without pointing out that attempts have been made to derive the entire existence of the <term>Brahmin caste</term> with its monopoly on worship from the privileged position of this priestly official. This view, unless significantly modified, hardly hits the mark. The separation of a hereditary priestly class is, as we have seen, a completed—presumably long-completed—fact in the <term>Rigvedic</term> <note>referring to the era of the Rigveda, the oldest of the four Vedas</note> period. Thus, such a development could only be derived, if at all, from the towering influence of pre-Vedic, perhaps pre-Indian Purohitas. Yet it is neither provable nor probable that the influence of such royal sacrificial officials was more than one contribution among others to that naturally developing process of priestly knowledge and skill becoming hereditary, and thus to the formation of the Brahmin caste—

---

...to suffer from the criticism that the word *brahman* is understood by him with all too great a preference as a technical priestly designation (cf. below p. 396 note 1). Likewise, the passage in the <term>Taittirīya Saṃhitā</term> <note>a collection of sacred hymns and ritual instructions</note> I, 8, 9, 1 (which G. <note>likely referring to the scholar Karl Friedrich Geldner</note> did not take into account) seems to me to prove nothing; it lists *brahman* and *rājanya* <note>the noble or warrior class, later known as Kshatriya</note> in the same context in which the <term>Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa</term> <note>an important prose commentary on the ritual</note> V, 3, 1, 2 names the *purohita* and the *sūyamāna* <note>the one being consecrated or the patron of the sacrifice</note>.

->### The Purohita. The Ṛtvijas.<-

...should have provided. From the <term>Vedic</term> <note>referring to the era of the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, c. 1500–500 BCE</note> perspective, at any rate, the dignity of the <term>Purohita</term> <note>the private chaplain and advisor to a king</note> does not appear as the root, but conversely as the consequence of the existence of the <term>Brahmin caste</term>. It is a consequence of the principle that one is only qualified to manage cultic affairs through birth within certain families. It remains probable enough, however, that those influential court officials played a significant role in the gradual increase of Brahmanical caste pride and Brahmanical claims to status. —

After the Purohita, let us consider the second type of representatives commissioned by a patron of sacrifice: the sacrificial priests (<term>ṛtvijas</term>), who are to be chosen for the individual sacrifice and who appear at every sacrifice in a specific number and with strictly defined duties.

We may find the oldest list of sacrificial priests¹) in a verse of the **Rigveda** (II, 1, 2), in which <term>Agni</term> <note>the god of fire, who acts as the divine priest</note> is identified with all of them in sequence: "Yours, Agni, is the office of the <term>Hotar</term> <note>the reciter of hymns</note>; yours is the office of the <term>Potar</term> <note>the 'Purifier' priest</note> according to the order; yours is the office of the <term>Neshtar</term> <note>the 'Leader' or 'Messenger' priest</note>; you are the <term>Agnidh</term> <note>the fire-kindler</note> of the pious; yours is the office of the <term>Praśāstar</term> <note>the 'Instructor' or director</note>; you perform the service of the <term>Adhvaryu</term> <note>the priest who performs the physical ritual actions</note>; and you are the <term>Brahman</term> <note>the high priest overseeing the whole rite</note> and the master of the house in our home" ²) — thus, if we omit the "master of the house" (the patron of the sacrifice), there are seven priests. These are likely the "seven Hotars" so often mentioned in the **Rigveda**, whose number is connected to that of the seven <term>Ṛshis</term> <note>the seven mythical 'Seers' or sages</note>, the mythical ancestors of the great Brahmin families.

->**The Sacrificer and the Priests.**<-

This same **sevenfold number** of priests has also been preserved in various parts of the later sacrificial ritual—appearing either directly or clearly visible beneath the surface—within both the spoken formulas and the actual ritual performance. For example, in the appointment of priests which the <term>Adhvaryu</term> <note>the "officiating priest" responsible for the physical labor and manual steps of the sacrifice</note> performs during the morning pressing of the <term>Soma</term> sacrifice¹) <note>a central Vedic ritual involving the pressing and offering of the juice of the sacred Soma plant</note>: this appointment extends to the <term>Hotar</term> <note>the priest who recites the hymns</note>, the two Adhvaryus, the two <term>Prashastars</term> <note>the "Directors" or assistants</note>, the <term>Brahman</term> <note>the high priest who supervises the ritual in silence</note>, the <term>Potar</term>, <term>Neshtar</term>, and <term>Agnidhra</term>. If we omit the second Adhvaryu and the second Prashastar as later additions to the original group²), we are left with the seven priests mentioned above. This provides new confirmation that this was the ancient composition of sacrificial priests: for it is indeed impossible to see what reasons in this list of priest appointments could have led to the omission of a priest who functioned with equal rights alongside those named—lower-ranking sacrificial servants are, of course, not considered here.

Likewise, a priest who was evidently added later (see below, p. 397), the <term>Achavaka</term>, addresses "the Master of the Sacrifice, Hotar, Adhvaryu, Agnidh, Brahman, Potar, Neshtar, and Upavaktar"³) in his request to be admitted to the enjoyment of Soma along with the others. Our list of priests also approximately corresponds—

# The Sacrificer and the Priests.

For the <term>Zaotar</term> <note>the chief priest and reciter of litanies in the ancient Iranian ritual</note>, there are no specific singers: a fact that deserves attention in connection with the fact that in the list of the oldest Vedic priests discussed by us, the three singers of the common Vedic ritual are likewise missing.

Let us now look at what concrete content is attached to the names of our list, and what traces of the gradual development of the cult can be read from them.

Let us focus first on the two priests in the list who are most prominent in the entire ritual, and who also lead the way in its prose formulation: the <term>Hotar</term> <note>the priest responsible for recitations and calling upon the gods</note> and the <term>Adhvaryu</term> <note>the priest responsible for the manual labor and physical steps of the ritual</note>. The difference between the two is clear and simple: the former has to recite, while the latter has to attend to the concrete actions of the sacrifice. The name of the **Hotar**, which designates the performer of the sacrificial pouring <note>the word "Hotar" is etymologically related to the Sanskrit root *hu*, meaning "to pour" or "to offer into the fire"</note>, seems to point back to an age in which it was the responsibility of one and the same priest to present the praise of the God, the invitation to the God, and to pour out the offering. In smaller offerings, this unity of the priestly function was preserved; for larger ones¹) — perhaps starting from the **Soma** ritual — the aforementioned separation of the speaker and the actual performer occurred, which is already to be established for the <term>Indo-Iranian</term> period <note>the prehistoric era before the Indian and Iranian cultures diverged</note>, so that it was the speaker who — not in accordance with the etymological meaning of the word — took over the old name of the single speaking-acting priest. It was his duty to recite the poem at the individual main offerings of the **Soma** sacrifice, which celebrated the deeds, power, and glory of the God worshipped at each time, invited him to the drink, and commended the wishes of the sacrificer to him —

---

¹) We have here the distinction of what are called the <term>juhotayas</term> and <term>yajatayas</term> <note>categories of offerings: those poured (juhoti) and those offered with a recitation (yajati)</note> in the systematic sacrificial texts of the <term>Veda</term>: in the latter, the **Hotar** speaks and the **Adhvaryu** acts; in the former, the old individual priest functions, to whom, moreover, the designation **Adhvaryu** has been transferred from the more substantial part of his duties.

<summary>This page explores the historical development of Vedic priesthood, specifically how the roles of the Hotar (reciter) and Adhvaryu (actor) split from a single original priestly function during the Indo-Iranian period. It highlights that the Hotar's name implies he was once the one who poured the offerings, a task later assigned to the Adhvaryu in complex rituals.</summary>

### The Hotar and his Recitations.

Poems (<term>uktha</term> <note>a type of recited hymn or "utterance"</note>), with which the recitation of the "rapture" (<term>mada</term> <note>referring to the state of religious exhilaration or the juice of the Soma itself</note>) was already associated in the time of the <term>Rigveda</term>¹), consist of prosaic invocations, likely composed here and there from disconnected verse fragments. These invite the God—while listing the titles of honor due to him—to intoxicate himself with the <term>Soma</term>²). At the conclusion, the **Hotar** cried out: "Ho! We offer worship to [Name of the Deity]!" <note>original: *ye yajāmahe*</note>³), and the <term>Adhvaryu</term> poured the offering into the fire.

For smaller offerings, no recitation was required, only the aforementioned sacrificial call. The later ritual, which has preserved offerings of this very form in many instances⁴), frequently has the **Hotar** accompany the offering with two individual verses in other common cases; the typical content of the first (<term>puronuvākyā</term> <note>an "invitatory" verse</note>) is the invitation to the God to approach; that of the second (<term>yājyā</term> <note>a "sacrificial" verse</note>) is an invitation to enjoy the sacrifice. It seems that of these two verses, the second was formed first; it can be viewed as an expansion emerging from the sacrificial call *ye yajāmahe*. Series of verses of this kind, which are intended for certain fixed sequences of offerings, belong to the characteristic stock of Rigvedic sacrificial poetry⁵). Associated first

# The Sacrificer and the Priests.

...verses are missing here; their type seems to be observable only in a few early stages within the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>the oldest collection of Hindu scriptures</note>¹). — It hardly needs mentioning that, besides the recitations accompanying the offerings, many other secondary tasks fell to the **Hotar** <note>the reciting priest</note>: for instance, during the <term>Soma</term> sacrifice <note>a major ritual involving the pressing of the sacred Soma plant</note>, he was primarily responsible for the great morning litany to the deities of the dawn, as well as numerous shorter recitations accompanying various phases of the sacred act²). The composers of these diverse litanies would, of course, have been the very priests who recited them. Thus, there is no doubt that we should think of the <term>Rishis</term> <note>the legendary "seers" or poets of the Vedic hymns</note> of Rigvedic poetry primarily as **Hotar** priests, or as individuals inspired to create their works by the occasions upon which they served as **Hotars**. There is also no doubt that the priest who had to devise or utter the skillfully crafted, effective word to the god was, in the consciousness of that ancient time, the most distinguished of the sacrificial priests. How else would the **Hotar**, among all the priests, have been chosen to serve as the human counterpart to **Agni**, the priestly god <note>Agni is the god of fire who acts as the divine messenger and priest</note>?

The **Hotar** is praised as "fair-tongued," while the **Adhvaryu** <note>the officiating priest who performs the physical ritual actions</note> is praised as "fair-handed." As a rule, the latter only has to speak in such a way that his consecrating formula—praying for success and warding off evil³) —marks the individual sections of his various...

# The Adhvaryu. The Agnīdh.

...manifold ritual actions. He shares these specific duties—likely in a way that was governed more by considerations of practical convenience than by fixed principles—with other priests, especially with the **Agnīdh** <note>the "fire-stoker"</note> whom we will discuss shortly. Overall, however, it is he <note>the Adhvaryu</note> who stands at the center of the concrete sacrificial work as the primary caretaker of the sacrificial fires and the <term>sacrificial grass</term> <note>the *barhis*, or kusha grass, strewn as a seat for the gods</note>, the organizer and cleanser of the ritual utensils, the preparer and offerer of the holy cakes, and the one who presses, purifies, and offers the **Soma** <note>the sacred ritual drink</note>.

# The Sacrificer and the Priests.

The situation during the **New and Full Moon sacrifices** <note>traditional ritual cycles marking the lunar phases</note>, where the **Hotar** <note>the chief reciter priest</note> touches the **Adhvaryu** <note>the ritual executive priest</note> with one hand and the **Agnīdh** <note>the fire-stoker priest</note> on the shoulder with the other, after which both of these priests sit down¹), provides a significant expression of the equality between the two²).

-># The Sacrificer and the Priests.<-

The priest who is to consume the relevant Soma offering—the <term>Agnīdh</term> <note>the "Fire-kindler" priest</note>—does so by sitting on the lap of the <term>Neshṭar</term> <note>the "Leader" priest</note>. The meaning of these latter actions is clear; however, the consumption of Soma by the priest sitting on the lap of the <term>Neshṭar</term> likely has a related significance; it must somehow involve an exchange of power between the priest who takes into himself the magic potion of the Soma dedicated to the divine wives, and the one who is about to lead the human wife to the sacrifice³). # The Singers. The Brahman.

recitations existing from antiquity and, alongside these, representing a kind of redundancy inserted for the praise of the most prominent Soma-drinking deities. Is it not, however, the case that the singing of the Soma songs itself should be denied to the ritual of the oldest priestly circle? The previously mentioned absence of the singers in the old lists of priests (p. 393)¹) as well as in the <term>Avestan</term> <note>ancient Persian sacred texts closely related to the Vedas</note> <term>Soma</term> <note>known as Haoma in the Avesta</note> ritual seems to lead to this view. But the possibility must not be overlooked that singing is older than the existence of specific singers; it would be conceivable that in ancient times, for example, the <term>Potar</term> <note>literally "the Purifier"</note> of the Soma—as his name suggests—was responsible for the performance of the songs during the purification process. Certainty on this point can, of course, not be reached.

Another priesthood, significant in later times, which I believe must be denied to the ancient period, is that of the <term>Brahman</term> <note>the silent supervising priest who monitors the entire ceremony</note>. In the ritual of the younger <term>Vedas</term> <note>the foundational sacred scriptures of ancient India</note>, the Brahman is the overseer of the entire sacrifice. He is meant to know all three Vedas; his work outweighs that of all other priests; he governs the sacrifice with thought, while they govern with the word. Sitting on the Brahman-seat next to the most prominent of the three sacrificial fires, facing this fire, stretching forth his solemnly folded hands, remaining silent himself amidst all the noise, he is the "physician of the sacrifice": all errors occurring in the vast tangle of sacred acts and recitations are reported to him, and he must make them right "as one joins limb to limb or as one ties together leather gear or something else that has come loose with a strap."

Clear traces, however, seem to suggest that this priesthood was not yet known in the oldest times.

# The Brahman.

If the term <term>Brahman</term> <note>here referring to the specific office of the supervising priest</note> is found in other technical uses, it becomes all the more probable that it did not exist in that specific technical capacity required by later periods. Finally, a tradition that appears entirely credible also points toward the relatively recent origin of this priesthood¹); according to this tradition, at one time only a member of the <term>Vasiṣṭha</term> <note>one of the most famous legendary sage-families of ancient India</note> lineage could serve as the Brahman. A certain litany, which is among the few things the Brahman must speak during the sacrifice, is said to have once been known to the descendants of Vasiṣṭha alone and—as the legendary version naturally expresses it—was revealed to Vasiṣṭha himself. One can see that we are dealing here with an innovation originating from the priestly practice of a single family—an innovation of recent date, if we may use the very modern appearance of that litany as a benchmark—which then became generally accepted. This was evidently favored by the same tendency to which it likely owes its creation: the increasingly anxious care for the scrupulous correctness of even the smallest minutiae, upon which the success of the sacrifice was believed to depend²).

## Dīkshā and the Sacrificial Bath.

A consecration of the sacrificer precedes the **Soma sacrifice** <note>the central ritual of the Vedic religion involving the pressing and offering of the sacred Soma juice</note>; corresponding to this at the conclusion of the holy act are rites which lift this consecration once again. The consecration is called **Dīkshā**, a desiderative formation <note>a grammatical form expressing a wish or desire</note> which probably means "the desire to serve the god"¹); the concluding act is called **Avabhṛtha**, i.e., "the carrying down": the sacrificer carries the pressed Soma shoots and other objects used during the sacrifice down to the water²); he cleanses them and bathes himself along with his wife and the priests.

The **Dīkshā**, initiated by a sacrifice to **Agni** <note>the god of fire</note> and **Vishṇu**³), is performed in a hut⁴) in which the sacrificer—the same applies to his wife—is bathed, shaved, and anointed, clothed in fresh garments, girded with the sacred cord, and [seats himself] on black antelope [skins]—

<margin>14, 8) seem to me to point directly to its addition in relatively recent times.</margin>

Weber (*Indische Studien* X, 358 note 1) considers a root *daṣ*, compare *daṣasyati* <note>original: "to be helpful"</note>, Latin *decus* <note>original: "grace" or "glory"</note>. More likely is *dāś* "to serve a god," which is recommended by its frequency in Vedic linguistic usage.

¹) Some texts also speak of one or two antelope skins as the upper garment of the sacrificer. The skin of the black antelope, which plays a significant role in the sacrificial ritual, is regarded in the **Brāhmaṇa** texts <note>ancient Indian commentaries on the Vedas</note> as the embodiment of holy essence (*brahman*). Sitting on this skin and clothing oneself with it would thus mean, according to the conception of the Vedic period, an impregnation of the sacrificer with the substance of holiness, just as sitting on the skin of the potent he-goat is an impregnation with generative power (cf. *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* V, 2, 1, 24). Thus the *Atharvaveda* (XI, 5, 6) describes the **Brahmacārin** <note>a student of the Vedas</note> as "clothed in the antelope skin, consecrated (*dīkshita*), with a long beard." A similar hallowing power, or one that protects against demons and impurity, evidently also belongs to the antelope horn (see immediately in the text): therefore it is also used during the royal anointing to stroke over the moistened body (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* V, 4, 2, 4; *Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra* XV, 6, 8). — Compare also the use of shoes made from the skin of the black antelope in the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* V, 4, 4, 4. — Does the sacred significance of the black antelope not ultimately go back to the frequent use of the color black (black garments, etc.) in primitive cults where the goal is to make the person invisible to pursuing evil spirits? This would be consistent, for example, with the practice of throwing sacrificial waste to the demons under the black antelope skin (Hillebrandt, *New and Full Moon Sacrifice* 171); was a darkening veil intended to be placed between them and humans? Or do totemic ideas <note>belief in a spiritual connection between humans and a specific animal</note> perhaps play a role with the black antelope (cf. page 87 above)?

²) *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* VI, 1, 4, 5 ff. Regarding the vigil: *Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā* III, 6, 3, *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* X, 12, 6 etc.

<header>The Dīkshā as a Magical Rite.</header>

[The Dīkshā] should be categorized among the rites occurring consistently across the most diverse primitive peoples <note>German: *Naturvölkern*</note>, which aim to bring about communication with gods or spirits through the arousal of ecstatic states. The standard means for this are contemplative residence in a lonely place, seclusion and hiding from disturbing spirits, various forms of self-mortification, then sweat baths in hot vapors, and above all, fasting—"the continuously filled stomach can see no secret things," say the Zulus¹). As a kind of mystical substance or a fluid, the magical power of this *Tapas* <note>Tapas: literally "heat," referring to the spiritual energy generated through asceticism</note> resides in the body of the one who has completed the *Dīkshā* <term>Dīkshā: a solemn consecration or preparatory rite for a Vedic sacrifice</term>. You wetters! Give me power, give me strength, give me power! Do not destroy my *Dīkshā*, my *Tapas*!”²) In this connection with the concept of *Tapas*, the *Dīkshā* proves to belong to a circle of observances that proceed from the application of heating to achieve supernatural results. Indeed, while the term *Tapas* encompasses the most diverse forms of mortification, the relationship to heat as the vehicle of asceticism stands in the foreground, especially in older times; after all, the word *Tapas* means nothing other than heat. “From the inflamed *Tapas* were Order and Truth born,” it says in the *Ṛgveda* <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational scriptures of Hinduism</note> (X, 190, 1). The priest heats the potsherds on which the sacrificial cake is to be baked by covering them with burning coals, and says: “Become hot (*tapyadhvam*) through the *Tapas* of the *Angiras* and the *Bhṛgu*³)” (*Vāj. S.* I, 18). In later literature, one frequently encounters the *Tapas* of the “fivefold heat”: heating by four fires that surround the ascetic according to the four cardinal directions, and the sun. # Dīkshā and the Sacrificial Bath.

A Jain text <note>original: "Jainatext"</note> describes the ascetic who, “rigid as a pillar, with his face turned toward the sun, allows himself to be burned in a place exposed to the sun's heat”^1). As a result, however, of these heatings and the other acts of self-mortification associated with them—fasting, vigils, holding the breath^2), and so forth—one envisioned enlightenment and supernatural power of the most varied kinds. “The gods have entered into them,” says the *Ṛgveda* <note>The oldest collection of Hindu hymns</note> (X, 136, 2) on one occasion regarding those excited in an ecstatic frenzy, touching upon a way of thinking that has played a significant role from the lowest forms of tribal religion to the highest. It is a poet of the *Ṛgveda* (VIII, 59, 6) who, in the vision produced by <term>Tapas</term> <note>Spiritual heat generated through asceticism</note>, perceives the ancient creations of the ancestors, the first sacrificers in the most distant past of the human race. From the soul filled with *Tapas*, the dream is born, as well as “the tapas-born speech that presses toward the gods.” Through *Tapas*, whoever has accomplished great *Tapas* reaches the sun; after he practiced *Tapas*, <term>Indra</term> <note>The king of the gods in Vedic mythology</note> won the sun. The king who has taken the wife of a <term>Brahmin</term> <note>A member of the priestly caste</note> is reminded of the seven <term>Ṛshis</term> <note>Semi-divine ancient seers or sages</note>, the ancestors of the Brahmin lineages, “who sat down for *Tapas*”: the magical power of *Tapas* inherent to the Brahmin will bring disaster to the one who insults him. *Tapas* gives the strength for the most mighty acts of creation;

# Dīkshā and Tapas.

The goddess *Ashṭakā*, performing <term>Tapas</term> <note>Ascetic heat or spiritual fervor</note>, gave birth to *Indra’s* greatness; the <term>Ṛshis</term> <note>The ancient inspired seers of the Vedas</note> were born from *Tapas*¹). In numerous places, the legends of the <term>Brāhmaṇa texts</term> <note>Vedic prose commentaries on ritual</note> show <term>Prajāpati</term> <note>The "Lord of Creatures," a creator deity</note>, the creator of the world, performing *Tapas*, through which he acquires the power to let the worlds and beings emerge from himself: thus he once performed such *Tapas* that lights came forth from all his pores; these are the stars²). *Tapas* also helps this or that other mythical being, in numerous passages of the *Brāhmaṇa* texts, toward an enlightenment in which some secret of the art of sacrifice is revealed to them. Regarding the sacrificer who keeps watch the night before the kindling of the sacred fires—here again we have the situation where *Tapas* prepares for a particularly sacred act—it is said: "Thus he turns toward the gods. United with the gods, exhausted, and rich in *Tapas*, he kindles the fires" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* II, 1, 4, 7). The Buddhist texts provide a vivid picture of how, in the age of the *Buddha*, people expected visionary enlightenments while fasting and sweating under mortifications that exhausted the body to the extreme.

These phenomena found in India are clearly an instance of a type spread across the earth; the cultivation of ecstatic communion with spirits is particularly characteristic of the lowest forms of religious life. Thus, even without such positive expressions of the *Ṛgveda* <note>The oldest collection of Indian hymns</note> as we have cited, it would be self-evident that these are not late innovations, but that this whole circle of ideas must have played its part even in the oldest Vedic period—a role more significant than, understandably,

# Consecration and Tapas. The Sacrificial Bath.

assign a prominent place if we compare the performer of this <term>Dīkshā</term> <note>The formal consecration for a Vedic sacrifice</note>—who sits hungernd and wakeful, speaking in stammering tongues, wrapped in an antelope skin beside the demon-dispelling magic fire—to those types of wild magic-priests so well known to ethnology, who seek to achieve a state of possession through <term>mortification</term> <note>German: *Kasteiungen*; refers to Tapas or ascetic self-discipline</note>. —

For the closing ceremony, which corresponds to the *Dīkshā* at the end of the sacrifice, the participants descend from the sacrificial site to the water. The sacrificer and his wife have removed the antelope skin and the girdle which they had worn since the *Dīkshā*. These items are thrown into the water; likewise the sacrificial vessels that had come into contact with <term>Soma</term> <note>The sacred, hallucinogenic ritual drink</note>. The pressed Soma shoots are also submerged in the water. Finally, the sacrificer and his wife, as well as the priests themselves, step into the water. Husband and wife wash each other's backs. Upon emerging, they put on fresh garments. The sacrificial offerings and verses that accompany these rites are addressed above all to <term>Varuṇa</term> <note>The Vedic deity of cosmic order and the waters, who punishes and forgives sins</note>, the liberator from all guilt; the plea for this liberation appears in the most diverse forms.

> “A hundred and a thousand physicians have you, O King. Broad and deep shall your grace be. Drive hatred and destruction far away. Release us even from the sin already committed.”

And in a verse addressed to the personified cleansing bath itself:

> “You have sacrificed away the sin committed against the gods by the gods, and that committed by humans against humans. From your vastness, O God, protect us from harm.”

Is the purification of guilt and sin truly the original meaning, and is Varuṇa the liberator the original god of the sacrificial bath? One sees that these connections, even if they were far from the actual essence of the rite, were nevertheless particularly easily [adopted] by those who interpreted the sacrifice and...

# Dīkshā and the Sacrificial Bath.

could be introduced by theologians who embellished them with their own inventions. The presence of water made it natural to honor the Lord of the Waters, <term>Varuṇa</term> <note>The Vedic deity of cosmic order and the waters, responsible for punishing and forgiving sins</note>, with offerings and worship. Furthermore, washings were common as a means of removing impurity and guilt, and Varuṇa was, after all, the liberator from guilt. Thus, these traits could naturally coalesce during the development of the sacrificial bath. However, we must evidently seek the original nature of the ceremony in another direction. It is a widely held concept that a person must not carry over into everyday life the traces of contact with supernatural powers, which cling to him and his possessions like a sacred and hazardous fluid¹). That contact had been opened during the <term>Dīkshā</term> <note>The formal ritual of consecration for a sacrifice</note>; here, it is concluded. The ritual garments and utensils with which the man and woman had equipped themselves during the *Dīkshā* are now laid aside. But a bath is required for the complete removal of this unsettling fluid. A <term>Brāhmaṇa</term> text <note>Prose commentaries on the Vedas that explain ritual significance</note> (*Maitr. S. III, 6, 2*) states explicitly: "When he descends into the water for the sacrificial bath, he carries the *Dīkshā* back into the water," and among the incantations, one encounters a phrase that perfectly captures this original sense of the action: "The pure waters, the releasing ones, the releasers from *Dīkshā* and <term>Tapas</term> <note>Refers to 'ascetic heat' or the intense spiritual fervor generated through ritual exertion</note>" (*Āpastamba Śr. XIII, 21, 3*). The correspondence between *Dīkshā* and the sacrificial bath expressed in these passages—and clearly confirmed by the rites themselves—truly leaves no doubt that, in the original sense, it was not sin and impurity, but rather the clinging traces of supernatural potencies from which the bath was intended to release the individual²).

# The Sacrificial Bath. 409

It may be noted here in passing that a ceremony entirely similar to the sacrificial bath is made known to us by younger Vedic texts: the bath or, more precisely, the washing that forms the conclusion of the period of study dedicated to the <term>Veda</term> <note>The oldest and most sacred scriptures of Hinduism, written in Sanskrit</note> undergone by a <term>Brahmin</term> <note>A member of the priestly and scholarly caste</note>. This washing relates to the consecration that opens the period of study exactly as the sacrificial bath relates to the <term>Dīkshā</term> <note>A formal ritual of preparation and consecration</note>. At the beginning of the period of study, the youth had taken vows that brought him into special contact with divine powers and generated in him the state of <term>Tapas</term> <note>Refers to 'ascetic heat' or the intense spiritual fervor and discipline required for sacred study</note>—which is also characteristic of the one performing the *Dīkshā*^1); now he lays down these vows: the washing rinses away the traces of that contact. Corresponding formulas for both occasions point toward one another: "Agni, Lord of the vow, I will practice the vow"—afterward:

---

Regarding the great <term>Horse Sacrifice</term> <note>Known as the Ashvamedha, one of the most significant and complex royal rituals in ancient India</note> it is said: "When the sacrificer has stepped out, evildoers step in, who previously needed to practice no further observances. They are called purified by the Horse Sacrifice." *Kātyāyana XX, 8, 17. 18.* — Regarding the ceremony of this sacrificial bath, it should also be mentioned here that a crippled, misshapen person (according to *Śāṅkhāyana*, from the family of Atri; the *Yajustexts* do not have this information) was led into the water until it ran into his mouth; then an offering was sacrificed upon his head for "the killing of the embryo" <note>In ancient Indian law, the destruction of a fetus was considered one of the gravest sins, often equated with the murder of a learned Brahmin</note>; he was then released and chased away (*Śāṅkh. XVI, 18, 18 ff.; cf. Kāty. cited above 16*). Presumably, this person represents the sinner who has fallen into the hands of <term>Varuṇa</term> <note>The deity of cosmic order and the waters, often depicted as a judge of human conduct</note> and therefore bears Varuṇa’s marks (*Taitt. Ār. I, 2, 3*) upon himself; the water running into his mouth purifies him of sins up to the heavy guilt of embryo-killing. The *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* explains—less likely, I believe—that this person is a direct symbol of Varuṇa (*XIII, 3, 6, 5; also Taitt. Br. III, 9, 15, 3*). In any case, the view of Weber (*Z. D. M. G. 18, 268* <note>original: "Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft," a prestigious journal of oriental studies</note>) is erroneous: that the actual meaning of the ceremony lies in a human sacrifice and that it is the death of the misshapen descendant of Atri (who in fact does not die at all) upon which the expiatory power of the Horse Sacrifice's <term>Avabhṛtha</term> <note>The final sacrificial bath or ritual purification</note> rests.
