## Ritual Observances.

The <term>Dīkshā</term> <note>A formal period of preparation, consecration, and self-denial before a major sacrifice</note> is the most prominent example in <term>Vedic</term> <note>Relating to the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</note> tradition of a complex of observances that prepare for the execution of a holy act. Thus, the discussions in our previous section can serve as an introduction to the attempt we are now undertaking: to survey, in a larger context, the various types of such observances. Some of these are incumbent upon the performer of specific rites, while others are associated with entering certain stages of life or with learning specific portions of the Vedic curriculum.

Sometimes it is a matter of—as seems to be the primary focus with the *Dīkshā*—filling the person with certain "magical" qualities; at other times, it concerns rites which, at least originally, were intended to ward off evil powers. For whoever prepares themselves for the performance of holy acts or for the reception of a particularly sacred knowledge thereby enters a sphere especially exposed to <term>demonic attack</term> <note>The belief that transitions between the profane and the sacred are moments of spiritual vulnerability</note> and requires increased caution. These positive and negative measures are, moreover, frequently blended together, and their individual interpretation is often—as could not be expected otherwise—

# Fasting and Similar Practices.

The primary precautionary measures <note>Vorsichtsmaassregeln: actions taken to protect the ritual's purity from spiritual interference.</note> against the attack of hostile powers appear to be fasting (or the avoidance of certain foods), the avoidance of sexual intercourse, sleeping on the ground or staying awake, and finally silence—or, with an ethical reinterpretation revealing the spirit of a later age, the avoidance of any untruthful speech. Thus, whoever wishes to kindle the sacrificial fires must spend the preceding night in silence and wakefulness¹). The performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifice <note>Darśapūrṇamāsa: the foundational ritual of the Vedic sacrificial system.</note> must abstain from meat and sexual intercourse on the day preceding the ceremony; for the evening meal, he is permitted to consume forest fruits and wild plants, but food of the kind he is to sacrifice the next day is forbidden. He should sleep on the floor with his wife that night²); there is also the prescription³) that husband and wife should spend this night, at least in part, awake with storytelling and the like⁴). He may only speak the truth. The young couple must lie on the floor during the first three nights after the wedding, observe chastity, and avoid salty or spicy foods⁵). For the Brahmin student <note>A young man undergoing religious apprenticeship under a teacher.</note>, the avoidance of sexual intercourse and a "high bed" <note>Lying on a raised bed was often seen as a sign of luxury or pride, unsuitable for a period of discipline.</note> is prescribed⁶). After the ceremony of admission to his apprenticeship, he must spend the rest of the day standing and in silence, and he must not eat anything salted for three days⁷).

# Ritual Observances.

Before a student is taught a portion of the curriculum considered particularly holy, he must "with bound eyes¹), in silence, abstain from food for three days, or for one day and one night"²). The teacher, too, before performing the rites associated with teaching such a section, is prescribed "to observe chastity for one day and one night and to eat no meat"³). The person performing the *Sabali-homa* <note>A specific Vedic sacrifice involving an offering to a "spotted" (Sabali) cow or divinity to obtain cattle.</note> lies upon the bare earth for twelve nights; he nourishes himself only on sweet milk, speaks only what is absolutely necessary, and observes chastity⁴). These examples should suffice; it would be easy to provide many more at will.

Writing the pre-history of these observances—which, in their main features, are found across the entire world⁵)—is the task of **ethnology** <note>The comparative study of different peoples and cultures.</note>. In regard to fasting in particular, ethnology will have to determine how the motive of abstaining from food (so that food might be available for the deity) relates to the motive of fear felt by the participant—

For the Vedic theologians, fasting is viewed on one hand as a primary form of ascetic exertion (<term>Tapas</term> <note>Literally "heat"; the spiritual energy or inner fire generated through self-discipline and abstinence.</note>)—“fasting is the entirety of Tapas,” says a <term>Brāhmaṇa</term> <note>A collection of ancient Indian commentaries on the Vedas used to explain ritual procedures.</note>²). On the other hand, fasting—provided it precedes a sacrifice—is perceived above all as a duty of what one might call "social etiquette" toward the gods whom the human intends to host: “It is simply not proper if someone wants to eat first while other people are not eating; how much more so when someone eats first while the gods have not yet eaten?”³)

In connection with fasting, the following noteworthy rite should also be mentioned. During the sacrifice of the <term>Vājapeya</term> <note>A high-ranking Vedic ritual; the name literally means "Drink of Strength" or "Drink of Victory."</note>, an anointing—or rather a pouring over—of the sacrificer took place, similar to a royal consecration, for the purpose of filling him with strength and superior power. For this ceremony, water mixed with milk was poured into a vessel, along with seventeen different types of food according to some⁴), or according to others, every type of food one could possibly imagine, with the exception of a single one. "That food which he does not take, let him renounce; let him never eat of it for the rest of his life."

### Cultic Observances.

...lies. The practice of leaving a certain type of fruit untouched or abstaining from catching a particular species of animal is extremely common—whether to protect a **totem animal** <note>An animal or natural object considered to have a spiritual connection to a group.</note> or out of consideration for spirits or the souls of the deceased. This can also take the form of an individual choosing, perhaps based on certain omens, to enter into a pact with a deity and undertaking a specific type of renunciation in their honor¹). Something of this nature—perhaps a "contract" of reciprocity <note>original: "Leistung und Gegenleistung," a legalistic term for mutual exchange</note> where one surrenders a portion of food to the spirits so they might leave the rest for humans and protect them while they enjoy it—could have been incorporated into these Vedic rites. Even the rule that the builder of the **Fire Altar** <note>original: "Agnialtar"; referring to the Agnicayana ritual</note> is forbidden from eating poultry²) seems to align with the taboo regulations of indigenous peoples, which have a very similar appearance.

Turning from fasting and similar customs to the other observances mentioned above (p. 411), the original motive for most of them is clearly evident: the fear of spiritual attack. Out of this fear, the person establishing the sacrificial fires dares not sleep or speak; the student accepted by a teacher spends the remainder of the day in silence; the student facing a particularly holy section of the curriculum remains silent and keeps his eyes bandaged—evidently to avoid seeing the terrifying apparitions that hover around him; and finally, the youth who, after completing his apprenticeship, transitions into the status of an adult through the performance of solemn rites, spends the day in

In my view, this also applies to the observances in which a dread of using clay vessels is evident. Anyone wishing to learn the <term>Jyeṣṭhasāman</term> <note>A specific melody or chant from the Sāmaveda, often considered particularly powerful or "senior."</note> must "neither eat nor drink from a clay vessel from the beginning of the instruction in the observance"¹), and similarly, for the vessel containing the water to be used during the recitation of secret texts, it is expressly prescribed that it must be made of metal²). Likewise, for those wishing to learn the secret knowledge of the <term>Pravargya</term> sacrifice <note>A potent Vedic ritual centered on a heated clay pot (the Mahāvīra), though here the restriction applies to the student's personal use of clay.</note>, the rule is not to drink from a clay vessel³). These customs cannot be considered in isolation from the regulations stating that the pot containing the milk for the New Moon sacrifice (<term>Sāṃnāyya</term> <note>An offering consisting of a mixture of fresh and curdled milk.</note>) must be covered with a non-clay vessel⁴), that the person consecrating themselves for the <term>Soma</term> sacrifice must consume the milk on which they subsist from a non-clay vessel⁵), and that the sacrificial butter for the oath-taking ceremony belonging to the <term>Soma</term> sacrifice (<term>Tānūnaptra</term> <note>A ritual where the sacrificer and priests pledge mutual non-harm by touching sacrificial butter.</note>) must be covered with a non-clay vessel⁶). The tradition of the <term>Brāhmaṇa</term> period <note>The era of prose commentaries on the Vedas, roughly 900–600 BCE.</note> explains the rejection of clay in one passage by stating that "what man speaks of untruth upon her (the earth) is, as it were, mixed into it"⁷); this likely approaches the original meaning, in that it indeed concerns impurities,

# Avoidance of Contact with the Dead. 419

<sig>27*</sig>

which have their seat in the soil, the place of origin of earthen vessels. Only the ethicizing turn that the cited passage gives to this impurity is clearly secondary. Other passages of the <term>Brāhmaṇa literature</term> <note>Prose commentaries on the Vedas composed roughly between 900–600 BCE, focused on ritual explanation.</note>, however, lead, as it seems to me, to exactly the right point. Regarding the prohibition of covering the milk pot at the New Moon sacrifice with a clay vessel, several Brāhmaṇas state: "If he covered it with something made of clay, the Fathers <note>The *Pitṛs*, or spirits of deceased ancestors.</note> would be the deity to whom it belongs"¹). The earth-substance is in constant contact with the dead and belongs to the dead; "the house of earth"²) is a term already used in the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundation of Hindu scripture.</note> to refer to either the grave or the earthen burial urn. Thus, the observances relating to the avoidance of clay vessels seem to be entirely of the same kind as those discussed previously and, like those, prompted by the fear of contact with the realm of the dead.

In the same or a related category belongs the duty imposed on the <term>Snātaka</term> <note>A Brahman who has completed his Vedic studies and performed a ceremonial bath, marking his transition to householder life.</note> not to go to another village toward evening and not to enter a village by a secret path³). Furthermore, a similar distancing—as practiced toward the dead—is prescribed toward women in childbed, menstruating women, and the like; for a similar impurity adheres to them as it does to the dead. We may refrain from gathering further details of the same kind; on the whole, the nature of these observances, which concern the avoidance of various dangers, will be clear.

Alongside them, however, as already touched upon above, stand observances of an opposite kind, the discussion of which—

As substances around which a magic of this form revolves, rain and thunderstorms stand out on the one hand, and heat and the glow of the sun on the other.

The curriculum of the <term>Sāmaveda</term> <note>The Veda of Melodies or Chants, primarily used by priests during the Soma sacrifice.</note> included a song, the <term>Ṣakvarī</term> song, in which one found the <term>Vajra</term> <note>The "thunderbolt," the primary weapon of the god Indra used to slay the demon Vritra.</note> embodied—the weapon of Indra and the symbol of his all-conquering power. Even the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>The oldest collection of Vedic hymns.</note> says of this song that through it, with a great roar, the <term>Vasiṣṭhas</term> <note>A famous lineage of Vedic seers and priests.</note> infused strength into Indra². It was one of those texts whose study, because of the "sacred dread" inherent in them, was banished from the village to the forest. For the student who wished to learn this song, certain observances were prescribed for a period of twelve, nine, six, or three years—according to some, even for just one year—among which the following are found³: three times a day he must "touch water"; he must wear black clothes and consume black food; when it rains, he must sit down but not go under a roof; he must say to the raining sky: "Water is the Ṣakvarī song"; when it lightens: "This is what the Ṣakvarī song looks like"; when it thunders: "The Great One⁴) makes a great noise." ->### Saturation with Sun Substance. Bathing.<-

During the second consecration, the sacrificer closes his fists even tighter and pulls the sacred sash even firmer (see above, p. 398 ff.). Here it says now¹): "He takes the heating-observance <note>This refers to the concept of *tapas*, or inner heat generated through asceticism.</note> upon himself²) (that is, he consumes only hot milk for nourishment). One sees how here, too, the observance is directed toward filling the sacrificer with the substance or power of heat.

Naturally, further observances follow here, the purpose of which is to prevent the loss of such power. This includes the prohibition of bathing and the shaving of hair and beard (the trimming of nails, etc.).

Bathing and shaving, both in clearly recognizable parallelism, appear in the ritual in very diverse contexts, which it will be useful to glance at on this occasion.

The bath, with its power to remove any substance adhering to a person, must be avoided or undertaken depending on whether it concerns a healing or harmful substance. Thus, it is very frequently encountered in the ritual with the meaning of purification, which is performed before any sacred act. Before the <term>Soma sacrificer</term> <note>A priest or patron performing the sacrifice of the sacred Soma plant juice.</note> enters the <term>Dīkshā</term> <note>A period of consecration and ascetic preparation.</note>, he bathes with a mantra <note>A sacred ritual chant.</note> in which the waters are invoked as purifying, carrying away all impurity from here³). On the other hand, however, anyone who has undergone exercises that impart a special holiness or consecration must not bathe before the expiration of the time during which this specific character is intended to dwell within him. The consequence of this is that such a period of forbidden bathing finds its conclusion in a bath which "washes away" that spiritual character and prevents its potentially dangerous transfer into profane <note>Non-sacred or everyday life.</note> life. We have previously considered (p. 408) the particularly distinct application of these views to the offerer of the <term>Soma sacrifice</term> <note>A major Vedic ritual involving the offering of the juice of the Soma plant.</note>, in the correspondence between the ***Dīkṣā*** <note>The state of consecration or initiation.</note>—which saturates him with a fluid of consecration—and the ***Avabhṛtha*** **bath** which removes that fluid.

We also already touched upon the perfect analogy in which this relationship stands to the customs applicable to the <term>Brahmin student</term> <note>A young man of the priestly class undergoing Vedic education under a teacher.</note>. For the student, a purifying bath¹) precedes the admission ceremony, which establishes the character of consecration peculiar to him; a bath then concludes the period of study by taking this character away. The logical consequence would be that bathing should have been forbidden in the meantime. This would have bordered on impracticality and was at least not enforced in the era of the ritual law texts available to us²). In a verse that describes the striving of one devoted to asceticism <note>original: *tapas*; literally "heat," referring to the spiritual energy generated through self-discipline and penance.</note> as useless³), it asks: "What is the use of dirt, what of the skin, what of the beard, what of asceticism?" Dirt—which here clearly refers to the avoidance of bathing—is thus a characteristic of someone who wishes to generate a state of special magical power within themselves through *Tapas*. It seems that this way of looking at human beings was also transferred to the animal involved in a sacred act: the sacrificial horse, which was consecrated before its offering and then allowed to roam free for a year, had to be kept away "from waters in which bathing is possible" during that time⁴).

Similar rules to those for bathing are established for hair-cutting <note>original: *Scheeren*; refers to both shaving the head and trimming the beard.</note>, as already mentioned. However, here we must add the ancient role of hair-cutting in those initiation ceremonies performed for a child one or several years after birth, and then later again for the growing youth. In these rites, the hair is trimmed and brought into a form peculiar to the individual family, serving as a family insignia; later, the beard is also cut. # Shaving

Shaving and the clipping of nails clearly also occur in instances where, following a death, the survivors perform these acts alongside a ritual washing, the renewal of the hearth fire, and the acquisition of new household utensils¹). The logic is that the old hair, which has come into close proximity with the powers of death, must not accompany the individual into their new stage of life. The performance of these same actions upon the deceased themselves before burial signifies exactly the same thing²): prior to the "quasi-offering" of cremation and the departure of the departed into a new existence, they must be liberated from the death-tainted impurity of the old life.

Now, however—in much the same way as we saw with ritual bathing—we encounter rites of a different nature regarding the cutting of hair; we find cases where the hair was required to remain untouched.

If a person's character is to be entirely permeated by a salvific or magically potent "fluid" <note>the author uses "fluidum" to describe an invisible spiritual essence or energy</note>, this essence is thought to be distributed throughout the entire body, including the hair and nails. Thus, it is said of one who recites the Vedic texts while fully understanding the mystical significance of the act, that even if he rests on a comfortable bed, perfumed and adorned, he is nonetheless "filled to the very tips of his nails with <term>Tapas</term>"³). <note>original: *Tapas*; often translated as "ascetic heat," it refers to the spiritual energy or fervor generated through ascetic practices or intense meditation</note>. Similarly, on the fourth day after the wedding, before the first marital union, the newlywed bride was "anointed, including her hair and nails"⁴) with water containing the remnants of sacrificial offerings used to ward off misfortune. > “This is the collected strength and the sap of the waters with which they sprinkle him (at the royal consecration): when he is sprinkled, it first reaches his hair. If he were to shave his hair, he would cause this glory <note>original: *Herrlichkeit*; likely referring to the Vedic concept of *Tejas* or *Varikas*, meaning radiant energy or majesty</note> to miss its mark and vanish: therefore, he does not shave his hair. For one year he does not shave it, for the duration of the observance is one year.”

The observance thus structured is, of course, concluded by shaving, just as the observance of not bathing is concluded by a bath. # 429

->### Shaving and Related Matters<-

In the ceremony of the student’s return home (<term>samāvartana</term> <note>original: *samāvartana*; the ritual marking the end of a student's Vedic education and his return to his family to start a household</note>), ritual bathing is accompanied by the shaving of the hair and beard, as well as the hair growing on the body and the trimming of the nails¹). The <term>Soma-sacrificer</term> <note>one who performs the elaborate Soma ritual, a central part of Vedic religion</note>, who bathed and was shaved before the initial consecration, sheds his status of "consecratedness" at the end through a new bath and by having his hair and beard shaved²).

It should also be mentioned here that even smiling was regarded as a loss of power in a sense similar to shaving. The ancient Vedic comparison between lightning and laughter is well-known; the idea was that a person who smiles radiates, as it were, a portion of their "light-power" from within. Therefore, a rule was established for the <term>Dīkshita</term> <note>the person undergoing the *Dīkshā* or ritual consecration</note>, the recipient of the Soma-consecration, to hold his hand in front of his face when smiling "to hold back the radiance"³).

Finally, I cannot suppress the suspicion that the avoidance of a loss of power or substance, which we identified as the purpose of the prohibitions against bathing and shaving, is also at play in the prohibition of sexual intercourse—though perhaps not as the sole motive here. When it is prescribed that the sacrificial horse must be kept away from waters suitable for bathing as well as from mares⁴), the parallelism between these two rules suggests itself, as well as their connection to the rules that prescribe human abstinence from bathing and sexual intercourse on specific occasions. A <term>Brāhmaṇa</term> text <note>a category of ancient Indian texts explaining ritual significance</note>, which prescribes the necessary atonement offering for an act of copulation performed by the sacrificial horse, explains the effect—

The sacrifice was accompanied by prayer. We have already described the way in which this was integrated into the sacred act³); this is the appropriate place for some further remarks on the form and content of the prayers, as well as on the views held by the Vedic poets regarding the nature and power of prayer.

It goes without saying that alongside the ritually prescribed prayer, there was also spontaneous prayer, as prompted by the need or desire of the moment. Through his prayer

->### Free Prayer and Fixed Rites.<-

It is unlikely that the free prayer of the Vedic period was anything other than a naming of an individual, concrete wish, perhaps combined with phrases that placed this wish and the person of the petitioner particularly urgently at the deity's heart; we cannot think here of a prayer that would have been the expression of an inner life feeling itself in constant connection with the deity. The ritually fixed prayer—or something resembling prayer—could also take the form of a mere thought. During the liturgical recitation of the verse in which the words “rich in strong sons” appear, the priest should think of a strong son if the wife of the sacrificer desires one; in a similar connection, he should think of offspring if the wife of the sacrificer longs for this; when he prepares to strike the <term>Soma shoots</term> <note>original: *Somaschösslinge*; the stalks of the sacred Soma plant from which a ritual drink was pressed</note> with the <term>pressing stone</term> <note>original: *Pressstein*; a stone tool used in the ritual extraction of Soma juice</note>, he should think of his enemy, in order to direct the power of the blows toward him; at a certain other point in the ritual, the sacrificer should think: “<term>Agni</term> <note>the god of fire</note>, <term>Vāyu</term> <note>the god of wind</note>, Lightning, Moon! May I attain fellowship with you”—or whatever else he desires¹). It can be doubted, moreover, whether the interpretation of such a ritually prescribed thought as a "prayer" in our sense of the word is accurate. It seems to involve not so much bringing a wish to the attention of the gods (as if they were readers of human thoughts), but rather imparting a specific direction to a procedure endowed with magical effects through the magical power of one's own thinking, thereby granting it a specific outcome.

Even if, as we have previously stated²), the liturgical prayer that praises and invokes the god during the sacrifice predominantly takes a poetic form, while the formula consecrating the sacrificial implements or the individual ritual gestures moves in prose, there are nevertheless many cases, and indeed some—

->### The Liturgical Prayer. ###<-

> “May the prince be born endowed with royal power, a hero, an archer, a mighty marksman, and a great chariot-warrior; may the cow yield much milk, the ox be strong for the plow, the horse be swift, the woman fertile, and the warrior victorious; may the youth be eloquent in speech. May a hero-son be born to this sacrificer. May <term>Parjanya</term> <note>the Vedic god of rain and thunderstorms</note> grant us rain whenever desired. May the grain ripen with fruitfulness. May our labor and our rest be blessed¹).”

These prose prayers, while not lacking in power and dignity, possess little of the warmth and intimacy, or the sacred sublimity, found in prayers where the Old Testament petitioner pleaded for his own salvation and that of his people. In a sober and factual tone, the priest lists the goods that one might expect from the offering for the sake of the sacrificer and the people—or more accurately, for the higher social classes. Everything remains entirely within the sphere of material prosperity: long life, wealth, high status, and favorable weather. There is no mention of spiritual or moral virtues²).

In this regard, the poetic prayers of the earliest period—those belonging specifically to the <term>Soma sacrifice</term> <note>a central ritual involving the offering of the juice of the Soma plant</note> and intended partly for recitation and partly for chanting—stand on exactly the same level as the prose ones just mentioned. These poetic prayers form the collection of the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>the oldest and most important collection of Vedic hymns</note> and thus the bulk of Vedic prayers. However, alongside and even before naming human desires, their primary concern is the praise of the deity; they glorify the god's greatness, power, mysterious nature, and deeds. We have already addressed the prevailing tone of these hymns of praise earlier (p. 3 ff.).

> “We have wishes, Lord of the tawny steeds,” one says to <term>Indra</term> <note>the king of the gods and deity of thunder and war</note>, “you are the giver; here we are: there are our prayers.”

These goods are mostly spoken of in rather general terms, as is consistent with the less individualized character of that liturgical poetry. One prays for gifts, for treasures, for blessings, for protection, and for victory over all afflictions. When the language of the petitioner becomes more specific, it usually speaks of long life and strong descendants, of cattle and horses, of chariots and gold, and also that it may go ill for the enemies, the misers, and the <term>Brahmin-haters</term> <note>those who show hostility toward the priestly class or the sacred order</note>; that the god might take away their possessions and allot them to the pious. Only rarely is there a prayer for such goods as "right thinking," or that one might not do what the gods punish. In the atmosphere of satisfied well-being that prevails here, the petitions for reconciliation with an angry god, or for liberation from the <gloss>fetters of guilt</gloss> <note>original: "Fesseln der Schuld," referring to moral or ritual transgressions viewed as physical bindings</note> that hold man captive²), recede far behind the prayers of the rich and the fortunate for power and victory. One supports his petitions by reminding the god of one's own zeal, of the old friendship with the deity, and of the god's former benefits; one gives him to understand that, if one were like him and he were like a mortal, the granting of the prayer and rich blessing would not be long in coming. ->### Content and Effect of Prayer. ###<-

...of human existence are foreign to the external nature of these prayers, whose image finds its completion in that monologue of the one who hears the prayer—the god who goes home from the sacrifice satisfied and cheered¹): “I will do it like this—no, like that: I will give him a cow—or a horse. The petition has come to me like a cow lowing for her dear calf. Like a carpenter turns the seat of a chariot, so I turn the petition over in my heart. Have I then drunk of the <term>Soma</term> <note>a sacred ritual drink believed to inspire and invigorate both gods and men</note>?” —

The view of the Vedic poets²) sees in prayer—this “sacrificial food fashioned from the heart”³)—a means to please and strengthen the god, which is hardly inferior in effective power to the actual sacrifice itself. Above all, it is naturally the element of praise upon which this effect of prayer rests; in these the god finds his pleasure; from the memory of his past deeds, he draws desire and courage for new ones. Special merits of individual prayers are added to increase its effect. Sometimes the poet recommends his song as time-tested, inherited from his fathers; at other times, he offers his “new, beautiful song of praise, coming from the heart” to the gods; he says: “Forward I bring my word, the new, the freshly born.” Above all, however, the <margin>/</margin> song must be of impeccably artistic beauty. The singer has fashioned it “like a skilled, industrious man fashions a chariot”; he has freed it from all flaws “as one cleans grain with a winnowing fan,” “like purified sacrificial butter.” “For <term>Agni Vaiśvānara</term> <note>The fire god Agni in his aspect as "belonging to all men"</note>, a new, radiant, beautiful prayer is prepared, just as one purifies the <term>Soma</term>.” Such

Prayers, "born from thought just as rain is born from a cloud," stream toward the god as rivers run to the sea, as cows go to the hurdle; like mother cows lick their calf, they lick him and bellow at him; they flatter and embrace him like wives embrace a husband, like lovers embrace their beloved; they strengthen him like <term>Soma</term>-drinks <note>a sacred ritual beverage</note>.

> "Through their hymns, those who offer Soma increase Indra’s mighty strength."

> "As great as he is, his body shall become even greater, he who is praised with songs of glory and hymns."

> "The priests, elevating Indra with songs, have made him great so that he might slay the serpent." <note>A reference to the demon Vritra, who obstructed the waters and was slain by the god Indra.</note>

> "To the broad, wide-yoked chariot, they harness through the song the tawny steeds of the swift god—the steeds that carry Indra, which are harnessed by the Word."

Here, the effect of the hymn and song upon the divine listener—intended to please him and communicate human wishes—already transitions into an independent magical effect based on the inherent power of the consecrated word. We encounter here again that mixing of prayer and magic formula, which we previously touched upon in another context (above p. 315) as an exact counterpart to the mixing of sacrificial acts and magical acts¹).

## The Sacrifices of the Daily, Monthly, and Yearly Cycle.

In this specific overview of the individual sacrifices of the <term>Vedic cult</term> <note>the ritual system of the ancient Indo-Aryans</note>, we place the regularly recurring celebrations first. Regarding these, apart from a few more or less hidden traces, we lack the evidence of the—

<meta>This page continues the transition from the general power of prayer and the "consecrated word" discussed on page 438 to a detailed examination of specific, recurring rituals in the Vedic tradition. The regular sacrifices: the fire sacrifice. 439

<term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>the oldest collection of Indian hymns</note>; given the almost exclusive focus of the ancient hymn poetry on the <term>Soma sacrifice</term> <note>a complex ritual involving the juice of a sacred plant</note>, this is not otherwise to be expected. However, the overall situation allows us to trace this circle of sacrifices back to the earliest times with great probability, at least in their basic features.

Regular sacrifices accompany the course of the day, the month, and the year. Regarding the two actions tied to the day—the morning and evening "**fire sacrifice**"—one can certainly be doubtful whether these possess the full character of a sacrifice according to their original intention; it seems more accurate to understand them primarily as the regular tending of the sacrificial fire, which is necessary for its preservation ¹). In addition to the fire sacrifice, food offerings are presented every morning and evening to all beings. One considers the gods and <term>genii</term> <note>guardian spirits or local deities</note> who preside in and around the house; food is placed on the threshold and in the mortar, in the bed, and in the water barrel. A libation is also poured out to the souls of the departed in the south, the celestial region of the dead; food is thrown for dogs and birds; pregnant women, boys, and the elderly are fed.

The month is followed by the **New Moon sacrifice** and **Full Moon sacrifice**. In the course of the year, there are primarily three festivals, each four months apart, held on the full moon days around the start of spring, the rainy season, and the cool season. The two main points of the lunar month—primarily the full moon—and then, receding behind them, the midpoint of a half-month, the eighth day of the waning moon: these are the regular festival times according to the simple order of the <term>Veda</term> <note>the body of sacred knowledge and scripture</note>. The demands of the numerous deities for a share in the regular sacrifices—which were surely felt ever more strongly by priestly diligence over time—were met not by establishing new festivals, but by allowing the old ones to apply to increasingly large **hosts of gods**: none of the regular Vedic sacrifices is—at least in the stage of development presented to us by the ritual texts—celebrated for a single god ¹).

Regarding the **cake offerings** <note>sacrificial cakes usually made from ground rice or barley</note> of the **Full and New Moon sacrifice**, **Indra** <note>the king of the gods and god of storms</note> seems to stand out as the most significant among the various deities involved according to the ritual texts. This is not because he had anything to do with the **moon phases** due to his mythological nature; rather, the moon simply indicated the time at which honors had to be shown to the most powerful of all gods. I am inclined to believe that this sacrifice, in its frequent recurrence, may be regarded as the centerpiece within the regular **cultus** <note>the system of religious veneration and ritual</note> ²). # The Full and New Moon Sacrifice. The Four-Month Festivals.

The moon—or more generally the **waning moon**—was also the time at which the **souls of the ancestors** received their monthly feeding.

While the aforementioned celebrations, linked to the course of the day and the month, appear essentially identical in the sacrificial ritual of both the single fire and the three fires (p. 348 ff.), the three festivals that accompany the course of the year—corresponding to the natural **three-fold division** of the Indian year into the hot, the rainy, and the cool seasons—belong solely to the **greater ritual** <term>Shrauta</term> <note>The complex "high" rituals requiring multiple priests and three sacred fires, as opposed to simpler domestic rites</note>; the prevailing view must have been that a person who maintained only a single **domestic fire** was not capable of or worthy of performing them. Alongside ritual "mass-produced goods," which clearly originate from the workshops of later Vedic ritual-organizers, one encounters here a series of ancient rites that have preserved the unadulterated color of **popular folk-worship**. At each of these festivals, the **Maruts** <note>a group of storm deities often described as a restless troop of young warriors</note> are particularly prominent; it is unlikely that the post-Rigvedic period <note>the era following the composition of the earliest Vedic hymns</note> would have emphasized these deities in such a manner. During the second celebration, performed around the beginning of the rainy season, the offering of **Karīra fruits**—which are thrown onto the sacrificial gifts—clearly represents a **rain charm** <term>Regenzauber</term> <note>original: "Regenzauber"; a ritual act intended to sympathetically induce rainfall</note>, consistent with the usual cultic use of these fruits¹); the goal is to promote the timely onset of the wet season. "That Karīra fruits are taken, happens for rain, for the attainment of the blessing of food," a **Brāhmaṇa text** <note>prose manuals used by priests to explain the significance and performance of the rituals</note> ²) explicitly states: as an incidental remark, this is, as far as I can find, the only certain connection recognizable in the ritual of the three festivals to the

---

original state [which] has been shifted by the well-known priestly preference for this **divine pair** <note>Likely Agni and Soma</note>, which belongs to a younger age, whereby the **identification of Soma with the moon** will also have played a part in securing a place for that god in the full moon celebration.

# The Four-Month Festivals.

...to the god Tryambaka, that he may make us good, that he may make us happy, that he may lead us to a firm goal. "You¹) are medicine: medicine for the cattle, medicine for horse and man, prosperity for the ram and the ewe." One circumambulates the fire three times to the left, clapping the hands on the left thighs, and three times to the right, clapping on the right thighs; the unmarried girls of the family also walk around and pray to the god Tryambaka, who gives husbands to maidens: "Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from here, not from there"—from the parental home, not from the husband's house <note>This prayer expresses the wish of a young woman to be "plucked" from her childhood home to join a new family through marriage, just as a ripe fruit is harvested.</note>. Finally, the remains of the sacrificial cakes <term>Opferfladen</term> <note>flat cakes made of flour, a standard offering in Vedic rituals</note> are tossed into the air, caught again, and hung high in two baskets at the ends of a balance beam, as provisions for Rudra's journey, so that he might depart into the distance without harming people.

So far for the ritual of the three seasonal sacrifices <term>Jahreszeitenopfer</term> with their characteristic, folk-style customs. It is likely only through the artifice of the sacrificial theorists that a fourth festival has been connected with these, the **Śunāsīrīya**. The name indicates that it is dedicated to spirits <term>Genien</term> <note>original: "Genien"; refers to protective spirits or minor deities</note> who bestow blessings upon the plow. When this "Plowman’s Festival" <term>Pflügerfest</term>—in keeping with the way the other three festivals span the twelve months of the year—is associated with the thirteenth month, the intercalary month <term>Schaltmonat</term> <note>a leap month added periodically to the lunar calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year and the seasons</note> used to balance lunar and solar timekeeping²), it is naturally just an idea that introduces an interpretation completely foreign to the festival's actual nature³).

# Individual Sacrifices and Festivals.

Continuing the rites related to the course of the year, we must mention the remnants that have been preserved from solstice customs—more specifically, from the rituals of the **winter solstice**¹). In the tradition, these appear in connection with a cycle of **Soma sacrifices** <term>Somaopfer</term> <note>Soma was a ritual drink of great importance in Vedic religion, often personified as a god</note> that runs through the year, following the sun's path. Thus, they are integrated into the framework of the Soma ritual and interwoven with its exclusive priestly ceremonial, if only superficially. "The drums are beaten. (The priest) beats the **earth-drum**. The noisemakers make a noise"²): evidently, this is about driving away the evil spirits and souls of the dead who are particularly powerful during the darkest time of the year.

An Aryan and a **Shudra** <term>Șūdra</term> <note>the lowest of the four traditional social classes in ancient Indian society</note> struggle over a white, round hide, which the tradition rightly explains as an image of the sun³); the Shudra must let go and run away; the other strikes him down with that very hide. The meaning seems clear: the sun is in danger of falling to the hostile, dark powers, but the Aryan people succeed in preserving it. It also seems to refer to the sun—which is called "the golden swing in the sky" in the **Rigveda** <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>the oldest and most sacred of the Hindu scriptures</note> (VII, 87, 5)—that one of the priests must sit on a swing. He touches the swing board and the earth with the span of his right hand and says: "The Great One has united with the Great One. The God has united with the Goddess": this likely means that

In an enclosed space on the sacrificial grounds, a couple engages in sexual intercourse <note>This act functions as a form of sympathetic magic, where a human action is believed to encourage a similar result in nature—in this case, fertility and abundance</note>. > The cows are the mothers of butter! The sweet juice!
> They shall multiply among us! The sweet juice!

Everywhere, the concern is clearly the fertility of both humans and nature. The union of the couple aims at the former. The arrow shots, it seems, are intended to open the closure of the clouds; the vital winter rains are meant to fall; there should be water for the cattle herds. The coarse, tangible nature of the old folk customs has been fully preserved and stands in sharp contrast to the ritual artifice in the midst of which tradition has placed them. —

Linked further to the course of the year is the festival, or rather—depending on the different types of crops—the festivals of the **first-fruit offerings** <term>Erstlingsfrüchte</term>¹): <note>The practice of offering the first portion of a harvest to the gods or priests before the rest of the crop can be eaten</note> in these, an attempt has been made to establish a certain connection—even if not perfectly fixed due to the nature of the matter—to the dates of the full and new moons, which were perceived as the normal festival times²).

### The Individual Sacrifices and Festivals.

Finally, several rites tied to fixed dates must be mentioned here, which exist outside the ritual of the three fires <note>The complex public ritual (Shrauta) involving three distinct sacrificial fires</note> and are to be performed solely with the domestic sacrificial fire: such as an offering presented at the full moon of *Ashvayuja* <note>the lunar month of September–October</note> (around the beginning of autumn) for the prosperity of the herds¹). Furthermore, there are the rites of the snake cult²) <note>German: *Schlangencult*</note>, which likely belong to a relatively recent period, occurring at the beginning and end of the season when snakes are most dangerous (at the full moon of *Shravana* [July–August] and *Margashirsha* [November–December]). Above all, however, are the celebrations of the three *Ashtakas*³) <note>festivals held on the eighth day after the full moon during the dark half of the month</note> to be performed during the winter months. The timing of these—the last quarter of the moon in those months—aligns with the significance that emerges from the vague and varying accounts in the texts as the primary one: it is primarily the **Manes** <note>the ancestral spirits of the deceased; from the Latin *di manes*</note> to whom the *Ashtakas* are dedicated. Consequently, these celebrations in the domestic sacrificial ritual should be ascribed a significance similar to that of the **Festival of Souls** <note>German: *Seelenfest*</note> in the ritual of the three fires, which is connected to the last of the great seasonal sacrifices (see p. 442 above)⁴). ->## Various Festivals. The Pravargya Ceremony.<-

**Manes** <note>the ancestral spirits of the deceased</note> the offering of grain-dumplings common in the cult of the dead and also an animal. “Even if he (the sacrificer) is ever so destitute, he should nonetheless celebrate the *<term>Aṣṭakā</term>* <note>a festival held on the eighth day after the full moon during the winter months</note> with an animal. The **<term>Pravargya</term> ceremony** <note>a potent ritual involving the heating of milk in a clay vessel</note>. As we now prepare to transition from these sacrifices, which constitute what might be called the regular Vedic festival calendar, to the **<term>Soma</term> sacrifice** <note>the central, most complex Vedic ritual involving the pressing of the sacred Soma plant</note>, a rite should first be mentioned here which appears in tradition as a preparatory ceremony belonging to the **<term>Soma</term> sacrifice**, but which was likely originally independent: the offering of hot milk to the *<term>Aṣvin</term>* <note>the twin gods of the dawn, often depicted as divine healers</note> (*<term>Pravargya</term>*, *<term>Gharma</term>* <note>literally "heat," referring to both the hot drink and the vessel used</note>) ²). A vessel as high as a span <note>approximately 9 inches</note> is heated ³). Beneath it lies a silver plate, and above it a gold plate. The milk of a cow and a goat is poured into it ⁴) and offered to the two *<term>Aṣvin</term>*; the sacrificer partakes of his portion of it. The ritual texts prescribe the repetition of this ceremony twice daily, morning and afternoon, throughout a series of days preceding the main Soma sacrifice ⁵); in the *<term>Ṛgveda</term>* <note>the oldest collection of Vedic hymns</note>, only the morning character of the ceremony seems to stand out—

If we now ask about the meaning of this sacrifice, it seems to me — even if I only venture to express this as a conjecture — that we have here a magical rite originally directed toward the sun ¹). “From the sun they have brought the **<term>Gharma</term>** <note>literally "heat," referring to both the heated milk and the vessel</note>,” it is already said in the **<term>Ṛgveda</term>** (X, 181, 3). The heat of the glowing drink represents the heat of the sun; the sacrifice is intended to secure and strengthen this heat, but above all, of course, to allow its power to benefit the sacrificer.

The proof, of course, as is self-evident given the state of our materials, can rely almost exclusively on the younger **<term>Vedas</term>** <note>the ancient sacred scriptures of India</note>: these, however, allow the concept of heat to emerge repeatedly as a leitmotif both in the ritual act itself and in the associated mantras, and a series of indications point specifically to the heat of the sun. Elsewhere (p. 422), mention has already been made of the observances associated with the study of this sacrifice, which is treated as a secret doctrine: it was, for example, forbidden to cover oneself in the sunshine, to spit in the sunshine, or to urinate: clear indications that the one offering the **<term>Gharma</term>** was regarded as standing in a particularly close alliance with the sun. Furthermore, an important passage of the **<term>Frog Song</term>** <note>Rigveda VII, 103; a famous hymn where the croaking of frogs at the start of the monsoon is compared to the chanting of priests</note> (Ṛv. VII, 103, 8. 9) should be pointed out here. The frogs, who raise their voices every year when the wet season returns, are compared with priests who hold a celebration throughout the year, with “**<term>Soma</term>**-sacrificing **<term>Brahmans</term>**,” with “**<term>Adhvaryus</term>** <note>the class of priests who perform the physical labor of the sacrifice</note> who sweat at the **<term>glowing kettle</term>** <note>original: "Gluthkessel", referring to the Gharma</note>.” 
> “They preserve the divine order of the twelve-part (year); these men do not miss the right time. When the rainy season has come in the course of the year, the heated glowing kettles are set to rest.” 
The later ritual prescribes putting away the glowing kettle on the day before the start of the **<term>Soma pressings</term>** (*Indische Studien* X, 365). One gets the impression that the glowing kettles of the celebrating frogs are related to the solar heat of the hot season which precedes the rainy season; when the rain comes, the sacrificers put the glowing kettles away. Thus, our assumption that the milk sacrifice represents a magic ritual directed at the sun and its heat seems to find confirmation from the Rigveda. However, when the Rigveda further points out that this relationship to the sun’s heat is also connected to the rain that succeeds it, this is initially in full harmony with the invocation communicated above (p. 449) to the ray “of the sun, the giver of rain,” but then also with the following **<term>Brāhmaṇa</term>** passage: 
> “They look toward the shining (kettle); from the shining (heaven) the rain god sends the rain: thus the rain god grants rain; the creatures prosper” 
(**<term>Taittirīya Āraṇyaka</term>** V, 6, 11). The use of a Rigvedic verse belonging to our sacrifice (X, 139, 4; cf. *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* IV, 11, 7), which speaks of Indra as he hastens after the path of the waters and thereby perceives the enclosures of the sun, likely leads into the same circle of ideas.

# The Pravargya Ceremony. The Soma Sacrifice.

29*

one therefore makes the milk glowing hot, one imparts the sun’s glow to it: and when further, corresponding to a frequently emphasized tendency, the magical act takes on the mantle of a sacrifice enjoyed by the gods, which deities could with such great right become recipients of this sacrifice as the **<term>Ashvins</term>** <note>the divine twin horsemen who represent the transition from darkness to light at dawn</note>, who rule the morning before the appearance of the sun? —

The **<term>Soma Sacrifice</term>**. In Vedic literature, the Soma sacrifice stands out beyond all comparison above all other cultic acts. Whether this precedence existed in real life quite as it does in tradition is, however, a question. The high esteem within the relatively narrow circles of priestly schools—who were drawn to the Soma sacrifice by material interests as well as by the enjoyment of their own poetic or sophisticated, mystery-mongering creative power—does not prove a correspondingly high standing in the religious life of the people. Only a few could have found it possible to organize a Soma sacrifice; where it was celebrated, it can have had for the masses at most the character of an incomprehensible spectacle, which one watched without being touched by its proceedings. Indeed, it plays no significant role in the depictions of ancient Indian popular life that do not belong to the specifically Vedic sphere, such as in the literature of the **<term>Buddhists</term>**.

The Soma sacrifice was not fixed calendarically, or at least not nearly with the same firmness as the celebrations discussed above. As for the rule found in the younger texts that it is to be offered in the spring, or that it is to be offered every spring,¹) it is first of all questionable whether the same

### Individual Sacrifices and Festivals.

The character of the **<term>Soma sacrifice</term>** <note>the central ritual of the Vedic religion involving the pressing and offering of the juice of the Soma plant</note> as an act of extraordinary generosity performed by the wealthy and the noble for the benefit of gods and priests is not overturned by that provision.

The Soma cannot be offered to one god or another according to circumstances, as is the case with sacrificial cakes or sacrificial animals. It is offered according to a fixed order of the **<term>morning pressing</term>**, the **<term>midday pressing</term>**, and the **<term>evening pressing</term>**¹) to a series of deities. While this sequence is capable of individual additions, in the main it is fixed once and for all and, by intention, clearly encompasses all deities²): the more important ones appear individually by name, and the inexhaustible mass of lesser ones is included in an offering addressed to "all the gods." Thus, the Soma sacrifice is a general drinking festival for gods and priests. Among the divine guests, however, one enjoys the chief honor: **<term>Indra</term>** <note>the king of the gods and the patron of warriors, often associated with storms and lightning</note>. Just as the songs and sacrificial formulas celebrate him above all other gods as the Soma-drinker—as the god to whom the eagle brought the Soma and who performed his greatest deeds in a Soma-induced trance³)—so

### The Three Soma Pressings and Their Deities.

...claim to the first drink of the **<term>Soma</term>** <note>a sacred ritual drink made from a plant of the same name</note>—then the pair **Indra** and **Vāyu** <note>the gods of storm and wind</note>, **Mitra** and **Varuṇa** <note>gods of contracts and cosmic order</note>, the two **Aśvins** <note>divine twin horsemen and healers</note>, **Indra** once more, the All-Gods, and finally **Sarasvatī** <note>goddess of both the sacred river and speech</note>. If we find in the ritual of the later texts that, during the morning pressing, the three assistants of the **<term>Hotar</term>** <note>the chief priest who recites hymns from the Ṛgveda</note> still recite litanies to Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra, and the pair **Indra-Agni** <note>the storm god paired with the fire god</note>, then these data add **Agni** <note>the god of fire</note> to the circle of aforementioned deities, though not as a deity standing on his own, but in the company of Indra: several **<term>Ṛgvedic hymns</term>** <note>hymns from the oldest layer of Indian scripture</note> make the great age of this divine pair as recipients of Soma likely¹).

Regarding the midday pressing, with its exclusive belonging to **Indra**, who is joined only by his retinue, the **Maruts** <note>storm deities who serve Indra</note>, this has already been discussed.

The evening pressing, according to the ritual of the later **<term>Vedas</term>** <note>ancient Indian religious scriptures</note>, includes Soma offerings for the **Ādityas** <note>a group of solar deities representing sovereignty</note>, **Savitar** <note>the sun-god representing the solar power of motivation</note, the All-Gods, and Agni as the one from the gods—

¹) The series of gods indicated here, which results from the litanies of the **Hotar** priests, agrees for the most part perfectly with the series suggested by the formulas to be recited by the **<term>Adhvaryu</term>** <note>the priest responsible for the manual ritual actions</note> when drawing the individual Soma portions (**Vājasaneyi-Saṃhitā** VII, 1 ff. etc.). To discuss the individual deviations here would lead too far. It should only be noted that from **Vājasaneyi-Saṃhitā** VII, 24–25, one should not conclude that there is a separate Soma offering to **Agni Vaiśvanāra** <note>Agni in his aspect as 'belonging to all men'</note>: cf. **Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra** X, 7, 7 and the Commentary to X, 7, 10.

Finally, to the above details about the morning pressing and its deities, let it be added here that a series of twelve Soma pourings, dating back to the **Ṛgvedic** period (**Ṛgveda** I, 15; II, 36–37), belongs to that pressing. These correspond to the six priesthoods of **Hotar**, **Potar**, **Neṣṭar**, **Agnīdh**, **Brahman** (that is, the **Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin**; cf. above p. 396), and **Praśāstar**, and simultaneously, as it seems, to the twelve months: their deities are in order—first corresponding to those six priests—Indra, the Maruts, **Tvaṣṭar** <note>the divine craftsman</note>, Agni, Indra again, and Mitra-Varuṇa: then four times the "Giver of Wealth" (**Draviṇodas**), the Aśvins, and Agni. I would assign a more superficial meaning to these combinations of priests with deities than Hillebrandt does in *Vedic Mythology* I, 262.

The Ṛgveda also allows the wives of the gods to enjoy the Soma, and similarly, the inclusion of Indra’s horses along with the god himself—regardless of whether it took place exactly in the location and form assigned to it by the later ritual—corresponds perfectly to the views of the Ṛgveda. However, I consider it unlikely that the Soma offering to **Savitar** <note>a solar deity representing the impulsive power of the sun</note> goes back to the ancient period. In the hymns of the **Ṛgveda** <note>the oldest layer of Indian sacred texts, c. 1500–1200 BCE</note> addressed to this god, almost any reference to the **Soma** <note>the sacred, intoxicating plant-drink of the rituals</note> offered to him would be missing¹), had the ritual in question already existed at that time. It is characteristic that for the individual verse used to hand over the offering to the god (<term>yajyā</term> <note>original: "yajyā"; the specific verse recited as the oblation is cast into the fire</note>), one had to choose a verse not contained in the **Ṛgveda**²)—or, more likely, compose one—in order to be able to refer therein to the Soma-drink of **Savitar**.

We should not shy away from lingering somewhat longer on these details, so that the relationship of the great Soma sacrifice to the older and younger layers within the **Vedic** world of gods may emerge. A deity who is of such overriding importance for the period of the later **Vedas** as the world-creator **Prajāpati** <note>literally "Lord of Progeny," the supreme creator god in later Vedic mythology</note>, could certainly find entry into the Soma sacrifice in secondary rites—in additions to the original ritual that are easily recognizable as such; yet he remained entirely removed from the actual foundations of that sacrifice. And what applies to **Prajāpati** applies at least approximately to **Savitar**. **Savitar**, celebrated in so many hymns of the **Ṛgveda**, is without doubt significantly older than **Prajāpati**, yet everything suggests that this god, with his abstract name (the "Impeller" <note>original: "Erreger"; one who rouses or stimulates life</note>) and abstract essence³), is to be counted among the younger formations of the **Vedic** world of gods. We have already touched upon the characteristic relationship of **Savitar** to the Soma sacrifice. When the reader of the later **Vedas** sees him occupying a fully legitimate position at this sacrifice, the **Ṛgveda** seems to exclude him: a fact which indeed hardly

# The Soma Sacrifice as Rain Magic.

side-effect is attributed to it: it is a **rain charm** <term>Regenzauber: a ritual intended to magically produce rain through imitation</term>, obviously not, or at least not primarily, in the sense that it stimulates the grace of the rain-giving gods, but rather by directly influencing the rain. The gushing of the **Soma** juice from its enclosure in the plant and its drop-by-drop trickling through the strainer were processes entirely in the manner of those common in rain magic: one produced some kind of image of rain or the wetting of the earth, herbs, etc., and then expected the corresponding result from nature. Thus, the **Soma** dripping through the strainer—himself a son of **Parjanya** <note>the Vedic god of rain and thunder</note>, whose fertilization made him grow—is a giver of rain. "He is united with the seed of heaven, the milk-rich," it is said of him. "He creates water; he makes the heaven rain." "Stream the rain of heaven to us." "Purify yourself for us into rain, into waves of water from heaven"¹). Invocations of a similar kind are frequent. —

->### Overall Picture of the Soma Sacrifice.<-

...horses, gold, and garments. The purification of the sacred drink through the sieve of sheep’s hair is accompanied by the monotonous chant, moving within only a few notes, of the three priestly singers who sit side by side, their gaze fixed unswervingly straight ahead at the horizon. Sitting as well, the reciting priests perform their verses, to whom the **Adhvaryu** <term>Adhvaryu: the priest responsible for the manual ritual duties and measurements</term>, sitting opposite them as the chief performer of the actual sacrificial acts, responds with the call **Om** (“Amen”) <note>original: "Om ('Amen')"; the author uses the comparison to help Western readers understand 'Om' as a ritual affirmation</note>—those recitations in which, amidst stereotypical formulas and the elaborate play of riddles and mysteries, many a thought of soulful poetry and many a word of bold beauty shines through. These are addressed to the invisible listeners imagined to be sitting upon the sacrificial straw: the entire host of gods along with the divine consorts, and above all the god **Indra**, who has arrived with his team of bay horses, unhindered by the prayers of other sacrificers, to feast upon the intoxicating drink beckoning to him. In this way, the actions and recitations continue throughout the day in the threefold sequence of the morning pressing, the midday pressing, and the third pressing—a colorful medley of rites from both ancient and more recent origins. There are invocations to gods who are new creations of the Indian spirit, and to those who stem from the shared past of Indo-Iranian or Indo-European life—all of them intermingled with even older elements: magical practices still bearing the raw, unmistakable stamp of the most distant, wild prehistoric times.

# The Individual Sacrifices and Festivals.

We begin with the wedding.

Recent investigations¹) have made it probable that the Indian wedding—and I believe the same will generally hold true for the other celebrations of this circle—preserves the Indo-European <term>Indo-European: the ancient linguistic and cultural ancestor shared by Indians, Greeks, Romans, and Germanic peoples</term> form of the rites²) in its essential features. While only sparse remains remind us of the primordial marriage by capture <note>original: "Raubehe"</note>, the wedding customs of the **Veda** instead express a union of man and woman taking place in a peaceful and solemn order. This union was often based on a purchase or at least bore traces of bride-purchase <note>original: "Frauenkauf"</note>; the woman is subordinate to the man and yet stands beside him in high esteem—though not always as his only companion. Furthermore, these rites serve to drive away all malevolent powers and to invoke shared happiness over many years and blessed offspring. On the whole, the wedding customs—and this also applies to other ceremonies of a related kind—naturally move more in the realm of magic than in that of the sacrificial cult³). The grasping of the hand <note>original: "Handergreifung"</note> placed the bride into the hand of the husband; the stone upon which she had to step communicated its own firmness to her; the seven steps, which she had to take while being led by her husband⁴), and the shared consumption of sacrificial food established friendship and togetherness—

It can hardly be said that the numerous verses and spells that pepper the wedding ritual—calling now upon this god, now upon that in fleeting invocation, or bestowing now this, now that magical blessing—rise much above the level of this simple benediction. The actual wedding hymn, the *Song of Sūryā*¹), which was recited by a **Brahmin** <term>Brahmin: A member of the highest, priestly caste, responsible for the performance of sacred rituals</term> during the wedding ceremony, deviates most from this tone, though in the least pleasant way. It was a song originating in the later **Rigvedic** <term>Rigvedic: Relating to the Rigveda, the oldest of the four sacred Vedas of Hinduism</term> period concerning the marriage of the Sun-maiden **Sūryā** to **Soma**—specifically that mystical Soma “whom the Brahmins know, but of whom no one else partakes,” <note>original: "den die Brahmanen kennen, von dem Keiner geniesst"</note> meaning the **Moon**. It is a song full of empty priestly mysticism, devoid of all poetry that might have known how to meaningfully connect the radiant image of the heavenly couple with the hopes for earthly domestic happiness. Thus, in keeping with the overall spirit of Indian intellectual life, the direction in which the Vedic wedding ritual moves away from that of **Indo-Germanic** <note>The author uses "Indo-Germanic" to refer to what we now call Indo-European ancestors.</note> antiquity leads neither into that sphere of free beauty in which the Greek wedding feast resides, nor into the regions of earnest, defined legal thought where the Roman ritual has its existence²); instead, it is the clutter and word-flood of pretentious priestly phrasing, which prepares to cover everything and increasingly drown out the expressions of natural human feeling.

Following the wedding in India, as with so many other peoples, there is a period of marital abstinence extending over three nights; it appears that this originally served the purpose of [averting] the dangers that might threaten the union...

# Rites for Birth and Childhood.

to tire out and distract the evil spirits¹). Expiatory offerings on the fourth day mark the end of this period; they drive away all the ruinous forces that reside in the woman: those that kill the husband, those that make her childless, and those that harm the herds.

The rites to be performed for the child's prosperity during **pregnancy** and then after birth and during childhood possess the very same predominantly magical character as the wedding; actual sacrificial acts take a backseat, just as they did there. A powdered magical medicine sprinkled into the pregnant woman's nose grants the fetus a male gender. In the fourth month²) of the first pregnancy, the "parting of the hair" <note>original: "Scheitelziehung"</note> is performed: the woman's hair is parted⁴) with a porcupine quill³) that is white in three places. Unripe **Udumbara** fruits <term>Udumbara: The cluster fig tree (Ficus racemosa), considered sacred in India and a symbol of fertility and nourishment due to its abundant sap</term> are tied around her—doubtless a symbol of the still unripe fetus, to which the juicy fullness of the Udumbara fig is to be imparted. # The Individual Sacrifices and Festivals.

tenth day after the birth—at the end of the period of impurity brought about by it—the naming ceremony occurs. In the third year¹) the ceremony of the **hair-cutting**²) is performed on the child. This ritual is famously endowed with religious consecration among many indigenous peoples as well; it involves the creation of the hairstyle peculiar to the child’s family. While bowls containing substances that bring fruitfulness and prosperity, such as bull dung, various types of grain, and the like, stand next to the fire, the child's hair is moistened with lukewarm water. A number of grass blades are placed into the hair³) and it is then cut off: in four passes on the right side and three on the left. The cut hair is placed upon the bull dung and buried with it in a place rich in herbs, near water, or in a cowshed. In a similar manner, the ceremony of **beard-shaving** follows later for the sixteen-year-old.

The most important of the consecrations, however, that are to be performed for the growing boy or youth, is the <term>Upanayana: The ritual of initiation where a young boy is introduced to his spiritual teacher (guru) and invested with the sacred thread, marking his "second birth" into the religious community</term>, the introduction to the teacher; we must devote a somewhat more detailed consideration to this.

### The Upanayana.

...postponing it to the 16th, 22nd, or 24th years: these are artificially constructed numbers which undoubtedly depend on the number of syllables in the <term>meters: poetic rhythms used in sacred verses</term> corresponding to the three <term>castes: the social classes of ancient India (Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas)</term> and their protective deities. Perhaps an older order, untouched by such artifice, shines through when the tenth year is specified for the Brahmin alongside the eighth year—a number that does not fit into those numerical games¹).

The teacher stands at the **sacred fire**²); between him and the fire stands the boy, bathed and adorned, with shorn hair. The teacher winds the girdle around him three times to the right; as the accompanying verse says, the girdle "protects from evil words, purifies our color as a cleanser, and gains strength through inhalation and exhalation: the friendly deity, the bringer of good fortune"³). Just as the groom takes the hand of the bride at a wedding, the teacher here grasps the hand of the pupil; then he has him turn to the right and places his own hand over the boy's shoulder so that it touches the location of his heart. The accompanying verses express that he thereby takes the boy's heart into his own will: "may your thought follow my thought; rejoice in my word with your whole soul; may **Bṛhaspati** <note>The god of prayer and the "teacher of the gods" in Hindu mythology</note> join you to me⁴)". ...there is yet another name, derived from the name of a god or a constellation, or relating to his <term>gens: the ancestral clan or lineage</term>, which is to be used during formal greetings¹). Finally, the teacher gives him the instruction:

> “A student (<term>brahmacārin: a chaste seeker of sacred knowledge</term>) you are; lay on the firewood; sip water; perform your service; do not sleep during the day; restrain your speech until the laying on of the wood.”

With this, the boy has entered his period of study. During this time, he must observe strict chastity, abstain from certain foods such as honey and meat²), place wood into the holy fire of his teacher every morning and evening, and walk through the village begging for food. Above all, however, he must learn the <term>Veda: the most ancient and authoritative scriptures of Hinduism</term> and, first and foremost, the <term>Sāvitrī: a sacred verse used as a prayer for enlightenment</term> which introduces Vedic study—the verse in which the god <term>Savitar: a solar deity representing the impelling power of the sun</term> is asked to stimulate the thoughts of man³).

Whoever has received this consecration of the <term>Upanayana: the 'leading near' of a student to a teacher</term> is a “Twice-born”; the first, physical birth has been followed by a spiritual rebirth.

> “The teacher,” says a <term>Brāhmaṇa: a prose text explaining Vedic ritual</term>⁴), “by laying his right hand upon the boy, becomes pregnant; on the third day, with the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*⁵), the <term>Brahmin: a member of the priestly caste</term> is born.”

From this moment on, the boy is considered capable of enjoying the remains of sacrificial food⁶).

The ceremony of the *Upanayana* described here is not even hintedly mentioned in the *Ṛgveda* <note>The oldest of the four Vedas</note>. So—

# The Upanayana.

If one were to adopt an exclusively <term>Vedic: relating to the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</term> perspective, one might be inclined to consider this ceremony a recent innovation—one that grew out of the soil of Vedic educational institutions and could only be interpreted within that context. However, it is all the more instructive to observe how the inclusion of "extra-Vedic" materials places the entire matter in a completely different light. We are led out of the sphere of <term>Brahminical: relating to the priestly caste and their teachings</term> instruction to see the prehistory of the <term>Upanayana: the initiation ritual for a young student</term> illuminated within the family institutions of the most primitive antiquity.

Even the <term>Avestan: relating to the Avesta, the primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</term> ceremony of girding with the sacred cord—through which a fifteen-year-old is received into the community of the <term>Zoroastrians: followers of the ancient Persian prophet Zoroaster</term>¹)—guarantees the origin of this practice from a distant, pre-Vedic past, as it proves to be of a common source with the Upanayana. Furthermore, we find essentially identical rites spread across the entire earth among <term>nature-dwelling peoples: a historical term for indigenous societies living in traditional ways</term>. We are dealing here with the celebratory reception of the growing boy into the community of men, whether this celebration is connected to the reaching of puberty or not²). Just as with the Vedic Upanayana, the concept of a "second birth" is found applied to this act among the most diverse peoples. "The thought seems to be," says <note>Sir James George Frazer (1854–1941) was a foundational Scottish social anthropologist whose work "The Golden Bough" compared various world mythologies and rituals.</note> Frazer³) in reference to an Australian tribe, "that a second birth or the beginning of a new life for the novice takes place here: therefore he receives"—just as in India—"a new name at the time when he is circumcised, or his tooth is knocked out, or the blood of his clan is [poured] out over him..." <note>The sentence ends abruptly due to the page break; the catchword "aus-" indicates the original German word was likely "ausgegossen" (poured out).</note>

---

¹) See <note>Wilhelm Geiger (1856–1943) was a German Orientalist specialized in Iranian and Indo-Aryan languages.</note> Geiger, *Eastern Iranian Culture* 238.
²) See Lippert, *History of Culture* II, 340 ff.; Frazer, *Totemism* 38 ff.; Ploss, *The Child*² II, 411 ff.; Kulischer, *Journal of Ethnology* XV, 191 ff. and other extensive ethnological literature.
³) Op. cit. <note>original: "A. a. O." (Am angegebenen Orte)</note> p. 47. Cf. Kulischer op. cit. 195, 199.

After all this, no doubt remains—from an ethnological perspective, this has long been recognized³)—that the Upanayana is nothing other than the specifically Vedic form of the ancient youth initiation. The admission of the boy into the community and into the undertakings of the men has, in the spiritual atmosphere of the <term>Brahmin caste: the social class of priests and scholars</term>, transformed into his admission to the sacred science of the <term>Veda: the oldest body of Sanskrit literature and Hindu scripture</term>, and a corresponding character has been imprinted on the rite; in particular, since it now concerned the establishment of a certain form of life-sharing between teacher and student⁴), rites have forced their way in that resemble the ceremonial of a similar community

# The Upanayana. Rites of Public Life.

...stemming from the marriage ceremony which establishes the household. But behind these innovations, the ancient core of the act—through which it joins the ranks of African, Australian, and American <term>youth initiations: rites of passage marking the transition from childhood to adulthood</term>—cannot remain hidden from the practiced eye. —

Corresponding to the **Upanayana** <note>the initiation ritual into Vedic study</note> at the end of the period of study is the **Samāvartana**, or "**the return**"; the main component of this rite is a bath already discussed above (p. 409), which is clearly intended to wash away the status of the **Brahmin student** <note>original: "Brahmanenschüler", a youth living and studying under a spiritual teacher</note>. —

Finally, we should speak of the **burial ceremonies** here. However, it seems appropriate to treat these in another place, in connection with the discussion of the belief in life after death and the **cult of the dead**.

Rites for **occasions of public life**. As we move on to some of the more prominent rites relating to public life, we must recall the fact set forth above (p. 370) that the acting subject in these rites—the one offering these sacrifices—was not the tribe or the people as such, but rather here too exclusively the individual, in this case generally the king. Essentially, the same relationship highlighted in the discussion of the wedding repeats itself here: rather than **sacrificial acts** <note>original: "Opferhandlungen", formal offerings to deities</note> in the stricter sense, rites that instead possess the character of magical acts stand in the foreground. This is a very natural phenomenon for ceremonies intended not so much to arouse the grace of the gods in general, but rather to win quite specific powers and successes for the person, and which therefore express the effort toward the goal as directly and concretely as possible.

A solemn anointing, or more precisely, a pouring of water (**abhisheka** <note>original: "abhisheka", a ritual lustration or consecration</note>), consecrates the king to his office; for greater power...

<page-num>472</page-num>

### Individual Sacrifices and Festivals.

...another act elevates him: the **royal consecration** (*rājasūya*)¹. Both ceremonies, though not mentioned in the oldest tradition <note>referring to the earliest layers of the Rigveda</note>, likely received their full expression only in the later Vedic period; however, the magical acts that form their main components seem entirely ancient. These celebrations are connected with **Soma rites** <note>sacred rituals involving the pressing and offering of the Soma plant juice</note>; it may be an old custom that the holy drink of the gods was prepared and consumed during royal festivals of this kind. 

The king receives the **anointing** <term>Abhisheka: a ritual bath or sprinkling that consecrates a monarch</term> while sitting on a throne-chair crafted from the wood of the **Udumbara fig tree**—the tree that, for the Indian person, embodies all the abundance of nourishment. A tiger skin covers the seat. A cup, likewise made of Udumbara wood, contains a liquid mixed from various components of diverse power and blessed significance, such as butter, honey, water from a **sun-shower** <note>original: "Sonnenregen", rain that falls while the sun is shining</note>, and so on: with this liquid, the king is sprinkled, thereby transferring to him all the power and abundance inherent in those substances. 

During the *Rājasūya*, in addition to a similar anointing², a larger series of further rites is added, which are intended to ensure the king successes of all kinds. For instance, there is a **raid** directed at a herd of cows; according to another version, there is the shooting of arrows at the king's "weak relatives" and the plundering of the same; furthermore, a **dice game** for a cow, in which the king is clearly intended to be the winner³.

²) Here, in a number of regulations, it emerges very explicitly that the saturation of the body with the respective substance is the decisively important factor.
