<page-num>473</page-num>

# Rājasūya, Vājapeya, Horse Sacrifice.

The *Vājapeya* (“drink of strength”¹) is considered even more sublime and effective than the celebration of the *Rājasūya*. A chariot race stands at the center of this rite, in which the sacrificer <note>the king or patron for whom the ritual is performed</note> naturally emerges victorious. This is clearly a magical act intended to bestow upon him the swift power (*vāja*), which is most visibly embodied in a running horse. This is followed by the "ascent to the sun" mentioned previously (page 88)—that is, climbing toward a wheel rim made of wheat flour that represents the sun, which has been placed atop the post intended for binding the sacrificial animals. Once he has descended again, the sacrificer receives an anointing², similar to the celebrations discussed earlier.

The highest sacrificial <note>original Latin: "sacrificale"</note> expression of royal power and royal splendor is the **horse sacrifice** (*aśvamedha*³). "He has marched victoriously across the whole earth and offered the sacrificial horse": these are the standard words of a text speaking of the greatness of the most legendary kings⁴). We already touched upon the fact (page 306) that this sacrifice, in its true essence, is not a thank-offering for successes achieved, but rather a petitionary sacrifice—allowable only after such successes—aimed at fulfilling the king's highest desires. While the ritual texts present the gods in their entirety as recipients of this sacrifice, with special emphasis on *Prajāpati*⁵) <note>a creator deity in later Vedic mythology</note>, there is also a trace of another con—

²) Regarding the dietary prohibition that follows this, see page 414 above.
³) Cf. especially Hillebrandt, *National Sacrifices in Ancient India* (Tribute to Boehtlingk, page 40 ff.).
⁴) Aitareya Brāhmana VIII, 21 ff.
⁵) Whose role, of course, cannot be ancient.

### Individual Sacrifices and Festivals.

-ception preserved: Verses which report on the horse sacrifices of ancient kings¹) speak several times of the sacrifice being offered to Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra <note>original: *Vṛtratödter*; Vṛtra was a demonic serpent representing drought and chaos, famously defeated by the storm-god Indra</note>: the most obvious deity for a celebration that moves entirely within the conceptual sphere of martial heroism. The royal animal²), the horse as a sacrificial animal, indicates—as we have already explained (p. 356)—the vigorous speed which the king desires to attain or increase within himself, and of which the horse is the preeminent bearer among animals.

During the bathing of the sacrificial horse, which consecrated it for its holy purpose, a man of base origin had to strike dead a "four-eyed dog"—that is, a dog that had two eye-like spots next to its eyes, clearly a symbol of hostile powers³)—with a club⁴); this dog was then made to swim in the water beneath the bathing horse. "Whoever seeks the life of the horse, Varuna’s plague <note>original: *Varuṇas Plage*; referring to the god Varuna, who punished sinners with disease, particularly dropsy</note> strikes them," went the accompanying verse. After the horse had received its consecration, it was allowed to run free throughout the land for a year; an entourage—

¹) In the section *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* XIII, 5, 4.

³) But see note 4.

⁴) "Four-eyed dogs" also appear as dogs of the god of death <note>Yama</note>. It is conceivable that the killing of this dog during the consecration of the sacrificial horse originally had the purpose—contrary to the interpretation given in the present ritual—of providing the horse with protection against ghostly stalking: that is why it had to swim up to it.

of armed youths accompanied and guarded it. Meanwhile, at home, various sacrifices, the recitation of solemn narratives, singing, and lute-playing filled the sacrificial grounds; young and old, high-born and lowly, took part in the ceremonies, which were rich in pageantry. Finally, the year had passed; amidst the splendor of a three-day <term>Soma</term> <note>A sacred ritual drink and the deity associated with it; the Soma festival was a central pillar of Vedic religion</note> celebration, the horse was offered, surrounded by a following of numerous sacrificial animals¹).

Beside the dead horse, the chief wife of the king had to lie down; the woman and the animal were covered with a garment. It is clear that this is a matter of magic intended to awaken fertility and procreation, and to saturate it with the blessing emanating from the horse sacrifice. Between the priests and the royal women, along with their entourage, obscene jests were exchanged—was this a piece of old folk-defiance that had attained ritual permanence? Or a kind of farcical entertainment for the invisibly present gods? Or perhaps something belonging to fertility magic? More serious discourses were exchanged among the priests; riddles regarding priestly wisdom <note>original: *priesterliche Weisheit*; often referred to as *Brahmodya*, these were formal intellectual contests</note> were posed and solved. What abundance of blessing was thought to reside in this sacrifice—the "barbarically grandiose" centerpiece of the Vedic cult—is shown in the magical power attributed to the water of the sacrificial bath performed after the horse sacrifice. This water has absorbed the aura of the holiness inherent to the sacrifice: "after the sacrificer has stepped out, evildoers who have performed no religious observances step into it: they are called 'pure' through the horse sacrifice" ²).

<header>Sorcery and Related Matters.</header>

## Sorcery and Related Matters.

The sacrificial cult, which we have had to describe, we found constantly interspersed with magical acts; it is necessary to consider the fundamental features of the <term>Vedic</term> <note>Relating to the Vedas, the oldest scripts of ancient India, dating roughly from 1500 to 500 BCE</note> system of sorcery here in a connected way.

To the connoisseur of magical customs—which appear essentially identical among both higher and lower-standing nations—the following presentation will confirm what for him can hardly require confirmation: that Indian tradition also provides an example of that very type which reaches across the entire earth. No doubt we have reached here a very primitive stratum of religious, or if you will, pre-religious concern of man for his well-being; no doubt that long before one had begun to revere sublime gods who protect the good and the right, one kept harmful spirits away through water and fire, through noise and blows, destroyed the enemy by destroying his image or his cut hair, and conjured up rain by creating an image of rain and an abundance of water.

On the lowest levels of culture, the cult of sacrifice and worship—so far as it is already present—is understandably most closely and firmly linked with the practice of sorcery; the priest is at the same time a sorcerer; indeed, he is more the latter than the former. But the later course of things must pull two spheres apart. One sphere, moving in the path of powerful historical currents, is raised ever higher by the progressing development of thought and not least by the ethicizing <note>The process of shifting religious focus from ritual mechanics to moral and ethical behavior</note> of the religious essence; the other sphere, remaining immobile, clothes itself with the character of a lack of culture and backwardness. If this separation of cult and sorcery, one can approximately—

...should we also speak of belief and "superstition" as already being present in the <term>Vedic period</term> <note>The era in ancient Indian history (c. 1500 – c. 500 BCE) during which the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, were composed</note>? The opposition between a prayer literature like that of the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>original: "Ṛgveda"; the oldest of the four Vedas, consisting of hymns to deities</note>¹) and the magic literature of the <term>Atharvaveda</term> <note>The fourth Veda, which contains spells for healing, protection, and daily life</note> might seem to support this. I believe, however, that closer examination reveals this appearance to be deceptive. Indeed, sacrificial invocations established themselves early as a distinct literary type, and these prayers to the great gods offered little opportunity for mentioning magical practices. But the ritual of these very sacrifices, for which the prayer hymns were intended, is described in other Vedic texts as being permeated from beginning to end with sorcery customs, the execution of which fell to the sacrificial priests. And, as we saw, whenever rituals exist that are attached to specific occasions, directed toward specific goals, and thus favor a more prominent emergence of the magical element—such as weddings, the <term>initiation of youths</term> <note>original: "Jünglingsweihe"; likely referring to the Upanayana rite of passage</note>, or the royal consecration—these indeed represent entire displays of magic of all kinds²); and this magic always moves in forms that bear the stamp of the highest antiquity. Should we assume that the Ṛgvedic sacrificial priests, the authors of the ancient hymns, lived as if on an island untouched by sorcery, surrounded by all this magic that stems from the distant past and, on the other hand, reaches through the priestly literature of more recent times? Certainly not; rather, even in the Ṛgvedic period, the sacrificial priest was simultaneously a sorcerer—

Against one who offers a sacrifice with hostile intent, one invokes the alliance of "the sorcerer, destruction, and the evil demon": "may they through injustice destroy his truth"²). The powers set in motion through magic for or against human well-being are only partially conceived as spirits—specifically those predominantly malicious and harmful spirits mentioned earlier (pages 262 ff.). Beside these spirits—and perhaps standing ahead of them in the <term>Vedic stage of development</term>—there is another class of entities with which magic operates: impersonal or semi-personal substances and forces. Endowed with the most varied modes of action, these sometimes exist independently and sometimes dwell within other entities; they reach humans and their possessions through all sorts of paths, bringing good or bad fortune. The most general expression in the Vedic language for such entities is "body" <note>original: *tanū*</note>. Hunger and thirst are "bodies"²); in a woman endowed with harmful, fatal qualities, there dwells the "husband-killing body," the "body of childlessness," or the "body of herdlessness" <note>An ancient reference to the loss of livestock or wealth</note>³). Or these substances are spoken of in neutral terms: "that which is fearful in you"—"that through which you became one who miscarries..."

In the Vedic epic of the bird Garuda²), Tarkshya drinks half of the ascetic heat <term>tapas</term> <note>spiritual energy or "heat" generated through intense self-discipline</note> along with the magical power inherent in it, which the wise Valakhilyas <note>a group of thumb-sized semi-divine sages</note> had acquired; through this drink, he gains the power to father Garuda. 

Magical technique indicates at every turn the belief that the substances being handled are transferred from one being to another through touch: therefore, either the initiation or the avoidance of touch plays a leading role in magic. These substances enter the body particularly easily through eating and drinking, as in the story of Tarkshya mentioned above: here we find one of the roots from which the widespread ritual requirement of fasting emerged³). 

But these "fluids" <term>fluida</term> <note>original: "Fluida"; invisible, flowing spiritual substances or essences</note> can also travel by airier paths. One can breathe them in: reason enough to hold one's breath on many occasions. They can be communicated through the gaze; the person looking can transfer them to others through their sight, but they can also take them into themselves by the same path, becoming "infected" by them: a reason, on many occasions, not to look at something or not to look back. 

Against these manifold ways of movement and communication of substances—we have only touched upon some of the main ones here—stand obstructions, such as those created by water, fire, mountains, or narrow holes: a brief mention must suffice, as the types of various magical acts to be presented later will provide a more complete and vivid picture of both the movements and the obstructions of these fluids. <page-num>484</page-num>
<header>Magic and Related Matters.</header>

and magic, on the one hand, cannot be fundamentally delimited from faith and ritual practice <note>original: *Cultus*</note>, there exists, on the other hand—especially in the more ancient state of things—a large portion of primitive natural science and hygiene. This is hardly separable from the spheres of religion and superstition even by the boundaries of our modern classification systems, and in truth and reality, it was absolutely never separated from them.

Following these introductory remarks, it will be easy to describe the primary types of magical acts. In a vast majority of cases, the magician seeks to achieve his goal by warding off demons or magical substances from himself or others; in another group of cases, he does so by directing them toward himself or others. Alongside this, and in the closest connection to it, stands the method of bringing about processes that one cannot evoke directly—natural occurrences that are not within human power, or influences on others that one is too weak or otherwise unable to inflict. This is achieved by performing the act in an image or upon an image, in order to evoke or influence the original model <note>original: *Urbild*</note>¹⁾, or by performing it on a part or a single specimen to influence the whole or the entire species. Given the strong sense of substantial unity between the image and the original, the part and the whole—which dominated ancient ways of thinking—it is obvious that this form of magic cannot be fundamentally separated from the process of directing a magical substance onto the being one wishes to influence.

<page-num>485</page-num>
# Main Types of Magic.

In complete internal similarity with these procedures, there remains one final main type of magic to be mentioned here: **divination magic** <term>divination: the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</term>. Here, the goal is to gain knowledge of something not directly knowable—such as a future event—through an indirect route. The most common method for this is to create a representation of the event in question, or to take possession of an existing representation—especially within the sphere of sacrifice, which is saturated with mystical significance—and then to draw conclusions about what one wishes to know based on the course of events observed there. Thus, just as the previously mentioned magical procedure consisted of creating an image of a process to bring that process about, here the main event itself is recognized by observing such an image.

**Defense Against Hostile Entities.** Let us now turn to illustrating the types generally described here in brief with a number of examples, beginning with the expulsion of hostile entities. While, on the whole, the same means are used against demons as against neutral magical substances, the struggle against these personal beings understandably often takes on a special appearance in its details.

The defense against evil demons does not under all circumstances take the form of open hostility; one also attempts to escape their harassment through friendly behavior, expressions of reverence, and offerings¹). One asks them to depart, to have mercy on the human; “Reverence be to you,” “revering you, we wish to serve you with sacrificial offerings”²). One

# Protective Magic.

Substances. Defense initially manifests as caution: one avoids everything that could attract them; one seeks to make access as difficult as possible. We already discussed above the significance of observances directed toward this goal, such as fasting, chastity, holding one's breath, silence, seclusion, dressing in disguising garments, and the like ¹). Just as one hides their person, one also hides from the wrongdoers <note>The "wrongdoers" here refers to malevolent spirits or sorcerers seeking to cause harm.</note> those parts of one's own being that could offer them points of attack—for example, one hides or buries the hair, beard, or nails cut from a child or youth during consecration rites ²). Furthermore, one naturally avoids any contact with beings in whom dangerous spirits or harmful substances dwell: for instance, after childbirth, touching the mother during the ten days of her impurity is considered dangerous; the stones to be laid down for the goddess of destruction (<term>Nirṛti: the Vedic personification of death, decay, and misfortune</term>) during the construction of the Agni altar <term>Agni altar: a complex brick structure used for Vedic fire sacrifices</term> are brought to their place without touching them ³). Closely related to not touching is the non-hearing of impure sounds, and above all, the non-seeing of impure or dangerous persons and objects: such as not looking during offerings to the dead, to Rudra <note>Rudra is a fierce Vedic deity, often associated with storms and disease, who required careful handling in rituals.</note>, and the like ⁴). Furthermore, there is the exceedingly common custom—encountered in India as well as in the most diverse parts of the globe, in regions of both higher and lower culture—of not looking back when leaving the site of any uncanny or eerie operations

# Magic and Related Matters.
<page-num>490</page-num>

In atonement ceremonies, bathing and washing play a significant role (p. 322 f.); the "sacredly dangerous" substance inherent in a sacrifice is removed—at least after major offerings—through a sacrificial bath, so as not to carry it over into profane <note>Profane: the ordinary, everyday world as opposed to the sacred or ritual space.</note> life¹). It would be pointless to provide extensive collections of material regarding the very clear role of bathing in religious cults and magic²); one should only mention the requirement that after reciting spells addressed to uncanny beings—to Rudra <note>Rudra: a fierce Vedic deity associated with storms and disease, later evolving into Shiva.</note>, evil demons, the dead, and the like—one must purify oneself with water from the contact inherent in such actions³). If in India, as elsewhere⁴), cow urine appears as a particularly valued means of purification, one may assume that this is based on the effort to use a substance for washing that simultaneously has the power to impart an abundance of nourishment to the person, as it participates in the nature of the cow.

Alongside washing, or simultaneously with it, wiping naturally also plays a role. The unlucky contamination caused by bird droppings is wiped and washed away. After a bad dream, one wipes one's face⁵). One wipes away dangerous substances with lead—which often appears in magic rituals with a somewhat disparaging significance—and with a black wool thread⁶). In various forms, the plant <term>Apāmārga: *Achyranthes aspera*, a plant whose name translates literally to "wiping away"; it was used in Vedic rituals to "wipe out" diseases and demons.</term> was used as a means of purification and healing; its name was interpreted through folk etymology as "wiping away," and from...

Here we are led to the role which the staff plays in the most diverse areas of ritual. The Vedic student (<term>Brahmacārin: a young man during his stage of life dedicated to spiritual study and celibacy.</term>), whom the observances imposed upon him characterize as a person particularly endangered by the attacks of spirits, receives a staff during the solemn act of his initiation, at the same time as the announcement of the duties incumbent upon him; he must carry it constantly and must not allow any passage between it and his body²). At the ceremony which concludes his period of study, the staff is "sacrificed into the water"³) along with the belt that was placed on the student at his initiation and some other objects filled with special holiness. At the same time, however, the Brahman—now entering a new stage of life and subject to new observances—receives a new staff made of a different material than the one the student had carried. A verse spoken during this act, in its various versions, indicates the purpose of the staff: "Protect me from all sides"—"from all powers of destruction protect me from all sides"—"strike all enemy hosts round about like the giver of treasures (Indra)": and here, alongside human enemies and harmful animals, the <term>Rakshas</term> and <term>Piśācas</term> <note>These are classes of malevolent demons or flesh-eating spirits in Hindu mythology.</note> are also quite explicitly named⁴). — In another context, it was pointed out (p. 409) that the consecrated state of the Brahman student is entirely comparable to that of the Soma sacrificer: here, as there, one is lifted out of profane existence by special ob-

The custom of pulling a person through a narrow hole—whereby the entity to be removed is "stripped off"—is found in the superstitions of many peoples and is not foreign to ancient India. The skin-afflicted Apālā <note>A woman from a Rigvedic hymn who was cured of a skin disease by the god Indra.</note> is pulled by Indra "through the hole of the wagon, through the hole of the cart, through the hole of the yoke"; the god "makes her golden-skinned, purifying her three times." And it is certainly interpreted correctly as a remnant of a similar form of purification when, during a wedding, the hole of a wagon yoke is placed upon the head of the bride²). — 

In many cases, the removal also takes the form of transferring the essence to be eliminated into objects (including living beings) that are brought into contact with it, which are then removed; or alternatively, one banishes the essence into the most distant possible dwellings through incantations or symbolic actions, thereby making it harmless. At a crossroads, one lets the hostile entity pass over onto someone else³). The garment with which the impurity of the bride has been wiped away is hung up in the forest; likewise, the dangerous substance of the bridal shirt is banished into a post or a tree, which is then "clothed" with that shirt⁴). # Sorcery and Related Matters.

Agents that have not been given their due in the previous discussions will be discussed specifically further below: such as the amulet and medicament, the magic spell, and the magic sacrifice.

### The Sending of Spirits and Substances.

In contrast to the expulsion of spirit beings and substances is the magical "sending" or directing of them toward oneself and others, toward friend and foe—the sending of both favorable and harmful things. As we have already touched upon in another context (above p. 268), when someone suffers under a hostile spell, it is considered the common state of affairs that his opponent has unleashed evil spirits upon him. Thus, the Rigvedic <note>Refers to the *Rigveda*, the oldest of the four *Vedas*, the ancient sacred hymns of India composed in archaic Sanskrit.</note> sorcerer sends the disease demon <term>Apvā</term> <note>A personification of a disease, likely dysentery or colic, intended to weaken an enemy's resolve and physical strength.</note> against the enemy army:
> "Go away, Apvā, to confuse their spirit, to seize their limbs.
Go at them; burn them with your glow in their
hearts; let the enemies fall into dark gloom!"

With such spells, magical acts might then be combined, as described in a ritual text: the release of a white-footed ewe—in which the power of the disease was thought to be incarnated—against the enemy army¹). The sorcerer could also—just like the spirits serving him—take on animal form and in this shape bring harm to his enemies; the belief in such transformations is characteristic of Vedic sorcery, as it likely is for that of all peoples. Thus, the person pursued by such magic calls upon the Storm Gods <note>The *Maruts*, a group of deities associated with the wind and thunder, often depicted as a young band of warriors.</note> to seek out and seize the hostile sorcerers among the villagers "who become birds and fly around at night"²).

The magic-infused substances which one [brings] to oneself...

This contact, however, can take on the most varied forms depending on the nature of the body that acts as the carrier of the substance in question. "Anoint yourself with one; make an amulet of the other; wash yourself with one, drink the other of those things," it says in one instance regarding **magical substances**²). It is also a kind of "immaterial contact," so to speak, that emanates, for example, from a favorable or unfavorable celestial body near which the moon stands, from the waxing or waning of the moon, or from the length of the day: in these conditions lies a magical potency that communicates itself to people or to the actions they perform.

Regarding the effect of contact, the following passage from a **ritual text**³) expresses itself, for instance, in which the correct and genuine logic of sacrificial magic finds its voice. It concerns the question of whether the sacrificer <term>sacrificer</term> <note>The *yajamāna*, the person who institutes and pays for the sacrifice to receive its benefits.</note> should touch the animal being led to the sacrifice.
> "There it is said: The sacrificer must not touch it. For it is being led to death; therefore he should not touch it. But he should touch it after all. One does not lead the animal being led to sacrifice to death; therefore he should touch it after all. He would exclude himself from the sacrifice if he did not touch it."

Thus the entire ritual is full of prescriptions stating that this or that officiating person should touch another person or an object; the fluid <note>The author uses the term "fluidum," referring to a semi-physical, semi-spiritual essence believed to flow between things.</note> of the sacrifice, the blessing-filled power dwelling within it, is thereby transferred. ### The Conveyance of Spirits and Substances.

Just as we encountered "wiping off" as an action to remove a hostile substance, "wiping on," anointing, pouring over, and similar actions are means of conveying them: the guilt of sin <note>original: *Sündenschuld*</note>, the dangerous substance of an evil dream, can be "wiped onto" a person¹). To destroy an enemy, one sacrifices reed arrowheads that have been smeared with one's own sweat²): the meaning of this action is likely to direct arrows against him that are saturated with the power of one’s own inner heat, one's own <term>tapas</term> <note>Sanskrit for "heat" or "ardor," referring to the potent energy generated through asceticism or ritual intensity</note>. Furthermore, one might point to the royal anointing, the anointing or sacrificial treatment of the war chariot³) and so forth: in every case, it is a matter of introducing a substance filled with magical powers.

Naturally, eating plays a very prominent role among the means for conveying such a substance. The magical power attributed to eating sacrificial food—the strengthening of the person with the blessing embodied in the sacrifice—has already been discussed in another context; likewise, the custom of giving a child, as its first nourishment, the substance which represents the specific quality desired for that child in each instance—

---

[It] plays a role in the *rite of vital essence* <note>original: *rasakarman*; a Vedic ceremony intended to grant vigor or essence</note> (Kauṣika Sūtra 21, 23), the sacrifice against poisoning (ibid. 31, 25), and so on. — I suspect another meaning for the anthill when, on various occasions, the remains and waste from the sacrifice, such as spoiled or boiled-over sacrificial food and the like, are poured into one (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa III. 7, 2, 1; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra III, 10, 23; Weber *Rājasūya* 12. 104 Note 2. 109 Note 1; compare Krauss, *Folk Belief and Religious Custom of the South Slavs* 158). It seems to me that this belongs under the category of disposing of dangerous sacrificial substances (see above p. 345 ff.). Similarly, among the Zulu people (Callaway, *The Religious System of the Amazulu* 315), the substance of an illness is buried in an anthill; the ants restore their mound and thus seal away the dangerous object.

The <term>Atharvaveda</term> <note>Atharvaveda: the fourth sacred book of the Vedas, consisting largely of spells, incantations, and prayers for healing and protection.</note> is full of verses expressing the fear of sorcery "that has been buried in the sacrificial straw, in the cemetery, or in the field," magic that has been placed in a well, or carefully prepared just as one adorns a woman for her wedding journey, whose parts have been joined together as a <term>Ṛbhu</term> <note>Ṛbhu: in Vedic mythology, one of three divine craftsmen known for their supernatural skill in fashioning objects like chariots.</note> (see above, p. 235) joins the parts of a chariot¹). However, one can restore the fortune of a person endangered by such magic by digging up the buried items while reciting the following verse:

> "Your fortune, which they buried under the three stones and the four stones, that I dig up again, along with your offspring and wealth."

### The Transmission of Spirits and Substances. 505

When one buried cut hair, nails, and so on in a cowshed or another auspicious location, the intention behind this—among other purposes—is clearly evident¹): to allow the person concerned to be saturated with **luck-substance** <note>original: "Glückssubstanz"; this refers to the ancient belief that "luck" or "fortune" was a physical essence that could be absorbed or transmitted.</note> in hidden stillness.

Finally, it must be mentioned that in order to transmit some substance or **power**, it was also considered effective if, during whatever **manipulations** were being performed, **tools** of any kind were **used** in which the relevant **power** was **embodied**. To a prince who had been driven away, one gave **magic food** to eat in order to bring him back: this food was cooked using wood that had grown out of the chopped-off stump of a tree, which thus signified the **restoration of a destroyed existence**²). During a **sacrifice** offered for the same purpose of **bringing back an exile**, the **sacrificial fire-place** (?) was sprinkled with earth from his homeland, and **materials** originating from that land were also used³). To remove troublesome **ants**, a **sacrifice** was performed: for this, a **sacrificial spoon** made of *Bādhaka wood* was used⁴). *Bādhaka* means "the **remover**" <note>original: "der Beseitiger"; the name of the plant *Bādhaka* (Cassia fistula) is linguistically linked to the verb meaning to drive away or oppress.</note>: in this way, one set the **power** of **removal** into **action**. In a **sacrifice** offered for **victory in battle**, earth was used for the **sacrificial altar** (*vedi*) <note>term: *vedi*—a shallow bed or trench dug in the ground, specifically prepared to serve as the altar for Vedic sacrifices.</note> that had been churned up by a boar, and in which the boar’s **strength** therefore resided⁵). ## **Magic by Means of Imagery and Similar Methods**

We now turn to describing several cases of the magical procedure characterized above (p. 484), in which the desired event is brought about by creating an image of that event. The higher cult, which is tied to the three sacrificial fires, is rich in rites that possess such significance, or where this meaning has attached itself to their original purpose. We have seen how the morning ignition of the sacred fire became a spell to bring about the sunrise, and how the trickling of the Soma juice through the purifying sieve became a rain charm¹). The chariot race during the royal sacrifice of the **Vājapeya** <note>term: *Vājapeya*—literally "the drink of strength," a prestigious ritual intended to rejuvenate a king or high-ranking priest.</note>, in which the king organizing the sacrifice wins, is a charm intended to gain victorious power and speed for him²): the individual success, artificially created for him, is an image of general, real victory. The solemn dice game is no different; it appears in the ritual on various occasions³) and clearly represents a charm that grants luck and profit to the sacrificer. When, during the solstice celebration, an Aryan wrestles with a **Shudra** <note>term: *Shudra*—the fourth and lowest social class in the Vedic system, often representing the non-Aryan population.</note> for a white, round hide and tears it away from him⁴), we recognize in this a charm through which sunlight is liberated from the threatening powers of darkness. The <term>Ashvins</term> <note>term: *Ashvin*—divine twin horsemen in Vedic mythology, known as physicians to the gods and heralds of the dawn.</note> and <term>Sarasvatī</term> <note>term: *Sarasvatī*—a major goddess associated with rivers, healing, and knowledge.</note> heal <term>Indra</term> <note>term: *Indra*—the king of the gods and the deity of storms and war.</note>, who is sick from excessive <term>Soma</term> consumption <note>term: *Soma*—a sacred ritual drink believed to grant immortality and divine inspiration.</note>: in the same way, the sacrificer suffering from any kind of failure shall be elevated to full strength and complete happiness. The type of magic we are considering here is frequently found in a context that tends to possess particular importance in all ancient ritual systems: that of rain magic. During the solstice celebration, one shoots at a hide (p. 445); presumably, this represents the seal of heaven, which one wishes to pierce. On the same occasion, girls with filled water jars dance around a fire; they pour out the jars and sing a song which speaks of the cows bathing (p. 445). This too is, by all appearances, a form of rain magic. Spheres filled with magical power, such as those of dreams, sacrifice, or burial, provide significant images of reality. The movements of a sacrificial animal or the rising smoke of the sacrifice allow one to glimpse the future. While in these omens, <term>divination</term> <note>term: *divination*—the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note> based on symbolic images already begins to blend with the kind that receives news of the future from the superhuman knowledge of gods and spirits, it is this latter aspect of divination that emerges most clearly in the interpretation of the movement, flight, or voice of animals. These animals are believed to stand in a special connection with gods or spirits, such as the owl, the crow, or the hyena (see p. 76 above)¹).

We shall limit ourselves to sharing just a few details.

Anyone wishing to know whether a girl will make a good wife should have her choose one of several clumps of earth. ¹) The <term>ordeal</term> <note>term: *ordeal*—a traditional trial used to determine guilt or innocence by subjecting the accused to a dangerous or painful test, believed to be under divine control.</note> (trial by fire, trial by water, and the like) also belongs to the category of determining hidden things with the help of the knowledge of superhuman beings. Its origin in Indo-Germanic times has been made probable notably by Kaegi (in the *Festschrift of the 39th Philologists' Assembly* 1887, pp. 40 ff.). The point is not that the divine element should punish the guilty, but rather that it should testify to guilt or innocence through its behavior. ### Amulets and Medications.

We must complete our presentation of Vedic magical practices by adding a few supplementary remarks here regarding the mode of operation of several magical agents that we have frequently encountered in the preceding pages: concerning amulets and medications, concerning magical spells, and concerning magical sacrifices.

We already noted above (p. 499) that the transmission of a power or substance is effected in the same way through internal or external use: through eating and drinking just as through ointments or the wearing of an amulet. The magical medication or amulet stems, in principle, from some being—preferably, it seems, from the plant kingdom—which embodies the effect to be achieved in whatever way, even if only through the sound of its name³). ## The Magic Formula.

The magical power of the word is already evident in the magical effects of the name¹) and those of lucky or unlucky ominous pronouncements, as accepted in Indian belief just like that of all peoples; this power reaches its peak in the magic formula, the curse, and the oath. The type of "auspicious dialogue" common in India as elsewhere²)—where the answer given to a question seems accidental, though in reality it is naturally prearranged—rests on the belief in the power of auspicious words; this answer provides the effective <term>omen</term> <note>term: *Omen*—a sign or prophetic symbol meant to predict the future.</note>. At the plowman’s festival, the wife asks the practitioner: "Have you plowed?" He answers: "That we have!" She asks further: "What have you brought back from it?" To which he replies: "Possessions, luck, prosperity, children, cattle, food, the enjoyment of food!" During the hair-parting ritual performed on a pregnant woman, the husband asks her: "What do you see?" And she answers: "Offspring!" During the rite to obtain male offspring, the husband asks the woman to whom he has given a magic potion: "What are you drinking? What are you drinking?" She re—

<page-num>517</page-num>
# Magic Formulas.

[Just as the speaking] of the name exerts a magical power over the named being, the naming of a desired process brings about the process itself, thanks to the same mystical bond between name and thing. The power of the magic is strengthened when the desired effect is compared with occurrences in nature or the world of the gods; these comparisons, so common in magic formulas, are clearly not accidental poetic ornament, but rather they contain a magical element: the entities or events mentioned in the comparison are intended to draw their counterpart into the present situation:

> “As the rising sun robs the stars of their luster, so I rob all women and men who are hostile to me of their strength” — “The cows have settled down at their resting place; the birds have flown to their nest; the mountains stand firm in their place: I have made the kidney stand firm in its place” <note>This is a healing charm intended to stabilize an internal organ or stop a physical ailment by comparing it to the stability of nature.</note> — “As the wind stirs the lotus pond from all sides, so shall your offspring <note>literally "fruit of the womb"</note> stir; in the tenth month <note>Ancient Indian tradition often counted pregnancy as lasting ten lunar months.</note> it shall emerge”¹)

Related to such comparisons is when the incantation recounts how the gods once achieved their successes through the very same magic intended here, or by using the same <term>amulet</term> <note>term: *amulet*—a physical object, such as a piece of wood or a plant root, worn for protection and empowered by a spoken charm.</note> being used now (cf. p. 514); the time-tested power of the magic will become effective once again. Other frequently recurring features of magic spells are as follows. In order to strike the harmful spirit, the seat of the evil, or whatever the case may be in every instance, one names the entire series of possibilities in succession:

> from eyes and nose, from ears and brain, from neck, back, and arms, I drive out the disease — whether you belong to <term>Soma</term> <note>term: *Soma*—a major Vedic deity and a sacred ritual drink; here, the spell addresses a spirit that might be under Soma's jurisdiction.</note>,

---

¹) <note>original: "Atharvaveda VII, 13, 1; 96, 1: Ṛgveda V, 78, 7. Wie solche Gleichnisse sich gelegentlich in rituelle Handlungen umsetzen konnten ist S. 481 Anm. 1 gezeigt."</note> <term>Atharvaveda</term> <note>term: *Atharvaveda*—one of the four Vedas, containing hymns, but also many charms for healing and magic.</note> VII, 13, 1; 96, 1: <term>Rigveda</term> <note>term: *Rigveda*—the oldest of the sacred Vedic scriptures.</note> V, 78, 7. How such similes could occasionally be converted into ritual actions is shown on p. 481, Note 1.

# Magic and Related Matters.

[...I] buy you for King Soma <note>In Vedic tradition, Soma is the personified deity of a sacred ritual drink.</note>; if you belong to Varuna <note>A major Vedic deity associated with the sky, cosmic order, and justice.</note>, I buy you for King Varuna; if you belong to the Vasus <note>A group of eight elemental deities representing aspects of nature, such as fire, earth, and wind.</note>, I buy you for the Vasus¹). However, if one knows the spirit one wishes to drive away, one lets it feel that knowledge: "This is your name; we know your birth; this is your father, this is your mother"²). The objects from which one expects a magical effect are often described as containing or originating from certain substances. For example, the drum is described as originating from the "Lord of the Forest" and being "covered with cows" (Atharvaveda V, 20, 1), meaning it is made of wood and covered with leather. This, too, is clearly not just a rhetorical flourish; rather, it serves the purpose of drawing upon the magical properties of those substances to aid in the magic.

**Curses and Oaths.** A special case in which the word appears as a primary carrier of magical power is that of the curse, including the oath. The gods curse the trees by which they have been offended: 

> "You shall be struck down as if by a thunderbolt with a handle that comes from yourselves." "Therefore, one strikes down trees as if with a thunderbolt using a handle that comes from them. For they are cursed by the gods"³). 

Agni <note>The Vedic god of fire and the messenger between gods and humans.</note> curses the fish that betrayed his hiding place in the waters, decreeing that it should be killed using various tricks: 

> "Therefore, one kills the fish with various tricks, for it is cursed"⁴).

<page-num>519</page-num>
<header>The Curse.</header>

That the curse played a role in the **Vedic period** <note>The era in ancient India (c. 1500–500 BCE) when the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, were composed.</note> is self-evident and is confirmed by the numerous spells intended to avert a curse or to turn it back upon the curser. “To the curser let the curse return. With the spell that is friendly to us, we crush the eye and ribs of the hostile spell” (Atharvaveda II, 7, 5): the curse here seems to take on a hint of a personal being, moving back and forth in ghostly concreteness between the **sorcerer** and the **counter-sorcerer**, who send it to one another. The harmful power inherent in the curse can be further strengthened by additional magical ceremonies: “Whose wife has a lover—if he hates him, he should set up the sacrificial fire in an unfired vessel and scatter a sacrificial strewing of reed arrows against the right direction <note>Vedic rituals usually move clockwise; moving "against" this direction signifies a destructive or "black" magic purpose.</note>; then he should offer three reed tips smeared with butter against the right direction with the spells: ‘In my fire you have sacrificed; I take from you hope and prospect, [Name]!’—here he speaks his name. ‘In my fire you have sacrificed; I take from you children and cattle, [Name]!’—here he speaks his name. ‘In my fire you have sacrificed; I take from you breath and out-breath <note>Original: "Atem und Aushauch," referring to the vital life-forces of prāṇa and apāna.</note>, [Name]!’—here he speaks his name. Robbed of power, robbed of the blessing of his good deeds, he departs from this world, whom a **Brahmin** <note>A member of the highest, priestly caste, responsible for performing rituals and maintaining sacred knowledge.</note> who knows such things curses” ¹).

The **Brāhmaṇa** texts <note>Ancient Indian commentaries on the Vedas that explain the symbolism and performance of rituals.</note> very frequently warn against some ritual error not in the form of saying: “This or that misfortune will follow from it,” but rather: “If someone then said: ‘This or that misfortune will occur,’ then one would be exposed to it” (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa XII, 4, 1, 4; similar phrases occur frequently): the error in question thus creates the disposition to succumb to a possible curse.</gloss>

<page-num>520</page-num>
<header>### Sorcery and Related Matters.</header>

The **Oath** is a curse that one directs against oneself, to take effect if one should break their word or if one has told an untruth <note>original: "sofern man sein Wort brechen wird oder sofern man die Unwahrheit gesagt hat." Footnote 1 clarifies the linguistic connection: the same verb *ṣap-* means "to curse" in the active voice, and "to swear" (literally "to curse oneself") in the middle voice.</note>. One stakes one’s life, the lives of one’s kin, and one’s earthly and eternal possessions—or perhaps specific items among these goods—for the truth of one’s word. Along with the spoken formula, which calls down misfortune upon one's own person, there may be gestures or symbolic acts that represent a magic that draws in hostile powers. The priest, who intends to bestow the great **royal consecration** <note>The *Rājasūya*, a complex ancient Indian ritual for the inauguration of a king.</note> upon a king, makes him swear:

> “All my merit from sacrifices and gifts from the day of my birth to the day of my death <note>Similar formulas appear in the law books of Baudhāyana and Nārada.</note>, my place, my good deeds <note>A common expression in oaths; since deeds decide one's fate in the afterlife, this is akin to swearing "by one's soul’s salvation."</note>, my life, and my offspring shall belong to you, if I deceive you.” <note>original: "ṣāpayitvā 'bhishincet" — "having made him swear, he should consecrate him." From the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa VIII, 15.</note>

As an ancient **Vedic** <note>Refers to the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, composed in Sanskrit.</note> verse already testifies, one called upon the god **Varuṇa** <note>The deity of the cosmic order and the sky, often associated with the punishment of liars.</note>, the cows, and the waters as witnesses; in later literature, rules are found stating that a **Kshatriya** <term>Kshatriya: the warrior and ruling caste</term> shall swear by his chariots and weapons, the **Vaiśya** <term>Vaiśya: the merchant and farmer caste</term> by his cows, his grain, and his gold—the **Brahmin** <term>Brahmin: the priestly and scholarly caste</term> shall swear by the truth—; <note>From the Laws of Manu, VIII, 113. This implies that one swears upon the things most vital to one's social standing and identity.</note>

In one story, girls swear that they wish to receive an old husband or no husband at all if they are speaking the untruth¹); a queen swears that she wishes to be reborn as an evil demon if she has deceived her husband²). Through the gesture of self-touching—the touching of one's own head or heart—the swearer directs the evil powers toward themselves and their own life. In the Epic <note>Refers to the *Mahābhārata*, one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India.</note>, **Satyavant** <note>A legendary figure known for his virtue; his wife Savitri famously rescued him from the god of death.</note> swears that he would not survive any misfortune that befell his parents: "by this truth³) I touch myself"—and another time it is said in a similar connection: "thus I touch my head"⁴). Apparently, it is this touching to which the regulation of a **Sūtra** <note>A "thread" or rule-book of aphorisms in Sanskrit literature.</note> text⁵) refers, which requires one to purify oneself with water if one has spoken a verse to **Rudra** <note>An early, fierce form of the god Shiva, associated with storms and destruction.</note>, to evil spirits, to the dead, "or if one has touched oneself": in this self-touching, too, lay an involvement with uncanny powers that [demanded] a purification...

If the oath is broken, punishment naturally follows: when the Moon God did not keep the oath he had sworn to <term>Prajāpati</term> <note>A Vedic creator deity, the "Lord of Progeny."</note>, he was afflicted with the disease <term>Rājayakshma</term> <note>original: "Lungenschwindsucht." This term, literally the "King’s Consumption," is historically identified with pulmonary tuberculosis; in myth, it describes the Moon's waning as a wasting disease.</note>¹).

**Magic in the form of sacrifice:** Already in previous passages, we have had occasion to observe many instances where the sacrifice—which by its true nature honors, delights, and appeases the gods—becomes intertwined with the sphere of magic, which seeks to direct the course of events through secret power²). An imagination accustomed to the conceptual world of magic transfers its mode of operation to the sacrifice; conversely, an imagination at home in the world of sacrifice adopts the form of sacrificial rites to clothe magical acts within them³). The sacrifice forces demons or sorcerers to appear and reveal themselves; the sacrifice drives demons away; the sacrifice overcomes all rivals for a wife; the sacrifice helps an exiled prince to return and achieve victory over his adversaries⁴). Two particularly common types are: first, a magical character is infused into an act that is predominantly sacrificial in nature, either through the choice of the sacrificial animal or other offering—which contains an allusion to the specific purpose of the act—or through the special form given to any other elements of the ritual. <header>### Magical Sacrifices.</header>

...[objects] that would be suitable for performing any kind of magical manipulations to achieve a specific purpose are presented as sacrificial offerings. Evidence for the first of these two procedures is offered by almost every page of the ritual texts¹); for the second of the designated types, it is perhaps not superfluous to provide a few examples here or to recall rites of this kind²) already mentioned. Ants are driven away by sacrificing poison³). One destroys one’s enemy by sacrificing arrowheads that have been anointed with one’s own sweat—the power of one's own <term>Tapas</term> <note>In Vedic tradition, *Tapas* refers to the "inner heat" or spiritual energy generated through asceticism and intense discipline, which was believed to grant the practitioner supernatural power.</note>—⁴). He who desires large cattle must sacrifice the dung of a pair of calves; he who desires small cattle, the dung of a pair of sheep⁵). He who wishes for a long life—who wishes, as it were, to nail down life through a hundred years—sacrifices a hundred nails made of Khadira wood⁶) <note>Khadira (*Acacia catechu*) is a tree known for its extremely hard, durable, and rot-resistant wood, making it a fitting symbol for longevity and stability in ritual use.</note>. Similar to all this is how the practice of sacrificing through a hole⁷) evidently developed based on the method discussed above (p. 495) of stripping away harmful substances by pulling the person at risk through a hole <note>This refers to a "passing-through" ritual where a person or object is moved through a narrow opening to symbolically "scrape off" disease or bad luck.</note>. Throughout, the blending of the two conceptual spheres of sacrifice and magic is clearly evident.

# SECTION FOUR.

## Belief in the Soul and Cults of the Dead.

---

->**The Soul. Heaven and Hell.**<-

The Soul. The conceptions of the Vedic Indians regarding death and life after death rest upon a belief in the soul that the <term>Indo-European</term> <note>The original German text uses the term *indogermanisch* (Indo-Germanic), which was the standard 19th-century term for what we now call the Indo-European language family and its associated cultures.</note> peoples brought with them from the prehistoric stage of development common to early cultures. This belief, which is essentially shared by traditional societies across the entire globe even today, can be expressed as follows: within the body dwells an airy or shadowy being, the soul. It can leave the body, which then sinks into unconsciousness, while the soul itself freely wanders through things near and far; at death, it departs from the body forever and—whether for a limited time or indefinitely—leads its own existence, either remaining invisible or assuming visible forms.

The question of how this "soul-being" was named—a question easily and briefly answered for Homeric Greece by the single word *Psyche* <note>original: *Psyche* (Greek: ψυχή), meaning breath, spirit, or soul.</note>—is not quite as simple to resolve for the <term>Veda</term> <note>The Vedas are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, composed in archaic Sanskrit.</note>. What a living human possesses that a dead body lacks could be viewed from many different perspectives: and so we find here, alongside other less prominent designations¹), the frequent use of *asu* <note>original: *asu*, often translated as "vital breath" or "life force," representing the energetic principle of life.</note>, which appears to be—

---

¹) Such as the word *ātman* (“breath,” then “soul,” “the self”), which later attained such outstanding significance. <note>In later Indian philosophy (the Upanishads), *Atman* became the central term for the eternal, individual soul that is identical with the universal reality, Brahman.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the Vedic concept of the soul as a shadowy or airy entity that can exist independently of the body, noting its roots in prehistoric Indo-European culture. It also distinguishes between various early Sanskrit terms for the soul, such as asu and atman.</summary>

...sometimes as the breath of life, sometimes of <term>manas</term> <note>Sanskrit: *manas*, the mind or spirit as the seat of thought.</note>, the spirit, as the essence whose departure signifies death. Among these expressions, <term>asu</term> <note>Sanskrit: *asu*, vital force or life-breath.</note> is evidently to be understood entirely as a potency lying within the realm of physical life, which also belongs to animals¹). Nothing indicates that thinking, feeling, or wishing was brought into connection with the *asu*. In contrast, we find phrases such as these: "The living *asu* has come to us," "(Agni,) producing the highest *asu*, the living, unconquerable one" (<term>Ṛv.</term> <note>Abbreviation for the Rigveda, the oldest collection of Vedic hymns.</note> I, 113, 16; 140, 8). And nothing seems to contradict what passages in the younger Vedic texts²) together with later linguistic usage suggest: that in this "living *asu*," the breath is intended as the carrier of life. *Manas*, on the other hand, is the spirit as the seat of thinking and perceiving, of wishing and willing, of joy and fear. Even the oldest Veda seems to possess the view, frequently and definitively expressed later, that the dwelling place of the *manas* is the heart³).

At the very least, we can tentatively attribute to this same antiquity a specific conception regarding the physical size of the *manas* <note>Sanskrit: *manas*, the mind or spirit as the seat of thought.</note>. According to the <term>Upanishads</term> <note>Ancient philosophical texts of Hinduism that explore the nature of reality and the soul.</note>¹) the life principle—called <term>purusha</term> <note>Sanskrit: *purusha*, meaning "person" or "being," here representing the inner self or cosmic man.</note> in these texts—dwells in the heart as a thumb-sized being; the epic poem of <term>Sāvitrī</term> <note>A famous legend in the Mahabharata about a devoted wife who rescues her husband from the god of death.</note> and her husband tells how this thumb-sized *purusha* is pulled out of the dying man’s body by the demon of death. # The Soul.

The instances are exceptionally frequent where living and dying appear dependent on the remaining or departing of now the <term>asu</term> <note>Sanskrit: the vital breath or life-force</note>, now the <term>manas</term> <note>Sanskrit: the mind or spirit, the seat of thought</note>, and sometimes both alongside each other. “Breath and strength depart; we call back your *asu* <note>Sanskrit: life-force or vital energy</note>.” “May your *asu* not leave the body.” “Stay here, do not go away. # The Soul.

In the numerous and extensive ritual texts of the <term>Veda</term> <note>The oldest layer of Sanskrit literature and the foundation of Hindu scripture</note> relating to the cult of the dead, it is worth noting that the invocations are never addressed to the *manas* or the *asu* of the deceased (represented as N. N. <note>original: "N. N.", a Latin abbreviation for *nomen nescio*, used here as a placeholder for the name of the departed</note>), but always directly to the individual—to the father, the grandfather, the ancestors, to Vasiṣṭha <note>A famous Vedic sage</note>, and so on. The true self of the departed was thus considered to be preserved in the realm of souls¹). Furthermore, the role of the *manas* <note>Sanskrit: the mind or spirit, the faculty of thought and intent</note> as described so far allows us to recognize with certainty that the Vedic conception of the soul living in the hereafter must have differed significantly from the Homeric one. The <term>Psyche</term> <note>Greek: soul or spirit</note> of the Veda could not possibly have resembled that unconscious shadow-being, deprived of all powers of will and thought, as depicted in Homeric poetry; since the *manas* has passed over into the afterlife, the "fathers" <note>The ancestral spirits</note> there will have retained all the functions of spiritual life that belonged to the *manas* on earth.

Moreover, the body also has a share in the existence in the beyond, as shown even in the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>The Rigveda, the oldest of the four Vedas</note> (X, 16, 6) by the concern for injuries to the body caused by birds or other animals²). Likewise, from the <term>Atharvaveda</term> <note>The fourth Veda, containing hymns, incantations, and magic spells</note>, among many other examples, we find the request to the fathers that everything of the bones in

The Buddhists imagine the devil hovering near the recently deceased like a cloud of smoke: he seeks to snatch away their *viññāṇa* <note>Pali: consciousness or cognition</note> (see my *Buddha*, 2nd ed., p. 289). ## Heaven. 
What then is the setting of this spiritual-bodily existence in the beyond? What is its content?

Well-known verses of the <term>Ṛgveda</term> <note>The Rigveda, specifically IX, 113, 7 ff.</note>, the prayer of a <term>Soma</term> <note>A sacred ritual drink offered to the gods</note> sacrificer to the holy draught, show us the shape of these pious hopes:

> "Where inexhaustible light is, the world in which the sun is placed: place me in that, O Soma, in the imperishable world of immortality. Let the draught flow for Indra²)." <note>Indra is the king of the Vedic gods; the "flowing" refers to the ritual preparation of the Soma drink</note>

# The Soul. Heaven and Hell.

The Rigveda <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the ancient sacred scriptures of India</note> already places the scene of the blessed life with **Yama** in heaven, as the passage shared above shows. Not all the Fathers <note>The *Pitris*, or ancestral spirits of the deceased</note> dwell there—we shall have to return to this point—but this is the most distinguished dwelling place of the Fathers. At times, the text speaks of the highest regions of light (see above) or the highest canopy of heaven (Rigveda X, 14, 8); at other times, of the center of heaven (15, 14) or the "bosom of the rosy dawns" (15, 7). The Atharvaveda <note>The fourth Veda, containing a mix of hymns, spells, and philosophical reflections</note>, which also speaks of the "highest world" (XI, 4, 11), the "third firmament" (IX, 5, 1. 8; XVIII, 4, 3), the "back of the firmament" (XVIII, 2, 47), and the "world of light" (IV, 34, 2), describes the location of the world of the Fathers most precisely in the following verse (XVIII, 2, 48): 

> "The 'Water-Abundant'—so the lowest heaven is named; the 'Myrtle-Abundant' <note>original: *Myrthenreiche*; likely referring to the *Pīlu* tree, often associated with the world of the dead in Vedic literature</note> is the middle one; the third is called the Upper Heaven, in which the Fathers sit." 

Within the celestial world, there are particularly favored places as a reward for the highest merits. This is especially true of the Sun¹): 

> "High in heaven stand those who have bestowed rich sacrificial gifts; those who give horses <note>A reference to the *Ashvamedha* or similar prestigious sacrifices</note> dwell with the Sun" (Rigveda X, 107, 2). 
> "Those who have reached the Sun through asceticism <note>original: *Askese*; referring to *Tapas*, the spiritual heat or fervor generated by self-discipline</note> . . . the wise, masters of a thousand paths, who guard the Sun" (X, 154, 2. 5).

To further illustrate this heavenly bliss, the verses addressed to **Soma** <note>The sacred ritual drink of the Vedas, personified as a deity</note> mentioned above (pp. 531 ff.) have already provided some details. The other expressions in both the Rigveda and the Atharvaveda are in complete agreement with this. Earthly imperfection is cast off: this does not mean an internal elevation toward ethical ideals, but rather the removal of physical ailments; the blessed "have the

<meta>This page follows the transition from the joys of the Vedic heaven to the logical necessity of a counterpart: hell. # Hell.

As the idea of continued existence had shaped itself into that of a reward in the hereafter for earthly virtues, the thought of punishment for earthly offenses in the afterlife must also have emerged. That the same imagination, which held the bright heights in readiness for the good and for friends, will also have disposed of dark depths for the wicked and the enemies, is a logical consequence that can hardly be avoided. To say nothing of more distant peoples—one should recall how, in the Avesta <note>The primary collection of sacred texts of Zoroastrianism, the ancient religion of Persia</note>, the fates of the soul of the good man and the wicked man, the path of the one into the heavenly world and the other into the hellish world, run in the most precise correspondence: no matter how much of the details here one might wish to attribute to the known tendency of Avestan theologians toward a uniformly schematic elaboration of the light and dark halves of the world, in its basic features the entire way of thinking is nonetheless the necessary product of internal consistency; it could very well—though this can only be conjectured—stem from the period of Aryan commonality <note>The ancestral period before the ancient Indian and Iranian peoples separated</note>. 

Attempts have been made to avoid the concepts of hell and hellish punishments by formulating the doctrine of the oldest Veda to suggest that immortality is a free gift from heaven, and that for the one who does not receive this gift, physical death brings an end to all existence¹). This seems to me to be entirely misunderstood. It is not Yama <note>The king of the dead and first mortal to die</note> or any other god who grants continued existence to the dying; rather, according to an ancient way of thinking reaching back into the times of savagery, continued existence is a matter of course; from the gods, one could only hope or fear that they would exercise their grace or their wrath upon the soul that continues to live.

We must therefore, without any question, expect the belief in a hell within the Veda. How then do the—

### The Soul. Heaven and Hell.

What do the texts say? Regarding the younger <term>Vedas</term> <note>The later collections of sacred Sanskrit hymns and rituals following the Rigveda</note>, there can be no doubt; the belief in hell is clearly present in all of them. One can only have reservations regarding the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, composed roughly between 1500 and 1200 BCE</note>. Yet even here, as has been emphasized by several scholars¹), the evidence is not entirely lacking. Admittedly, one should hardly place much weight on the concept of <term>Yama’s</term> <note>The first mortal to die, who became king of the dead</note> two four-eyed, dappled dogs (<term>Rigveda</term> X, 14, 10–11)², past which the deceased are wished a safe passage during the funeral rites. It is indeed possible that, according to the Rigvedic poet’s conception, these dogs were meant to keep the wicked away from the entrance to the realm of the blessed. However, they could just as easily be understood within—and inherited from—a traditional framework that gathered the dead into a general <term>Hades</term> <note>A term for the underworld, used here to compare the Vedic afterlife to the Greek concept of a collective place for all the dead</note> without distinction between good and evil. In that case, they would simply belong to the whole apparatus of ghostly terrors that surrounded the transition from earthly life to the world of darkness³. Nevertheless, some other testimonies for a belief in hell in the <term>Rigveda</term> cannot be dismissed without forced interpretation.

> “<term>Indra</term> <note>The king of the gods and god of storms</note> and <term>Soma</term> <note>The god of the sacred ritual drink that grants immortality</note>, hurl the evildoers into the prison⁴), into bottomless darkness⁵): so that not one of them comes out again, thus shall your...”

²) Compare above, p. 474, note 4. One should recall the dogs that guard the <term>Chinvat Bridge</term> <note>In ancient Persian religion, the bridge of judgment that souls must cross</note> in the Zarathustrian faith (Vendidad 13, 9).

# Hell

"...[may] fierce power subdue them" (VII, 104, 3).
> "Beneath all three earths <note>Vedic cosmology often envisioned three heavens and three earths stacked upon each other</note> shall he dwell . . . who by day and by night plots deception against us" (ibid. v. 11).

And regarding the evil sorceress:
> "she who comes forth at night like an owl, veiling her body with deception—may she plunge down into the endless dungeons¹)" (ibid. v. 17).

The expressions in these passages are far too concrete <note>Original German "positiv" here refers to the specific, descriptive nature of the language</note> to be interpreted as referring to mere annihilation. The last of these verses is supported by a passage from the <term>Atharvaveda</term> <note>The fourth Veda, which contains many spells, incantations, and speculative hymns</note> (II, 14, 3), which curses all sorceresses into "that house down there." The poets must have envisioned a dark depth from which the outcasts desire to escape back into the light, and from which they would escape, were it not for the firm seal and the heavy, burdensome wrath of the gods that restrained them. Consider also the following verse:
> "Those who wander like brotherless girls²), who lead an evil life like women who deceive their husbands, who are wicked, false, untrue—they have created for themselves that deep place" (Ṛv. IV, 5, 5).

The "deep place" (<term>padaṃ gabhīram</term> <note>Sanskrit: a deep step, station, or location</note>) seems, if one interprets the word naturally, to include the idea of a dwelling or residence, and thus of a continued existence. Certain other passages are less clear, where sinners or those pursued by misfortune or divine wrath are said to be cast into the "pit" (<term>karta</term>): it can hardly be proven that this means something more specific than an end marked by terror. The passages are as follows:
> "Protect us, you gods³), so that the wolf does not devour us⁴),

# Hell.

“...from East to West” (XVIII, 3, 3<gloss>1)</gloss>). Everywhere the darkness is that of death; we therefore have no right to apply that <term>Ṛgvedic</term><note>The Ṛgveda is the oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational sacred texts of ancient India.</note> invocation to the darkness of hell.

As we can see, there is very little that we hear about the belief in hell during the oldest period. It seems that, on the whole, it was reserved for a later age to shake the imagination through that terrifying depiction of the torments of hell, as was practiced with preference by the Buddhists and of which the <term>Atharvaveda</term><note>The fourth Veda, which focuses more on spells, rituals, and everyday concerns than the earlier hymns.</note> (V, 19, 3) gives a first foretaste in the image of the sinners sitting in streams of blood, consuming their own hair—those who on earth have insulted a <term>Brahmin</term><note>The priestly and scholarly class in ancient Indian society.</note>. In the gods, who took the primary place in the sacrifices glorified by the ancient Vedic poetry, one saw dispensers of earthly blessing rather than the administrators of dark, otherworldly pain. And even for the spells spoken at the burial of the pious sacrificer—our main evidence for the belief in that life—there was hardly a reason to mention hell, against which one felt secure through the possession of one's good works. Perhaps a more definite exploration of the great final decision regarding the soul's fate in the afterlife would appear in these spells if this decision had been conceived in the form of a judgment to which everyone must submit. But it is doubtful and hardly probable that such a formal judgment of the dead was already assumed in ancient times<gloss>2)</gloss>. In a Vedic ritual (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* VI, 5, 13) it says: “By King <term>Yama</term><note>The first mortal to die, who became the king and judge of the dead.</note>, son of Vivasvant, the people part ways: those who are faithful to the truth here below and the un[faithful]—”

# The Soul. Heaven and Hell.

"...speaking truth": but that this separation was carried out by a court of judgment is not found in the words¹). The gods know the innocent and the guilty and send each to their place: this simple idea may have sufficed for that era. —

Let us now attempt, looking at the whole, to find an expression for the character of the Vedic belief in immortality, and to measure the significance of these hopes for heaven and fear of hell for worship and life.

The goods of which one knows are material goods—health, enjoyment, wealth, and the power of the individual and the lineage: therefore, the afterlife can bring no other than material joys and sufferings for the soul, which even in death does not separate itself from physicality, and to which all the needs and habits of bodily life remain attached. To be sure, imagination has used the wide, airy scope of the afterlife to heighten the image of suffering in hell—and especially in heaven, which seems to have occupied it much more intently—to the highest peak reachable; however, this peak in the Vedic ideal of heaven hardly rises above the level of a Land of Plenty <note>original: "Schlaraffenland" — a mythical land of extreme luxury and ease where food flows freely.</note> relocated to the world of light, with inexhaustible streams of milk and honey and no less inexhaustible pleasures of the harem. The casting off of all imperfection, which one expects, signifies only the liberation of the body in the afterlife from all physical infirmities— <meta>The text cuts off here at "Ge-", likely "Gebrechen" (infirmities) or "Gefahren" (dangers).</meta>

It is only said of them that they collect a tribute from the reward for good works, which follows the deceased into the afterlife as their possession. — How an allusion to a judicial sentence by Yama can be found in <term>Rig Veda</term> X, 14, 11 (<gloss>Scherman, Visionary Literature 152 ff.</gloss>) is incomprehensible to me.

-> General character of the Vedic belief in immortality. <-

[physical in]firmities and thus the restoration of the fullest capacity for enjoyment; the union with the gods means pleasant interaction amidst music and full cups: joys and desires of a distant, pale future, which are completely overshadowed by the tangible joys and urgently present desires of daily life. In those infrequent passages where the Veda speaks of the afterlife—outside of the sections dedicated to the funeral ritual and the cult of the dead—the motif of heavenly reward for those who give generously to the priests, and of hellish punishments for those who do harm to the priests, stands quite dubiously in the foreground. In prayers, death primarily plays the role of something one wishes upon one's enemies, while wishing for oneself a long life of "a hundred autumns" <note>A traditional Vedic expression for a full life span of one hundred years.</note>. In the cult <term>Cultus: the formal system of religious worship and ritualized practice</term>—if we set aside the gifts to the priests connected with ritual acts—the time to care for salvation in the afterlife comes above all at the funeral: there begins the petty concern that Agni <note>The Vedic god of fire, who consumes the body on the pyre.</note> might do no harm to the body, and that he and Soma <note>The deity associated with the sacred ritual drink, often linked to healing and immortality.</note> might heal all injuries inflicted upon the deceased by crows and ants, so that every rite might be duly performed to let the soul reach the right place. What a transformation from here to the sentiments that filled Indian souls in the times of early Buddhist monasticism, where life was the preparation for death, illuminated by the thought of the triumph of eternity over all things transitory.

### Traces of Older Forms of Belief in the Soul. ###

originates from religious concepts. We have no reason to date it even further back, or to assume it was a possession of the undivided Indo-Europeans <note>The ancestral group from which most European and Indian languages and cultures descend.</note>. In general, this belief—as much as it seems to bear the stamp of spiritual childhood when measured against the standards of the most highly developed religious formations—actually represents, as we cannot doubt, a comparatively young form of the human race's thoughts about the afterlife. Now, as is known from experience regarding all religious matters, and especially those concepts and customs relating to death and the hereafter, it is almost never and nowhere the case that new formations have achieved dominance without allowing the foundation of the older beliefs to peek through their only half-covering veil. Should this relationship, recently demonstrated convincingly for the beliefs of Homeric Greece <note>original: "homerischen Griechenland"</note>¹), not also apply to the Veda? I believe that this question may be answered in the affirmative.

First of all, I would like to touch upon some expressions which, as it seems to me, belong to such traces of older ideas and concern the path of the departed faithful into their future existence. In many places, this path is indeed conceived in the way that is natural for a belief in a heavenly afterlife: the soul rises through the realm of the air to heaven, whereby it is natural to assign a role as leader or companion to the fire or fires that consume the corpse. Thus, Āśvalāyana <note>An ancient Indian teacher and author of ritual texts.</note> says in his presentation of the cremation ritual (<term>Gṛhya: a collection of rules for domestic life and rituals</term> IV, 4) that if, of the three sacrificial fires ignited simultaneously, the eastern one reaches the corpse first, one may know that the fire has overtaken the soul in the heavenly world; if the western fire, in the world of the air; if the third, the south—

# Traces of Older Forms of Belief in the Soul #

fellowship with **Ahura** <note>Short for Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity in Zoroastrianism, corresponding to the Vedic Varuṇa.</note>; likewise, the **Avesta** <note>The sacred scriptures of Zoroastrianism.</note> knows of **Yima’s** (= Yama’s) realm. But here, these two ideas are entirely separate. Yima's realm is located not in heaven, but on earth, in the fabulous reaches of the wonderland **Airyana Vaējah** <note>The mythical homeland of the ancient Iranians.</note> or even, as one of the texts says, beneath the earth. Its inhabitants are not—or as we might say, *no longer*—the blessed dead, but rather a race of fortunate mortals blessed with long life. The fact that the dead were originally intended had been forgotten, and indeed had to be forgotten, because the dead were now believed to dwell in the bright heaven of Ahura.

One can perhaps express the shift in ideas seen here, as in the **Veda** <note>The oldest layer of Sanskrit literature.</note>, by saying that the dead—to whom a cult similar to that of the heavenly gods was dedicated—were attracted, as it were, by the gods and had become heavenly beings just like them. The desires for power, happiness, and glory for the departed fathers, and for the power, happiness, and glory of one's own soul after death, had intensified the more the imagination grappled with these problems. Belief in the bliss of the heavenly gods had shown the direction in which hopes for the human psyche could be satisfied; the thought that pious works were entitled to a reward gave these wishes the character of legal claims. To this was added the fact that the funeral rite of **cremation** <note>Burning the body allowed the soul to rise with the smoke to the sky, whereas burial suggested a journey into the earth.</note>, alongside that of burial, had introduced a path upward in addition to the path downward. Is it not understandable that the realm of the dead thus rose from the depths of the underworld, or from the distance of an earthly land of fable, to the heights of heaven?

# The Sacrifice to the Dead #

We now turn to these customs themselves: it appears that the rites for the dead have survived with great tenacity, outlasting the very ideas from which they originally sprang, and have thus preserved a particularly significant testimony of ancient views concerning the afterlife.

I provide here the main content of the description of the sacrifice to the dead—which was to be repeated partly at fixed times (around the new moon) and partly on special occasions—according to the presentation by <term>Gobhila</term> <note>An ancient Indian sage and author of one of the most important manuals on domestic religious rites.</note> (<term>Gṛhya</term> <note>The *Gṛhyasūtras* are ancient Sanskrit texts detailing domestic rituals and life-cycle ceremonies.</note> IV, 2. 3).
