### The Sacrifice for the Dead.

This stems from the most primitive stage of religious custom. Nothing here points to a heavenly dwelling for the souls; the gifts for them are not sent upward through the sacrificial fire. Instead, they are placed in the earth: the soul dwells in the depths of the ground or even on the earth, near human dwellings¹) and waits for the living to still its hunger and clothe it. It approaches for the meal, sits in the place prepared for it²) or slips into the water vessel³); it enjoys the heat of the food given to it and leaves the cooled substance behind⁴). Once it has received its portion, care is taken that the uncanny guest does not linger any longer. This should be understood as a last, faded remnant of more material forms of "driving out souls," such as are found elsewhere—through striking the air with clubs and the like. This is similar to the Athenian cry: "Out the door, spirits, the Anthesteria is over!" <note>original Greek: θύραζε Κῆρες, οὐκ ἔτ’ Ἀνθεστήρια. The Anthesteria was a three-day festival in Athens where the souls of the dead were thought to walk among the living.</note> Just so, the Indian sacrificer, who first invited the souls with the words "O fathers, enjoy yourselves!", afterwards says: "The fathers have enjoyed themselves." This is even clearer in other versions of the ritual⁵): "Go away, fathers, friends of Soma <note>Soma is a sacred ritual drink and the deity associated with it</note>, on your deep, ancient paths. But in a month's time, return to our house to eat the sacrifice, rich in descendants, in men." There is also a shaking out of the gar—

...shaking the hem of the garment¹) is mentioned, which is undoubtedly a shaking off of the souls.

We learn all of this from sources that are consistently younger, and in some cases significantly younger, than the Rigveda <note>The *Rigveda* is the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns, dating back to the second millennium BCE.</note>. However, this should not shake our belief in the ancient origin of these rites. The simple offering of food balls <note>original: *Speiseklössen*; these are the *pindas* or sacrificial dumplings offered to ancestors in Hindu ritual.</note> laid down for the dead did not receive the elaborate adornment of hymns and songs addressed to the most powerful gods, such as those invented for the Soma sacrifice <note>Soma was a sacred ritual drink and a major deity in the Rigvedic religion; its sacrifice was highly complex and prestigious.</note>. It is, therefore, understandable enough that one reads nothing of this ceremony in the book of hymns. Yet, the entire character of the ritual would be incomprehensible if it had truly only emerged in the era of the texts that report it. It does not correspond to the living thoughts dominant in that later age, but rather to the ideas and forms of expression of a cultural stage for which most, perhaps all, of the deities of Rigvedic poetry still rested in the womb of a distant future.

**Belief in Ghosts and Related Matters.** We must touch upon a few more customs here which seem to point to the belief that the deceased does not immediately join the other host of souls upon their departure, but at first leads a separate existence for a time—remaining particularly close to the living and, therefore, according to the original conception, particularly dangerous.

In this regard, it must be mentioned above all that the regular monthly sacrifices for the dead (*śrāddha* <term>śrāddha: a ritual performed in honor of one's deceased ancestors</term>) offered to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the sacrificer were not yet celebrated for the recently deceased in the initial period following their death.

<page-num>555</page-num>
<header>The Recently Deceased.</header>

The deceased was honored individually through an <term>individual sacrifice for the dead</term> <note>original: *Einzeltodtenopfer*; a specific ritual performed for a person who has recently died, separate from the general ancestors</note> and was usually admitted into the sacrificial community of the "fathers" <note>the *Pitris*, or ancestors who have already passed into the afterlife</note> who preceded him only after a year had passed. This practice is clearly based on the idea that the dead person only takes the place due to them among the other dead in the afterlife after a certain period of time, remaining in an intermediate state until then. Some small ritual deviations of the <term>individual sacrifice</term> from the usual form of the <term>ancestor sacrifice</term> <note>original: *Todtenopfer*; the general offerings made to the collective body of ancestors</note> seem to confirm this. The summoning of the dead is omitted. At the conclusion, where the fathers are normally dismissed (“Go away, you fathers,” etc., p. 553), the text here says: “May one tarry in peace”¹). Instead of a prayer asking that the gift granted to the fathers belong to them eternally, one prayed only that it might exist for the [specific] deceased person²). The concept expressed in these variations can only be that the deceased lingers in the immediate proximity of the living during this time, and that this state is a temporary one as opposed to a later, permanent condition. The entirety of the more recent literature³) explicitly establishes the distinction between the one who is honored individually—

<header>Belief in Ghosts.</header>

Strictly speaking, one should certainly expect that the transition from the individual veneration of the deceased to their participation in the general <term>cult of the dead</term> <note>original: *Todtencult*</note> would coincide with the final burial, whereas the ritual texts instead represent these processes as completely independent of one another. Yet it can indeed hardly be surprising if the two ritual modes of expression for the deceased entering into their full rest have ultimately gained such an independent existence that—perhaps through the fixing of the duration for individual sacrifices to the dead at one year—the connection between them has been obscured. —

We have already mentioned that the term for the deceased who has not yet been accepted into the community of the "Fathers," the <term>Preta</term> <note>Sanskrit for "the departed"</note>, is also used directly in the sense of a "ghost." The existence of the dead person still wandering in the vicinity of the living bears a ghostly character; proper burial has the power to give the ghost its rest¹). ### Traces of Older Forms of Belief in the Soul.

...is not, or not yet, connected to the completed burial¹); it could also arise independently of considerations regarding burial customs, or subsequently become independent of them—specifically in such a way that the belief in retribution <note>the idea that one's actions in life determine their fate after death</note> played a role, and instead of a lack of burial, it was various sins for which a ghostly existence formed the punishment. Here, however, is the place to provide an overview of the main features of the ancient Indian belief in ghosts.

The **Rigveda** <note>the oldest of the sacred Hindu scriptures, dating to the 2nd millennium BCE</note>, in which we naturally should not expect many explicit references to this belief, does speak at least in one passage (X, 15, 2) of the Fathers "who sit in the earthly air-realm or who sit in the well-fenced settlements"²): where it is natural to think of a ghostly lingering of souls in the vicinity of the living. A younger Vedic text introduces the element of guilt and punishment: whoever sheds the blood of a **Brahmin** <note>the priestly and scholarly class</note> shall "not be allowed to see the World of the Fathers"³) for as many years as the blood wets grains of sand.

The Vedic texts seem to offer no material for a more detailed depiction of this existence of ghostly souls who are excluded from the World of the Fathers⁴). This fact is noteworthy, but not difficult to understand. Heaven and hell—especially as the **belief in the transmigration of souls** <note>reincarnation, or the soul's journey through different lives</note> became increasingly vibrant—enjoyed a prominence in a worldview directed toward extremes—

³) *Taittiriya Samhita* II, 6, 10, 2; compare *Laws of Manu* IV, 168; XI, 207.

<header>The Belief in Ghosts.</header>

...theological imagination the priority; they had nearly emptied the earth of its ghostly inhabitants; the world of ghosts was little more than a vestige lingering in popular belief outside the vibrant intellectual currents of the time: "the living and the fathers," it is now said <note>Śatapatha Brahmana XIII, 8, 4, 12. A voluminous prose text detailing Vedic rituals and mythology.</note>, "do not appear together." Thus, even the beings we encounter as the instigators of disease and misfortune in the literature of protective charms directed against evil demons and tormenting spirits do not present themselves as ghosts. While it is likely that these **Rakshas** <note>a type of malevolent being or demon in Hindu mythology</note>, **Piṣāca** <note>flesh-eating demons</note>, etc., trace back in no small part to the ill-willed souls of the deceased <note>See above, page 60 ff.</note>, this connection had long been obscured for the poets of the **Atharvaveda** <note>the "Veda of magic formulas," the fourth sacred scripture of Hinduism</note>. Those types had become independent entities, so that we do not encounter the belief in ghosts even in the literature of magic.

We only hear more about ghosts in the texts of ancient **Buddhism** <note>Specifically, the story collection known as the *Petavatthu*, or "Stories of the Departed," is relevant here.</note>. Here, ghosts who are punished for the sins of their earthly lives are popular as warning examples and, at the same time, as an incentive for generosity toward pious monks; for through gifts given in honor of the deceased, one can alleviate their suffering in the afterlife. If we set this specific point aside, it is likely that the Buddhist belief in ghosts provides an essentially faithful image of the Vedic belief, which is nearly hidden from our direct knowledge; there is no reason to suspect many new developments here. It will therefore be justified at this point to take a look at the Buddhist conceptions of ghosts. That these were by no means viewed by the Buddhists themselves merely as poetic-edifying set dressing, but were taken quite seriously, is shown by the fact that the...

Monastic law <note>original: "Gemeinderecht"; referring here to the *Vinaya*, the regulatory framework for the Buddhist community</note>, in its invariably sober tone, discusses—for example, when prohibiting sexual sins—even the case of a monk having relations with a female ghost. Similarly, in the prohibition against theft, it addresses the case of a monk appropriating an object belonging to a ghost: such an object was considered ownerless, just like one belonging to an animal ¹). In the narratives, ghosts are found especially frequently in lonely places where a traveler might encounter them, or where a monk, having withdrawn into the silence, might be addressed by them. The King of Surāṣṭra <note>a region in western India, modern-day Gujarat</note>, returning from the capital of the Maurya <note>the imperial dynasty that ruled much of India from roughly 322 to 185 BCE</note> to his own land, comes at midday to a path that runs through a swamp; there, a sinister smell wafts by and a gruesome noise is heard ²). He realizes that he is near the people from Yama's realm <note>Yama is the Hindu and Buddhist lord of death and justice</note>, and under a massive **Nyagrodha tree** <note>the Banyan tree, *Ficus benghalensis*, often associated with spirits in Indian folklore</note>, a man of god-like appearance, beautifully adorned, approaches him. This man reveals himself to be a ghost (<term>preta</term> <note>a "hungry ghost" or departed spirit suffering in the afterlife due to past misdeeds</note>) and tells the king of the wicked life he had led ³). Other ghosts appear on the banks of the Ganges, in a sugar field, on a dung heap, or outside the city of Vesālī ⁴). They are not irrevocably bound to the place where they appear; a husband invites his wife, whom he encounters as a ghost, to come home and see her children ⁵); another ghost goes into the royal city of Rājagṛha <note>modern-day Rajgir, an important city in ancient Buddhist history</note> to the king, in order to show him how the spirit can be redeemed ⁶). dwellings are swarmed by the ghosts of deceased family members: 
> "Behind the walls they stand, at borders and crossroads; at the doorposts they stand; to their house they return; — whoever has a compassionate heart gives them food and drink; to them the ghosts wish a long life." 

> "Among them there is no agriculture, and no herds are tended there; there is no trade, no buying and selling for money. Just as rainwater that has fallen on the heights flows down into the depths, so does what is given here benefit the deceased." 

Here it looks quite as if the ghostly lingering in the vicinity of the old home was considered the regular lot of the dead. Usually, however, the existence of ghosts appears as an exception, as a punishment for debts <note>original: "Verschuldungen"; referring to moral failings or karmic debts</note>, laden with plagues of all kinds. Naked or clothed only in their own hair, pursued by heat against which water, shade, and wind offer no refuge, hungering or eating filth, thirsting in the midst of the waters of the **Ganges** <note>the sacred river of India, often depicted as turning to blood or pus for those with bad karma</note>, which turns to blood for those who desire it, rushing about like madmen or hunted game: thus Buddhist poetry describes the ghosts—suffering themselves rather than causing harm to people they encounter, just as we already found in the Vedic period that the ability or inclination of the souls of the deceased to harm the living had receded into the background.

Finally, a peculiar trait of these Buddhist poems should be highlighted: repeatedly¹) the ghost, telling its story to the person it encounters, says that in so-and-so many months it will "die" and then enter into such-and-such a hell.

<page-num>562</page-num>
<header>Traces of Older Forms of Belief in the Soul.</header>

Does the idea we touched upon earlier—that the existence of a ghost is a transitional stage preceding the soul’s arrival at its final destination—re-emerge here, translated into the language of the belief in reincarnation <note>original: "Seelenwanderungsglaubens"; literally the belief in the wandering of souls</note>? —

Naturally, one cannot venture to judge how far specific concrete features of later ghost-lore may be traced back to the Vedic world of ideas <note>The Vedas are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, dating roughly to 1500–1200 BCE</note>—features such as the "City of Ghosts" in the *Divyāvadāna* <note>A Sanskrit collection of Buddhist legends</note>¹) or the islands inhabited by ghost-women in the *Jātaka* <note>Stories concerning the previous births of Gautama Buddha</note>²) or the frequently encountered scenes of ghostly terror set in cemeteries (for instance, in the *Mālatīmādhava* <note>A 10th-century Sanskrit drama</note>, or in the "Story of the Sunshade with Five Rods"³)). However, we are justified in using the general picture of that circle of ideas, according to its approximate content, to fill a gap that the Vedic tradition leaves in our knowledge of ancient Indian views on life after death.

Within the older Indian literature, as far as I can see, these instances appear only quite sparsely. ## The Dead and the Living.

That the souls of the ancestors, even after they had reached their final destination in the afterlife, were nevertheless—unlike the Homeric Greeks with the inhabitants of Hades—attributed the ability to enter into contact with the living and to influence their fates, is already shown by the existence of the cult of the dead. This cult, deeply interwoven with all family orders, continues throughout the year, new moon after new moon, or monthly during the half of the waning light—also preferring the afternoon, the time of waning daylight³). Additionally, there are certain specific times—the festival of the *Sakamedhas* (p. 442), the *Ashtakas* in winter towards the end of the year (p. 446), and likely at yet another date during the rainy season—

# The Intervention of the Dead in the Existence of the Living.

Before a battle, warriors offer prayers to their ancestors—the "fathers"—envisioned as spear-bearing, mighty with the bow, and conquerors of enemy hosts¹). During the *Pravargya* sacrifice <term>Pravargya: a significant Vedic ritual involving the heating of milk in a clay vessel representing the head of the universe</term>, the ancestors, alongside the gods, grant their approval to the one performing the ritual²). It is, however, especially the continuation of the lineage that stands under the protection of the ancestors.

> “Give me strong sons, you great-grandfathers! Give me strong sons, you grandfathers! Give me strong sons, you fathers!”

This is the prayer offered during the sacrifice for the dead³); the sacrificer gives one of the dumplings <note>original: "Klösse," referring to *piṇḍas*, the ritual balls of rice or flour offered to spirits</note> prepared for the *Manes* <term>Manes: the ancestral spirits or souls of deceased ancestors</term> to his wife, if she desires a son, with the verse:

> “Bestow a fruit of the womb, you fathers, a boy crowned with lotus, so that a man may be here”⁴);

The sacrificer who desires a son also moistens his face with the remains of the water poured out for the fathers⁵). Before a wedding, a dumpling sacrifice is brought to the fathers⁶), evidently to ensure offspring for the marriage, and it is believed that when the bridal procession is held, the spirits come forth to see the young bride⁷).

Certainly, the belief would not have been lacking that the deceased, with their supernatural knowledge, can come to the aid of the living; here we may include—while setting aside the framework based on the belief in the transmigration of souls <note>original: "Seelenwanderungsglauben," or reincarnation</note>—those instances appearing frequently in Buddhist tales⁸)...

<page-num>568</page-num>
-># The Dead and the Living.<-

...to present the encounter in such a way that a "kindred deity" imparts good counsel to a person¹). —

There is little mention of evil inflicted upon the living by the deceased, as might be expected given the contexts to which the relevant Vedic texts mostly belong—primarily the rituals of burial and ancestral offerings. That the general notion of harm-inflicting souls was not entirely absent is clear and is confirmed by sufficient traces. Already in the <term>Rigveda: the oldest and most sacred collection of Indian hymns</term> (X, 15, 6), a prayer associated with the sacrifice for the dead states:

> “Do us no harm, O fathers, if we, after the manner of men, have committed any offense against you.”

And in a later Vedic text²) it is written: “What they take for themselves is the portion of the fathers.” One's own ancestors will only be angry and cause harm when guilt or the withholding of due offerings provokes them. To a stranger, however, spirits will more easily become dangerous: recall the invocation mentioned earlier (p. 566), where the fathers are asked to turn the merit of their good deeds toward the destruction of the petitioner's enemy. The priestly focus on the "merit of deeds" is secondary here; the core belief is in the souls of the fathers who destroy their descendant's foe. Specifically, the souls of unborn children—in India as elsewhere—are also considered malevolent; they are regarded as bloodsuckers³). In general, the various precautions permeating the entire <term>funeral ritual: the complex series of Vedic rites (Samskaras) performed to ensure the soul's safe passage to the world of the ancestors</term> toward the souls point to the belief that these can easily come closer to the living than is good for those who do not guard themselves.

In the era of the <term>Atharvaveda: the fourth Veda, focusing largely on spells, charms, and healing rituals</term>, the idea of malevolent, disaster-causing souls must have already been fading significantly. <header>The Burial.</header>

## The Burial.

In the preceding sections, burial customs have been mentioned many times; it will not be superfluous to return to them here once more in context.

Cremation was the normal, though by no means universally practiced, form of burial during the <term>Vedic age: the period in ancient India (c. 1500 – 500 BCE) when the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, the Vedas, were composed</term>. When later authors describe graveyards full of discarded, decaying bodies, when the law books prescribe burying or discarding the corpses of small children, "leaving them lying in the forest like a piece of wood"¹) or the great epic poem²) says that the dead person "is burned or buried or cast away," then these various forms of burial or non-burial were naturally also known in the Vedic period. The <term>Rigveda: the oldest and most important of the four Vedas, containing hymns to the gods</term> (X, 15, 14) speaks of the dead—not some common folk or non-Aryans, but the pious ancestors living in heavenly joys—"those who are burned by fire and those who are not burned by fire," and alongside this passage, the *Atharvaveda* (XVIII, 2, 34) places a verse in which <term>Agni: the Vedic god of fire and the mediator who carries sacrifices to the gods</term> is invoked in a similar but more concrete way: "Those who are buried and those who are cast away, those who are burned and those who are exposed: lead them all here, Agni, the fathers, so that they may eat of the sacrifice."

---

...the soul [comes] through clearly enough when it is told how a <term>Rakshas: a malevolent spirit or demon</term> emerged from the severed head of Namuci, whom Indra had killed in violation of a truce <note>According to myth, Indra promised not to kill the demon Namuci with anything "wet or dry," but eventually killed him using foam at dawn</note>: it pursued Indra and said to him: "Where will you go? Where will you get rid of me?" (*Shatapatha Brahmana* V, 4, 1, 9; cf. *Taittiriya Brahmana* I, 7, 1, 7. 8; *Maitrayani Samhita* IV, 3, 4). Evidently, this is fundamentally the soul of the slain pursuing the perpetrator as a spirit of vengeance.

²) I, 3616 Calcutta edition <note>Referring to the *Mahābhārata*, one of India's two major Sanskrit epics.</note>.

<header>Different Types of Burial.</header>

It may be doubtful who the "exposed" (*uddhitāḥ* <note>original Sanskrit: "those set up or out"</note>) actually are. Another passage, in which this not-so-frequent expression appears, deals with the case where, during the sacrifice of a cow that must not be pregnant, an unborn calf nonetheless appears. "Then it is said: Where shall he put the calf? One should expose it (*uddadhyuḥ*) on a tree . . . Against this, however, it is said: Whoever should pronounce the curse against him: 'One will expose him on a tree when he is dead,' that would come to fulfillment" (<term>Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa: a major prose text detailing Vedic rituals and mythology</term> IV, 5, 2, 13). The custom of fastening corpses to trees, thereby securing the existence of the living from contact with them, occurs among many peoples: are we to understand that expression of the <term>Atharvaveda: the fourth Veda, containing hymns, spells, and incantations</term> as referring to such or a similar exposure¹)?

Burial <note>specifically inhumation, the practice of burying the whole body</note>, the factual occurrence of which among the Vedic Indians is established as we have shown, is nevertheless not considered in the ritual texts, evidently because it was not regarded as normal. And it is hardly with justification that scholars tend²) to read the description of burial ceremonies into one of the <term>Rigvedic: relating to the oldest collection of Vedic hymns</term> funeral songs (X, 18). There it is said to the dead man: "Go hence to Mother Earth"—"as the mother covers the child with her garment, so do you cover him, Earth"—"I set up the earth around you." But one must not overlook that all of this fits the ritual of cremation just as well as that of burial. The bones which remain after the cremation are lowered into the earth: it is simply not evident from the text³) that this act is not what is meant, but rather the burial of the entire body. ## Cremation

"animal to be laid around" <note>original: *Anustaraṇī*—a sacrificial animal, usually a cow or goat, whose body parts were placed upon the deceased to protect them from the fire's intensity</note> is slaughtered; limb by limb, the corpse is covered with the parts of this animal; the fat-streaked omentum <note>the fatty membrane surrounding the internal organs</note> is placed upon the face, and the two kidneys are placed in the hands as protection against the dogs of the God of Death¹); the hide, including the head and feet, is draped over the whole. And next to the funeral pyre, a he-goat is tied with a thin cord so that it can easily break free. Now the funeral pyre is set ablaze²); invocations to <term>Agni</term> <note>the Vedic god of fire, who acts as a messenger between the world of the living and the dead</note> plead for the deceased to reach the ancestors unharmed. Certainly, sacrificial offerings took place at this point even in ancient times³), although the verse that accompanies the most important of these offerings in the later texts is missing from the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>the oldest and most sacred collection of Vedic hymns</note>⁴):

> "From this one (the deceased) you (Agni) were born; may he in turn be born from you"

: the fire, which the living person once ignited <note>referring to the sacred household fires a householder was required to maintain</note>, creates new life for the dying.

# Mourning Observances: The Collection of the Bones

...the original state; it is natural that the mourning customs incumbent upon the living are dependent on the rites concerning the remains of the deceased, and thus the deceased himself.

On the third day¹) after the cremation of the corpse, the gathering of the bones takes place. First, rites are performed at the cremation site—which reappear similarly in other ritual contexts—that express the extinguishing of the fire and the arrival of coolness in place of the heat. Various water plants and a female frog are brought there:

> “The one whom you have burned, O Agni <note>the Vedic god of fire</note>, extinguish him again; let <term>Kiyāmbu</term> <note>a water plant, possibly a variety of lily</note> grow here, along with small millet and <term>Vyalkaṣā</term> <note>another aquatic plant often identified as a creeping grass</note>. Cool herb, rich in cooling, fresh herb, full of refreshment, come together with the female frog to gladden this fire²).”

The later texts speak of sprinkling the fireplace with water and milk—water and milk are also, according to the testimony of a <term>Sūtra</term> <note>a manual of ritual or aphoristic rules</note>³), set out for the deceased under the open sky on the night after the cremation, with the words: “O deceased, bathe here!”—the water plants may⁴) have been placed into the liquid with which the sprinkling of the cremation site was performed.

Now the bones are collected, placed in a jar⁵), and showered with all kinds of fragrant substances. The various sources differ as to where they then

³) <term>Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra</term> III, 10, 28.

...and [the idea] that in the unconsciousness of approaching death the soul has already entered *Yama's realm* <note>original: *Yamas Reich*; in Hindu mythology, Yama is the lord of death and the first mortal to die, becoming the king of the departed</note>, would stand in direct contradiction to this. Of course, it must not be overlooked that this very view also does not fit with the established idea of *Agni* <note>original: *Agni*; the Vedic god of fire, who acts as a messenger between humans and gods</note> as the conductor of the soul into *Yama’s realm*, or of cremation as the specific moment of this transition. Clearly, the discrepancy is explained by the development of the entire complex of ideas. The interpretation of cremation in this sense has nothing to do with the original nature of this type of burial. In its origin, the burning of the corpse—appearing in India, as in so many other places, as an equivalent to burial—evidently belongs to a large group of other ritual cases in which a threatening object is sometimes burned and sometimes buried¹). The actual pollution emanating from the corpse, but even more so the dangers based on the soul’s attachment to the body, on the "death-substance" <note>the ritual or physical essence of mortality thought to reside in a body</note> inherent in it, and on the magic that could be linked to the corpse, are intended to be removed. It is probable that cremation practiced in this sense is older than the belief in a heavenly life for the soul. Anyone who reads Homer’s description of the funeral of Patroklos <note>the close companion of Achilles in the *Iliad*; his funeral involved an elaborate pyre and sacrifices</note> while keeping the Vedic cremation ritual in mind will find it difficult to escape the impression that cremation, with a series of distinct details, reaches back into the *Indo-Germanic* <note>a historical term for Indo-European</note> or, if you will, the *Graeco-Aryan period*: but the belief in a blessed life in a heavenly kingdom can hardly be attributed to this era. # The Totality of the Burial Ritual.

Whether this or that element contributed more or less to the emergence of that belief—attempting an estimate here is not possible—it is in any case hardly doubtful that the idea of Agni <note>the Vedic god of fire</note> as a psychopomp <note>original: *Psychopompen*; a guide who escorts newly deceased souls to the afterlife</note> leading toward heaven entered into an existing mass of ideas regarding the soul's fate during death and the burning of the body. In this context, it should not be surprising that the old and the new have not merged into a perfectly smooth unity.

It is not only the cremated dead who are thought of as dwelling in heaven: "those burned by fire and those not burned by fire rejoice in the midst of heaven at the soul-food," it says in the *Rigveda*¹). <note>The *Rigveda* is the oldest of the sacred Hindu scriptures, composed in archaic Sanskrit</note> But despite this, it remains true that the concept of heavenly life stands in a specific, often expressed relationship to the rite of cremation; the normal path for the dead to reach the heavenly world is the one led by Agni. Certainly, it was this very relationship which—alongside other factors, such as the general preference of Vedic theologians for Agni and all rites that could be linked to him²)—secured for cremation its precedence over competing types of burial.

As that which Agni burns—or according to the more precise

---

¹) Book 10, Hymn 15, Verse 14; compare Bergaigne Volume I, page 79.
²) A certain similarity to the sacrificial rite is indeed present in cremation—as Abel Bergaigne <note>a prominent 19th-century French scholar of Sanskrit</note> has emphasized in Volume I, page 81. In a free manner of speaking, the Rigvedic poet (Book 10, Hymn 16, Verse 5) could say that the dead man was "offered as a sacrifice" <note>original: *āhutaḥ*</note> to Agni. But for all that, the act of cremation did not possess the technical construction of a sacrifice in any way; it was simply not equipped with all the poetic-liturgical decorations that are inseparable from such an act: though this is, of course, very well compatible with the fact that certain sacrifices were connected to it.

...form of symbolic fiction—it does not burn but rather cooks and makes ready—the whole person seems to be understood as present: the body as well as the soul, which is likewise thought of as being there. "Do not burn him up, Agni," <note>Agni is the Vedic god of fire, acting here as a transformative force</note> says the *Rigveda* (Book 10, Hymn 16, Verse 1), "do not hurt him with your heat, do not strike his skin and his bones; when you have cooked him ready, God Jātavedas, <note>Jātavedas is an epithet of Agni, often meaning "knower of all beings"</note> then send him to the fathers." One will not be surprised by the fluctuation of this conception when, after "he"—the deceased with body and soul—has gone into the afterlife, at a later stage of the ceremony during the interment of the bones, the same "he" is laid in the earth. As it is said there, the earth shall not press upon him; there his house shall be, his place of refuge, and there Yama <note>the king of the dead and the first mortal to find the path to the afterlife</note> shall prepare a seat for him (see above, page 580)¹). Here, there is no more talk of life in the heights of heaven; the older layer of ideas regarding the afterlife comes to the surface. What is more natural than this unresolved transition? And what is more natural than the fact that, in whichever direction the ritual act may move, "he"—the self of the dead—is thought of as present everywhere as the object toward which the action is directed?

The dead man does not cross over into the afterlife naked and unaccompanied. When clothes and jewelry are placed upon the corpse, this must not be understood as a mere expression of vague piety; the thought is that the deceased shall wear what is given to him on the "other side." This meaning of the custom is still completely alive in the *Veda*. "This garment," it is said to the deceased in the *Atharvaveda* (Book 18, Hymn 4, Verse 31), "God Savitar <note>a solar deity representing the impulsive power of the sun</note> gives you to wear. With it..."

<page-num>587</page-num>
# The Whole of the Burial Ritual.

“...clothed in the linen garment, <note>The translation of the original word *Linnengewande* is uncertain.</note> enter into the realm of Yama <note>The king of the dead and the first mortal to reach the afterlife</note>.” The ancient and widespread custom of providing the dead with the primary items of their personal property has left its mark, first and foremost, in the burning of <term>sacrificial utensils (Opfergeräthe)</term>. This was likely done because these specific objects were thought to possess a particular "holiness" that was fraught with danger for the survivors. However, the fact that a bow or gold was taken out of the hand of the deceased <note>See above, page 575, note 2.</note> also indicates that such possessions were once left with them. In these cases, as the rights of the living began to be felt as more dominant, a specific rite was developed to express the release of these things from the dead man's sphere of power.

The situation is no different regarding the widow. There is no doubt that the Vedic ritual excludes the actual burning of the widow. However, she does mount the funeral pyre, and a specific ritual act is required to lead her back from there to the world of the living. This is a clear enough sign that this is a remnant of the actual practice of <term>widow-burning (Sati)</term>, which, as is well known, later saw a revival—or perhaps, despite the authority of the Veda, was never truly extinguished. <note>This point was already very clearly explained by E.B. Tylor in *Primitive Culture* (Vol. I, p. 459); see also Bergaigne (Vol. I, p. 78, note 1). In the *Atharva Veda* (XVIII, 3, 1) and similarly in the *Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka* (VI, 1, 3), we read the verse: “This woman, choosing the world of her husband, lies down by you, O mortal <note>referring to the deceased husband</note>, keeping the old custom; may he grant her offspring and wealth here in this world.” Does such an explicit emphasis to the dead man—that the "old custom" has been fulfilled—not raise the suspicion that the old custom actually demanded more, and that people were still quite aware of that fact?</note>

The burning of a goat or a cow along with the corpse is unlikely to have the meaning of giving the animal to the dead as a possession. The covering of all his...

# The Burial.

The practice of covering the deceased's limbs with the corresponding parts of an animal seems to indicate, first and foremost, a form of substitution: an animal was offered to the hostile powers that stalk the dead, serving as a proxy to secure mercy for the departed. The <term>Rigveda (Rgveda)</term> <note>The oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns, dating back to roughly 1500–1000 BCE.</note> itself interprets the rite in this way—specifically in relation to the all-consuming power of the fire.¹) alongside this, however, other explanations are found. The <term>Maruts</term> <note>Vedic storm deities and companions of Indra.</note> are said to provide cooling for the dead by means of a goat—though I do not fully understand how this was intended to work;²) and furthermore—not impossibly an authentic ancient trait—there is mention of paths traversed by goats, upon which the god **Pūshan** is meant to lead the dead into the afterlife. These were perhaps steep mountain paths that are impassable for any animal other than the goat, the creature of the divine master of the ways and <term>psychopomp (soul-guide)</term>.³)

While the rites discussed so far related to the journey of the deceased to the afterlife and their fate on the other side, another circle of actions deals with the purification and protection of the living. These include the erasing of footprints, the setting of a boundary stone, and the use of water in its two functional types—as a purifying agent and as a barrier—among others. The significant space allotted to these rites leaves no doubt that they represent one of the dominant perspectives of the entire burial ceremony. Detailed explanations of these specifics seem unnecessary; I will only comment on the mourning customs mentioned above (p. 578), specifically the observances tied to the <term>ritual impurity (Unreinheit)</term> of the survivors—such as celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and eating only food that has been purchased or provided by others...

Among the **Alfurese** <note>The Alfurese (or Alfur) are Indigenous peoples of the Moluccas and neighboring islands in Indonesia.</note> in the Malay Archipelago, for a certain period, the widower is not permitted to consume any food prepared in the house where the death occurred. Among the **Samoans**:
> "*while a dead body was in the house no food was eaten under the same roof; the family had their meals outside, or in another house.*"

Undoubtedly, then, it is not at all a matter of expressing a sorrowful state of mind through abstinence from food; the danger lies in the self-cooked food, or rather, the food cooked in the house of death. This food carries the possibility of being infected by a **deadly substance** or by the **soul-substance** of the deceased, thereby transferring this **death-matter** into the body of the person eating it²). Sleeping on the ground is likely based on similar conceptions. Is it perhaps intended that whoever has been in the vicinity of the deceased might transfer traces of this contact to their own bed and thereby infect it for the future? Or is the underlying thought that the soul will haunt the survivors at night, and one escapes it by avoiding the accustomed resting place? Finally, I would interpret **sexual abstinence**³) to mean that, just like the food prepared in the house of death, the semen of someone who had been near the deceased was considered suspect of being polluted by death, and a transmission of the infection to the woman or the newly conceived being was feared. —

It is costly, overloaded with a ceremonious ritualism devised by priests, and adorned with the beauty of a liturgical poetry in which an awkwardly tangled formlessness and the first clear signs of that lush, sophisticated over-refinement—so overwhelmingly prominent in later Indian verse—have formed a peculiar alliance. This world is infinitely older than those newer structures and is destined to outlast them with a tenacity that seems inexhaustible. ## Soma and the Moon.

->(Regarding p. 183 ff.)<-

In the first volume of his *Vedic Mythology* <note>original: "Vedische Mythologie"; a landmark work by Alfred Hillebrandt published in 1891.</note>, Hillebrandt attempted to demonstrate that the identification of Soma <note>Soma was both a sacred plant used in rituals and the god who personified the pressed juice of that plant.</note> with the Moon—which, according to the view prevailing before him, was thought to appear first in only a few late passages of the *Rigveda* <note>original: "Rgveda"; the oldest collection of Vedic hymns, dating to roughly 1500–1200 BCE.</note>—is in fact one of the most important foundations of the entire Vedic mythology. The Moon-god, primarily in his capacity as Soma, stands at the center of Vedic belief and cult <note>original: "Cult"; the system of religious ritual and worship.</note> (p. 277). Indra <note>The king of the gods, often associated with storms and war.</note>, who previously appeared as the supreme ruler in the realm of the Vedic cult, can only be recognized as the second most popular Vedic god after the Moon (p. 315). The entire ninth book of the *Rigveda*, which celebrates Soma Pavamana <note>Soma "Pavamana" refers to the ritual juice as it is being purified or strained through a wool filter.</note>, is in fact “dedicated to the glorification of the great Moon-god, to whom almost every one of its hymns is linked; it is a moon-songbook” (p. 274).

In the following, we wish to present our position regarding Hillebrandt's theory.

We formulate two questions:

Is it correct that everywhere in the *Rigveda*, the lunar nature of Soma comes to the fore as an important or the most important factor?

And in case this question is to be answered in the negative, second:

Does the concept in question exist at least with secondary significance in the *Rigveda*, even outside of its latest portions?

In my opinion, the answer to the first question is not in doubt. However the explanation of a few perhaps debatable passages may turn out, the vast majority of statements in the *Rigveda* relating to Soma move in

# Excursus.

...a circle of thought that shows no connection to the moon, but rather permits and demands a different, simple, and clear interpretation.

This applies equally to the expressions that run through the songs addressed to other gods, namely to **Indra**, as well as to the songs to **Soma Pavamana** <note>Soma "Pavamana" refers to the ritual juice as it is being "clarified" or strained through a wool filter.</note>.

To **Indra** it is customary to say: Drink the **Soma** that the stone has pressed. May it gladden you. In your intoxication, slay the enemies. Many pressings are consecrated to you. You **Adhvaryus** <note>The Adhvaryus were the priests responsible for the physical labor of the sacrifice, such as preparing the ground and pressing the plant.</note>, bring the **Soma** to **Indra**; it belongs to him.

Here, one is dealing solely with the plant and its intoxicating juice, with the god who loves this state of ecstasy, and with the deeds of power performed by the god while intoxicated. The importance accorded to **Soma**, the exalted words with which he is praised, are fully explained by the fact that he is the mysterious inducer of intoxication¹ <note>original: "Rausch"; refers to a state of ritual ecstasy or altered consciousness.</note>, the favorite drink of the god, and the contributing cause of his deeds; for man, however, it is the most effective means of winning the god's favor. All of this requires no connection to the moon to be understood.

The songs to **Soma Pavamana** are similar. At least the vast majority of their content refers to the concrete sacrificial drink dripping through the strainer. They speak of the manipulations performed by the priests, of the vats, the strainer, the additions of water and milk, of the gods who are to intoxicate themselves with it, and the blessing it brings to mortals. All of this is, of course, overloaded with the most diverse ornamentations, but the main point remains clear: in the foreground stands the earthly, tangible **Soma** and the rites revolving around it, during which these songs are recited.

Even if it should turn out that the decorative additions to the Pavamana songs link themselves to an identification of the divine drink with the moon in one place or another, it is nonetheless certain that it is an absolute shift in perspective to make the moon the center of Vedic mythology, or even just of **Soma-mythology**, and to declare the ninth **Mandala** <note>A "Mandala" (literally "circle") is one of the ten books or sections that comprise the Rigveda.</note> to be a moon-songbook: at the very most, it can only—

¹) The religious significance usually attributed to intoxication and related states in the spheres of lower cults, and often far beyond them, is well known.

# Soma and the Moon.

...it is to be discussed that among the numerous motifs worked into the "marginal decorations," so to speak, of Soma poetry, a place is also assigned to the moon motif.

Whether this is indeed the case, we shall now examine. We thereby move to the second of the questions posed above.

**Soma**, who is imagined sometimes as a bird flying into the forest (i.e., into the wooden vat), sometimes as a bellowing bull—this must refer to the noise produced during the relevant ritual manipulations, which is certainly quite insignificant in itself—sometimes as a swift horse running, and in many other forms besides, is placed in many passages in relation to the concepts of light, heaven, and the sun. The eagle has brought him from heaven—the passages are well known; he is the **beestings** <term>piyusha: the rich, first milk of a mammal after birth, used here metaphorically for the divine nectar</term> of heaven (IX, 51, 2; 110, 8 etc.), the pillar of heaven (IX, 2, 5; 86, 8. 35 etc.), the lord of heaven (IX, 86, 11. 33); he purifies himself in heaven (IX, 83, 2; 86, 22 etc.), traverses heaven (IX, 3, 7. 8), enters heaven (IX, 85, 9), shines above the three lights while ascending to heaven (IX, 17, 5), has his place at the highest vault of heaven (IX, 86, 15), and looks down from heaven, or as a heavenly bird, upon the earth (IX, 38, 5; 71, 9). He has generated the sun, bestowed its light (or generated light in general), made the dawns shine, made the sun rise, impelled the sun, attained the sun, and bestows the sun (IX, 4, 5; 7, 4; 17, 5; 23, 2; 28, 5; 35, 1; 36, 3; 61, 16; 63, 7; 66, 24; 83, 3; 84, 5; 86, 14; 91, 6; 96, 5; 97, 31. 41; 107, 7. 26; 108, 12; 110, 3 and frequently elsewhere). He shines like the sun, stands above all beings like the sun, glows with the sun, clothes himself in the rays of the sun, and mounts the chariot of the sun (IX, 2, 6; 10, 8; 54, 2. 3; 61, 8; 66, 22; 71, 9; 75, 1; 86, 32. 34 etc.). The **Daughter of the Sun** purifies him (IX, 1, 6; 72, 3. Cf. 97, 47? 113, 3). His brightness, his rays, and the like are often mentioned. Regarding the relationship of Soma to heaven, it must also be added that heaven is spoken of particularly frequently in such a way that it is to be understood as a mystical name for the strainer made of sheep's hair through which the Soma runs¹). Even the common designation <term>sanu: literally "surface" or "back"</term> for the strainer, or rather for its surface, is characteristic of this identification; it clearly contains an allusion to the "back of heaven" <term>divah sanu</term>. Navel of Immortality, upon it rests the whole world (IV, 58, 1. 11); the sacrificial horse is called Yama and Aditya <note>original: *Yama and Aditya*; Yama is the god of death, and Aditya is a solar deity.</note> (I, 163, 3). If one now keeps in mind the entire appearance of these attributes of Soma described here, and considers in this context the passages intended to prove the equation Soma = Moon, one will become quite doubtful about their significance. Take, for instance, the verses from IX, 54, 2-3 discussed by Hillebrandt (p. 272), which (in his translation) read:

> “A sight like the sun, he runs through the seas, the seven heights²) and the heaven. Soma stands, purifying himself, above all worlds, like the god Surya <note>original: *Surya*; the Sun god.</note>.”

It is unlikely that anything more is intended here than Soma running through the strainer (= heaven), mixing with water (= seas, the seven *pravatah* <note>original: *pravatah*; steep paths or slopes.</note>), to whom sun-like qualities are attributed in the manner discussed above. — Or consider I, 91, 22 (Hillebrandt 308) *tvam jyotisha vi tamo vavartha* <note>original: "you warded off the darkness with your light."</note>. “Can it be doubted,” Hillebrandt asks here, “given an unbiased exegesis, that the moon is this Soma who wards off the darkness?” I must confess that I doubt this very seriously. Once Soma came to be regarded as a champion of light—and he could arrive at this from sides other than his alleged moon-nature—nothing was more natural than that the stereotypical phraseology regarding the expulsion of darkness by light (cf. I, 92, 4; IV, 52, 6; V, 31, 3 etc.) was also applied to him. Or rather, it was likely that, just as other deeds of Indra (e.g., the victory over Vritra <note>original: *Vrtrasieg*; the slaying of the chaos-serpent.</note>, the finding of the cows, etc.) were transferred to Soma, so too was this one (V, 31, 3).

Furthermore, I exemplify my difference from Hillebrandt regarding IX, 70, 7 (“whetting the yellow horns”) “where *srnge harini* <note>original: *srnge harini*; yellow or golden horns.</note> can be nothing other than the ‘yellow horns of the moon’” (p. 339, note 1). # Appendix

606

"As confirmation serves the use of the verse prescribed by Hiranyakesin <note>An ancient teacher and author of ritual manuals (Sutras).</note> (*Gṛhya S.* I, 16, 1) at the time of the new moon."

Does the passage from the *Satapatha Brahmana* <note>original: *Satap. Br.*; a massive prose work of the late Vedic period that provides symbolic and ritual explanations for the sacrifices.</note> really remove every doubt? We already knew that by the era of this *Brahmana*, the equation Soma = Moon had long existed; it also goes without saying that the authors of the *Brahmana*—regardless of what the real view of Rigvedic antiquity was—would not hesitate to interpret the *Rigveda* <note>original: *Rgveda*; the oldest collection of Indian hymns, composed centuries before the Brahmanas.</note> based on this equation. One certainly cannot speak of any "doubt-removing" authority of such an interpretation. A strange picture of the world of ideas in the *Rigveda* would emerge if we attempted to reconstruct it based on such starting points. It is no different regarding the fact that Hiranyakesin, among a series of other verses, has *Rigveda* I, 91, 16 and 18, addressed to the new moon: it is self-evident that for him, these verses alluded to the waxing of the moon, but the point is to refute the view that a change in perspective took place between the time these verses were composed and the time of the later authors.

We now ask on our part: by what right does Hillebrandt translate <term>visvebhir amsubhih</term> <note>original: *visvebhir amsubhih*; literally "with all stalks/rays."</note> in the two cited verses as "in all rays," thereby giving them a relationship to the waxing moon? By what means is the meaning "ray" proven or even made probable for <term>amsu</term> <note>original: *amsu*; traditionally understood in the older language as the stalk of the Soma plant.</note> in the older language¹)? What gives us reason to cast doubt on the only truly secured meaning of the word for the ancient language—the one established in so many passages of the *Rigveda* and appearing regularly and technically in the ritual texts—which is its use for Soma stalks (which, after all, also belongs to the Avestan language <note>The ancient Iranian language of the Zoroastrian scriptures, closely related to Vedic Sanskrit.</note>)? Why doubt it in a verse that points so clearly to the Soma juice flowing out of the stalks through the phrase <term>pra syandasva</term> <note>original: *pra syandasva*; "flow forth" or "stream forward."</note>²)? And further, what gives us reason to either [separate] the verses that occupy us from those expressed in exactly the same terms—

...[concerning] texts of the Yajurveda <note>one of the four Vedas, primarily containing the formulas for sacrifices</note>, or to detach the latter from the rites described with exactly the same catchwords, to which they fit most precisely? Above all, what comes into consideration here is *Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā* V, 7: "Stalk by stalk, O divine Soma, may you swell . . . may Indra swell for you, may you swell for Indra, make us and our friends swell with gain and wisdom" <note>original: *amsur - amsush te deva somapyayatam . . . a tubhyam indrah pyayatam a tvam indraya pyayasva, apyayayasmant sakhint sanya medhaya*</note> etc.: for which the ritual prescribes either a real moistening with water, or a symbolic making-juicy of the pressed Soma shoots, which is expressed by the verb <term>ā-pyāyayati</term> <note>to cause to swell or increase in juice</note>¹). > which the inexhaustible ones drink as the inexhaustible,
> with that, may King Varuna, Brihaspati,

### Digression

After all this, it seems to me that the following results for the interpretation of our verses. Just as we are otherwise accustomed to finding the ritual terms of the *Ṛgveda* <note>the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns</note> in the later ritual and understanding them from that context, we must also interpret the phrase *a pya* (or *pra pya*) <note>meaning "to swell" or "to increase"</note> in IX, 67, 28 and I, 91, 17 as referring to the restoration of juice and strength to the Soma shoots. It is in this sense that we must understand the words *visvebhir amsubhih* <note>original: "with all stalks"</note>. The ritual continuity that emerges so clearly in the whole situation must show us the way; only secondarily can it be considered whether a similar continuity should be assumed regarding the mystical equation Soma = Moon. For this, it seems to me that there is far too little firm evidence. In any case, even if the idea of the waxing moon was involved in the command "swell up!" (*pra [a] pyayasva*), it can only be a secondary mystical allusion added to the most obvious primary ritual meaning of the passages, which it remains completely inadmissible to highlight alone in a translation.

Hillebrandt also attempts to demonstrate the "moon-nature" of Soma within the ritual of the Soma sacrifice (p. 296 ff.).
> "The Soma, which is solemnly brought into the sacrificial site under the symbol of the plant and used as a drink, is regarded as the Moon-god himself."

This is supposedly proven beyond doubt both by the spells used in this rite and by the explanations added by the Brahmanas <note>ancient prose commentaries on the Vedas</note>. I do not dispute the explanations; they can only teach us what everyone already knows: that in the Brahmana period, the identification in question was fixed and popular. Even encountering this identification occasionally in the spells would hardly surprise us, given the overall situation. But do we really encounter it there? When the Soma is driven to the sacrificial site, the Hotar <note>the presiding priest who recites the hymns</note> says—according to Hillebrandt—:
> "All rejoice over the arrived splendor."

Is this "arrived splendor" really intended to prove that the organizers of the ritual were thinking of the moon? In fact, it must be translated—it is verse X, 71, 10 of the *Ṛgveda*—as:
> "All friends rejoice over the arrived glorious friend, who is powerful in the assembly."

In the word *yasás*¹) there does not lie

<note>This fragment likely belongs to a note discussing the origin of the verse</note>
...verse was composed for this use: note that it does not originate from the *Ṛgveda*.

¹) Not *yaśas*, although the Brāhmaṇa paraphrases this word with easily understandable freedom.

# Soma and the Moon.

...both the significance of physical radiance and the glory that belongs to an outstanding person. The god who approached as a guest was praised with a verse that spoke of the joy at the arrival of a noble friend or guest. This has nothing to do with the moon. — Furthermore, Hillebrandt points to the verse <term>Rv. IV, 53, 7</term> <note>Rigveda Book 4, Hymn 53, Verse 7</note> recited on the same occasion:

> “The God has approached with the seasons¹). May he increase the house. May <term>Savitar</term> <note>a solar deity representing the impulsive power of the sun</note> give us rich offspring and food.”

Do the seasons here prove anything in favor of the moon? I doubt it. At this point in the sacrificial ritual, a god approached the sacrificial site of the humans: so the ritualists chose for this situation the verse that began “The God has approached.” The fact that it was actually addressed to <term>Savitar</term> did not matter; the seasons simply happened to occur in the text. Even if the ritual organizers here associated them with the moon, such an allusion in the era when the ritual was fixed would still hardly teach us anything that we did not already know. — <term>Yajus-formulas</term> <note>sacrificial prayers or mantras from the Yajurveda</note>, which belong to the same ritual setting, address the <term>Soma</term>:

> “Go forward, O Lord of the Earth” — “Stride along the atmosphere.”

He is placed upon a throne; he is honored with the words:

> “Revere the great <term>Varuna</term> <note>a major deity of cosmic order</note>, revere the wise guardian of the <term>Amrta</term> <note>the nectar of immortality</note>.”

I find in all this only, on one hand, the usual, well-known <term>Yajus-style</term>, which loves to connect every small and minute process with the universe — the saying “stride along the atmosphere” occurs on the most varied occasions wherever any kind of walking is involved²); on the other hand, the glorification of <term>Soma</term> as a divine king, the reference to his significance as the drink of immortality, but absolutely no reference to his lunar nature. — Hillebrandt does not mention that in the same ritual context, the following verse was also addressed to <term>Soma</term>:

> “Reverence to the eye of <term>Mitra</term> and <term>Varuna</term> . . . to the son of heaven, whom <term>Surya</term> <note>the Sun-god</note> proclaims³).”

It is surely no inadmissible supposition that Hillebrandt [would find] a similar verse addressed to the moon...

Let us therefore renounce all the risky—or more than risky—translations and interpretations characterized here. Let us renounce seeing proofs for his identification with the moon in those passages that highlight the heavenly nature or the light-nature of <term>Soma</term>, or his connection with the sun and the like. # Soma and the Moon

The ambiguous expressions for these ideas, which we encounter again and again in the literature of the subsequent period, are missing here. From the expressions that the <term>Rigveda</term> <note>the oldest collection of Hindu scriptures</note> uses, it would be easy to prove a mystical connection between Soma and the Sun that stands out strongly in the imagination of the <term>Rishis</term> <note>the inspired poet-seers who composed the hymns</note>; by contrast, regarding the connection with the Moon, a peculiar game of hide-and-seek must have governed the hymn-composers, which nowhere allows us to lay our hands on a testimony that is not entirely vague.

I wish to exercise the utmost caution where an <term>*argumentum ex silentio*</term> <note>original Latin: "argument from silence"; a logical conclusion based on the absence of evidence</note> is concerned, so as not to exaggerate the evidentiary power of the considerations I have presented. Thus, I will concede it as at least conceivable that in one or another of those passages celebrating Soma's nature as light—perhaps also in the concept of his "swelling" (<term>*apyayana*</term> <note>a technical term for the replenishment or "fattening" of the Soma, later associated with the waxing moon</note>)—the identification of Soma with the Moon, which appears as a fixed rule later on, might already be at play. I will further acknowledge it as an open question, though likely forever unanswerable, whether this equation—common among younger Vedic theologians—is to be seen as the revival of a primitive, pre-Vedic belief of this kind,¹ and whether in the Vedic ideas of Soma's—

# Excursus: Soma and the Moon

—heavenly origin, his nature as light, etc., a faded trace of this belief is involved¹) — faded in a similar way as the last faded traces of a moon-god, or of the morning and evening star, remain recognizable to research in the figures of <term>Varuna</term> <note>an ancient sky deity associated with cosmic law</note> and the <term>Ashvins</term> <note>divine twin horsemen associated with the transition between night and day</note>, though these traces have long since vanished from any living understanding. These are possibilities. But what is certain, in my opinion, is this: for the poets of the *Rigveda*—with the well-known exception concerning the most recent phase of *Rig*vedic poetry—Soma is not a moon-god. At the very most, within the kaleidoscopic play of countless, constantly shifting modes of representation, he is a god who might perhaps be identified with the moon once or twice; he is primarily the god of the miraculous plant and the drink prepared from it.
